papers.abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
bullets: Addresses tasks where coordinated hand forces and whole-body motion cannot be defined by kinematic trajectories alone.
Learns from robot-free demonstrations using force-sensing handheld grippers and wearable body-motion trackers.
A diffusion policy combines vision, proprioception, and measured contact wrenches to predict actions and per-hand force commands.
A hybrid compliance controller tracks commanded forces while maintaining balance and preserving motion accuracy in simulation.
Across three robot tasks, FLORE succeeds in 80% of rollouts versus 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations.

papers.selection_reason: Learns force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation policies from demonstrations with whole-body force control, directly fitting robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: FLORE enables humanoids to perform contact-rich loco-manipulation by learning force-reactive actions from multimodal demonstrations and executing them with compliant whole-body control.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxc\'e-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io
authors: Gijeong Kim, Seungbin Oh, Dongyun Kang, Hae-Won Park
bullets: Addresses the lack of first-order information when frictional contacts transition between modes.
Uses a central-path relaxation of frictional complementarity only during backpropagation, while retaining the exact hard-contact forward solve.
The resulting sensitivity is continuous across contact-mode transitions and approaches the exact sensitivity as relaxation vanishes.
With 100,000 samples and under 2 minutes of desktop training, the learned policy transfers to hardware without fine-tuning.
Hardware and trajectory-optimization demonstrations show robustness to pushes, debris, slippery ground, and contact-rich solutions missed by baseline gradients.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces differentiable contact dynamics for legged locomotion policy learning and trajectory optimization, directly fitting robot learning and control.
papers.title: Differentiable Contact Dynamics for Legged Locomotion: Policy Learning and Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization
papers.tldr: A smooth contact gradient enables feasible policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged robots, including hardware transfer without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Expanding multilingual ASR systems to new languages is challenging when adaptation must preserve previously supported languages without replaying source-language training data. We study this problem in connector-based Speech LLMs, where a trainable connector maps speech representations into a frozen large language model. We evaluate target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting the connector while preserving source-language performance. In single-target expansion, target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging learn new languages but cause severe source-language forgetting, while SSU-Wanda+TIES gives the best source-preserving trade-off. In multi-target expansion, update merging provides stable source retention, whereas recursive expansion can improve target adaptation under favorable orders but is highly order-sensitive. These results show that multilingual ASR expansion requires balancing target acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Haralambos Mouratidis, Ravi Shekhar
bullets: Problem: Add new languages to connector-based Speech LLM ASR without replaying source-language data or degrading existing languages.
Method: Compare target-update construction and merging strategies for adapting a trainable speech-to-LLM connector while keeping the LLM frozen.
Single-target finding: Target-only fine-tuning and standard TIES merging cause severe source-language forgetting; SSU-Wanda+TIES offers the best reported trade-off.
Multi-target finding: Update merging provides stable source retention, while recursive expansion can improve target adaptation but is highly order-sensitive.
Scope: Expansion requires balancing new-language acquisition, source retention, and interactions among target-language updates.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: GPT-6-Astra is evaluated as a robot-control agent under the same visual and proprioceptive observations as post-trained policies.
Direct control performs competitively, especially on short-horizon tasks and across generalization dimensions.
It underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon, tabletop, and high-precision contact-rich manipulation.
A harness that invokes VLA or WAM policies combines complementary strengths, reaching the strongest standalone policies’ overall success level with lower token cost.
Remaining gaps stem from suboptimal policy invocation, fixed instructions without subgoals, and grasp disruption when control returns to the agent.

papers.selection_reason: Profiles frontier MLLM agents controlling robots directly and via VLA/WAM policies, directly relevant to embodied VLA and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Profiling a Frontier Agent with EBench: From Direct Control to Harness with Policy
papers.tldr: Evaluating GPT-6-Astra on EBench shows that direct MLLM control is strong on short-horizon tasks, while combining it with VLA/WAM policies improves overall performance and reduces token cost but remains limited by imperfect policy orchestration.

papers.abstract: Selection bias in large language models (LLMs) can persist despite instructions to ignore presentation order or prompts that elicit reasoning. Recent efforts to reproduce Jev-style System One behavior have produced a growing family of models that predict probabilities directly over supplied candidates. Yet systematic comparisons of selection bias across Jev versions, Jev reproductions, and generative LLMs remain limited in multi-option tasks. This leaves a central question: does Jev-style decision structure reduce selection bias? We address this question with a simple test that shuffles options while keeping question and candidate content fixed. Across two Jev versions, twelve Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs, we trace individual answers through eight presentations and compare them with fixed-order repetition. On our primary collection of 1,700 questions from two benchmarks, Jev's accuracy varies by less than two percentage points, yet its cumulative failure set expands by 27--29\% relative to the original order, with first failures continuing into the final presentation. This loss of initial successes is substantially larger than under fixed-order repetition, even for highly repeatable Jev reproductions. Nor does Jev show a general advantage over the LLM baselines in preserving correct choices. Aggregation offers limited protection: voting yields modest gains for Jev, while even unanimous answers are frequently wrong. These results expose a gap between repeatable decisions and decisions that remain correct across equivalent presentations, showing why stable accuracy alone cannot establish resistance to selection bias.
authors: Mingyang Song, Mao Zheng, Zhiyuan Ma, Xinpeng Zhou
bullets: The study tests selection bias by shuffling options while keeping questions and candidates unchanged.
It compares two Jev versions, 12 Jev reproductions, and six generative LLMs across eight presentations and fixed-order repetition.
On 1,700 questions, Jev accuracy changes by under two percentage points, but its cumulative failure set grows 27–29% relative to the original order.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate multiple tokens in parallel, but often require many decoding rounds to complete a response. Efficient generation depends not only on which tokens are easy to predict, but also on how committing to them helps predict the remaining positions. A highly predictable token may provide little useful context, while revealing a less predictable token can help several other positions become predictable sooner. We propose dSpark, a new schedule distillation-based framework for learning when to commit tokens for faster diffusion language generation. To achieve this, we construct unmasking schedules that prioritize tokens whose reveal makes other positions easier to predict, reducing uncertainty earlier in decoding. We then distill these schedules into the model to enable faster parallel sampling, with a KL-divergence regularizer to help preserve generation quality. We extensively evaluate our approach across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. On GSM8K, our method achieves remarkable 10.12$\times$ and 5.12$\times$ speedups over the various baselines on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct, respectively, while maintaining superior task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/dSpark.
authors: Aidar Myrzakhan, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel but can still be slow because they require many decoding rounds.
The method prioritizes tokens whose unmasking makes other positions easier to predict, rather than only selecting individually predictable tokens.
These schedules are distilled into the model for faster parallel sampling, with KL-divergence regularization to preserve generation quality.
Evaluated on mathematical reasoning and code generation, dSpark reports up to 10.12× speedup on GSM8K while maintaining superior task performance.
The approach is demonstrated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes dSpark, a schedule distillation framework for diffusion language models (dLLMs) that learns when to commit tokens to achieve significant speedups in parallel sampling while maintaining quality.

papers.abstract: Deep research, or any use of large language models (LLMs) to read a large document collection and produce insights, requires synthesizing information from different sources. In this work, we find that LLMs produce long-form research reports that read as confident syntheses but which fail to accurately reflect the underlying documents. We call this failure smoothing. In collapsing diverse and potentially conflicting sources into a single narrative, the model discards the evidential "jaggedness" of its corpus and asserts conclusions more decisive than the citations can support. We introduce a claim level scoring pipeline, SmoothScore, to quantify this effect. Our pipeline extracts key conclusive claims from model generated reports, then finds evidence relevant to each claim and clusters that evidence along high level aspects. Finally, each claim is scored with respect to the evidence to quantify the degree of smoothing done by the agent. Across 7 systems and 4 datasets, we find that agents consistently produce stronger claims than warranted.
authors: Tiasa Singha Roy, Manya Wadhwa, Greg Durrett
bullets: The study examines how long-form LLM research reports can misrepresent their source documents.
“Smoothing” occurs when agents discard evidential nuance and make conclusions more decisive than the citations support.
SmoothScore extracts report claims, retrieves relevant evidence, clusters it by aspect, and scores each claim against that evidence.
Evaluated across 7 systems and 4 datasets, agents consistently produced claims stronger than warranted.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in text-guided 3D editing, particularly with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have shown promise but still lag behind the flexibility of 2D editing tools. Existing methods face a critical trade-off between preserving multi-view consistency and allowing structural modifications. Image-based editors can also struggle to apply the intended edit to objects viewed from unusual angles. To address these limitations, we introduce VidEdit3D, a framework that reformulates 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. By drawing a parallel between camera movement in static 3D scenes and temporal dynamics in video, we leverage the robust spatiotemporal priors of pre-trained Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) to encourage semantic and structural coherence across views. Specifically, we propose Trajectory-Guided Rendering (TGR) to select informative keyframes and construct smooth video clips aligned with VDM input requirements. To propagate edits from an anchor view to these clips, we develop Flow-Aligned Video Editing (FAVE), a training-free framework incorporating an Editing Consistency Guidance (ECG) mechanism. ECG contrasts source and edited image conditions at a shared latent state, using scheduled source-image amplification to strengthen adherence to the edited reference while maintaining original scene context. Finally, we introduce Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement (RS-GS) to strictly confine geometric and appearance updates to target primitives, reducing background attribute leakage. Experiments demonstrate stronger instruction alignment and better multi-view consistency than the baselines.
authors: Yanming Yang, Chenxi Song, Tong Zhao, Juntao Xu, Wenhao Rao, Yiwen Chen, Yiwei Wang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between structural editability and multi-view consistency in existing 3D and image-based editors.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Rendering to select keyframes and create smooth camera-aligned video clips.
Applies Flow-Aligned Video Editing with Editing Consistency Guidance to propagate an anchor-view edit across views.
Uses Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement to limit geometry and appearance changes to target regions and reduce background leakage.
Experiments show stronger instruction alignment and improved multi-view consistency than baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of VidEdit3D. We reformulate 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. This module incorporates ECG for semantic alignment and a self-attention-based mask for background preservation. (3) RS-GS: We lift the 2D edits back to 3D via inverse rendering to confine updates to the target Gaussians.

papers.abstract: Existing jailbreak attackers fall into two classes: static planners fix their single- or multi-turn adversarial plans in advance, remaining simple but losing sight of the victim's replies, wasting turns and limiting transferability; interactive generators read each victim reply to generate the next-turn attack but require in-loop evaluators for success signals or hints, incurring substantial costs and inflated performance. Bridging this gap, we propose SEMA-Auto, a sighted and efficient multi-turn attacker with autonomy, interacting with the victim model and terminating the session by itself upon success. To stabilize its behaviors and boost its capabilities, SEMA-Auto is trained in two stages. Synthetic bootstrap tuning installs the notion of attack targets and conforming decisions by fine-tuning the base model with bootstrapped trajectories. Decision-supervised reinforcement learning then optimizes two objectives jointly yet separately, reinforcing the attack with higher jailbreak reward while supervising the decision at each turn against an absolute target. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack success rates (ASR) across multiple datasets, victims, and judges, outperforming all static and interactive baselines, within almost the fewest turns, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency. For example, SEMA-Auto performs a $76.0\%$ ASR@1 within an average of $3.0$ turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash on AdvBench, while the best static baseline is $54.8\%$ with fixed $7$ turns and the best interactive baseline is $43.8\%$ in $3.7$ turns. Against safety-hardened frontier models, GPT-oss-120B, GPT-5.4, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and GPT-6-Astra, our counter-trained attacker achieves an average $59.6\%$ ASR@1 on HarmBench, $13.8\%$ over prior SOTA. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/SEMA
authors: Mingqian Feng, Xiaodong Liu, Weiwei Yang, Chenliang Xu, Jialin Song, Qiyao Ma, Chengquan Guo, Carolyn Buractaon, Christopher White, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fixed attack plans that ignore replies and interactive attackers that require costly in-loop evaluators.
Uses two-stage training: synthetic bootstrap tuning, followed by decision-supervised reinforcement learning for attack effectiveness and per-turn stopping decisions.
Autonomously terminates sessions upon success, improving efficiency and reducing unnecessary turns.
Reports state-of-the-art attack success across multiple datasets, victim models, and judges; on AdvBench, it achieves 76.0% ASR@1 in an average of 3.0 turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
On HarmBench against safety-hardened frontier models, a counter-trained attacker reaches 59.6% average ASR@1, exceeding prior SOTA by 13.8 percentage points.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SEMA-Auto, a reinforcement learning-based jailbreak attacker that achieves state-of-the-art efficiency and success rates by training on decision supervision and bootstrapped trajectories.
papers.title: SEMA-Auto: Sighted and Efficient Multi-Turn Attack with Autonomy

papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones.These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.
authors: Marius Henry, Michael Rizvi-Martel, Michael Hahn
bullets: Addresses the interaction between in-distribution generalization and extrapolation to longer sequences.
Derives guarantees based on model parameter sizes, quantization space, and sequence alphabet size.
Characterizes the trade-off between the number of training samples and their lengths.
Shows theoretically that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing sample count.
Experiments support the theory’s predictions.

papers.selection_reason: Joint statistical and length-generalization bounds for transformers inform long-context training and length-scaling tradeoffs.
papers.title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
papers.tldr: The paper develops joint theoretical generalization bounds for fixed-precision, multi-layer transformers across both sample distribution and sequence length, showing that longer training strings can be far more valuable than more samples.

papers.abstract: Attention over tens of thousands of visual tokens dominates the inference of video diffusion transformers (DiTs). Existing methods reduce this cost through sparsity, low precision, or both, but use a single precision for all kept tiles. We observe that the output error introduced by approximation varies widely across tiles. Many tiles can be skipped with little error, others must be computed but gain little beyond low precision, and a few retain substantial error even at low precision. We present Triage, a training-free attention method that assigns each tile one of three approximation tiers: skipping it by replacing it with its block means, skimming it in NVFP4, or refining it with NVFP4 residual correction. A lightweight router predicts each tile's error under each tier from block statistics and moves a tile to a more accurate tier only when the predicted error reduction justifies the extra compute, with a single price setting this trade-off. A fused kernel executes all three tiers in a single pass on the FP4 tensor cores of RTX Blackwell GPUs. Across Wan2.2, HunyuanVideo, and LTX-2.5, Triage accelerates end-to-end generation by up to 2.32x over dense FlashAttention, and in each of five settings it runs faster than every baseline while reaching 0.3-3.0 dB higher PSNR than the highest-PSNR baseline.
authors: Yeonjae Kim, Omin Kwon, Seong Hoon Seo, Jae W. Lee
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.
Assigns each tile to skip, NVFP4 skim, or NVFP4 residual refinement.
A lightweight router uses block statistics and one price parameter to balance error against compute.
A fused kernel executes all tiers in one pass on RTX Blackwell FP4 tensor cores.
Across three video diffusion models and five settings, it achieves up to 2.32× end-to-end speedup and 0.3–3.0 dB higher PSNR than the strongest baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Tiered attention-tile skipping and low-precision refinement for video diffusion transformers, directly relevant to efficient attention and token/tile pruning.

papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), model-reported self-confidence is often miscalibrated, yet it may still be useful for efficient evaluation. At the same time, LLM-as-a-judge offers a scalable alternative to direct human auditing, but its practical benefit depends on calibration quality and inference cost. This paper develops a unified statistical framework for both evaluation routes under alternative sampling strategies. For direct auditing, confidence-stratified sampling is used to recover population accuracy from partially verified outputs without requiring calibrated confidence. Finite-sample uncertainty is characterized, and the analysis shows how highly uneven confidence strata affect audit efficiency and label allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, the judge is modeled through sensitivity and false-positive rate, yielding an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty. The two routes are then compared through human-label and total-cost efficiency boundaries. Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro show that miscalibrated self-confidence can still support statistically valid stratified auditing. Under highly imbalanced confidence distributions, proportional allocation substantially reduces estimation error relative to equal-per-stratum allocation. For judge-assisted evaluation, only a small subset of target--verifier pairs satisfies the idealized human-label efficiency condition, and automated inference costs can further limit potential savings. These findings clarify the statistical and economic conditions under which confidence-guided auditing and automated verification are useful.
authors: Harine Choi (Texas A&M Transportation Institute, Texas A&M University System), Chenchen Kuai (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zihao Li (Department of Civil, Construction and Environmental Engineering, Marquette University), Jiwan Jiang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Yunlong Zhang (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zhiwen Fan (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Texas A&M University), Zhengzhong Tu (Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Texas A&M University), Yang Zhou (Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A&M University)
bullets: Confidence-stratified sampling estimates population accuracy from partially human-verified outputs without calibrated confidence.
Finite-sample analysis links uneven confidence strata to audit efficiency and label allocation.
Judge-assisted evaluation uses sensitivity and false-positive rates to form an error-corrected estimator with calibration uncertainty.
Experiments on MMLU-Pro and MMMU-Pro favor proportional over equal-per-stratum allocation under imbalanced confidence distributions.
Only a small subset of target–verifier pairs meets the idealized human-label efficiency condition; inference costs can erase savings.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified statistical framework for evaluating LLMs using self-confidence stratified sampling and LLM-as-a-judge, characterizing finite-sample uncertainty and cost efficiency.

papers.abstract: Conversational QA systems should fix errors when users push back and signal which answers to trust. We split each follow-up into its speech act (re-ask, agree, or challenge) and its payload (an answer string, correct or not), and measure four confidence signals on the same transcripts: verbalized confidence, length-normalized likelihood, a frozen hidden-state probe, and P(True). Answers change when the user supplies an answer string and almost never under the speech act alone: in every retained full-size cell, the correct answer converts at least four times as many wrong answers as re-asking or agreement. The four signals disagree. On Qwen2.5-7B the frozen probe rises with answer persistence rather than truth; this holds on held-out questions, with Llama-3-8B (cleaned answers) as support, but not on four other models. Among 81 Qwen2.5-7B errors that survive one re-ask, re-asking, a fresh chat, or abstain repair almost none, while a gold answer repairs 75-95%. In two preregistered replications, every repair rate without an answer string stays below 0.15; a larger post-hoc rerun excludes 0.15 except for the empty elicit. With BM25 TriviaQA evidence, sentences that contain the answer repair 67-76% of persistent errors versus at most 12% when they do not. An end-to-end contain-gate cuts harm on TriviaQA, but a deployable gate that does not know the gold answer repairs few errors.
authors: Duc-Vinh Tran
bullets: Separating speech act from payload shows that re-asking or agreeing rarely changes answers; supplied answer strings drive correction.
Four confidence signals disagree, and Qwen2.5-7B’s frozen probe increases with answer persistence rather than correctness; this pattern does not generalize to all tested models.
For persistent errors, re-asking, fresh chats, and abstention repair almost none, whereas providing a gold answer repairs 75–95%.
Evidence containing the answer repairs 67–76% of persistent TriviaQA errors, versus at most 12% for evidence without it.
An answer-containment gate reduces harm, but a deployable gate without gold-answer access repairs few errors.

papers.title: Not One Belief: Answer Payloads, Persistence, and Dissociated Confidence Signals in Conversational Question Answering

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach's practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
bullets: Targets weak VLM image interpretation and grounding in specialized robotic domains.
Uses a reactive cyclic planning pipeline with online grounding and dynamically selected vision preprocessing.
Requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations.
Evaluated across five diverse domains, including real-world robot disassembly.
Field tests indicate practical integration in brownfield settings with limited domain-specific data.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely adopted for reflective error correction in task planning; however, existing approaches primarily rely on autonomous exploration, rendering them prone to accumulating erroneous experiences during early interactions with new environments. To address this limitation, we propose the Flexible Instructional Scaffolding Reflection Framework (FISRF), an agent--mentor architecture that estimates the robot's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) in task planning and adaptively selects reflection strategies and mentor guidance, thereby facilitating the accumulation of effective error-correction experience. Experiments in ALFWorld and on real-world robotic platforms demonstrate that FISRF reduces the average number of error-correction rounds by 37% and redundant reasoning by 25.1%, while improving the overall task success rate by 8%. Project webpage : https://fisrfplanning.github.io/
authors: Qingmiao Liang, Jiatao Zhang, Runxin Zou, Yufan Song, Wei Song, Yuhua Zheng
bullets: Targets the tendency of autonomous exploration to accumulate incorrect experiences in new environments.
Uses an agent–mentor architecture to estimate the robot’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD).
Adaptively selects reflection strategies and instructional guidance for error correction.
Experiments in ALFWorld and on real robots reduce error-correction rounds by 37% and redundant reasoning by 25.1%.
Improves overall task success by 8%.

The resulting reflections and planning trajectories are stored in a memory module for long-term retrieval.

papers.abstract: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses unseen subject surfaces and inconsistent 3D structure during viewpoint changes.
Uses an automated pipeline to synthesize videos with geometry-driven camera motion, including full 360° orbits.
Conditions generation on surface-normal maps reconstructed from reference views without requiring temporal alignment.
Introduces Showcase-4K for training and ShowcaseBench for evaluation with known meshes and camera parameters.
Reports state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency with competitive video quality and motion.

papers.abstract: Robot corrections allow people to adjust a robot's behavior, but a single correction changes many features. Also, preferences about object attributes and relationships between objects cannot be expressed by moving the robot. We propose environment edits as a complementary form of feedback. The robot's motion is held constant as the human edits the scene, so the only explanation for the edit is the moved object. We introduce Feature Learning from Environmental and Robot-Relational Edit Traces (FERRET), which learns preferences from both robot and environment corrections. We show that environment edits are able to disambiguate features and learn preferences that robot corrections alone cannot.
authors: Isaac Ngui, Courtney McBeth, Nancy M. Amato
bullets: Robot corrections can change multiple features at once, making preferences ambiguous.
They cannot directly express preferences about object attributes or inter-object relationships.
FERRET learns preferences from both robot corrections and environment-edit traces.
Keeping robot motion fixed makes the edited object the likely cause of the feedback.
Experiments show environment edits disambiguate features and reveal preferences that robot corrections alone miss.

papers.abstract: JEV decision models pair a language model backbone with a lightweight scoring head to select among natural-language options. Direct selection compares candidate answers within one request, whereas entailment reranking evaluates each candidate in a separate natural language inference (NLI) request over fixed relation options. We examine whether the readout and adaptation choices used for direct selection remain effective for cross-request reranking. We combine a mean-span readout with selective backbone adaptation. Mean-span pooling replaces the option-ending pointer with an average of the contextualized states inside each NLI option, without adding head parameters. Selective adaptation retains low-rank updates in attention and gated DeltaNet projections while removing feed-forward adapters. On MC11, which averages accuracy over eleven reranking configurations from seven sources, selective adaptation improves NeoHorse-1-4B accuracy over the all-module baseline while cutting trainable parameters by more than half, and mean-span pooling yields further consistent gains at the same parameter count.
authors: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Ye Yuan, Enhua Wu, Chao Xu, Allen Chen, Kai Han, Yunhe Wang
bullets: Studies whether direct-selection design choices transfer to cross-request NLI reranking.

papers.abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$
authors: Richard Fechner, Peer Neubert
bullets: Introduces 16 database–query datasets from terrestrial Space Analog Domains, covering environmental, viewpoint, and illumination variation.
Defines matches by whether a relative pose estimator can produce a useful pose for downstream SLAM, rather than by fixed pose thresholds.
Provides ground-truth matrices derived from an ensemble of state-of-the-art relative pose estimators.
Evaluates nine state-of-the-art VPR methods and finds substantial room for improvement.
Offers a pre-release dataset and evaluation resources via GitHub.

papers.abstract: An offline language-based support tool is presented to assist pilot training and tactical decision-making in air combat operations. The system, named MATE (Mission Assistant for Training and Evaluation), applies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to answer natural language questions using content extracted from doctrinal and tactical manuals. Built entirely with open-source components, it performs text preprocessing, embedding generation, semantic search, and language generation locally, ensuring full offline functionality. The tool was evaluated by three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots, who rated the answers produced with three open-weight language models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Mistral NeMo 12B) to five tactical questions derived from a publicly available air combat manual. Average ratings ranged from 4.00 to 4.40 on a five-point scale, with Mistral NeMo 12B obtaining the highest score, and the pilots rated the response time of the tool as fully adequate compared to manual search. The relevance of the retrieved content was identified as the main point for improvement. Potential applications are discussed in onboard mission systems, flight simulators, and training environments.
authors: Joao P. A. Dantas
bullets: Uses open-source components for local preprocessing, embeddings, semantic search, and language generation without internet access.
Answers questions from doctrinal and tactical manuals using three open-weight language models.
Three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots evaluated five tactical questions, giving average answer ratings of 4.00–4.40/5.00.
Mistral NeMo 12B received the highest rating, and response time was considered adequate compared with manual search.
Retrieved-content relevance was the main identified improvement area; proposed uses include mission systems, simulators, and training.

papers.abstract: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic data collection remains a major bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) policy learning, especially for tasks requiring accurate end-effector positioning and camera-action alignment. This challenge is particularly severe in electronic-waste disassembly, where robots operate in cluttered assemblies of densely packed, visually similar components. Full digital-twin simulation is difficult because many parts are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level meshes and contact models difficult to obtain. In this work, we focus on pre-contact reaching and propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based data generation pipeline for wrist-camera VLA adaptation. Our method reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders diverse wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses. These observations are paired with smooth, structured reaching trajectories to provide robot-aligned visual-action supervision for VLA fine-tuning. We further augment the VLA policy with an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that estimates target proximity and provides reliable termination before physical interaction. Experiments in motherboard disassembly demonstrate precise VLA-based reaching using wrist-camera observations alone, without an external side-view camera. With $\pi$0.5, 1,500 generated trajectories achieve 80.0\% precise-reaching success across three targets, compared with 58.7\% using 150 teleoperated demonstrations, while requiring less than 10 minutes of active human capture. Project website: https://001-wang.github.io/PrecisionReach-GS/

papers.abstract: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual trajectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer-evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assessment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful trajectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with Pi. Across both benchmarks, 10 skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improve coding performance across all evaluated settings, demonstrating transfer across benchmarks, coding models, and agent harnesses. We further evolve the skill library from target-benchmark trajectories without verifier feedback, relying solely on the learned evaluator for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills.

papers.abstract: Expressive robot motion positively impacts human-robot interaction by improving user engagement, likability, or task performance. We present a novel approach to automatically generate and modulate complex, expressive full-body gesture sequences from a multimodal (text, audio, video) context description. Based on a unified mathematical implementation of the Principles of Animation using Dynamic Movement Primitives, we use multimodal foundation models to generate such sequences along with parametric motion variations that are highly context-aware. This method extends the state of the art in terms of flexibility and generality by being interpretable, composable, and working across different robot morphologies. Moreover, we integrate the system into a continuous control framework and leverage knowledge distillation to learn a much smaller model, significantly improving token efficiency and system latency. Results from a user study with a human-like platform indicate that participants judged our system's motions to be better aligned with the interaction context than motions produced under a non-modulated or API-level condition. We also demonstrate how the system generates expressive motion for robots with different kinematics, showcasing its versatility. Paper webpage: https://gen-mod-expressive-motion-behavior.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Modeling the latent, multi-step reasoning processes of learners is a core challenge for adaptive tutoring systems, which often rely on simple right/wrong answers rather than understanding how students think. Instantiated here for grammatical reasoning, this study introduces a diagnostic framework that makes students' step-by-step problem-solving visible by analyzing their action sequences in an interactive learning game. The framework computes five interpretable strategy dimensions (e.g., systematic error correction, random guessing), estimates coordination demand from task structure and behavioral patterns, and classifies reasoning into four distinct states. Analyzing 36,234 interactions from 234 students working on 42 morphosyntactic exercises, we found that reasoning strategies vary primarily by context rather than stable traits (intraclass correlation = 0.14), and students show high persistence in unproductive states; specifically, 74.6% of failures driven by high coordination demand (rather than simple knowledge gaps) are followed by another failure without intervention. Our early warning model predicts validation success with strong accuracy (AUC = 0.826 using strategy patterns alone; 0.902 with additional sequential context) while avoiding circular reliance on current error counts. These findings demonstrate that making latent reasoning processes visible enables earlier, more targeted scaffolding that responds to how students are thinking rather than simply whether they succeed. While demonstrated in language learning, the framework provides a generalizable, interpretable architecture for diagnosing complex, structured reasoning in any domain.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation is essential for deploying modern video diffusion models. Among existing approaches, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) has emerged as a highly promising paradigm by achieving strong output-space fidelity without adversarial training, while remaining flexible across various student architectures. We observe, however, that DMD fundamentally relies on an output-space objective, lacking explicit regularization on the model's internal representations. As the distillation step count aggressively shrinks, this output-only supervision becomes insufficient, causing the distilled student to degrade in both fine-grained spatial structures and coherent temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce Self Flow Forcing (SF$^2$), which incorporates a predictive representation loss into the DMD framework without altering its output objective. By providing the student and an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) teacher with heterogeneous noise levels, we establish an information asymmetry. This formulation forces the student to predict the teacher's internal representations from a more corrupted input, effectively integrating self-supervised representation alignment into distribution matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SF$^2$ effectively mitigates temporal flickering and consistently improves both spatial fidelity and motion quality. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism is architecture-agnostic - seamlessly supporting both bidirectional and causal models - and requires no external feature extractors, introducing minimal computational overhead.
authors: Junyi Chen, Haiyu Zhang, Zhoujie Fu, Tengfei Wang, Chunchao Guo
bullets: DMD’s output-only supervision can fail at very low step counts, harming fine spatial detail and coherent motion.

Experiments report less temporal flickering and consistent gains in spatial fidelity and motion quality.
The method is architecture-agnostic across bidirectional and causal models and needs no external feature extractor.

Hidden states from asymmetric layers are aligned via learnable projectors with a stop-gradient cosine loss Lrep. The teacher is updated by EMA and requires no external pre-trained features.

papers.abstract: Coordinating many miniature robots in a confined arena, with no leader, central planner, or global map, is a core challenge for swarm robotics. As the swarm grows denser, collision avoidance becomes the limiting factor, and the number of safely coexisting robots depends on the formulation of the inter-robot safety constraint. We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a $0.64\,\mathrm{m^2}$ arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.
authors: Prajol Shrestha, Siddhant Mohapatra, Filip Novkoski, Julian Oelhaf, Nicolas Vandewalle, Ana-Sun\v{c}ana Smith, Andreas Maier
bullets: Targets leaderless swarm coordination without a central planner or global map, where dense packing makes collision avoidance the key challenge.

Six barrier and control-barrier-function safety formulations are compared in a digital twin; the look-ahead discrete-time CBF yields the fewest collisions and widest inter-robot margins across nearly all tested swarm sizes.
Experiments cover phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus, from ten robots to the arena’s geometric packing limit.
Collisions rise sharply near the packing limit, but coordination and cohesion degrade gradually; local alignment remains high, indicating safety and order are maintained together.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed. To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings,with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence. Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption. Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.
authors: Zerun Liu, Lechao Cheng, Yimin Liu, Shengeng Tang, Yaxiong Wang, Zhun Zhong
bullets: Targets runtime preemption and resumption when higher-priority instructions interrupt an unfinished navigation sequence.
Introduces single, repeated, and nested interruption scenarios with stage-specific evaluation metrics.
Measures inserted-task completion, original-task resumption, and full-sequence completion separately.
Finds that recovery varies by interruption condition and that aggregate success can hide these differences.
Provides a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline for re-grounding navigation targets after interruption.

papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly considered for clinical decision support, where their answers should be grounded in clinical evidence and remain robust to irrelevant information. Prior work shows that a single irrelevant sentence can lower the accuracy of medical models, but not where inside the model its effect can be removed, or how to do so without knowing which sentence it is. We find that blocking attention to a known distractor restores the answer, whereas head masking can suppress correct answers. We also show that the model's hidden states mark the distractor as the sentence that least fits the case even when the model follows it. To remove a distractor's effect without knowing which sentence it is, we propose EXCISE, an inference-time method that blocks the sentence most influencing the answer, but only if the model's hidden states mark it as inconsistent with the case. On MedQA-TD (MedQA with Targeted Distractors), a benchmark we construct in which each distractor targets a specific wrong option, EXCISE gains 16.7-22.8 accuracy points at a 1.5-2.1-point cost on the same questions without distractors, outperforming prompting, rewriting, and steering baselines for all three models. Its gains extend to MedDistractQA and BiasMedQA, as well as chain-of-thought generation.
authors: Yerim Hong, Sohyun Son, Heeseung Chung, Mujeen Sung
bullets: Irrelevant sentences can substantially reduce medical model accuracy, even when the model follows them.
The model’s hidden states often identify the distractor as the sentence least consistent with the case.
EXCISE operates at inference time without requiring the distractor to be known in advance.
On the authors’ MedQA-TD benchmark, it improves accuracy by 16.7–22.8 points, with a 1.5–2.1-point cost on distractor-free questions.
Benefits also transfer to other benchmarks and chain-of-thought generation.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase computation per token by repeatedly applying a shared backbone, offering a way to improve language modeling and downstream task performance at a fixed backbone parameter count. However, each loop depends on the preceding loop, so increasing recurrent depth also increases decoding latency. Existing approaches include Parallel Loop Transformers, which reduce latency by overlapping loop computation across token positions, but yield rapidly diminishing marginal accuracy gains at larger depths. To address this challenge, we introduce LoopFold, which folds computation at multiple recurrent depths into parallel batches for the same token prefix. A lightweight predictor estimates inputs to later loops so they can start before earlier loops finish. A corrector then refines the outputs of these later loops using newly available results from earlier loops. All components are trained jointly using only the final next-token prediction loss. In experiments with 1.4B models, deeper LoopFold configurations achieve progressively higher average zero-shot accuracy across eight tasks, rising from 53.41% to 56.38%. Vanilla looped models and PLT show limited gains over the same depth range. Compared with a nine-loop vanilla model, LoopFold uses five sequential stages and additional parallel computation to reduce decoding latency by 46%.
authors: Feichen Song, Boyi Zeng, Yiqin Hao, Shixiang Song, He Li, Yizhou Yang, Zitong Wang, Yifan Liu, Ziwei He, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Looped Transformers improve modeling capacity through repeated use of a shared backbone, but sequential loops increase latency.
LoopFold folds multiple recurrent depths into parallel batches for the same token prefix.
A predictor estimates later-loop inputs early, while a corrector refines them when earlier-loop outputs become available.
Joint training uses only the final next-token prediction loss.
In 1.4B-model experiments, average zero-shot accuracy rose from 53.41% to 56.38%; five sequential stages reduced latency by 46% versus a nine-loop vanilla model.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers offer a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling by repeatedly applying a shared backbone. Vanilla looped Transformers use each backbone output directly as the input to the next iteration. These outputs may contain information useful several iterations later, but retaining it across the loop depends entirely on the single hidden state. We introduce StateLoop, which maintains one additional persistent state per token to retain information across iterations. At each iteration, a learned gate controls how much of the previous state is retained and how much information from the backbone output is incorporated. The updated state is projected back and added to the backbone output for subsequent iterations and final prediction. This design reduces Pile perplexity and improves average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks over Vanilla Looped. Its perplexity advantage over Vanilla Looped grows with trained loop depth, consistent with persistent state becoming increasingly useful as recurrent computation deepens.
authors: Feichen Song, Boyi Zeng, He Li, Shixiang Song, Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Yizhou Yang, Yifan Liu, Ziwei He, Zhouhan Lin
bullets: Vanilla looped Transformers rely on a single hidden state, which may lose information needed in later iterations.
StateLoop maintains an additional persistent state for each token across loop iterations.
A learned gate balances retaining prior state with incorporating new backbone output information.
The updated state is projected back into the backbone output for later iterations and final prediction.
It reduces Pile perplexity and improves average accuracy across eight zero-shot tasks; its perplexity benefit grows with loop depth.

papers.abstract: Uniform frame sampling can miss brief evidence in sparse-event videos when the VLM sees only K frames. We propose EARS (Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and motion), a training-free, query-free front-end that ranks frames using optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity. The evidence score alone has frame-level AP 0.39; used only to select frames for the VLM, EARS with temporal diversity reaches localization AP 0.94, compared with 0.88 under Uniform sampling. In the updated matched study, at K = 1 EARS reaches XD-subset F1 0.660 versus 0.614 for centered Uniform (the paired interval includes zero); earlier backbone studies use separate protocols. On mostly-silent UCF-Crime, however, EARS slightly trails Uniform. A single configuration is used across both benchmarks; the new controls do not repeat the original held-out search. EARS therefore targets low-budget videos whose salient evidence aligns with motion or audio; on dense narratives or stealthy events, uniform or semantic selection remains preferable, and cheap modality statistics cannot reliably route between them. Code: https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/EARS
authors: Shih-Yao Lin
bullets: Targets sparse-event videos where uniform sampling may miss brief evidence under a frame budget.
Training-free, query-free retrieval ranks frames by optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity.
With temporal diversity, EARS achieves localization AP 0.94 versus 0.88 for uniform sampling; at K=1, XD-subset F1 is 0.660 versus 0.614, with an interval including zero.
Performance slightly trails uniform sampling on mostly-silent UCF-Crime videos.
Scope is limited: uniform or semantic selection may be better for dense narratives or stealthy events, and modality statistics cannot reliably choose the strategy.

papers.abstract: Both models and minds not only encode features that describe an entity, but can specifically represent which features of that entity are relevant for a given context. This core capability underlies in-context learning in language models and a variety of cognitive phenomena in minds, yet it is unclear how intelligent systems identify and promote relevant features. In this work, we propose Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA), an algorithmic hypothesis that provides an explanation for how relevance is determined in the context of few-shot concept induction --- the ability to infer a latent concept from a small number of positive examples. Under ADA, concept induction proceeds by forming a summary representation of the examples in a feature space that is shaped by amortized knowledge about which features tend to be useful for finding commonalities between items. We investigate and validate ADA in language models using a few-shot concept induction task. This work provides a novel perspective on the mechanisms supporting contextualization in language models and a promising hypothesis for a core aspect of cognition.
authors: Michael A. Lepori, Laila Johnston, Aalok Sathe, Zhuonan Yang, Roman Feiman, Ellie Pavlick
bullets: Addresses how models determine which entity features matter in a given context.
Models concept induction as summarizing positive examples in a feature space shaped by prior knowledge of useful commonalities.
Introduces ADA as an algorithmic hypothesis for relevance determination.
Investigates and validates ADA in language models on a few-shot concept induction task.
Offers a perspective on contextualization in language models and a hypothesis about a related cognitive mechanism.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Few-Shot Concept Induction and Amortized Direction Accentuation. (Left) Given a set of support items, a concept induction task requires a learner to infer the concept that generated those items from a potentially infinite set of candidates. Inferring a latent concept enables a learner to produce novel instances of that concept. (Right) Amortized Direction Accentuation (ADA) proposes that learners produce representations of inferred concepts based on an aggregation of the support set (visualized here as a prototype representation), which is then biased by an accentuation matrix that amortizes the learner’s experience about which features tend to be helpful when assessing commonalities between items (e.g., a model might learn that it is typically more important to represent whether an item is a bird than to represent whether the item has a vowel for its second letter).

Figure 2: Performance on the concept list task across language models. We measure the boost in token probability due to the presence of a support set. Across models, tokens that belong to the latent concept that generated the support set consistently receive a greater change in log probability than tokens that do not belong to the concept.

Figure 5: Leave-One-Concept-Out Behavioral analysis results. We model the context-induced change in token probability using a score function that accounts for feature accentuation (ADA) or uncontextualized embedding geometry (Generic). We find that accounting for feature accentuation usually, but not always results in a stronger account of LM output behavior. (Significance markers according to a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over concepts; ∗ = p < .05, ∗∗ = p < .01, ∗ ∗ ∗ = p < .001)

Figure 4: Regression analysis results. To distinguish between the alternative hypotheses, we fit rotation matrices (Generic), ridge regressions (ADA), or MLPs (Ad-Hoc) to predict context displacement vectors from the average embeddings of support items. We compute a noise ceiling that captures variation due to ordering effects. (Left) For held-out support sets, ADA is robustly supported across layers, achieving >80% of the upper bound while outperforming the Generic Feature alternative and matching the Ad-Hoc alternative. All alternatives beat a baseline that uses raw prototype representations, and another baseline that shuffles (prototype, displacement vector) pairs independently. Shaded region indicates SEM. (Right) This pattern holds when entire concepts are held-out (all alternatives are significantly different at p < .001 according to a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over concepts).

Figure 3: Visualization of context displacement vectors as the number of support examples grows. The sport vector denotes the mean context displacement vector over 20 support sets. Context displacement vectors are placed end-to-end for visualization purposes, so an optimal vector for the concept is parallel to the sport vector. When the concept list begins with canonical sports, the context displacement vectors quickly align with the sport vector. When the list begins with less canonical sports, it takes several examples before the context displacement vector aligns. Axes are the top 2 principal components of a matrix of mean displacement vectors for all concepts in the dataset.

Figure 7: Steering with average context displacement vectors on gemma-2-2B. Steering in the direction of average context displacement vectors boosts the probability of held-out in-concept items while suppressing out-ofconcept items. Steering in the negative direction does the opposite, and steering in control directions does not have a large impact.
Figure 6: RSMs created from concept vectors and context displacement vectors at a middle layer of gemma-2-2B. Individual context displacement vectors approximate the rich geometry of concept vectors.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models keep the KV of past chunks as retrieval memory so that revisited places stay consistent. On a single consumer machine (one RTX 4090, 32 GiB of host memory, one NVMe SSD), long sessions with such memory hit two walls. The first is capacity: the KV of Matrix-Game 2.0 exhausts host memory after 45 seconds of video in bf16 and after 2.8 minutes in int4. The second is the model's positional horizon of 4.3 minutes. We show that this memory is capacity-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and that its access set is known before compute, because the camera pose is an input. An analytical model built on these observations predicts spill points to within one chunk and classifies zero versus non-zero stalls correctly on held-out configurations. Guided by it, WorldPager stores int4 KV in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy instead of recomputing it, prefetches each chunk's memory from the extrapolated pose, never waits on a miss, and writes back in the background; to our knowledge, it is the first to place the KV memory of an interactive world model on an NVMe tier with zero-stall prefetching. With training-free position handling, it generates 37.5 minutes of video continuously with zero stalls and constant host memory, at about 9.5 frames per second. On a sealed test set, int4 storage shows no measurable quality loss; on long-gap revisits it lowers image quality by about one MUSIQ point.
authors: Bingnan Liu, Ruini Xue
bullets: Addresses host-memory exhaustion and the model’s limited positional horizon during long interactive sessions.
Uses an analytical access model based on known camera poses to predict spill points and classify potential stalls.
Stores KV memory in a GPU/DRAM/NVMe hierarchy, prefetches before computation, avoids waiting on misses, and writes back asynchronously.
Generates 37.5 minutes of continuous video at about 9.5 FPS with zero stalls and constant host memory on a single RTX 4090 system.
Reports no measurable quality loss with int4 storage on a sealed test set, but about a one-point MUSIQ drop for long-gap revisits.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. WorldPager overview. KV of past chunks is stored as int4 blocks (one block per layer and chunk) in a pinned DRAM pool and spills to NVMe. While chunk c is denoised, the retrieval set of chunk c+1 is computed from the extrapolated camera pose and staged to the GPU by a prefetch thread. A miss reuses the previous retrieval set instead of waiting. Cold dirty blocks are written to NVMe by a background thread.

Fig. 3. Prefetching keeps the median stall at zero down to 0.25 GB/s, whereas on-demand swap-in stalls at every bandwidth. Stall per chunk (P50; triangles: P99 of prefetching) when NVMe reads are limited by a software token bucket and every retrieved block comes from NVMe (32 GiB, 36 chunks, 99–165 chunks per point). Crosses: predictions of the analytical model registered before the runs; predicted zero stalls are drawn at the axis floor.

Fig. 1. Two walls for MG2 on one RTX 4090. Capacity stops every design without an NVMe tier early (chunk 21, 60, or 226 at 32 GiB), and without position handling every design stops by the positional wall at chunk 341; WorldPager reaches 3000 chunks. All bars are measured; the 64 GiB int4 run uses an extended position table so that it isolates the capacity wall, and it stops at chunk 496 against a registered model prediction of 492. WorldPager runs under 32 GiB with an NVMe tier (37.5 min of video).

Fig. 4. Chunk time and host memory stay flat for 3000 chunks while KV spills to NVMe. One 3000-chunk session (37.5 min of video) under 32 GiB with all components enabled (1 rollout). Top: chunk time; the step at chunk 341 is the position re-mapping. Bottom: host RSS stays flat while KV spills to NVMe after the pool fills at chunk 226.

papers.abstract: Recovering an object's 3D structure and camera motion from a few uncalibrated views is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Classical structure from motion methods recover 3D geometry consistent with the input images but cannot recover unseen regions; native generation methods produce plausible 3D objects which are related but not necessarily faithful to the input images. Methods simply concatenating reconstruction and generation allow error to cascade across the two stages, instead of producing a 3D object consistent with both the distribution and the input. We propose GenSfM, which integrates image-based 3D reconstruction with a native 3D diffusion model. In particular, we use a multi-modal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise the shape latent and per-view pose latents under shared self-attention, grounding generated geometry in the observed views while using object-level priors to infer unobserved regions. A compact 3D-native UV-volume tokenization keeps the joint sequence small as views are added, and a pose-aware stage refines geometry and texture by sampling per-voxel image features at the recovered camera poses. On Toys4k and GSO, for $4$ uncalibrated views, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by $3.2$-$4.5$ dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by $2.8$-$3.8\times$ over a strong native-3D generation baseline, while recovering input-view poses over $96\%$ Acc@$5^\circ$ without any external pose-estimation backbone, post-hoc optimization, or known intrinsics. Project page: https://dotb1ue.github.io/GenSfm/.
authors: Haobin Duan, Binbin Huang, Mochu Xiang, Yiqun Zhao, Zibo Zhao, Yi Ma, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses the gap between classical reconstruction, which misses unseen regions, and unconstrained generation, which may not match inputs.
Uses a multimodal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise shape and per-view pose latents with shared self-attention.
Employs compact 3D-native UV-volume tokens and pose-aware refinement using image features sampled at recovered camera poses.
On Toys4k and GSO with four uncalibrated views, improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2–4.5 dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8–3.8× versus a native-3D generation baseline.
Recovers input-view poses with over 96% Acc@5° without external pose estimation, post-hoc optimization, or known intrinsics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GENSFM. We cast pose-free multi-view 3D recovery as a single coarse-tofine generative problem. The coarse stage (Sec. 4.1) jointly denoises the sparse-structure latent and per-view 3D-native pose tokens with a multi-modal shape-pose DiT, recovering shape and multi-view camera poses together. The fine stage (Sec. 4.2) refines geometry and appearance with per-voxel pose-sampled image conditioning, producing the final structured-latent set.
