Each added component sharpens local geometry and texture, with the full model best matching GT.

For methods that produce a canonical 3D output without input camera poses, we align predictions to the ground truth via similarity ICP on 100K points sampled from the rendered surface of the output mesh of each side, then evaluate photometric quality on novel views and 3D geometric accuracy in the ground-truth coordinate frame.

Table 1: Comparison of paradigms for sparse-view object structure-and-motion recovery. “Where” denotes camera-motion recovery and “what” denotes object-structure recovery, with observed and hidden geometry referring to visible and unobserved object regions, respectively. “Unified joint inference” means jointly recovering complete object structure and camera motion in one model, while “native 3D prior” denotes a generative prior over complete 3D shapes. ✓: explicit support; △: partial or indirect support; –: not a primary objective.

We report relative rotation error (RRE) with Acc.@{5◦, 15◦} thresholds, relative translation error (RTE; the angular error between predicted and GT relative-translation directions), and mean absolute FOV error (RFOV; intrinsic-only); see supplementary for the full evaluation protocol. CD is the median across objects.

Table 6: Pose VAE autoencoding accuracy on Toys4k across latent spatial resolutions. We sweep the latent grid in {43, 83, 163} at a fixed 8 channels per token (yielding {64, 512, 4096} latent tokens respectively), encode each held-out 643 ground-truth UV volume, decode, and recover camera pose via the DLT solve. Each cell reports median / mean / 95% quantile over ∼77K (image, pose) pairs. UV distance is in normalized image coordinates (×10−4); pose errors are in degrees.

papers.abstract: Point-supervised temporal action localization (PTAL) aims to recognize and localize action instances in untrimmed videos using only point-level annotations. Existing pseudo-label-based methods have made substantial progress in PTAL. However, confidence-based initialization can overlook well-localized proposals. Meanwhile, existing methods either keep pseudo-labels fixed during detector training or update them without fully exploiting alternative boundary evidence from the original proposal pool. These limitations constrain supervision quality, thereby hindering detection performance. To learn high-quality pseudo-labels, we propose a framework that integrates prior-guided initialization with consensus-guided refinement during detector training. Our framework comprises two modules: Prior-Guided Initialization (PGI) and Consensus-Guided Refinement (CGR). PGI combines proposal confidence with point-derived priors to establish instance-specific reliability for initial pseudo-label selection and candidate retention. CGR continually uses the retained original candidates to construct boundary targets, combining their consensus with evolving detector predictions to refine pseudo-labels throughout training. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves competitive detection performance compared with existing methods. In particular, our method achieves 68.5\% average mAP over tIoU thresholds 0.1--0.7 on THUMOS14, surpassing PseR by 3.7 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/zhenyingfang/LHQP
authors: Zhenying Fang
bullets: Addresses missed well-localized proposals and weak pseudo-label updates in existing PTAL methods.
Prior-Guided Initialization combines proposal confidence with point-derived priors to select reliable initial pseudo-labels and retain candidates.
Consensus-Guided Refinement uses retained original proposals and evolving detector predictions to refine action boundaries throughout training.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving 68.5% average mAP across tIoU 0.1–0.7 on THUMOS14, 3.7 points above PseR.

papers.abstract: Mental health research on social media has been dominated by English-language datasets and DSM-5-centered resources, limiting cross-lingual and cross-cultural understanding of online mental health expression. We introduce MATCHA, the first Chinese multi-disorder mental health dataset that links disorder-specific Weibo Super-Topic communities with users' broader public timelines. MATCHA covers seven DSM-5 disorders and a control group, comprising 46,025 cohort-level users and 1.8 million posts. The dataset distinguishes users with explicit self-disclosure evidence from broader disorder-related participants through an LLM-assisted annotation pipeline, and is released in a rigorously de-identified, controlled-access format. Using MATCHA, we analyze behavioral, linguistic, symptom-related, and life-event-related patterns across disorders, and conduct cross-lingual comparisons with Twitter-STMHD. Our analyses show that Weibo Super-Topics function as concentrated spaces for affective and health-related expression, while cross-platform differences between Weibo and Twitter often exceed cross-disorder variation. MATCHA provides a new resource for community-aware and cross-lingual mental health NLP research.

papers.abstract: Learning-based structure-from-motion methods such as ACE-Zero have demonstrated strong performance in estimating cameraposes and scene coordinates from unordered image collections without requiring ground truth supervision. However, the lack of global and multi-view consistency constraints in ACE-Zero can lead to pose drift and misalignment, particularly in complex or ambiguous scenes. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework that integrates pose graph optimization (PGO) into ACE-Zero to refine camera poses and suppress incorrect refinements. We construct pose graphs directly from ACE-Zero outputs by extracting relative pose constraints from predicted scene coordinates. Furthermore, we introduce an uncertainty-aware optimization strategy by estimating confidence scores using geometric priors, including epipolar and optical flow consistencies across views. Our approach improves the robustness and accuracy of pose estimation, demonstrating that global geometric reasoning can effectively complement learning-based inference in structure-from-motion.
authors: Tze Ho Elden Tse, Jizong Peng, Angela Yao
bullets: Addresses pose drift and multi-view misalignment caused by limited global consistency in ACE-Zero.
Builds pose graphs from ACE-Zero-predicted scene coordinates and relative pose constraints.
Uses uncertainty-aware optimization with confidence scores from epipolar and optical-flow consistency.
Reports improved pose-estimation robustness and accuracy through global geometric reasoning.
Scope: targets unordered image collections and ambiguous or complex scenes.

papers.abstract: Training robotic manipulation policies in simulation is widely adopted due to safety and cost efficiency; however, tasks involving obstacles remain under-performing and often converge slowly under Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). To address this challenge, we propose a task decomposition framework for DRL that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) with Reward Redesign (RR) to improve learning efficiency and robustness in obstacle environments. The TL strategy selectively transfers only the first-layer critic parameters across structurally related tasks, since that layer captures general state--action representations while deeper layers encode reward- and obstacle-specific value geometry; RR decomposes tasks into staged sub-objectives to provide denser optimization signals. Experiments on the PyBullet Panda platform show consistent gains in obstacle settings. On Push with obstacle, our method achieves $0.83 \pm 0.05$, outperforming the strongest baseline (Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC), $0.77 \pm 0.06$) by approximately $7.8\%$. On Slide with obstacle, performance reaches $0.95 \pm 0.02$, exceeding Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) ($0.84 \pm 0.06$) by about $11\%$ success rates. In addition to higher final performance, forward transfer reduces convergence time by up to $70\%$ in obstacle tasks, and RR shortens sparse-reward Pick-and-Place training from roughly $0.75$M to $0.20$M steps ($\approx73\%$ reduction). The best policy is deployed on a real Franka Emika FR3 robot as a qualitative feasibility demonstration.
authors: Yuanzhi He, Victor Romero-Cano, Jiayu Xu, Juan David Hern\'andez, Gualtiero Colombo

On PyBullet Panda tasks, success reaches 0.83 for Push with obstacle and 0.95 for Slide with obstacle, with reported gains over the strongest stated baselines.
Forward transfer reduces convergence time by up to 70%, while reward redesign reduces sparse-reward Pick-and-Place training from about 0.75M to 0.20M steps.
The best policy is qualitatively demonstrated on a real Franka Emika FR3 robot.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) on resource-constrained embodied agents for 3D visual question answering necessitates cloud-edge collaboration. However, offloading massive visual data to the cloud over bandwidth-limited and noisy channels introduces severe latency and transmission distortion. To address this, we propose TP-JSCC, an efficient token pruning and joint source-channel coding method for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration. First, we develop a Local and Global Semantics-based Hybrid Token Pruning (LGS-HTP) module to significantly reduce the visual token count. By decoupling foreground-background tokens and jointly selecting local and global semantics, LGS-HTP effectively reduces redundancy while preserving reasoning-critical tokens. Second, we introduce a lightweight Token Joint Source-Channel Coding (T-JSCC) module to further compress the pruned tokens and ensure their robust transmission over error-prone channels. By employing lightweight cascaded linear layers and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-adaptive mechanism, this module adapts to fluctuating channel conditions while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanQA and SQA3D datasets indicate the exceptional efficiency and robustness of our approach. Specifically, on ScanQA validation set, the LGS-HTP module could achieve 90% pruning ratio while incurring less than a 1% CIDEr loss. Building on this, the T-JSCC further compresses the tokens by 18 times, resulting in an overall 180 times data volume reduction for robust transmission, while saving 90% in computational complexity for LVLM deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhui0325/TP-JSCC.
authors: Zhengxin Li, Chongzhen Tian, Hui Yuan, Hao Liu, Sam Kwong
bullets: Targets latency and distortion caused by offloading large 3D visual inputs from resource-constrained agents.

On ScanQA validation, it prunes 90% of tokens with less than 1% CIDEr loss and achieves 18× further compression.
The combined approach reduces transmitted data volume by 180× and deployment computational complexity by 90%, as reported on ScanQA and SQA3D.

papers.abstract: Social media enables cross-lingual communication, yet the meaning of user-generated content (UGC) is often distributed across text, images, and cultural knowledge, making translation challenging. Existing evaluations typically treat images as optional and assume textual information is sufficient, obscuring whether errors stem from missing visual evidence or inadequate cultural adaptation. We introduce \textbf{Culture-MMT}, a diagnostic benchmark for \textbf{distributed-evidence pragmatic reconstruction} in social-media translation. It contains 498 curated, de-identified UGC instances across 20 domains, categorized into Symbol, Visual, and Hybrid by their required evidence. We also develop a human-aligned domain-specific judge, Judger, and a controlled evaluation framework that systematically varies the evidence available to translators. Across 17 model configurations, real images improve performance by +0.280 on Visual and +0.197 on Hybrid, but only +0.050 on Symbol, while random images provide no comparable gains. Human-authored descriptions further show that jointly dependent cases remain more challenging even when visual facts are explicit. These results characterize culturally effective social-media translation as {meaning reconstruction from distributed evidence}, highlighting visual grounding and cultural-pragmatic adaptation as distinct model bottlenecks.
authors: Dingming Li, Yiwen Qiu, Linjuan Wu, Hongxing Li, Zixuan Wang, Xinze Lyu, Ye Guo, Daoxin Zhang, Zhe Xu, Weiming Lu, Yongliang Shen

papers.abstract: Automated fake news detection is vital on social media, where fake news is easily rewritten to fool detectors. However, existing approaches typically rely on superficial writing cues or single-style text rewrites, resulting in poor robustness under diverse cosmetic modifications. We construct MANTIS-Bench, a multi-axis presentation-attack benchmark that pairs original news with rewritten views across writing style, emotional expression, and dissemination framing. We further propose MANTIS, an instance-adaptive adversarial framework enabling dynamic worst-case training tailored to each news article with zero inference-time overhead. This reframes fake news defense from heuristic format smoothing into targeted, fact-invariant credibility assessment. Experiments on MANTIS-Bench show that MANTIS reduces the Union Attack Success Rate (UASR) by 3.55 percentage points relative to SheepDog on GossipCop and consistently outperforms prior single-axis defenses on Macro-F1 while maintaining competitive clean accuracy, demonstrating the effectiveness of multi-axis and instance-adaptive worst-case training.
authors: Dexin Liu, Fan Yang, Zimu Wang, Xunfei Zhu, Bolin Ren, Bingyan Zhang, Wei Wang, Qi Chen

papers.abstract: Existing manipulation data collection methods typically offer either accurate robot-state acquisition through kinematic-chain-based teleoperation or convenient, portable operation through vision-based approaches. We present DEX-PHD, a portable handheld device that combines these advantages for dexterous manipulation by integrating a dexterous robot hand, continuous per-finger control, and multimodal logging. The system records proprioceptive information, fingertip contact data, and wrist-camera video, while the operator directly controls the robot hand through joint-level mapping. Its untethered design enables data collection across diverse environments. We demonstrate DEX-PHD on contact-rich tasks requiring coordinated multi-finger manipulation and deploy the collected demonstrations through open-loop replay on a physical humanoid robot. The results show that open-loop replay preserves the main temporal patterns of finger motion and task-relevant contact. Therefore, DEX-PHD provides a practical platform for portable, multimodal dexterous manipulation data collection.

papers.abstract: Data-enabled predictive control has recently emerged as a promising control paradigm, enabling a transparent optimal-control formulation without the need to learn an explicit dynamics model. This paper presents a number of extensions paving the path towards its use in real-time robotics tasks. Following recent work, we utilize a nonlinear predictor based on Gaussian kernels to represent the relationship between input and output data. We propose a damped Gauss-Newton method that enables real-time control by efficiently exploiting the least-squares structure of the control problem. In addition, we introduce a hybrid buffer management strategy that incorporates informative online data while retaining relevant offline data, allowing the predictor to account for changes in the dynamics. We demonstrate the tracking performance and computational suitability of the proposed method in MuJoCo using a Franka Research 3 arm pushing a block across surface, without prior knowledge of its changing friction values.
authors: Akshun Sharma, Zhongqi Wei, Buqing Ou, Frederike D\"umbgen
bullets: Targets real-time robotic control without learning an explicit dynamics model.
Uses a Gaussian-kernel nonlinear predictor to model input–output relationships.
Introduces a damped Gauss–Newton solver that exploits the control problem’s least-squares structure.
Maintains a hybrid data buffer combining informative online data with relevant offline data to adapt to changing dynamics.
Demonstrates tracking and computational suitability in MuJoCo for a Franka Research 3 pushing task with unknown, changing friction.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.
authors: Khaled M. Seyam (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Julian Wiederer (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Samar Fathalah (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Markus Braun (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Bin Yang (University of Stuttgart, Germany)
bullets: NeuroNCAP analysis attributes 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions to planning failures rather than perception.

Cross-planner transfer is limited, indicating that targeting the specific planner is important; scope is demonstrated on two planners and NeuroNCAP.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce \textbf{Omni-InteractScope}, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) \textbf{Timely tool invocation remains unreliable}: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) \textbf{Query-free reminders remain poorly covered}: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) \textbf{End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited}: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu

Across 12 models, on-time first responses for tool invocation reach at most 40%, while joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0%.
Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0%, and nine of 12 models complete none of the 26 guidance sequences.
Controls show that tool-use scores do not alone prove event grounding, while reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot teams executing predefined missions must adapt to runtime changes and sustain mission management despite robot failures. This paper proposes MATE-BT (Mission, Allocation, and Task Execution with Behavior Trees), a hierarchically decentralized framework that separates mission execution, allocation, and task execution. An active onboard leader manages mission progression and team-level task assignment, with authority transferable to another leader-capable robot after failure. Interchangeable decentralized methods resolve target assignments, while each robot adapts its local behavior through planning and acting with behavior trees. Webots simulations and real-robot experiments demonstrate mission continuity despite new targets and robot failures, including active-leader failure. In the physical experiments, all MATE-BT computation runs onboard. Hardware-in-the-loop resource measurements further support onboard execution on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 5. By updating only the affected layers without full-plan regeneration, MATE-BT maintained a response time of approximately 130 ms with 30 robots and 120 targets. Comparisons of four target-assignment plugins reveal scenario-dependent trade-offs between mission completion time and total travel distance.
authors: Sunbeen Lee, Hoseon Gi, Jik Hur, Inmo Jang

papers.abstract: Text-in-image translation aims to translate all textual content embedded in an image. In Text Image Translation (TIT), the output is translated text; In-Image Machine Translation (IIMT) additionally renders the translation back into the image. We introduce ImgMT, a massively multilingual dataset and benchmark mined from localized SVG illustrations on Wikimedia Commons, focusing on diagrams, maps, and infographics. ImgMT contains 35,612 aligned image pairs grouped into 1,855 image sets, spanning 129 languages, 20+ writing systems, and 4,886 language pairs. We propose a multi-level evaluation protocol that measures source-side text-region detection and OCR accuracy alongside target-side translation quality. We benchmark several multimodal large language models and a dedicated TIT system in English->X and X->English settings, and find that the source language and writing system substantially affect TIT quality. Finally, we show that ImgMT is not well suited for isolating the contribution of visual information in multimodal translation.

papers.abstract: In the past few years, Vision Transformer (ViT) has achieved excellent performance in the field of computer vision. However, there still some problems remain. For instance, ViTs heavily rely on large-scale training data since they simply contain a large number of trainable parameters, which slows down their learning efficiency and limits their applicability in resource-constrained scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning model, namely All-Convolutional Self-Attention Network (ACSAN), which applies convolution operations to replace fully-connected matrices multiplications in the ViT framework. To implement ACSAN, we firstly design Dynamic Convolutional Self-Attention (DCSA) as the basic module, which employs multi-scale dilated convolutions to generate Query, Key, and Value. We defined spatial self-attention and channel self-attention to generate attention features respectively. The two attention features are finally merged as the output of the DCSA module. Based on DCSA, we then construct the basic ACSAN block. Comparing with ViT, we use DCSA to replace the regular self-attention operations, and use convolution layers to replace MLPs. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we train ACSAN on three widely-used image classification databases, i.e. CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1k, from scratch. Experimental results show that ACSAN achieves excellent classification accuracy comparing with standard ViT with comparable or fewer parameters, as well as other state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies verify that each component contributes positively to the final performance.
authors: Zimian Wei, Tianqi Zhang, Hengyue Pan
bullets: Targets ViT’s reliance on large training datasets and many trainable parameters, which limits resource-constrained use.

Combines spatial and channel self-attention features within each DCSA module.
Builds ACSAN by replacing standard self-attention with DCSA and MLPs with convolutional layers.
Trained from scratch on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1k; reports accuracy comparable to or better than standard ViT and other state-of-the-art methods with comparable or fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a promising representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. For practical deployment, recent studies have explored pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, which reconstructs Gaussian representations directly from unposed input images. However, these methods remain sensitive to residual pose errors, which perturb canonical-space Gaussian transformation, introducing noisy supervision for geometry and attribute learning. To address this problem, we present SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that improves robustness to pose uncertainty and stabilizes the learning of Gaussian primitives. SG-Splat decouples geometry estimation and Gaussian attribute prediction into two dedicated branches, reducing error coupling between pose-sensitive geometry and Gaussian attributes. We further introduce a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline, consisting of Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC), to improve geometric alignment before Gaussian attribute reconstruction. Specifically, FGPR refines camera poses with flow-based correlation features and differentiable bundle adjustment. RGC then corrects initial point maps using depth residuals derived from FGPR, producing more reliable Gaussian centers. To stabilize training, we introduce a dual-path strategy that mixes ground-truth and predicted poses for canonical transformation. It provides clean supervision for Gaussian attributes while improving geometry robustness to residual pose errors. Extensive experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that SG-Splat achieves state-of-the-art performance in both novel view synthesis and pose estimation.
authors: Xiaohan Lu, Jiaqi Zhang, Weijia Jiang, Siwei Ma
bullets: Targets noisy geometric and attribute supervision caused by residual pose errors in unposed input images.
Uses separate branches for geometry estimation and Gaussian attribute prediction to reduce error coupling.
Applies coarse-to-fine refinement through Flow-Guided Pose Refinement and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction.
Uses a dual-path strategy mixing ground-truth and predicted poses to stabilize training and improve robustness.
Reports state-of-the-art novel view synthesis and pose estimation on DL3DV and RealEstate10K.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the pipeline. The input images are processed by separate geometry and attribute branches. The geometry branch predicts initial local point maps and camera poses through the point head and camera head, while the attribute branch predicts the remaining Gaussian attributes. Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) refines the initial poses and produces depth residuals, which are used by Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC) to correct the local Gaussian centers µlocal . The corrected centers are transformed into the canonical space with the refined poses and combined with the predicted attributes to form the final Gaussian representation.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparisons on the DL3DV dataset with 24 input views. With more accurate camera pose estimation, our model produces geometrically consistent Gaussian primitives, yielding sharper boundaries, finer details, and fewer artifacts in novel views.

Fig. 7. Qualitative comparisons on the RealEstate10K dataset with sparse-view inputs (6 views). Even with only a few input views, our model reconstructs more coherent scene geometry and more realistic novel views, with clearer details and reduced artifacts.

Fig. 1. Comparison of pose usage strategies in pose-free feed-forward 3DGS training. (a) AnySplat [1] uses predicted poses with pose supervision, maintaining consistency between training and inference but suffering from perturbations caused by pose errors. (b) WorldMirror [2] uses ground-truth poses with pose supervision, stabilizing training but introducing inconsistency between training and inference. (c) E-RayZer [3] relies on predicted poses without pose supervision, making optimization sensitive to pose errors. (d) Our method uses mixed poses with pose supervision, balancing stable learning and robustness to residual pose errors.

Fig. 5. Dual-Path Training Strategy. The refined predicted pose and the ground-truth (GT) pose are sampled with equal probability. The selected pose is used to transform local Gaussian centers into the canonical space for rendering. When the ground-truth pose is selected, reliable rendering supervision updates both the geometry and attribute branches. When the predicted pose is selected, rendering gradients are detached from the attribute branch and only the optimize geometry branch. This asymmetric optimization stabilizes attribute learning while improving geometry robustness under residual pose errors.

Fig. 3. Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR). At each iteration, FGPR uses the current pose and geometry estimates to build flow-based correlation features and optical flow of camera motion. Together with context features, these cues are fed into an update operator to predict correspondence corrections ∆pij . The corrected correspondences p∗ ij are optimized by differentiable bundle adjustment (DBA) to jointly update camera poses and depths. Over T iterations, FGPR progressively improves pose accuracy and produces depth residuals for subsequent geometry correction.

Fig. 4. Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC). RGC uses the residual depth map ∆D̂i from FGPR to correct the initial local point map M̂i. The residual depth map and the initial point map are embedded and fused with geometry tokens to predict a bounded multiplicative correction, producing the corrected point map M̃i.

papers.abstract: Voronoi tessellations have recently emerged as an adaptive, space-partitioning discretization for shape and appearance reconstruction from multi-view images. However, the irregular cells they produce make the repeated reconstruction of the tessellation during optimization costly. We therefore explore adaptive centroidal Voronoi tessellations (CVTs), which extend standard CVTs with non-uniform cell sizes while preserving the regular, well-shaped cells that make them efficient to compute. In CVTSplat, cell size is modulated by the evolving signed distance field, concentrating sites near the zero level set while keeping cells nearly centroidal. This regularity lets us specialize the whole pipeline, with GPU algorithms for nearest-neighbor queries and approximate Voronoi construction, and a rasterizer tailored to small, nearly isotropic cells. Our Voronoi construction is 5 to 10 times faster than general-purpose alternatives in this regime. On DTU and BlendedMVS, CVTSplat reaches geometric accuracy competitive with the best Gaussian-splatting surface methods while training in about 2.5 minutes on a single GPU.
authors: Briac Toussaint, Diego Thomas, Jean-S\'ebastien Franco, Edmond Boyer, Christian Theobalt
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeatedly reconstructing irregular Voronoi tessellations during optimization.
Modulates cell sizes using the evolving signed distance field, concentrating sites near the zero level set while maintaining near-centroidal cells.
Introduces GPU-optimized nearest-neighbor queries, approximate Voronoi construction, and rasterization for small, nearly isotropic cells.
The specialized Voronoi construction is reported as 5–10× faster than general-purpose alternatives in this setting.
Achieves competitive geometric accuracy with leading Gaussian-splatting surface methods on DTU and BlendedMVS, with training taking about 2.5 minutes on one GPU.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our approach during optimization. Top row: Construction of the tessellation. (a) The sites are processed to obtain a list of their 32 nearest neighbors, (b) before building the Voronoi diagram as an adjacency graph. (c) The center of mass of each cell is then computed to regularize the distribution of the sites via the CVT loss. (d) The Voronoi diagram is optionally converted to a Delaunay triangulation to extract the zero-level set with marching tetrahedra. Bottom row: Differentiable volume rendering from posed images. (e) The sites’ attributes (learnable SDF and features) are smoothed with a Gaussian kernel. (f) The gradient of the SDF is also computed to produce normal vectors, which define a piecewise linear SDF over the cells. Then, for all viewpoints in the mini-batch, (g) a per-site color is computed based on the camera’s position, (h) before rasterizing the scene and comparing against the ground-truth image.

Figure 13: We remove one loss on each example to ablate our model. Bottom: The multi-view (ZNCC), depth and normal losses as well as the reflection probes are important for geometric accuracy. The mean is ≈ 14.2, corresponding to 14 bisector planes contributing to each cell on average. Middle and Right: zero-based index of the last detected Voronoi neighbor in the KNN list, with linear and logarithmic frequency scales respectively. papers.abstract: Constrained decoding guarantees that Large Language Models (LLMs) produce outputs conforming to predefined formats, but is often assumed to inherently degrade reasoning. We examine this assumption through a taxonomy of three constraint types: \emph{format constraints}, which enforce output structure; \emph{validity constraints}, which mask invalid answer; and \emph{reasoning constraints}, which restrict reasoning trajectories. We theoretically show that appropriate constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths. Across four model families and eleven open-source models, causal ablations on diverse benchmarks using state-of-the-art constrained decoding strategies reveal that apparent performance degradation largely stems from non-equivalent prompting and output formats rather than from decoder-level masking. Meanwhile, validity constraints improve reliability and extractability by eliminating invalid answers, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and, consequently, accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories. These findings show that the impact of constrained decoding depends on the type of constraint and the output space it removes. Our code is available.
authors: Ngoc Trinh Hung Nguyen, Alonso Silva, Armen Aghasaryan, Mehwish Alam
bullets: The study distinguishes format, validity, and reasoning constraints.
Theoretical analysis shows suitable constraints can preserve or improve performance by eliminating invalid paths.
Across four model families and eleven open-source models, apparent degradation mainly came from mismatched prompting and output formats, not decoder masking.
Validity constraints improve answer reliability and extractability, while reasoning constraints can improve reasoning and accuracy when they enforce beneficial trajectories.

papers.abstract: Large language models incur substantial training and inference costs in personalized search and recommendation, as growing interaction histories lengthen request inputs and repeatedly expose the same item text to the model. We propose \textbf{C}omposable and \textbf{R}eusable \textbf{I}tem \textbf{M}emory (CRIM), a framework that separates item-level semantic encoding from request-level history modeling. A small set of learnable summary tokens compresses each item into compact continuous memories, while segment-level readout tokens (REC tokens) introduce predictive supervision within the interaction history. These memories are independent of users and queries and can therefore be reused across requests. At inference time, CRIM composes cached memories in interaction order and incorporates an optional query to produce a personalized retrieval representation, reducing repeated item-text encoding while retaining request-dependent contextual modeling. We further introduce a joint training mechanism that combines cached memories with sampled live re-encoding. Re-encoding only a few history items per request allows the retrieval objective to jointly optimize the item and request encoders at limited computational cost, while periodic cache refreshes maintain consistency. Extensive evaluation and cost analysis on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and our new LazSeq dataset show that CRIM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale, while limiting item re-encoding during joint training. We will publicly release our code and dataset.
authors: Haolin Li, Haipeng Zhang, Mang Li, Zhaohui Xia, Xun Zhu, Miao Li, Yu Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses rising training and inference costs caused by long interaction histories and repeated item-text encoding.
Separates item semantic encoding from request-level modeling using learnable summary tokens and predictive REC tokens.
Composes cached, user- and query-independent item memories in interaction order, with an optional query for personalization.
Jointly trains cached memories with limited live re-encoding and periodic cache refreshes to maintain consistency.
Evaluations on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and LazSeq report state-of-the-art retrieval with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale.

papers.abstract: Monocular occupancy prediction in indoor scenes aims to recover a scene's 3D geometry and semantics from a single RGB image. Existing methods are restricted to a closed set of predefined categories, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen categories. This limitation is particularly critical in indoor scenes, where objects exhibit highly diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. We study open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes and present OVM-Occ, a Gaussian-based occupancy framework with an instance-aware vision-language teacher. Specifically, we adopt Language-Embedded Gaussians as the intermediate scene representation, propose a geometry-aware deformable attention module to refine Gaussian semantic features, and construct instance-level vision-language embeddings to provide reliable semantic supervision. We further introduce geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation to mitigate the interference between geometry learning and semantic learning. To evaluate open-vocabulary occupancy prediction performance, we introduce OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica, two extended benchmarks with more diverse and fine-grained semantic categories. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in open-vocabulary monocular occupancy prediction for indoor scenes, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art approach by 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU on the Occ-ScanNet dataset, with consistent gains under new open-vocabulary evaluation protocols.
authors: Shuyang Yu, Haibo Qin, Shaohan Hu, Wei Shan, Xiaoqing Guan, You Wang, Guang Li
bullets: Addresses the limited category generalization of existing closed-set monocular occupancy methods.
Represents scenes with Language-Embedded Gaussians and refines semantic features through geometry-aware deformable attention.
Uses instance-level vision-language embeddings and geometry-aware decoupled semantic distillation for semantic supervision.
Introduces OpenOcc-ScanNet and OpenOcc-Replica benchmarks with more diverse, fine-grained categories.
Reports gains of 12.2 mIoU and 0.6 IoU over the previous state of the art on Occ-ScanNet, with consistent improvements under new protocols.

At inference, the LE-Gaussians are aggregated into LanguageEmbedded Occupancy (LE-Occ), where the occupancy features are matched with query text embeddings via cosine similarity to produce open-vocabulary occupancy predictions.

papers.abstract: Adaptive robot perception systems must balance detector accuracy, inference latency, and energy consumption, particularly when high ambient temperatures cause processors to thermally throttle. We propose Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), a lightweight model-selection policy that forecasts processor temperature using a closed-form RC thermal model and excludes detector configurations predicted to cross a throttling threshold. We evaluate THR with four YOLO11 configurations across seven real-world perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds, comparing it with latency-aware routing, fixed-threshold thermostats, duty caps, and a matched-compute-budget control. At ambient temperatures of 45-55 degrees C and a tight inference deadline, THR eliminates throttling in simulation, reduces deadline misses by 3.9-7.5 percentage points, and reduces energy per on-time frame by approximately 12-13% relative to a latency-belief router. A separate experiment using deadline-paced, nonoverlapping frame execution yields miss-rate reductions of 6.2-9.5 percentage points. A tuned thermostat or duty cap can match THR at a fixed operating point; predictive routing is most useful when ambient conditions or calibrated thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies. Measurements on an Apple M5 support the single-node heating approximation but do not validate hardware throttling. The results characterize the conditions under which thermal forecasting improves the efficiency and timeliness of resource-constrained robot perception.
authors: Sparsh Roy, Kevin Zhou, Arhaan Shah, Shreyan Garg, Vihaan Joshi-Apte, Maxim Kudryashov, Nanda Cheruvanthala
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between detection accuracy, latency, and energy when high temperatures cause processor throttling.
Uses a closed-form RC thermal model to predict temperature and avoids detector configurations likely to exceed a throttling threshold.
Evaluated four YOLO11 configurations across seven perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds against static and latency-aware baselines.
At 45–55°C with tight deadlines, it eliminates simulated throttling, lowers deadline misses, and cuts energy per on-time frame relative to a latency-belief router.
Predictive routing is most beneficial when operating conditions or thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies; hardware throttling itself was not validated.

papers.tldr: Thermal-Headroom Routing uses thermal forecasting to select robot perception models, reducing throttling, deadline misses, and energy use in extreme heat.

papers.abstract: Effective video agents must learn not only how to answer, but also where to look next. Transferring this capability to smaller models is challenging because each observation serves two purposes: supporting an answer and guiding the search for further evidence. Textual descriptions may capture what is currently visible while omitting cues needed for subsequent acquisition. We introduce Latent Agentic Reasoning for Video Analysis (LARVA), a framework that distills multi-round video agents through jointly learned latent reasoning and visual observations. Rather than communicating through captions, an observer passes compact continuous representations to a reasoner that selects the next acquisition action or produces the final answer. Crucially, action and answer supervision propagate through this interface, training the observer to communicate information useful for downstream decisions. Observation reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment provide auxiliary supervision from textual teacher trajectories. Across five video-understanding benchmarks, LARVA achieves strong performance with 4B and 7B backbones. On VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, the 7B model outperforms a textual CoT student trained on the same teacher trajectories by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points, respectively. These results highlight the value of jointly learning how agents represent evidence and act on it when distilling video-understanding capabilities.
authors: Junzhang Liu, Hao Yuan, Qi Zhang, Yiming Wu, Long Chen, Zhecan Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring agentic video understanding when observations must both support answers and guide future evidence acquisition.
Uses compact continuous latent representations between an observer and a reasoner instead of textual captions.
Jointly trains observation and reasoning through action/answer supervision, with reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment as auxiliary signals.
Evaluated with 4B and 7B backbones across five video-understanding benchmarks.
The 7B model surpasses a same-trajectory textual CoT student by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points on VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, respectively.

papers.abstract: We present GaussianSpline, a dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting method that models per-Gaussian motion using adaptive, non-uniform piecewise cubic B\'ezier splines. Unlike approaches based on global deformations, fixed-order polynomials, or uniformly parameterized splines, GaussianSpline jointly learns the B\'ezier control points and the temporal partition of each Gaussian's trajectory. This adaptive representation allocates greater temporal capacity to highly dynamic regions while maintaining compact trajectories for near-static regions, enabling high-fidelity reconstruction of complex and rapidly changing motion. To jointly achieve globally smooth motion and local adaptivity, we enforce $G^1$ continuity between consecutive B\'ezier segments using a reflection-based constraint on their control points. This produces smooth, fully differentiable trajectories while preserving the flexibility of non-uniform temporal parameterization. Experiments on the Neural 3D Video benchmark, the Google Immersive dataset, as well as on synthetic scenes demonstrate that GaussianSpline substantially improves reconstruction quality in scenes with highly non-uniform and challenging dynamics, while maintaining competitive performance on general dynamic scenes compared with state-of-the-art 4D Gaussian Splatting methods.

papers.abstract: Existing multi-agent collaboration (MAC) methods have primarily explored a group thinking collaboration topology, where agents independently generate solutions and aggregate their outputs. In this work, we investigate an alternative relay thinking topology, where reasoning ownership is dynamically transferred across agents, allowing subsequent agents to inherit and refine an evolving reasoning trajectory. We introduce Multi-Agent Confidence-guided Relay (MACR), a framework that enables dynamical relay collaboration among agents. The key challenge is determining when reasoning should be relayed and which agent should continue the process. method addresses this challenge through confidence-guided relay triggering and a bidding mechanism that selects the next agent based on its confidence. Experiments on four benchmarks show that method outperforms the strongest single-model strategies in accuracy, e.g., +3.3% on MathVista and +3.9% on MMStar, and remains on par with multi-agent strategies while consuming 6.0x less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar.Further analysis demonstrates that relay collaboration enables heterogeneous agents to progressively integrate complementary insights, combining heterogeneous capabilities across reasoning stages. Our source code is available at https://github.com/67L1/MACR.
authors: Xu Liu, Jungang Qiao, Guikun Chen, Xiaojuan Qi, Wenguan Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of group-based multi-agent collaboration, where agents reason independently before aggregation.
Uses confidence-guided triggering to decide when to relay reasoning and a confidence-based bidding mechanism to select the next agent.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, MACR outperforms the strongest single-model strategies, including gains of 3.3% on MathVista and 3.9% on MMStar.
Matches multi-agent strategies while using 6.0× less token overhead on HallusionBench and MMStar.
Relay collaboration helps heterogeneous agents combine complementary capabilities across reasoning stages.

papers.abstract: Neural synchrony is hypothesized to help the brain organize visual scenes into structured multi-object representations. In machine learning, synchrony-based models analogously learn object-centric representations by storing binding in the phase of complex-valued features. Rotating Features (RF) instantiate this idea with vector-valued activations, encoding object presence in magnitudes and affiliation in orientations. We propose Orthogonal Rotating Features (OrthoRF), which enforces orthogonality in RF's orientation space via an inner-product loss and architectural modifications. This yields sharper phase alignment and more reliable grouping. In evaluations of unsupervised object discovery, including settings with overlapping objects, noise, and out-of-distribution tests, OrthoRF matches or outperforms current models while producing more interpretable representations, and it eliminates the post-hoc clustering required by many synchrony-based approaches. Unlike current models, OrthoRF also recovers occluded object parts, indicating stronger grouping under occlusion. Overall, orthogonality emerges as a simple, effective inductive bias for synchrony-based object-centric learning.
authors: Despoina Touska, Bastiaan Onne Fagginger Auer, Alexandru Onose, Tejaswi Kasarla, Luis Armando P\'erez Rey, Maximilian Lipp, Lyubov Amitonova, Martin R. Oswald, Pascal Cerfontaine
bullets: Addresses reliable organization of visual scenes into multi-object representations, including overlap, noise, distribution shifts, and occlusion.
Adds an inner-product orthogonality loss and architectural changes to Rotating Features.
Produces sharper phase alignment and more reliable object grouping without post-hoc clustering.
Matches or outperforms current models in unsupervised object discovery while recovering occluded object parts.

papers.abstract: Recent studies on generalizable human Gaussian splatting have achieved the notable progress in synthesizing novel views of unseen human subjects from multi-view images. Despite this progress, existing methods still struggle to represent fine-grained details of human subjects, which inherently involve high geometric and textural complexity. This is because previous methods do not impose a constraint on how densely Gaussians are placed, which often leads to blurry rendering results in complex regions. To address this problem, we propose a complexity-guided regularization scheme. The key idea is to leverage a complexity prior computed via the local entropy in geometric and textural characteristics of a clothed human. This effectively prevents Gaussians from being coarsely placed in complex regions, which facilitates the faithful reconstruction of intricate structures. Furthermore, we sample local patches predominantly from complex regions according to this complexity prior, which allows the model to be sufficiently supervised by local details. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance while maintaining the real-time inference speed in generalizable human Gaussian splatting. The code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/DCVL-3D/CGR-GS_release.
authors: Gun Ryu, Gi-Mun Um, Won-Sik Cheong, Wonjun Kim
bullets: Targets blurry rendering of fine-grained geometric and textural details in unseen human subjects.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative video models have improved visual realism, making detection increasingly dependent on subtle temporal inconsistencies. However, these signals are weak and spatially localized, while most of the video content is redundant. This creates a fundamental mismatch: existing detectors rely on heavy backbones to model full videos, which leads to high computational cost and limited scalability. In this work, we rethink AI-generated video detection from a representation perspective. Instead of modeling entire videos, we restructure them into compact temporal slice representations that isolate informative temporal evolution. We introduce a lightweight framework using frequency-aware temporal slice consistency learning, where informative spatial rows and columns are aggregated over time to form slice-domain inputs. This reparameterization suppresses redundant appearance while preserving discriminative temporal dynamics, enabling efficient and targeted detection. By constructing slices from both high- and low-frequency regions, our method exposes complementary temporal artifacts, including unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness. We instantiate this idea in a Temporal Slice Consistency Network, which integrates task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer to model cross-slice and cross-frequency dependencies. We further introduce AI-Artist, a new benchmark with artist-curated videos from recent high-fidelity generators, including Seedance and Kling. Experiments on GenVideo and AI-Artist show that our method achieves strong performance while requiring over 400$\times$ fewer model-forward FLOPs and 3.6$\times$ faster model inference than the strong video-based baseline ReStraV (2.9$\times$ faster end to end, including preprocessing), enabling scalable and practical deployment.
authors: Wei Shang, Zhiyuan Li, Shengfeng He
bullets: Targets the redundancy and high computational cost of full-video detectors, where generation artifacts are weak and spatially localized.
Aggregates informative spatial rows and columns over time into compact slices, suppressing appearance redundancy while preserving temporal dynamics.
Uses high- and low-frequency slices to capture complementary artifacts such as unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness.
Implements Temporal Slice Consistency Network with task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer.
Evaluated on GenVideo and the new AI-Artist benchmark; reports strong performance, 3.6× faster model inference, and 2.9× faster end-to-end processing than ReStraV.

papers.abstract: A cooperative 3D detector can miss a vehicle even when the LiDAR points on it remain unchanged. We study this failure under adverse weather as Weather-Induced Context Interference. To our knowledge, this is the first controlled study of how weather-related exterior changes remove cooperative benefits while preserving all points inside annotated objects. Controlled experiments on simulated and real roadside inputs show that exterior loss changes object representations before fusion and removes previously useful assistance. On real inputs, restoring object-neighborhood features recovers 30 of 31 induced failures; three equal-area exterior controls recover none. The failure condition also appears with a second fusion model. These findings motivate Adverse-Weather Cooperative Repair (AWCR), with separate implementations for the available supervision. Point Classifier filters added weather returns in simulation. On real inputs, Local Correction refines candidates and Quality Selection checks them against current measurements, without naturally paired clear/adverse-weather recordings. Candidate tracing shows that correction supplies accurate geometry for some targets that original candidates cannot localize at the evaluation threshold. On natural adverse-weather CoInfra development data, AWCR improves car bird's-eye-view (BEV) AP@0.7 by 4.66 points with V2X-ViT and 5.56 with AttFuse. On simulated V2X-R fog, it improves vehicle BEV AP@0.7 by 4.47 points at a fixed 4,096-candidate budget.
authors: Mengxu Ma (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
bullets: Identifies Weather-Induced Context Interference: unchanged object LiDAR points can still yield missed detections when exterior context is altered.
Controlled simulated and real-roadside experiments show exterior loss damages object representations before fusion and removes useful cooperative assistance.
Restoring object-neighborhood features recovers 30 of 31 induced failures, while equal-area exterior controls recover none; the effect also appears with another fusion model.
AWCR uses Point Classifier for simulation and Local Correction plus Quality Selection for real inputs, adapting to different supervision settings.
AWCR improves car BEV AP@0.7 by 4.66 points with V2X-ViT and 5.56 with AttFuse on natural adverse-weather data, and by 4.47 points on simulated fog.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.
authors: Junze Wang, Lei Fan, Dezheng Zhang, Donglin Di, Yang Song, Sidong Liu, Cong Cong
bullets: Addresses two failure modes in test-time prompt tuning: excessive update magnitude and inconsistent directional drift.
Decomposes prompt-update trajectories into magnitude plus persistent, oscillatory, and residual directional components.
Uses Adaptive Koopman Control to shrink expansive updates and Hankel Update Router to preserve persistent directions while suppressing unstable components.
Prompt-agnostic: integrates with existing visual and text TPT methods without changing the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss.
Across 15 datasets, improves 10 baselines, with reported gains of 3–8% for visual prompts and over 2% for text prompts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TPD. The base prompt update ut from visual or text TPT is delay-embedded with a Hankel window and projected into a local Hankel subspace. AKC regulates update magnitude and HUR refines update direction. The controlled magnitude and refined direction are then combined into a stabilized prompt update gtu hur t , which is applied to the prompt state at step t.

The zoomed windows show accuracy, magnitude (spectral radius ρ), and direction (ℓ2 distance between consecutive update vectors, decomposed in (b)) in unstable and stable regimes. Figure 12: Persistent ratio versus accuracy gain for TPT+TPD. Each point corresponds to a local trajectory segment, and the red dashed line shows the fitted trend for each dataset.

Figure 11: Sensitivity of HUR routing weights on cross-dataset transfer. The triangular βc–βn sweep is consistent across VPT+TPD and TPT+TPD: retaining persistent components while attenuating oscillatory and residual components yields a broad high-performing region, whereas weights near one reduce HUR to weak routing and degrade performance.

Each gray point denotes one short temporal window. The red dashed curve is a piecewise linear fitted trend line.

Figure 10: Sensitivity of HUR routing weights on domain-generalization datasets. Warmer colors indicate higher perpanel accuracy. The high-performing region favors small residual weights and moderate oscillatory attenuation, supporting selective routing rather than using the raw update unchanged.

Figure 8: Sensitivity of AKC on domain-generalization datasets. Each heatmap sweeps the spectralradius threshold ρ̄ and gain floor gmin for VPT+TPD or TPT+TPD. Colors are normalized within each panel. Performance is strongest in a broad region around ρ̄ = 1.0 with a small gain floor, indicating that AKC benefits from suppressing locally expansive dynamics without over-damping stable updates.

papers.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.
authors: Jinhu Qi, Minda Hu, Wentao Zhang, Zixing Song, Irwin King
bullets: Implicit requirements are common: over 80% of CL-bench Life rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request.
Direct answering passes 67% of implicit rubrics, compared with 81% of other rubrics.
QERA builds a requirement checklist, asks typed information needs, verifies quoted evidence in code, and performs guarded repair without training or rubrics.
Across 405 tasks and four frontier LLMs, QERA averages a 21.0% solving rate, versus 18.2% for the strongest baseline and 14.6% for direct answering.
Its gains come mainly from the pre-answer protocol and request-specific questions, especially for implicit rubrics; post-answer checking mainly helps numeric requirements.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Answering directly (left) misses what a request leaves unsaid: the four LLMs of our study, answering directly, pass 81% of the rubrics whose wording the request largely contains but only 67% of the others. QERA (right) first asks what the reply must deliver (checklist 𝑂) and what must be found in the context (needs 𝑁 ); code filters Φ keep these questions 𝑄 faithful to the user’s words. The reply is drafted from the whole conversation under 𝑄 ; the check asks 𝑄 again and returns evidence 𝐸 with quotes, which code audits; a local repair is kept only if the guard Γ accepts it. papers.selection_reason: Proposes an inference-time question-driven reasoning architecture for in-context learning.
papers.title: Ask Before You Answer: A Question-Driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture (QERA) for In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: QERA improves LLM reasoning over users’ long-term web traces by asking targeted, evidence-grounded questions before answering.

papers.abstract: Understanding and operating with scientific charts is a standard approach in data analysis, and while humans are good at interpreting such charts, open vision-language models (VLMs) are known to perform poorly when it comes to question answering based on such data types. Motivated by an initial observation that many of their errors are due to inexact answering, we raise the following natural question: how much accuracy can we recover without changing the model at all? In this paper, we study this question by searching over inference programs and the code around a "frozen" version of the model. Using ideas from autonomous evolution (famously used in AlphaEvolve), we first start from a baseline inference program, and in each round we show an LLM judge the code together with a few failures on training questions, and ask for an improving evolutionary move. As usual in autonomous evolution approaches, the candidate programs are kept in a small pool ranked by training accuracy, and the next edit is performed on top-scorers from this pool. We run this approach on three VLMs and four popular benchmarks on scientific charts, and we measure the fraction of descriptive questions whose answer exactly matches the ground truth. The accuracy improves in all experimental settings. On average, it rises from 16.6% with the starting program to 41.3% with the evolved one, and the largest single increase is 55.2 percentage points. As a side benefit, our evolved program is 3.8x faster than the starting program, because short answers are easier to grade and faster to generate. Our results demonstrate that a large part of the observed errors arise due to the inference pipeline, and that optimizing it can improve the "frozen" VLM without the need to retrain it.
authors: Abhinav Sudhakar Dubey, Vidushi Goel, Kiran Rana, Shikhar Mathur, Vaggos Chatziafratis
bullets: Open VLMs often fail on scientific-chart questions, particularly through inexact answers.
The method evolves inference programs using an LLM judge, failure examples, and a pool of high-scoring candidate programs.
Evaluated across three VLMs and four scientific-chart benchmarks, accuracy improved in every setting.
Average exact-match accuracy increased from 16.6% to 41.3%, with a largest gain of 55.2 percentage points.
The evolved program was also 3.8× faster, suggesting inference-pipeline errors account for many failures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Our autonomous evolution framework for better VLMs. Fixed inputs (left) feed an evolution engine (middle) that outputs deployable inference programs (right). The model id, greedy decoding, and the train/holdout split never change during a run; only the code inside the EVOLVE-BLOCK of a candidate is being mutated. An LLM mutator (in our case Gemini-2.5-flash) proposes edits, a validator rejects broken candidate programs before any GPU work, an evaluator scores survivor programs by exact-match accuracy, and a population manager keeps the best-by-holdout program. The same engine produces all twelve runs by swapping the seed program and the benchmark evaluator.

Figure 2: Seed vs. our evolved descriptive exact-match accuracy on all 12 model-benchmark pairs. Annotations give the absolute gain in percentage points by our method. As observed, every pair improves with the largest improvement being +55.2 percentage points. The largest jumps are on Qwen3-VL-2B, whose naive seed produced verbose, wrongly formatted answers; the smallest is SmolVLM2/CharXiv, whose seed was already clean (EM stands for Exact-Match).

Figure 5: Absolute gain in descriptive exact match for each of the 12 runs, sorted. Color denotes model. Gains cluster by whether the seed’s failure was one of formatting (large, recoverable) or perception (small headroom).
Figure 4: Accuracy vs. throughput, Qwen3-VL-2B/ChartQA. Evolution moves the program up and to the right of the seed; best_speed dominates on both axes.

Figure 3: The evolution loop. In every generation, the split loader feeds the train and holdout windows to the evaluator. The LLM-mutator proposes edits, the validator checks them before any GPU work is performed, and the population manager selects the next parent and writes the best-by-holdout candidate to disk. Every five generations, a crossover step combines two strong parents into one child.
Table 4: Qwen3-VL-2B / ChartQA, all six programs (128 descriptive and 64 reasoning samples). best_speed is both the fastest and the highest on the aggregate score, beating the hand-tuned baseline.
Table 2: The five validator invariants. Checks 1–4 are cheap string tests run before the costlier syntax and import stage; the whole gate runs before any GPU work.

Table 3: Examples of incorrect instances (abbreviated). The seed baseline perceives incorrectly and often returns a long, verbose response; the evolved program returns the exact answer. papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments. Maintaining persistent episodic memory remains a challenge for VLM-based streaming agents in long-horizon navigation. We present MEMVLN, a streaming episodic memory framework that maintains a bounded bank of compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, and produces compact memory tokens via cross-attention. We pair the proposed memory with a frozen pretrained geometry encoder. To learn the memory module, we design a masking-based trajectory summarization task with multi-granularity sub-trajectory decomposition, encouraging route reconstruction exclusively from episodic memory. Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, MEMVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, MEMVLN improves success over the VLM baseline from 17% to 40%, and post-training further raises it to 47%.
authors: Yan Wang, Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful past observations during long-horizon VLN.
Stores compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, then converts them into memory tokens via cross-attention.
Uses a frozen geometry encoder and a masking-based, multi-granularity trajectory summarization task to train the memory module.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across standard VLN-CE benchmarks under R2R/RxR trajectory restrictions.
In a physical-scene evaluation, success improved from 17% for the VLM baseline to 40%, and to 47% after post-training.

papers.abstract: Tube-wise video completion reconstructs temporal trajectories at spatial locations unobserved in every frame. We propose a two-stage framework combining regularized masked Kronecker product decomposition (KPD) with cross-fitted self-supervised residual learning. First, we estimate a compact structural backbone directly from observed entries using cyclic component-wise least-squares updates, spatial and temporal factor regularization, and regularizer-optimal scale balancing. The exact updates yield a nonincreasing objective. Second, we address the mismatch between in-sample fitting errors and the prediction errors encountered at missing tubes. We partition observed tubes into folds and construct residual targets using backbone models fitted without the corresponding target tubes. A lightweight 3-D convolutional neural network then predicts corrections from the backbone, visible residual context, observation mask, and local detail features. Exact data consistency preserves observed measurements. Experiments include ablations, sensitivity analysis, grayscale and RGB video completion, and structured missing patterns. Our method achieves the highest mean PSNR and SSIM at the higher tested sampling rates on the grayscale benchmark. On eight selected DAVIS RGB sequences, it achieves the highest mean missing-region PSNR and full-frame SSIM and the lowest mean missing-tube temporal-gradient MAE at every evaluated sampling rate.
authors: Qi Qi, Yanfei Wang, Yanjun Cui, Jun-e Feng
bullets: Targets reconstruction of spatial-temporal tubes missing across every video frame.
Builds a regularized masked Kronecker product decomposition backbone with exact cyclic least-squares updates and scale balancing.
Uses cross-fitted residual targets to reduce the mismatch between in-sample errors and missing-tube prediction errors.
A lightweight 3-D CNN predicts residual corrections from backbone outputs, visible residuals, masks, and local detail features.
Reports strongest performance on the tested grayscale and DAVIS RGB benchmarks across the stated sampling settings, with ablations and sensitivity analyses.

papers.abstract: Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks. Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensor data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine the magnitude, direction, and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape. Since DLOs are not actuated and are typically thin, like cables and wires, strain gauges and actuation readings are usually impractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only, thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks. Realistic tests are performed by introducing noise into the measurements while the DLO follows a prescribed path in the presence of external forces that are accurately estimated.
authors: Annika Delucchi, Vincenzo Di Paola, Bruno Marco Quadrelli, Matteo Zoppi
bullets: Addresses reliable contact-force estimation for underactuated DLOs such as cables and wires.
Models the DLO state and sensor observations through conditional probability distributions.
Infers force magnitude, direction, and location alongside DLO shape.
Designed to avoid impractical strain-gauge or actuation measurements by using one sensing type.
Realistic noisy-measurement tests show accurate force estimation as the DLO follows a prescribed path under external forces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) ground a referring expression in one of two ways. They decode the box as coordinate tokens, which is precise but takes one sequential step per token, or they regress it from a hidden state with a small head, which takes one step but loses accuracy at high IoU. The two fail differently: a head usually finds the right object but places its edges loosely, while coordinate tokens place edges precisely. We therefore use the regression head as a speculative drafter for the model's own coordinate tokens. Locus writes the head's box as coordinate tokens and checks them with the same backbone by Jacobi iteration over a shared image prefix. The fixed point is the model's greedy coordinate-token answer, reached in about 5.60 sequential passes on average instead of 18.46 decoding steps; head and verifier are one set of weights, trained jointly. On the 8 RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification raises Locus-2B's Acc@0.9 from 54.87 for its own head to 59.13, and the one-pass head is ahead at Acc@0.5 of every published model with at most 3B parameters except Florence-2-L. Against Jag, the strongest open regression-head model, at its own size and training budget, Locus ties at Acc@0.5 and, with typical acceptance, gains +4.52 points at Acc@0.9, with paired significance tests. Exact answers come 1.5x faster than vLLM greedy-decoding the same coordinate tokens with the same weights; a pure regression head remains faster still.
authors: Muhammad Talha
bullets: Uses the regression head to draft a box, then verifies and refines its coordinate tokens via Jacobi iteration with the same backbone.
Reaches the model’s greedy coordinate-token answer in about 5.60 sequential passes on average, versus 18.46 decoding steps.
On RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg splits, verification improves Locus-2B Acc@0.9 from 54.87 to 59.13.
The one-pass head achieves strong Acc@0.5 performance, while verified outputs provide more precise box edges.
Exact answers are obtained 1.5× faster than vLLM greedy decoding with the same weights, though pure regression remains faster.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture and inference of Locus, illustrated with Locus-2B on the RefCOCO val expression “right elephant” (dashed white: ground truth). (a) The image and a fixed prefix are prefilled once. Each question then runs as a short branch over the cached prefix (attention mask on the right), so all box and verifier branches of an image share one prefill. The head reads the final state of the learned [BOX] token; the verifier branch is the backbone’s own grounding prompt, read by its LM head. Head and verifier are trained jointly. (b) The head’s box is rendered as the coordinate tokens the model would write, and the model checks all of them in one parallel pass, keeping the longest prefix it agrees with (green) and correcting the next token (orange). Repeating this until the draft stops changing yields the model’s greedy answer, here in 3 passes instead of 19 decoding steps. Blue tokens are those that verification changed.
