papers.selection_reason: Draft-and-verify visual grounding improves VLM coordinate-token decoding; relevant to multimodal LLMs, spatial grounding, and inference efficiency.
papers.title: LOCUS: Locate Once, Check Until Settled. Draft-and-Verify Visual Grounding with a Box Head and Coordinate-Token Verification
papers.tldr: LOCUS combines a fast box-regression head with coordinate-token verification to improve high-IoU visual grounding while reducing sequential decoding passes.

papers.abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.
authors: Zhang Zhang, Shengjun Zhang, Simin Huang, Min Chen, Chong Xia, Xin Fei, Yueqi Duan
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static, post-hoc rollout reflection, which updates harnesses without autonomously validating them through interaction.
Maintains a harness graph to track version lineage, reuse effective mechanisms, and avoid repeated failed explorations.
Generates rollouts, probes failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively updates the harness based on execution evidence.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin, where it progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of VISTA. The meta-agent develops an embodied harness from versioned implementations and multimodal execution evidence. Within a development iteration, it interleaves code revision, active exploration, and autonomous candidate testing. After submission, the frozen candidate undergoes a separate autonomous evaluation under the declared development conditions. The selection rule determines whether it replaces the incumbent; both promoted and rejected versions remain in the history. The inner loop acquires evidence and refines a candidate, while the outer loop selects and retains harnesses across development iterations.

Figure 1 VISTA actively explores the environment to improve embodied-agent harnesses. Starting from an initial harness, a meta-agent inspects prior execution evidence, proposes revisions, and actively interacts with the environment to test hypotheses and refine candidate harnesses before formal evaluation.

Figure 5 A representative harness development process on Goal-t09. The initial harness achieves 0.0% success. The first development round adds lift verification, a bounded re-localization and grasp retry, and an explicit transportand-release procedure, improving performance to 56.3%. Analysis of the remaining failures then leads to a revision of the lift-state interpretation and release behavior, after which the final harness achieves 100.0% in autonomous evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Active self-exploration meta-agent for embodied policy and harness improvement.
papers.title: VISTA: Active Exploration for Self-Improvement in Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: VISTA enables embodied agents to actively test and refine their control harnesses through iterative environment exploration, improving success with fewer rollouts.

papers.abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Hanchao Leng, JiaHui Huang, Hanbing Li, Jingwei Zhao, Kuiyuan Yang, Chen Gao, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses information loss and cross-modal inconsistency caused by modeling driving modalities separately.
Encodes appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories into a shared continuous latent.
Uses a frozen tokenizer with a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents.
On NAVSIM, the unified design improves future prediction and planning while reducing downstream computational cost.
With reinforcement-learning post-training, DriveUniWAM reaches a PDMS of 91.54 and state-of-the-art performance among evaluated WAM planners.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced rapidly with the development of foundation models that demonstrate strong zero-shot generalisation across diverse visual domains. However, the applicability of these models to visual perception for lower-limb prosthetics remains largely unexplored. Reliable depth perception is particularly important for prosthesis users, who often experience significant challenges when navigating stairs, uneven terrain, and other complex environments. To address this gap, we introduce the Lower-Limb Prosthesis (LP) dataset, a benchmark designed to evaluate depth perception from an emulated knee-level prosthetic viewpoint. Using this dataset, we evaluate four state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation foundation models. Our results provide the first systematic benchmark of monocular depth estimation performance from a prosthetic viewpoint, while highlighting both the challenges and the potential of deploying foundation models in prosthetic perception systems. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Ishivijay/lp_dataset.
authors: Ishi Vijayvergiya, Marc H\"olle, Youssef Dawoud, Amir El-Ghoussani, Michele De Vita, Rohan Asthana, Philipp Beckerle, Vasileios Belagiannis
bullets: Introduces the Lower-Limb Prosthesis (LP) dataset for evaluating prosthetic-view depth estimation.
Addresses depth-perception challenges relevant to stairs, uneven terrain, and complex environments.

Provides a first systematic benchmark of depth estimation from a prosthetic viewpoint.
Releases the dataset and code publicly.

papers.abstract: Text-steerable visual encoders condition a frozen Vision Transformer on a natural-language prompt and point at the matching image region, producing prompt-conditioned heatmaps and features. We audit the released SteerViT model and find that its steering interface turns language-driven pointing into demographic profiling. On counterfactual face mosaics and real multi-person photographs, "the person" selects a man more often than the base rate, crime words select Black people more often than occupation words do, "the man" among four women selects the Black woman 75.6% of the time on SocialCounterfactuals, and "the monkey" selects Black people. None of them is in the backbone's unsteered saliency, and the crime association is not in the frozen text encoder; the race effects grow with steering strength and enter through the last two cross-attention layers: giving the prompt to those layers alone reproduces them. Four other grounding models, CLIPSeg, Grounding-DINO, SAM 3, and Qwen2.5-VL, show no crime routing and weaker race routing. The model cannot refuse. Its patch softmax must place its mass somewhere, and its heatmap separates a groundable request ("the police officer") from one that is absent ("the pizza") or that would require a stereotyped demographic inference ("the criminal") only at chance (AUROC 0.52). We introduce SafeSteer, which adds a learned abstention output and counterfactual-invariance training on the same 23M steering parameters. SafeSteer separates should-point from should-abstain prompts at AUROC 0.997, generalizes to held-out sensitive and absent words (0.998; at a 0.5 threshold it refuses 99.8% of trained and 62% of held-out sensitive words) with no over-refusal of visible people on the benchmark, and removes most race routing while keeping localization and retrieval within 1 point of the released model. Code, benchmarks, and the curated mosaic sets will be released.
authors: Seyedarmin Azizi, Parsa Razmara, Sajjad Ghiasvand, Ardalan Aryashad, Tina Khezresmaeilzadeh
bullets: The released model profiles people: crime prompts disproportionately select Black individuals, and “the man” selects a Black woman in 75.6% of four-woman mosaics.
These effects are absent from unsteered saliency and the frozen text encoder, increasing with steering strength through the final two cross-attention layers.
SteerViT cannot recognize when a prompt is absent or requires a stereotyped inference, separating valid from unsafe requests at chance (AUROC 0.52).
SafeSteer achieves AUROC 0.997 on refusal detection and generalizes to held-out sensitive and absent words, while reducing race routing.
Localization and retrieval remain within 1 point of the released model, with no benchmark over-refusal of visible people.

figures.caption: Figure 2. SteerViT and the SAFESTEER fix. A frozen DINOv2 ViT is steered by a text prompt, encoded by a frozen text encoder, through six gated cross-attention layers (blocks 1, 3, . . . , 11); only the cross-attention layers, connector, and heads are trained (23M parameters). The patch head outputs a softmax over image patches, which always sums to one, so the model must point even when it should not; Sec. 4 shows the demographic routing enters through the last two gated layers (blocks 9, 11). SAFESTEER appends a learned null logit s∅, computed from the steered global feature g, to the patch logits s, which gives the model an explicit abstention output.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can select among discrete candidates for pick-and-place manipulation or generate continuous action chunks for motion control. Improving both forms of decision making through a common mechanism while retaining the capabilities of a pretrained policy is an important adaptation problem. Inspired by Jev's structured, probabilistic decision interface, we propose JevVLA, a lightweight energy-based adaptation framework for VLA policies. JevVLA instantiates this inspiration by modeling the relative quality of action proposals: with the base policy frozen, it learns a differentiable scalar energy conditioned on observations, task context, and actions, using execution feedback, expert corrections, or demonstration-derived preferences. JevVLA uses this single learned action preference function in two ways: its values compare discrete candidates, while its action gradients correct continuous actions or guide their generation. Candidate selection and continuous control thus share one trainable decision core. Each benchmark uses independently trained weights and fixed input/output encodings, while retaining the same core network with approximately 80,000 trainable parameters. On the held-out test sets, JevVLA improves task success over the respective matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points on MetaWorld MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort, respectively. These results support the feasibility of a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy model for adapting both discrete action selection and continuous action guidance. The JevVLA implementation will be open-sourced at https://github.com/ZJU4EmbodiedAI/JevVLA.
authors: Wei Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Zheng Dong, Yingjie Niu, Jiaqi Zhu, Jun Xiao, Chao Li, Yueting Zhuang

papers.abstract: Intelligent operating rooms require accurate awareness of surgical workflow for better intra-operative decisions, teamwork, and surgical documentation. Therefore, accurately recognizing surgical phase during surgery is crucial. However, previous artificial intelligence-based methods provide fluctuating predictions for the transitions, restricting their clinical use. To address this challenge, we propose a clinically meaningful framework that integrates a Swin Transformer and Temporal Transformer Encoder (TTE) for effective surgical phase recognition and a parallel YOLOv11s network for real-time surgical instrument localization. To avoid phase flickering and to produce stable workflow predictions, a causal temporal smoothing is applied. The proposed framework is tested on the Cholec80 dataset for the simultaneous recognition of the surgical phases and instruments. The overall phase recognition accuracy of this model was 92%, and the macro average F1-score was 0.86. This performance surpasses CNN based methods such as EndoNet (81.7%) and SV-RCNet (85.3%), as well as temporal convolutional and transformer-based approaches including TeCNO (88.6%), Trans-SVNet (90.9%), and LoViT (91.5%). Besides, the module of instrument detection achieved mAP@0.5 = 0.863. The reliability of the results is confirmed, obtaining a high recognition rate of the workflows, and a high accuracy of the localization of the instruments. The proposed framework can serve as a foundation for intelligent surgical assistance, enriching situation awareness, and potential robotic surgery applications. Code will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/ac005sheekar/LapChol-Surgery-Swin-Cholec80

On Cholec80, achieves 92% phase accuracy, 0.86 macro-F1, and instrument-detection mAP@0.5 of 0.863.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view 4D reconstruction is highly under-constrained when only a few cameras are available. Generative priors can recover missing appearances, but video models are computationally impractical for iterative reconstruction, whereas single-view models produce temporally inconsistent pseudo-observations. Moreover, directly absorbing uncertain generative outputs into Gaussian optimization often creates redundant primitives and floating artifacts. To address these challenges, we propose DUET4D, a self-corrective coupled guidance framework for sparse-view 4D Gaussian splatting. The core of our approach is a self-corrective framework where the 4D representation guides generative prior for spatio-temporal consistent supervisions. We first construct sequential alignments from current Gaussian evidence to steer the latent restoration. Then we use Sequential Fidelity Resampling to lift generative supervisions into Gaussian space to selectively distinguish repeatedly supported primitives. The corrected representation then provides more reliable Gaussian evidence for the next restoration cycle. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET4D significantly improves rendering quality and rendering efficiency.
authors: Beizhen Zhao, Nanjie Yao, Boyi Fu, Qingsong Yan, Haofan Ren, Kaiyong Zhao, Hao Wang
bullets: Addresses the under-constrained nature of 4D reconstruction from only a few cameras.
Uses sequential alignment to guide latent generative restoration with current Gaussian evidence.
Introduces Sequential Fidelity Resampling to transfer generative supervision selectively into Gaussian space.
Iteratively corrects the representation to reduce redundant primitives and floating artifacts.
Experiments report improved rendering quality and efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons of state-of-the-art methods. Visual differences are highlighted with red insets for better clarity. Our approach outperforms other models on different scenes, demonstrating advantages in challenging scenarios. Best viewed in color.

Then we design a training-free anchor-driven latent steering mechanism within the latent space of SDM for temporally consistent generative outputs. The frames and confidence map will be used to locate Gaussians with weak spatial and temporal consistency for optimization. The reserved Gaussians are controlled by a spatial grid and Fourier spline priors for motion smoothness and regularization.

Red indicates lower error for DUET4D, and blue indicates the opposite.

papers.abstract: Long-video generators increasingly retrieve past visual observations to prevent identity drift. The intuition is compelling: more access to history should make future video more consistent. But an image can be faithful to the past and wrong for the present. Does visual memory always improve the generated story? We investigate this question through VMem-Bench, a two-track diagnostic study. Track-A measures which references are selected from 92 real films (16,548 segments), before generation and without generator confounds. Track-B compares four retrieval policies with no-memory and gold-informed last-seen controls on 30 causally generated stories (2,824 segments) using a shared generator. Retrieval increases entity recall from 0.559 to 0.628-0.693 and improves similarity to past appearances, but decreases precision from 0.977 to 0.915-0.938 and forbidden-entity avoidance from 0.968 to 0.845-0.898. It can also reinforce obsolete appearances after the story changes them. Conversely, high long-gap recall can arise without memory when the prompt itself supplies the appearance; an appearance-stripping analysis exposes this confound. These results distinguish historical fidelity from current-story correctness and show why retrieval relevance or final-video consistency alone does not establish memory utility.
authors: Yuzhuo Chen, Huafeng Shi, Xinyu Wang, Yulong Xu, Yucheng Wang, Haoqin Hong, Guoxin Zhang, Zehua Ma, Weiming Zhang
bullets: Introduces VMem-Bench, a two-track diagnostic study of visual-memory retrieval.
Across 92 real films, Track-A evaluates which references retrieval systems select before generation.
Across 30 generated stories, Track-B compares four retrieval policies with no-memory and gold-informed controls using a shared generator.
Retrieval raises entity recall and similarity to past appearances, but lowers precision and forbidden-entity avoidance.
High long-gap recall may come from prompt-provided appearance details rather than memory, so retrieval relevance or final consistency alone is insufficient evidence of memory utility.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic study of visual memory in long-video generation, distinguishing historical fidelity from story correctness.
papers.title: More Memory, Better Videos? A Controlled Study of Visual Memory in Long-Video Generation

papers.abstract: Road anomalies such as collisions, violations, and sudden hazards demand more from video understanding than detection: a practical system must verify what happened, describe the scene, and explain the cause. We find these competences pull in opposite directions for vision-language models: closed-form questions reward precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended answers are scored by similarity to reference text, where matching the annotation style matters as much as reasoning correctly. We present Reason-or-Recite (RoR), a two-specialist framework for the Traffic Anomaly Reasoning track of the 2026 AI City Challenge. RoR (1) rewrites the official chain-of-thought annotations into a structured, temporally grounded schema and LoRA-tunes a 9B vision-language model on the enhanced traces; (2) fine-tunes a 4-bit-quantized 27B model on answers alone, absorbing the annotation style; and (3) selects between the two candidates per question with a training-free LLM judge. RoR ranks first on the in-domain leaderboard with mean score 0.6788.
authors: Mayur Kulkarni
bullets: Traffic anomaly video understanding requires verifying events, describing scenes, and explaining causes.
Closed-form questions favor precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended scoring also rewards matching annotation style.
RoR LoRA-tunes a 9B model on structured, temporally grounded reasoning traces and fine-tunes a 4-bit 27B model on answer text.
A training-free LLM judge selects the better specialist response for each question.
RoR ranks first on the in-domain 2026 AI City Challenge leaderboard, scoring 0.6788.

papers.abstract: End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training. We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.
authors: Junho Kim, CheHyun Lee, Donghun Kang, Youngho Cho, Dongwook Lee, Heeseung Kim, Sungroh Yoon
bullets: Long sessions cause declines in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency.
A closed-loop evaluation framework measures stability, information retention, and efficiency over extended interactions.
Self-distillation with lightweight LoRA adaptation mitigates degradation across three architecturally distinct models.
Two-resolution context preserves recent exchanges in detail while compressing older history into key-value representations.
LoRA improves stability over ten-minute sessions, while TRC extends gains beyond training-session lengths and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.

papers.abstract: Camera-based bird's-eye view (BEV) perception methods such as Fast-BEV have demonstrated promising results with fast inference speed and competitive accuracy. However, their robustness to real-world corruptions remains insufficiently explored, posing risks for autonomous driving deployment where environmental variations are inevitable. In this paper, we propose Sparse Recovery Bird's-Eye View Model Soup (SR-BEVS), a sparse recovery learning approach that simultaneously improves clean accuracy and corruption robustness without requiring additional data or architectural modifications. Our method identifies pruning candidates based on layer-wise weight magnitudes, applies random pruning to create diverse sparse models, and retrains each model with a randomly sampled learning rate. By averaging these diverse recovered models into a single dense model, we achieve enhanced robustness against various corruptions while introducing zero inference overhead. We further provide a mode connectivity analysis demonstrating that our pruning-based diversification preserves the connected low-loss basin necessary for stable weight averaging. Experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate up to 33.8% improvement in corruption robustness and a 1.8% gain in clean accuracy over the Fast-BEV baseline, with consistent improvements across sensor noise, weather distortions, and illumination changes. Our simple yet effective approach may be applicable to other BEV models.
authors: Jinwoo Chung, Sangho An, Hyunsung Park, Jangho Kim
bullets: Targets insufficient robustness of camera-based BEV detection under real-world corruptions.
Prunes weights by layer-wise magnitude, randomly sparsifies models, retrains them with varied learning rates, and averages the recovered models.
Mode connectivity analysis suggests pruning-based diversity preserves a stable low-loss basin for weight averaging.
On nuScenes, reports up to 33.8% better corruption robustness and 1.8% higher clean accuracy than Fast-BEV.
Improvements cover sensor noise, weather distortions, and illumination changes; applicability beyond BEV models is suggested but not established.

papers.abstract: Pretrained transformers spend a large share of their inference compute inside self-attention, yet the per-head query-key interaction is structurally low-rank by construction. We ask a diagnostic question: across layers and architectures, which heads actually use the full rank budget on real data, and which do not? We propose SVD-Attention, a post-hoc method that decomposes the per-head interaction matrix $M_h$ and scores every singular mode by both its spectral magnitude and its activation variance across tokens on a small calibration set. The score keeps the modes the head can amplify and that real data actually activates, and discards the rest; the resulting factorization is exact for the retained modes and needs no finetuning. Across seven pretrained models and five task types, the diagnostic finds a task-dependent pattern: redundancy sits in the early to middle layers for sentiment and image classification and for generation, and in the late layers for dense prediction and extractive question answering. It is also predictive: truncating the layers it flags costs at most $1.75$ F1, while truncating the same number of layers elsewhere in the same model costs up to $50$ F1. SVD-Attention is an analysis tool rather than a compression method: acting on it reduces inference FLOPs by $0.8$-$1.5\%$ on its own and by $8$-$11\%$ when composed with weight pruning, with $0$-$4\%$ change in task quality.
authors: Debopam Sanyal, Hongjie Chen, Riya Elizabeth Kuriyan, Arth Tak, Divya Kothandaraman, Akshay Mehra, Joshua Kimball, Alexey Tumanov
bullets: Motivation: Transformer self-attention is costly, but many heads may not use their full rank capacity.
Method: Decomposes each head’s interaction matrix and scores singular modes using spectral magnitude and token-level activation variance from a small calibration set.
Finding: Redundancy appears in early-to-middle layers for sentiment, image classification, and generation, but in late layers for dense prediction and extractive question answering.
Validation: Flagged-layer truncation costs at most 1.75 F1, versus up to 50 F1 when truncating the same number of other layers.
Scope: The method is primarily diagnostic; it yields 0.8–1.5% standalone FLOP reduction and 8–11% with weight pruning, with 0–4% task-quality change.

papers.abstract: GUI agents built on vision-language models interact with continuously evolving interfaces, yet conventional inference repeatedly recomputes representations of largely overlapping observations and histories. This mismatch makes multi-step interaction costly, while changes in context, interface content, and action arguments prevent straightforward cache reuse. We introduce GUIFlow, a framework for full-pipeline incremental inference in multi-image GUI interaction. Our central insight is that advancing a decision need not require rebuilding all supporting representations: each interaction step can instead selectively update computational states maintained across the trajectory. To support new decisions as the context evolves, GUIFlow adapts how past computation is reused: historical KV states are position-aligned and injected into the current context; change signals guide selective updates of current-observation states in the vision encoder and language model; and earlier action responses serve as speculative drafts verified by the target model. Together, these mechanisms enable cross-step reuse throughout visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without additional training, a separate draft model, or changes to the model-visible inputs and action interface. Experiments demonstrate up to 3.39x geometric-mean speedup across offline multi-image benchmarks and up to 3.49x in online, closed-loop interaction on OSWorld, while maintaining task performance broadly comparable to the dense baseline.
authors: Ye Li, Haoran Ding, Huanan Liu, Yuan Meng, Yutian Shen, Yuansong Wang, Kangye Ji, Hanyun Cui, Hongbo Duan, Chen Tang, Jiawei Li, Shu-Tao Xia, Zhi Wang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of repeatedly recomputing overlapping observations and histories during GUI interaction.
Reuses position-aligned historical KV states and uses change signals to selectively update vision-encoder and language-model states.
Speculatively reuses prior action responses and verifies them with the target model.
Provides full-pipeline reuse across visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without a separate draft model or additional training.
Reports up to 3.39× offline and 3.49× online speedups, with task performance broadly comparable to dense inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GUIFlow. GUIFlow treats successive GUI decisions as incremental updates to existing computation rather than independent inference passes. (A) Historical State Integration. Historical KV states are positionally aligned and injected into the current context. (B) CurrentObservation Refinement. Pixel changes guide visual-encoder updates, while source-aware KV deviations guide deeper language-model updates. (C) Verified Incremental Decoding. Conditioned on the prefill state formed by (A) and (B), the target model verifies historical response drafts, accepting matching tokens and correcting mismatches. Together, these mechanisms exploit temporal redundancy across visual encoding, prefill, and decoding without additional training or a separate draft model.

Figures 4–7 provide eight additional successful OSWorld trajectories spanning presentation editing, file operations, document editing, image manipulation, email organization, system configuration, and code editing. In every example, Dense inference and GUIFlow follow the same interaction stages and reach the completed state, while GUIFlow consistently accumulates less task execution time. Across these trajectories, the observed speedups range from 2.01× to 2.24×, with 8.97–22.61 seconds saved per task. These trajectories complement Figure 3 by illustrating lower cumulative task execution time across applications and trajectory lengths. All timelines report task execution time.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Gaussian reconstruction requires compact scene features to support coordinated changes in geometry and appearance. A factorized grid provides efficient local queries, but accurate interpolation alone does not ensure that the resulting dynamic attributes remain compatible across space and time. We introduce DimFlow, a framework that learns these features through bidirectional interaction between a multi-resolution grid and a coordinate-based expert branch. Feature-level adversarial alignment connects their distributions, adaptive fusion transfers complementary information, and activation-masked residual feedback refines the grid during training. Four attribute experts organize deformation, rotation, opacity, and temporal information before Gaussian rendering. In the aggregate comparison across D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, and DAVIS, DimFlow achieves 39.73 dB PSNR, improving on 4D-GS by 1.92 dB while matching its reported 85 FPS rendering speed. The model occupies 18.9 MB, compared with 18.3 MB for 4D-GS. Component and attribute-expert ablations reveal complementary contributions from feature alignment, adaptive exchange, and temporal processing.
authors: Gabriel Adineera, Jinoh Kim
bullets: Targets spatially and temporally compatible dynamic attributes beyond what grid interpolation alone provides.
Uses feature-level adversarial alignment, adaptive fusion, and activation-masked residual feedback between grid and expert branches.
Employs four experts for deformation, rotation, opacity, and temporal information before Gaussian rendering.
Reports 39.73 dB PSNR across D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, and DAVIS—1.92 dB above 4D-GS—with 85 FPS rendering.
Ablations indicate complementary benefits from feature alignment, adaptive exchange, and temporal processing.

papers.abstract: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1--31.2\% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.
authors: Bing Sun, Yue Lin, Canhui Wen, Xin Chen, Yang Liu, Dong Wang, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Targets visibility-preserving navigation around obstacles with smooth, feasible motion.
Predicts control sequences and differentiably converts them into trajectories so trajectory-level objectives train the policy directly.
Uses decaying expert guidance to transition from effective initial behavior toward task-driven learning.
Adds a predictive safety lock that switches to classical planning and control when motion is unsafe or target prediction fails.

Across simulated settings, it achieves the highest tracking success, reduces RMS linear jerk by 14.1–31.2% versus the best competing method on that metric, and runs in 4.25–5.63 ms per cycle; robot tests cover indoor passages and outdoor forests.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of LECO, a kinematic-integrated neural control framework. (2) Optimization-to-policy learning transfers expert behavior and physics–geometry objectives into the neural policy. papers.abstract: An action seen once and the same action seen three times receive the same action-recognition label, so that supervision does not require a model to count. Answers shared across histories that differ in event order, accumulation, or relations leave those distinctions unconstrained; we call this state under-specification. Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) addresses it by training on source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency; under the same recent-frame interface it improves OVO-Bench over a strict-matched generic temporal supervision baseline while remaining comparable on StreamingBench, with the largest gain in hallucination detection. Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) then adapts evidence access while keeping the learned model fixed, expanding from recent frames to sparse event and compact history views on demand. The two interventions separate representation from view selection: supervision particularly benefits hallucination detection and causal reasoning, access particularly benefits event recall and forward reasoning. Together they reach the best reported accuracy among the published systems compared here on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench at a fraction of the processed frames of exhaustive selection, and strict replay shows that most of the remaining gap to a three-view oracle is a correct answer that was later replaced. Streaming accuracy depends on what supervision asks the model to keep, what evidence inference exposes, and whether the model keeps a correct answer once it has one.
authors: Yihao Hu, Pan Wang, Yitong Lin, Zhihao Wen, Deyuan Liu, Hang Wang, Mingda Wan, Yiwen Zhao, Yutong Li, Yuchen Mao, Tao Lin
bullets: Streaming supervision can under-specify distinctions such as event order, accumulation, relations, and whether an answer is sufficiently supported.
Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) uses source-grounded probes targeting event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency.
Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) expands evidence from recent frames to sparse events and compact histories without changing the learned model.
ViSS mainly improves hallucination detection and causal reasoning; TVS mainly improves event recall and forward reasoning.

Together, they achieve the best reported accuracy among compared published systems on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench, using a fraction of exhaustive-selection frames; answer replacement remains a key residual error.

Phase 2, TVS (Section 4.2): the checkpoint is frozen; the event view is acquired when the recent margin is low, the history view when the two disagree, and a calibrated margin rule keeps one proposal.

papers.abstract: In surgical instrument segmentation, the increasing variety of instruments over time poses a significant challenge for existing neural networks, as they are unable to effectively learn such incremental tasks and suffer from catastrophic forgetting. When learning new data, the model experiences a sharp performance drop on previously learned data. Although several continual learning methods have been proposed for incremental understanding tasks in surgical scenarios, the issue of data imbalance often leads to a strong bias in the segmentation head, resulting in poor performance. Data imbalance can occur in two forms: (i) class imbalance between new and old data, and (ii) class imbalance within the same time point of data. Such imbalances often cause the dominant classes to take over the training process of continual semantic segmentation (CSS). To address this issue, we propose SurgCSS, a novel plug-and-play CSS framework for surgical instrument segmentation under data imbalance. Specifically, we generate realistic surgical backgrounds through inpainting and blend instrument foregrounds with the generated backgrounds in a class-aware manner to balance the data distribution in various scenarios. We further propose the Class Desensitization Loss by employing contrastive learning to correct edge biases caused by data imbalance. Moreover, we dynamically fuse the weight parameters of the old and new models to achieve a better trade-off between the biased and unbiased model weights. To investigate the data imbalance problem in surgical scenarios, we construct a new benchmark for surgical instrument CSS by integrating datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving significant performance improvement against existing baselines.
authors: Shifang Zhao, Long Bai, Kun Yuan, Feng Li, Jieming Yu, Wenzhen Dong, Guankun Wang, Mobarakol Islam, Nicolas Padoy, Nassir Navab, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Existing continual segmentation models struggle as new instruments arrive, forgetting previously learned instruments.
It targets both imbalance between old and new classes and imbalance among classes at the same time point.
Synthetic surgical backgrounds and class-aware foreground blending rebalance training scenarios.
Class Desensitization Loss uses contrastive learning to reduce edge bias, while dynamic old/new weight fusion balances model knowledge.
A new integrated benchmark is introduced, and experiments show significant improvements over existing baselines.

papers.abstract: Training-free few-shot adaptation of vision-language models typically constructs a classifier from CLIP's final projected image representation, leaving intermediate representations unused. Combining them is not straightforward. Class scores from different representations differ in spread by orders of magnitude for the same query. Direct averaging allocates influence by numerical scale rather than predictive information. We propose Layer-Ensemble Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (LE-GDA), a method that fits regularized shared-covariance discriminants independently to intermediate and final representations extracted in one frozen encoder pass. LE-GDA standardizes each discriminant's class scores per query, selects a small representation multiset on labeled validation data, and combines it with the zero-shot classifier without gradient-based optimization. Across 11 datasets, four CLIP backbones, five shot counts, and three independently sampled K-shot training sets, LE-GDA achieves the highest mean accuracy of all evaluated methods on every backbone, raising the 16-shot mean from 78.01% to 79.54% over a matched GDA-CLIP (final-feature) baseline and improving that baseline for every backbone-shot combination. At one shot, LE-GDA retains a 1.20-point mean gain over the baseline even though covariance estimation is unavailable and per-query standardization is neutral. A control with richer per-class structure inside a single representation does not reproduce the gain, indicating that the benefit comes from combining representations. These results show that intermediate CLIP representations carry information beyond the final embedding and can improve training-free few-shot adaptation. Code and evaluation resources are available at https://github.com/pavodi-NM/le-gda.
authors: Pavodi Maniamfu, Vogel Kiketa, Zezina Kuzulu Kuetu, Jakin Mukendi Kabongo, David Mayoya Kutangila, Pescie Honore Kinkani Mampuya, L'Or Wolo Sieka
bullets: Addresses the underuse of intermediate CLIP representations and scale mismatches between their class scores.
Fits regularized shared-covariance discriminants independently in a single frozen encoder pass, then selects and ensembles representations using labeled validation data.
Combines the learned ensemble with CLIP’s zero-shot classifier without gradient-based optimization.
Across 11 datasets, four backbones, and five shot counts, it achieved the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods for every backbone.
Improved 16-shot mean accuracy from 78.01% to 79.54% over a matched final-feature GDA baseline, with a 1.20-point mean gain at one shot.

papers.abstract: Outcome RL raises pass@1 but not pass@k at large k (Yue et al., 2025). But every pass@1 is scored under a token budget. Every recipe also trains under one. On physics and math problems at fixed token budgets, we compare the pass@1 of 20 released RL models (1.5B to 32B) with that of the thinking models they started from. We ask whether each pass@1 gain is changed behaviour or new knowledge. We divide each change in pass@1 into three parts. Finishing measures answering before the budget runs out. Reliability measures being right once finished. Reach measures problems RL solves that its base answered wrongly in all eight tries, minus problems the base solves that RL answered wrongly in all eight. We find four things. (1) Where the base often hits the token budget before answering, most of the change, gain or loss, is finishing (82% at 4k and 8k). Given more tokens, the base closes most of the finishing gap itself. (2) Where the base has enough tokens, the gain is reliability: the RL model is graded right more often, even on problems both finish. (3) By our definition, RL rarely solves what its base cannot. Reach adds at most 2.1 percentage points on any of our four physics and math sets. We checked 144 physics problems that only the RL model solved. Of these, 3.5% hold up when resampled or read. In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human confirmed also appear in the base's samples. (4) In a small-scale RL run on an 8B model, the gain on new problems is finishing, with reliability flat. Supplying each problem's physical setup was not shown to improve on plain RL.
authors: Shan Yang
bullets: Compared with 20 released 1.5B–32B RL models and their base thinking models on fixed-budget physics and math tasks, the study decomposes pass@1 changes into finishing, reliability, and reach.
When base models often time out, finishing explains most gains or losses—82% at 4k and 8k tokens—and extra tokens largely close this gap.
When bases finish reliably, RL improves correctness among completed answers rather than discovering substantially new solutions.
Reach contributes at most 2.1 percentage points; only 3.5% of 144 apparent RL-only physics solutions held up under resampling or review.
A small 8B RL run likewise attributed new-problem gains to finishing, with flat reliability; providing physical setups did not improve over plain RL.

papers.title: What Outcome RL Buys: Finishing, Reliability, Rarely Reach

papers.abstract: Grasping is a foundational capability in robotic manipulation. Scene-level 6-DoF grasp synthesis relies on point clouds for metric geometry, yet real-world point observations are often noisy, incomplete, and over-smoothed. RGB images provide object-region, boundary, and appearance cues, yet two bottlenecks limit their effective use in scene representation and local grasp reasoning. We present MMGNet, a Multi-Modal Grasp Synthesis Network that addresses these bottlenecks through hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection and rotational graspness modeling. Hierarchical injection integrates multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation, while the rotational graspness jointly predicts the grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation before organizing local image-informed features through grasp-shaded grouping. Ablation studies show that these two modules provide complementary gains. MMGNet achieves a mean AP of 60.34 on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense, surpassing all compared methods. In real-world experiments with adversarial grasp objects, MMGNet improves the grasp success rate over AnyGrasp by 8.46 percentage points. \emph{Code, models, and data will be released upon publication.}
authors: Rui Cao, Jia-Hui Pan, Yichuan Li, Yunfan Yu, Chi-Wing Fu, Jiangliu Wang, Yun-Hui Liu
bullets: Addresses incomplete, noisy, and over-smoothed point clouds by incorporating complementary RGB cues.
Injects multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation.
Jointly predicts grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation, then organizes local features via grasp-shaded grouping.
Achieves 60.34 mean AP on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense and improves real-world grasp success by 8.46 percentage points over AnyGrasp.
Ablations indicate the two proposed modules provide complementary gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of MMGNet. Given a single-view RGB-D observation, the image backbone extracts dense image features, which are aligned with the scene points through pixel–point correspondence and injected into successive stages of the 3D backbone to form image-informed 3D features. Rotational graspness prediction then scores joint view–in-plane rotations at candidate grasp centers. Based on the selected rotations, grasp-shaded grouping aggregates local image-informed features within the corresponding gripper frames. Finally, the operation head predicts the remaining depth-wise grasp scores and gripper widths to produce the final 6-DoF grasps.

papers.abstract: Controlling personality in large language models is important for building conversational agents that can be customized to different users and interaction settings. However, existing personality control methods often face a tradeoff between strong trait expression and natural dialogue generation. We introduce FATE-5, Faithful Alignment of Trait Expression for the Big Five, a two-stage framework that separates personality encoding from naturalness alignment. FATE-5 first learns continuous soft prompt representations of Big Five profiles using dialogue supervision and an auxiliary survey objective. It then improves dialogue naturalness through preference alignment based on both dialogue quality and personality agreement. Across three language model backbones, FATE-5 maintains strong trait expression while achieving substantially higher dialogue naturalness than other trait-strong methods. On held-out questionnaires, it achieves monotonicity correlations of 0.97-0.99 and recovery RMSE of 8.9-12.4, substantially improving over the evaluated baselines. These results demonstrate effective continuous personality control while maintaining natural conversational behavior.
authors: Gunhee Cho, Hongyeob Kim, Yun-Gyung Cheong
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between strong personality expression and conversational naturalness.
Uses a two-stage framework: personality encoding followed by naturalness alignment.
Learns continuous soft prompts with dialogue supervision and an auxiliary survey objective.
Aligns responses using preferences that account for both dialogue quality and personality agreement.
Across three backbones, reports monotonicity correlations of 0.97–0.99 and recovery RMSE of 8.9–12.4 on held-out questionnaires.

The encoder is trained jointly with dialogue loss and survey loss to strengthen trait expression. Stage 2 freezes the encoder and backbone, attaches a trainable LoRA adapter, and performs offline DPO using preference pairs scored by an external LLM judge. This stage improves dialogue naturalness while preserving the personality representation learned in Stage 1.

papers.abstract: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.
authors: Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Pashmina Cameron
bullets: Targets the memory-bandwidth bottleneck of long-form reasoning by compressing model weights to roughly 2 bits.
Assigns ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit precision per layer using sensitivity, then searches quantization codewords block by block with Gumbel-softmax.
Recalibrates shared scales using knowledge distillation and applies short quantization-aware training to better match the base model’s output distribution.
Uses paired reasoning tests to select between recalibration and QAT checkpoints rather than relying only on perplexity or multiple-choice accuracy.
On Qwen3-1.7B, reports 46.7 MATH-500 after recalibration and 73.0 after QAT; a 3.74 GB model reaches 94.8 versus 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.

papers.selection_reason: Two-bit weight quantization with bitwidth allocation and scale recalibration reduces LLM memory footprint while preserving reasoning.
papers.title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning
papers.tldr: ThinkBit is a scalar 2-bit quantization framework that preserves challenging mathematical reasoning through sensitivity-based bit allocation, codeword search, scale recalibration, and reasoning-guided checkpoint selection.

papers.abstract: Document layout analysis (DLA) faces a long-standing dilemma: existing methods either capture rich local details at prohibitive computational cost (e.g., Transformer-based approaches with quadratic complexity) or achieve efficient global modeling but sacrifice fine-grained structural awareness (e.g., state-space models). This trade-off hinders deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. We present LayoutMamba, a hybrid framework that synergistically combines sparse-attention Transformers for localized feature extraction (O(n) complexity) and the recurrent state-space mechanism of Mamba for dilution-free long-range dependency modeling across the 2D document canvas. Our two-stage paradigm first uses a lightweight Transformer encoder to hierarchically distill salient local semantics; second, Mamba propagates global contextual dependencies without attention dilution, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable layout understanding. We further identify a critical yet overlooked issue in existing DLA benchmarks: the inherent low-overlap distribution bias of layout objects, which we mitigate through a novel Geometric Overlap Penalty Loss (GOPLoss), a dual-optimization objective that minimizes redundant bounding box overlaps and encourages geometrically consistent predictions. Extensive experiments on PubLayNet and D4LA show that LayoutMamba surpasses state-of-the-art AP on PubLayNet with 8x fewer parameters and maintains leading performance on D4LA, ranking top-3 among published methods, achieving an unprecedented balance between accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. Our work pioneers a cognition-inspired paradigm for document analysis, advancing practical deployment in edge computing and resource-limited environments.
authors: Kehua Chen, Mingyi Chen
bullets: Targets the trade-off between Transformer-based detail and state-space-model efficiency in resource-constrained DLA.
Uses a two-stage design: a lightweight Transformer extracts local semantics, then Mamba models long-range 2D document dependencies.
Introduces Geometric Overlap Penalty Loss to reduce redundant bounding-box overlaps and improve geometric consistency.
Outperforms prior methods on PubLayNet with 8× fewer parameters and ranks among the top three published methods on D4LA.
Designed for scalable deployment, including edge and resource-limited environments.

papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation asks which level of a rubric a response meets. It is usually done by prompting a large language model (LLM) as a judge, which needs a generative call per judgment and reads every level description, so its cost grows with the rubric. We present RubriX, a rubric judge whose architecture is inspired by contrastive language models (CLM): a LoRA-adapted encoder embeds the input and each level description, and a softmax over scaled cosine similarities gives a probability for every level without text generation. Trained on public rubric data and proprietary synthetic data, RubriX reaches 75.4% exact accuracy on held-out rubrics, against 57.1% for TypeSafe's Jev and 49.8% for a Qwen3-8B judge. On eight human-labelled benchmark sets it is within 6 percentage points of Jev's accuracy on most of them, while Jev keeps a larger lead on two and ranks responses best on average; against the results reported in the G-Eval paper, RubriX outperforms G-Eval with GPT-3.5 on every SummEval dimension and both QAGS subsets. With level embeddings cached, RubriX's latency stays at about 28 ms per judgment as level descriptions grow from 10 to 3,000 tokens, while Jev's (approximate network time subtracted) rises from 44 ms to 211 ms and the Qwen3-8B judge's from 32 ms to 516 ms, making RubriX 7.7x faster than Jev and 18.8x faster than the Qwen3-8B judge at 3,000 tokens per level.
authors: Balamurugan Paramasivam (CobuildX), Sudalai Rajkumar (CobuildX)
bullets: Addresses the cost and latency of LLM-based rubric judging, which requires generation and processes all level descriptions.
Uses a LoRA-adapted encoder to embed responses and rubric levels, then predicts levels with a softmax over scaled cosine similarities.
Achieves 75.4% exact accuracy on held-out rubrics, exceeding the reported baselines in the abstract.
Remains about 28 ms per judgment as level descriptions grow to 3,000 tokens, substantially faster than Jev and a Qwen3-8B judge.
On human-labelled benchmarks, it is close to Jev on most sets, though Jev leads on two and ranks responses best on average.

papers.abstract: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. The source code is publicly available.
authors: Siyuan Yang, Junning Lyu, Xiaoyu He, Lakmal Seneviratne, Shaoming He
bullets: Addresses cascading inter-UAV localization uncertainty in multi-hop GNSS-denied swarm operations.

Combines hierarchical Voronoi targeting with formation keeping for forward-looking coverage.
Demonstrations with 6–30 UAVs, Monte Carlo deployments, and MBZIRC runs show feasible control and robust search containment; source code is available.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve factual grounding without guaranteeing that every generated claim is supported. Previous work has studied claim-level conformal factuality in single-stage RAG and, more recently, multi-hop RAG. We examine its behavior in agentic RAG, where a language-model policy adaptively issues follow-up retrieval queries or terminates retrieval before response generation. We retain the retrieval-based relevance-scoring formulation and post-generation conformal filtering and evaluate six model-dataset configurations: GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B on HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. Each configuration uses 60 fixed questions, 100 seeded 30/30 calibration-test partitions, five conformal target levels, and a no-conformal-prediction baseline. Across the six configurations, higher target levels are accompanied by higher observed full-support rates and reduced answer availability. At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage ranges from 17.23% to 60.17%, claim retention from 10.72% to 43.16%, and full support among non-empty outputs from 89.14% to 95.56%. We formulate the adaptive retrieval trajectory explicitly and characterize the reliability-informativeness trade-off when conformal factuality is applied after agent termination.
authors: Muhammad Aimal Rehman, Chi-Kuang Yeh
bullets: Studies claim-level conformal factuality in agentic RAG, where retrieval adaptively continues or stops before generation.
Evaluates GPT-6 Luna and Llama 3.1 8B across HotpotQA, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA.
Across six configurations, stricter target levels increase full-support rates while reducing non-empty response coverage and claim retention.
At the 95% target, non-empty response coverage is 17.23%–60.17%, claim retention is 10.72%–43.16%, and full support is 89.14%–95.56%.
The paper characterizes the reliability–informativeness trade-off of applying conformal factuality after adaptive retrieval termination.

papers.abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.
authors: Asad Gohar, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Moon-Il Joo, Hee-Cheol Kim

papers.abstract: Much of the information needed for data analysis is buried in text columns: an analyst may infer customer frustration from complaint text and use it to explain resolution time. We call workloads in which processing text columns is central to subsequent data analysis TADA (\emph{Text Analysis in Data Analytics}). In an agentic setting, the user's query dynamically specifies this processing, and answering it interleaves LLM-based semantic steps with exact SQL or Python operations. This mixed execution raises two design questions: which work should be neural and which symbolic, and which semantic outputs later steps can reuse. We address them for agent-planned TADA workflows with two complementary, query-driven semantic atoms. Each atom takes a sequence of text items and a natural-language query specifying the semantic task: \textbf{Tagging} returns one string per input item, while \textbf{Categorization} returns $M$ category objects over $N$ input items. Tagging results are materialized as a row-aligned column and Categorization results as a category table; SQL or Python then performs exact computation over this exposed state. We realize this interface in TADA-Agent, whose atoms run inside generated Python programs and internally handle inputs beyond a reliable context window. We evaluate TADA-Agent on TABench, a benchmark of 40 complete analysis requests over spreadsheet tables spanning workflow composition, input--output structure, and literature-grounded analytical scenarios. Against a semantic-operator baseline and relative to a held-out TADA reference run, TADA-Agent delivers comparable row-level semantic quality, has higher complete-artifact preservation estimates, and uses over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests under the evaluated native execution paths.
authors: Jinxiang Xie, Zihao Li, Rui Ding, Bartuer Zhou, Shi Han, Dongmei Zhang
bullets: Targets text-analysis-in-data-analytics (TADA), where insights from text columns support downstream structured analysis.
Introduces Tagging for row-aligned labels and Categorization for category tables, both driven by natural-language queries.
Embeds these atoms in generated Python programs and handles inputs larger than a reliable context window.

On the 40-request TABench benchmark, it achieves comparable row-level semantic quality, higher estimated complete-artifact preservation, and over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests than the evaluated baselines/reference paths.

papers.abstract: Point cloud models are increasingly deployed through score-only black-box interfaces. Under this access model, test-time rotations outside the training distribution can substantially degrade performance. Although existing mitigations such as equivariant retraining and gradient-based adaptation are effective, they are infeasible without access to model weights or gradients. To address this limitation, we propose CanDO, a test-time canonicalization method that recovers lost performance using only forward queries. Specifically, CanDO searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence and uses derivative-free optimization to perform this search without gradients. We further identify three conditions for successful recovery: a training augmentation gap, an accuracy-aligned confidence surrogate, and global search over a multi-modal objective. Across multiple architectures and benchmarks, CanDO recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal misorientation and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation. These results show that frozen score-only point cloud models can recover from rotation-induced distribution shifts through post-deployment canonicalization alone.
authors: Seonghwan Park, Min-Gyu Park
bullets: Targets pose-induced performance degradation when only forward confidence scores—not weights or gradients—are accessible.
Searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence via derivative-free, global optimization.
Successful recovery depends on an augmentation gap, confidence aligned with accuracy, and handling a multimodal objective.
Recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal shifts and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation.
Scope: addresses rotation-induced shifts through post-deployment canonicalization of frozen models.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Rotation-induced shifts within each frozen point cloud model’s augmentation gap collapse performance, and CANDO recovers a large share of the gap to the supervised oracle from forward queries alone. (b) A frozen point cloud model on S3DIS collapses under tilt despite yaw augmentation; the star marks the mIoU recovered by CANDO over the shaded deployment band, without labels or gradients.

Figure 3. (Left) For one shape, the confidence objective is multi-modal yet peaks at the same pose as the true mIoU, so a local search is trapped while a global one is not. (Right) Across shapes and poses the objective tracks accuracy, with a pooled Pearson correlation of 0.51.

The identity prior preserves canonical inputs but struggles with near-inversions. Conversely, omitting the prior improves largerotation recovery but degrades well-posed inputs.

(Left) Categories with distinctive canonical frames exhibit the largest gains, whereas rotationally ambiguous categories show limited or negative recovery. (Right) Recovery increases with corruption magnitude, indicating that residual failures arise primarily from geometric ambiguity rather than optimization.

Table 3. Conditions for recoverability on the S3DIS PointNet++ model. Recovery requires performance headroom (an accuracy drop) and an accuracy-aligned confidence surrogate. The unseen tilt (green) best satisfies both prerequisites. Recovery ∆ denotes the accuracy change after label-free recovery.

Table 19. Mixed-stream single-policy sweep, averaged over three seeds. Part segmentation admits a do-no-harm operating point with positive net gain, whereas classification trades canonical harm for the rotated gain at every threshold.

papers.abstract: Learning an unfamiliar visual category requires more than adapting a classifier: the model must connect its visual evidence to a useful semantic name. A pre-trained vision-language model can retain discriminative image features while providing a weak textual anchor for the target concept. We address this imbalance through context-grounded semantic anchoring. Our framework, SynerNet, learns concept-specific name embeddings, exposes them to compatible linguistic contexts, and conditions their representations on visual evidence. Difficulty-aware processing and adaptive objective weighting coordinate this adaptation while retaining the pre-trained backbone. On four VISTA-Beyond domains, SynerNet reaches a mean 16-shot accuracy of 74.35%, compared with 72.45% for few-shot name learning. Across 14 domains in the name-masked transfer setting, it improves mean accuracy from 45.17% to 46.74%. Ablations identify concept-specific name embeddings and cross-modal context integration as important components. These results support treating concept acquisition as the construction of visually grounded semantic anchors.
authors: Gabriel Adineera, Jinoh Kim
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between strong pre-trained visual features and weak textual anchors for unfamiliar categories.
Learns concept-specific name embeddings, integrates compatible language contexts, and conditions representations on visual evidence.
Uses difficulty-aware processing and adaptive objective weighting while retaining the pre-trained backbone.
Achieves 74.35% mean 16-shot accuracy versus 72.45% for few-shot name learning, and 46.74% versus 45.17% in name-masked transfer.
Ablations highlight concept-specific embeddings and cross-modal context integration as important components.

papers.title: Seeing Before Naming: Context-Grounded Learning of Novel Visual Concepts
papers.tldr: SynerNet improves novel visual concept learning by grounding learned semantic names in both visual evidence and linguistic context.

papers.abstract: Recent multi-view Transformers (e.g., DUSt3R and VGGT) have advanced 3D reconstruction by scaling training data and model capacity from two views to many views and long sequences, subsuming the classical SfM/SLAM pipeline of feature extraction, matching, and pose estimation in a single feed-forward pass. Yet this subsumption hides the interfaces between pipeline stages---correspondences, geometry, and pose are entangled in a single forward pass, leaving supervised fine-tuning as the major path to improvement and offering no mechanism to correct predictions from geometric evidence at test time. We propose PosePlaner to close this gap by reviving the classical coupling between correspondences and pose via flow matching, treating pose refinement as a conditional generation problem that takes coarse geometric matches and initial pose as input condition and fuses the resulting pose hypotheses into a single refined estimate, providing a continuous, data-driven analog of RANSAC voting. Our method is trained efficiently on two-view data, yet serves as a periodic refiner for streaming n-view pose estimators with no retraining. Empirically, it corrects failures of feed-forward predictors, substantially improves correspondence-based solvers, and reduces accumulated drift in long streaming sequences.
authors: Yihang Chen, Bin Tan, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu, Nan Xue
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of correspondences, geometry, and pose in modern multi-view Transformers.
Conditions pose refinement on coarse geometric matches and an initial pose, then fuses pose hypotheses into one estimate.
Provides a continuous, data-driven analogue of RANSAC voting.
Trained efficiently on two-view data and used as a periodic refiner for streaming multi-view pose estimators without retraining.
Corrects feed-forward failures, improves correspondence-based solvers, and reduces drift in long sequences.

A score head softly fuses the hypotheses into the final refined pose Trefined, used to align the two-view reconstruction.

papers.title: PosePlaner: Denoising Any Feed-Forward Pose Predictor from Pairwise Planar Geometry
papers.tldr: PosePlaner refines feed-forward camera poses at test time by using pairwise geometric matches and initial predictions in a flow-matching pose-generation framework.

papers.abstract: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.
authors: Haoyang Jiang, Dana Kulic, Michael Burke, Pamela Carreno-Medrano
bullets: The paper identifies an objective mismatch between generative behaviour quality and downstream RL training utility.
It evaluates human behaviour models in highway driving and object handover HRI domains.
Common behavioural metrics are compared across multiple human trajectory representations and against RL policy performance.
Metric rankings vary with trajectory representation and do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains.
Training on a distribution different from the true testing behaviour distribution can sometimes produce better policies than training directly on the true distribution.

papers.abstract: Language models now answer questions alongside other claims: a note in the system prompt, a message from another agent, their own earlier answer. We ask what it takes to talk a model out of an answer it gets right on its own, and separate three factors that earlier studies vary together: where the advice sits in the prompt, who is said to have written it, and what the model has already written. On Qwen3.5-27B and four-option MMLU-Pro items, with the rest of the advice held fixed in each comparison, we find three things. First, position matters far more than the API channel, in opposite directions for a bare claim and an argument: a bare "the answer is X" does most harm just before the model answers, while the same claim with a false rationale does most harm before the question, where it raises error on items the model otherwise almost never misses from 1% to 67%; moving the claim between the system message and the user message at the same position changes error by a few points. Second, attributing the note to an authority rather than to another participant, and phrasing it assertively, each raise error by 10-27 points, while the two authorities we tested differ by under two. Third, replaying a correct worked answer before the advice protects it whether the text is shown as the model's own or as someone else's, and the same replay keeps wrong answers from being corrected by a bare correct note. The position result replicates under an independently written prompt. Code, items and all result tables are released at https://github.com/coolkillercat/safety.
authors: Xinyi Ni
bullets: The study separates prompt position, stated authorship, and the model’s prior answer while holding advice fixed.

A bare incorrect claim is most harmful immediately before the answer; an incorrect claim with false reasoning is most harmful before the question, increasing error from 1% to 67% on otherwise easy items.
Moving the same claim between system and user messages at the same position changes error by only a few points.
Authority attribution and assertive wording each increase error by 10–27 points, while the tested authorities differ by under two points.

Replaying a correct worked answer protects it from misleading advice, but also prevents a bare correct note from fixing an existing wrong answer; results replicate with an independently written prompt.
