papers.abstract: Cities must coordinate domains like infrastructure, mobility, environmental management, emergency response, and public services as conditions evolve. An urban Spatio-Temporal Intelligence (STI) system helps the city monitor citywide states, analyze problems, plan and execute interventions, and adapt through feedback, making urban governance more timely, effective, and transparent. Recent urban twinning and agentic AI techniques provide foundations for such systems. From a twin-agent perspective, this survey takes a system-level view of how these disparate techniques can be coherently integrated into an urban STI system. Specifically, we review how the twin reconstructs and represents a persistent, information-enriched urban environment, and how the agent understands the twin via interfaces, reasons over it, acts reliably, and continuously evolves with the city. Built upon this synthesis, we summarize a two-loop blueprint, where an inner agent loop for grounding, reasoning, and verification, and an outer system loop linking data, twin, agentic action, feedback, and update. We then use this to structure an STI research agenda and show how a shared prototype supports diverse urban domains.
authors: Zhen Dong, Haiping Wang, Wei Tu, Yuan Liu, Bing Wang, Xuan Sun, Jinzhou Cao, Ronald Clark, Zhiheng Fu, Mohammed Bennamoun, Danfeng Hong, Yuanzheng Cui, Gemine Vivone, Pedram Ghamisi, Bisheng Yang, Qingquan Li, Deren Li
bullets: Motivates STI systems that coordinate infrastructure, mobility, environment, emergencies, and public services as conditions change.

Examines how agents interface with the twin, reason over urban states, act reliably, and evolve through feedback.

Uses the framework to organize a research agenda and describe a shared prototype spanning diverse urban domains.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Detailed technical organization of this review. Urban twinning reconstructs, completes, represents, and enriches city states; urban agents access these states through textual and feature interfaces, reason over them, and operate through governed agentic architectures; the future vision couples both subsystems through a two-loop blueprint and adapts it across urban domains. Leaf labels summarize closely related technical topics.

Fig. 8. The four-layer organization of urban agent. General language models are grounded in city evidence, strengthened with spatio-temporal reasoning, embedded in agentic architectures, and constrained for reliable operations.

Fig. 3. The four-stage urban twinning framework. Recovery and completion determine the physical state contained in the twin, while physical representation and information embedding organize and enrich that state for subsequent operation.

Fig. 7. Strategies for embedding information in an urban twin. Inside-out methods lift or learn semantic features from reconstruction signals, whereas outside-in methods ground external fields, attributes, and relations on twin carriers.

Fig. 9. Urban agent systems organized by task. Analysis and planning transform urban evidence into analytical results and plans; interaction and control apply decisions to environments; mobility prediction and urban simulation model individual futures and collective dynamics.

Fig. 5. Inferring unobserved scene states. Generation synthesizes new 3D scenes or 4D evolution from weak conditions, whereas completion extends partial scene observations while preserving consistency with the measured spatial and temporal evidence.
Fig. 4. Recovering observable urban states. Analytical and feed-forward paradigms process images, 3D data, or multimodal observations to recover static or dynamic scenes.

Fig. 6. Three forms of physical representation. Explicit representations enumerate directly addressable primitives, implicit representations encode continuous scene functions, and hybrid representations attach learned features or attributes to explicit spatial anchors.

Fig. 10. The proposed system blueprint. The inner loop grounds, reasons, and acts, then replans before action. The outer loop updates the twin, executes an approved decision, observes the outcome, and starts the next full cycle.

papers.abstract: User memory helps personalized systems build on their understanding of users over time. In e-commerce, users convey their preferences and needs through both explicit language and implicit interactions with products. We study memory built from logs of these interactions, examining how it can \emph{remember} concrete evidence and established interests, and use that evidence to \emph{infer} underlying needs and preferences that inform judgments beyond well-observed product domains. Existing memory methods primarily target language-based interactions, and evaluations offer limited real behavioral data and limited separation of these capabilities. This leaves open how to jointly support and separately evaluate remembering and inference from behavioral logs. We formulate the problem of continual behavioral user memory around these joint requirements and develop a dedicated evaluation framework and memory method to address them. \textbf{BehaviorMemBench} is a benchmark built from real e-commerce logs covering 1{,}194 users and 17{,}462 behavioral batches over more than three years, with automatic future-behavior labels and a task-independent memory interface to separately evaluate remembering and inference under a common protocol. \textbf{BehaviorMem} is a memory design that organizes explicit behavioral facts and inferred user characteristics across long-term and short-term scopes in a two-axis state, with evidence-grounded formation, continual maintenance, and query-independent readout. Experiments across two builders and two task readers show that BehaviorMem leads the evaluated agentic memories on remember and infer, and reveal different method rankings across the two capabilities and competitive statistical baselines. Validation on a public dataset further supports its usefulness for downstream tasks based on behavioral histories.
authors: Sizhe Wang, Xinghao Fang, Rui Qiu, Zhenjia Ma, Dagui Chen, Kun Kuang, Hongcheng Guo

papers.abstract: Recent generic reference-based image generation models natively support multiple conditions by concatenating all reference image and text tokens into a joint sequence processed by a single Diffusion Transformer (DiT). However, this versatile paradigm comes at an efficiency cost: accommodating multiple references leads to a token explosion, incurring massive $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ computational complexity. Most acceleration methods operate inside the DiT, showing limited capability in reducing spatial redundancy and failing to alleviate peak VRAM. While some pre-model token reduction alternatives exist, they inevitably introduce external models. This raises a question: Is it possible to achieve acceleration and memory savings while preserving compatibility with in-model techniques and requiring no additional parameters? In this work, we realize this goal by proposing the early Token reduction via Downsampled self-Probing (ToDoPro). By executing a few denoising steps on spatially $2\times$ downsampled reference images, this cheap probing stage utilizes the DiT model itself to effectively and efficiently extract reference token importance. Using the probed importance, we apply a hierarchical reduction before the main denoising stage: we completely discard low-importance tokens, substitute mid-importance tokens with their downsampled counterparts to cheaply preserve global context, and keep high-importance tokens. Experiments across three base models and two benchmarks demonstrate that our early reduction accelerates inference significantly and mitigates peak GPU memory. Furthermore, we can improve generation quality by safely filtering out noisy, uninformative reference tokens, enabling the model to concentrate its limited attention capacity on genuinely useful tokens. The code will be released at https://github.com/scy639/ToDoPro
authors: Caiyi Sun, Yujing Sun, Siu-Ming Yiu
bullets: Addresses token explosion and quadratic compute from combining multiple image and text references.
Runs a few denoising steps on 2× downsampled references to estimate token importance without adding external models or parameters.
Hierarchically discards low-importance tokens, downsamples mid-importance tokens, and preserves high-importance tokens before full denoising.
Experiments on three base models and two benchmarks show significant inference acceleration and reduced peak GPU memory.
Filtering noisy, uninformative tokens can improve quality by focusing attention on useful references.

papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated or incorrect knowledge in large language models without full retraining. Existing parameter-editing methods remain limited for long-sequence knowledge: single-point editors provide insufficient coverage for extended targets, while fixed chunk-based editors distribute editing effort uniformly across rigid predefined windows, failing to prioritize difficult, information-dense tokens. In this work, we show that token entropy is closely associated with both editing difficulty and semantic importance: high-entropy regions are harder to edit and often contain key factual content. Motivated by this observation, we propose DynEdit, a dynamic framework for long-sequence knowledge editing. DynEdit uses token-level entropy to guide non-uniform sliding, increasing the coverage of difficult high-entropy regions, and further applies entropy-guided token-level optimization to strengthen updates on information-dense tokens within each editing window. Experiments on three benchmarks and two backbone models show that DynEdit consistently outperforms competitive baselines across diverse long-form editing settings, achieving gains of up to +14.0 BLEU points on challenging paraphrase queries and near-saturated semantic scores on several diverse knowledge domains.
authors: Jinhu Fu, Yan Bai, Yihang Lou, Li Sun, Jiahong Wu, Xiangxiang Chu, Sen Su

papers.abstract: Multi-modal video fusion aims to generate temporally coherent videos with salient targets and rich structural details by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous sensors. However, existing video fusion methods commonly rely on optical flow estimation and feature warping for inter-frame alignment and cross-frame information aggregation to maintain temporal consistency, thereby introducing considerable computational overhead and making the fusion performance vulnerable to flow estimation errors. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an efficient multi-modal video fusion network with dynamic region-guided temporal interaction. Specifically, the proposed spatio-temporal interaction module leverages the Test-Time Training paradigm to model temporal dependencies with linear complexity. Building on this design, the module restricts temporal modeling to key dynamic regions in the video sequence, as static background regions provide limited temporal cues. By excluding low-variation tokens from unnecessary temporal interaction, this selective strategy contributes to improved fusion quality and temporal consistency. In addition, leveraging the strong ability of pretrained MAE features to capture global structural dependencies, we introduce a feature-level temporal consistency constraint to suppress local flickering by aligning the inter-frame variation directions of the fused and source videos. We further propose a new MAE-based temporal metric that quantifies directional distance between their temporal variations within dynamic regions. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior fusion quality and temporal consistency on multiple benchmark datasets, while exhibiting high computational efficiency under edge-device deployment settings.
authors: Jingxue Huang, Xiaosong Li, Yi Lin

papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Standard all-layer LoRA applies adaptation throughout the transformer, despite heterogeneous contributions from its components. In this work, we conduct a systematic mechanistic interpretability analysis to understand how LoRA affects model internals. We observe that LoRA's adaptation effect is highly non-uniform, with significant component-wise and layer-wise sparsity. Most critically, we find that important layers are highly task-dependent, with limited overlap across tasks. Motivated by these insights, we propose Adaptive-LoRA, a calibration-driven method that automatically identifies task-specific layers via frozen-base zero-ablation, enabling efficient layer selection without exhaustive search. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-1.5B across 11 diverse reasoning tasks demonstrate that Adaptive-LoRA outperforms full-layer LoRA while using only 30% of layers, achieving a $3.5\times$ reduction in adapter parameters. This work bridges mechanistic interpretability and practical efficiency, providing both fundamental insights and a principled approach for adaptive fine-tuning.
authors: Fei Zuo, Yizhou Huang, Kezhi Wang

papers.abstract: Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation. To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants ("digital sisters") and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry's F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.
authors: Luke Hollis, Tianxing Fan, Heng Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of turning 3D/4D captures into usable simulation environments with accurate geometry and physics.
Coordinates segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation using simulator-based visual feedback.
Supports 3DGS, photogrammetry, LiDAR, AI-generated scenes, and 4D dynamic captures.
Generates diverse object variants (“digital sisters”) and scripted demonstrations for policy learning.
Improves reported reconstruction metrics substantially on cluttered and dynamic-scene benchmarks, with preliminary transfer to a real robot.

papers.abstract: Vision--language--action (VLA) models increasingly run on edge devices aboard robots, where inference latency constrains closed-loop robot control. However, it remains unclear how to design VLA models, their inference software and edge hardware so that robots can run VLA inference in real time. Most VLA models report only task success, while prior studies cover limited action-generation strategies, divide inference into at most three stages, and lack comparisons of inference optimizations on the same models.benchmarking 18 open VLA models across released and alternative backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, with a seven-stage inference breakdown. Our study reveals three insights. First, action-generation strategy matters more than model size. It dominates 14 of 19 Jetson configurations, latency varies by $82\times$ on Jetson and $157\times$ on AMD, and parameter count explains at most 15% of latency variance. Models that generate long action chunks in a few flow-matching steps keep up with control, whereas token-by-token decoding does not. Second, kernel fusion with 4-bit weights helps most, running $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 2.6--2.9$\times$ faster than PyTorch with \texttt{torch.compile}, but it exists for only these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12\% to 39\% of the GR00T N1.7 call. Third, after optimization, memory bandwidth limits only the stages that process few tokens on the Jetson, such as the denoising steps, whereas software limits all other stages, from unfused kernels to serial preprocessing on the host CPU. Overall, low-latency edge VLAs should use few action-generation iterations, inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit weights to more models and platforms, and edge hardware needs high memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU.
authors: Borui Xu, Hongshi Tan, Wenqi Jiang, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich
bullets: Benchmarks 18 open VLA models across multiple backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, using a seven-stage latency breakdown.
Action-generation strategy dominates latency in most Jetson configurations; long action chunks with few flow-matching steps are more control-friendly than token-by-token decoding.
Kernel fusion with 4-bit weights substantially accelerates the two supported models on Jetson, while optimization shifts bottlenecks toward CPU preprocessing.
After optimization, memory bandwidth limits selected Jetson stages, whereas software inefficiencies constrain other stages across the pipeline.
The study recommends few-step action generation, broader low-bit kernel fusion, high-memory-bandwidth hardware, and faster host CPUs.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer large multimodal models to compact models for autonomous driving, but uniform token-level matching can dilute planning-relevant semantics and amplify teacher errors. We propose RSKD, a semantic-consistency-guided distillation framework that routes supervision according to both the task importance of an answer phrase and its semantic consistency with the teacher prediction. Task-critical semantic phrases are localized in the ground-truth answer, and a phrase-level consistency score controls the balance between Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) distillation and ground-truth supervision. Teacher information is emphasized only where it is semantically consistent, while semantically inconsistent phrases receive stronger ground-truth supervision. We evaluate RSKD on DrivingVQA, LingoQA, and MapLMv2. RSKD improves over the compared student-based baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA and remains competitive on MapLMv2.
authors: Chuchu Xie, Yang Zhong, Kangan Qian, Hao Ye, Kun Jiang, Diange Yang
bullets: Uniform token-level distillation can dilute planning-relevant meaning and propagate teacher errors.
The framework identifies task-critical phrases in ground-truth answers and scores their semantic consistency with teacher predictions.
Phrase-level consistency dynamically balances JSD distillation against ground-truth supervision.
RSKD improves over compared student baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA, while remaining competitive on MapLMv2.

papers.abstract: Language-Only Vision-Language Model Selection (LOVM) aims to identify the Vision-Language Model (VLM) with the highest zero-shot accuracy on a target task using only textual information. We revisit the existing LOVM evaluation protocol and argue that ranking metrics, such as top-5 recall and Kendall's rank correlation, do not directly assess the performance of the selected model. We therefore adopt simple regret (SR), defined as the performance gap between the best and selected models, and introduce Outlier-Robust Normalized Regret (ORNR) to account for the varying performance ranges across tasks while reducing sensitivity to outliers. Building on this revised evaluation protocol, we propose Target-Conditioned Expected Source Regret (TC-ESR), a training-free method that selects the model with the lowest similarity-weighted mean regret across source tasks. Across 22 target tasks and 43 VLMs, TC-ESR achieves the lowest mean SR and ORNR among all compared methods. Separately, we identify two sources of target performance leakage in the prior ranking-based evaluation protocol and provide corrections that remove both.
authors: Hyuk Kwon, Jaebyeong Jeon, Hyeonseo Jang, Kibok Lee
bullets: Existing top-5 recall and Kendall correlation can reward good rankings even when the selected model performs poorly.
The authors use simple regret and introduce Outlier-Robust Normalized Regret (ORNR) to compare selection quality across tasks with different performance ranges.
Target-Conditioned Expected Source Regret (TC-ESR) is a training-free selector based on similarity-weighted regret across source tasks.
TC-ESR obtains the lowest mean simple regret and ORNR among compared methods.
The study identifies and corrects two sources of target-performance leakage in prior ranking-based evaluation.

papers.title: Good Rankings, Poor Choices? Rethinking Language-Only Vision-Language Model Selection

papers.abstract: Humans have been shown to use a "straightened" encoding to represent the natural visual world as it evolves in time (H\'enaff et al. 2019). In the context of discrete video sequences, "straightened" means that changes between frames follow a more linear path in representation space at progressively deeper levels of processing. While deep convolutional networks are often proposed as models of human visual processing, many do not straighten natural videos. In this paper, we explore the relationship between network architecture, differing types of robustness, biologically-inspired filtering mechanisms, and representational straightness in response to time-varying input; we identify strengths and limitations of straightness as a useful way of evaluating neural network representations. We find that (1) adversarial training leads to straighter representations in both CNN and transformer-based architectures but (2) this effect is task-dependent, not generalizing to tasks such as segmentation and frame-prediction, where straight representations are not favorable for predictions; and nor to other types of robustness. In addition, (3) straighter representations impart temporal stability to class predictions, even for out-of-distribution data. Finally, (4) biologically-inspired elements increase straightness in the early stages of a network, but do not guarantee increased straightness in downstream layers of CNNs. We show that straightness is an easily computed measure of representational robustness and stability, as well as a hallmark of human representations with benefits for computer vision models.
authors: Anne Harrington, Vasha DuTell, Ayush Tewari, Mark Hamilton, Simon Stent, Ruth Rosenholtz, William T. Freeman
bullets: Studies how architecture, robustness, and biologically inspired mechanisms affect straightness in learned visual representations.
Finds adversarial training increases straightness in CNNs and vision transformers, but not necessarily for segmentation or frame prediction.
Shows straighter representations improve temporal stability of class predictions, including on out-of-distribution data.
Biologically inspired components increase straightness early in networks but do not consistently improve deeper CNN representations.
Positions straightness as a simple measure of representational robustness and stability, with task-dependent limitations.

papers.abstract: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
authors: Hyunwoong Bae, Jisu Han, Jiyeon Choi, Dohoon Kim, Taesup Moon
bullets: Introduces OSMA-Bench, using spatially matched scenarios that vary only by obstacle type.
Proposes the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure obstacle-conditioned clearance, speed, and smoothness.
VLM and VLA policies inconsistently adapt motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts.
Policies distinguish obstacles semantically but fail to reflect that distinction in motion parameters or actions.
For VLM-based systems, inserting an explicit parameter-inference step improves motion adaptation.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that serve users across many sessions must choose, for every request, the few stored memories that enter a limited context window. This choice largely decides whether the agent answers correctly, and it runs on every request at Web scale. This selection faces three challenges: a large and growing store, a per-request cost budget, and multi-session questions that need all of their evidence. Many memory systems build notes or graphs with hundreds to thousands of LLM calls per history, and each is designed on its own, so it is unclear which component yields the accuracy. These challenges mirror the properties of recommendation, so we formalize agent memory as budgeted slate recommendation, with the request as the user, stored memories as items and the context window as a slate. The formalization places memory systems in one design space of recommender cascades and factorizes accuracy into the completeness that each stage controls. Guided by it, we propose AgentMemRec, which adapts candidate generation, learning to rank and slate construction from recommender systems and selects memories without any LLM call. On multi-session questions of LongMemEval, AgentMemRec outperforms memory and context-selection methods, including A-Mem, HippoRAG 2, DynamicRAG and T-Mem, by 10 to 31 points of accuracy. It matches an LLM reranker that makes 64 calls per query at 3.2 times lower serving cost, and on LoCoMo it outperforms Mem0 and Zep without any LLM call at write time. The factorization attributes the gains to slates that more often hold all of the evidence, so recommender-system design offers an effective and efficient foundation for the long-term memory of LLM agents.
authors: Xinyu Zhang, Weiwei Sun
bullets: Frames memory retrieval as slate recommendation: the request is the user, memories are items, and the context window is the slate.
Uses recommender-system components—candidate generation, learning-to-rank, and slate construction—to select memories without LLM calls.
Addresses large memory stores, per-request cost limits, and questions requiring evidence across multiple sessions.
Outperforms several memory and context-selection methods on LongMemEval by 10–31 accuracy points, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Video world models trained on large-scale robot data promise a safe and scalable approach for learning and evaluating policies that act in the physical world. However, they still struggle with long-horizon rollouts and out-of-distribution generalization, and they remain computationally demanding at inference time. Typically, video world models make predictions in the latent space of a reconstruction-trained autoencoder, which however is not directly optimized for dynamics modeling. On the other hand, world models designed for latent planning usually optimize latents to be predictable, but they forgo accurate prediction of observations in pixel space. In this paper, we show that it is possible to achieve the best of both worlds: a latent geometry optimized to make future prediction as simple as possible without sacrificing accurate prediction of future observations. More precisely, we find that temporal objectives for representation learning, paired with a past-conditioned decoder architecture, lead to consistent improvements in generative video world models at the same training budget. The gains include up to 5x cheaper inference, over 7x faster training, and 15-24% lower pixel and perceptual errors out of distribution and over long horizons. Our world models also agree more closely with real-world policy evaluation when using a vision-language model to judge task success from their pixel-space predictions. Overall, our study indicates that temporal predictability is an important design criterion for the latent space of video world models, and provides concrete guidance on how to incorporate it into the training of autoencoders.
authors: Mattia Scardecchia, Sherry Yang
bullets: Reconstruction-trained autoencoder latents are not optimized for dynamics, limiting rollout quality and generalization.
The approach combines temporal representation-learning objectives with a past-conditioned decoder.
This yields up to 5× cheaper inference and over 7× faster training at the same training budget.
Pixel and perceptual errors decrease by 15–24% on long-horizon and out-of-distribution predictions.
Generated-video task evaluations align more closely with real-world policy evaluations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Method overview. (1) An autoencoder is fine-tuned on pairs of nearby video frames xt, xt+1, with a reconstruction loss and a temporal objective on the latents zt, zt+1 and the action at; the decoder D conditions on the past frame xt to reconstruct xt+1 from its latent. (2) An actionconditioned diffusion world model is trained on the latents from the frozen encoder E. (3) From a context frame x1 and a sequence of actions a1:T , the world model generates latents, which D decodes conditioning on x1 as the past frame. We highlight in orange and green the two components that distinguish our recipe from a standard video world model: the temporal objective, and the past-conditioned decoder.

Figure 5: World models at equal reconstruction quality, across sampling steps, rollout steps and training. The four pipelines of Table 1, all with the ordinary decoder, against the number of DDIM sampling steps (top), along the long rollouts (middle) and over world-model training (bottom). Gray shading: prediction steps reached by fewer than half of the videos. Mean and standard error over three training seeds. Latent prediction gives the largest perceptual gains with few sampling steps, and the lowest LPIPS from the fourth prediction step on and throughout training.

Figure 2: Latents can be predictable and informative in a synthetic setting. Left: Synthetic observations have a predictable component (signal, the dot) and an unpredictable noise component (the static). An encoder E is trained with reconstruction, temporal contrastive learning or both, and three readouts are then trained on its frozen latents: a world model predicts the next latent from the current latent and action, a probe predicts the signal, and a decoder D reconstructs the observation. Right: the error of each readout at latent size 100, divided by the error of the same readout trained on the raw observation; geometric mean and standard error over 3 seeds, lower is better. Reconstruction alone leaves the next latent as hard to predict as the raw observation and reads the signal far less accurately; contrastive learning alone loses the observation; their combination avoids both failures.

Figure 6: World models at equal training budget, across sampling steps, rollout steps and training. The pipelines of Table 2 against the number of DDIM sampling steps (top), along the long rollouts (middle) and over world-model training (bottom). Gray shading: prediction steps reached by fewer than half of the videos. Mean and standard error over three training seeds. The temporal objectives improve LPIPS and SSIM in all three rows, and inverse dynamics also gives a lower pixel MSE than either reconstruction-only pipeline.

Figure 20: Latent maps at equal training budget. One held-out Bridge frame encoded by the encoders of the three past-conditioned pipelines, one training seed. Columns average channels 0–4, 5–9 and 10–15 of each 16× 32× 32 latent. Each map is standardized separately, black low and white high, so intensities are not comparable across maps. Latent prediction and inverse dynamics produce smoother regions around the arm and the objects than reconstruction alone.

Figure 3: The information-predictability frontier and the decoder’s reliance on the past frame. Left: reconstruction error against the unpredictable share of the latent variance, for autoencoders fine-tuned for 80,000 updates with latent prediction at weight λ, with the ordinary decoder or the past-conditioned decoder. Points are means over two training seeds at λ = 0 and 0.3 (faint: individual seeds) and one seed elsewhere. Raising λ trades reconstruction for predictability, and the pastconditioned decoder improves the frontier at every weight. Right: reconstruction error of each past-conditioned autoencoder with its past-frame pathway disabled (Appendix G.4), divided by its error with the correct past frame (log scale); same seeds as on the left. As the pressure from the temporal objective on the latent space increases, the decoder relies more on the past frame for accurate reconstructions.

Figure 23: World-model improvement over reconstruction as the temporal weight varies. Latent prediction at each weight against reconstruction (λ = 0, zero by construction, open marker), both with the past-conditioned decoder and the same training seed; panels have independent scales. One training seed, and two more at λ = 0.7 (dots). LPIPS improves at every weight in distribution, out of distribution and with two sampling steps; long-rollout gains favor larger weights.

Figure 8: Policy evaluation inside the world models. Three robot policies on the 17 Bridge tasks of WorldGym, inside the five world models of Table 2. One training seed; error bars: standard error over the 170 starting frames (left) and bootstrap standard error over tasks (right). With 2 sampling steps, the temporal world models keep their agreement with the real world and the real ranking of the three policies, while the reconstruction-only world models lose both.

Figure 19: Policy evaluation after 200,000 world-model updates. The three past-conditioned world models of Table 11, one training seed; panels, rows and error bars as in Figure 8. With 2 steps, the temporal world models keep the real ranking of the policies and their agreement with the real world.

Figure 25: Effect of latent prediction across world-model sizes. Improvement of latent prediction over reconstruction, both with the past-conditioned decoder and the same seed: relative reductions of pixel MSE and LPIPS, and increases of SSIM. Rows of the equal-budget autoencoders show the mean and standard error over training seeds, with dots for single seeds; rows of the second autoencoder pair show one run each. The gains persist out of distribution and with two sampling steps at both widths; in distribution, the effect is mixed at width 384 and negative at width 1,024, where the long-rollout gains also shrink.

Figure 9: AutoEval rollouts with video world models trained on different latent spaces. The baseline learns its latent space through reconstruction, as is standard; our recipe adds a temporal objective (latent prediction or inverse dynamics) and a past-conditioned decoder. One AutoEval trajectory, out of distribution: the recorded actions are replayed from one context frame for three times the length of the training clips, with 2 sampling steps. Figures 10 to 17 show more examples, selected and random.

Figure 4: The synthetic study at every latent size and weight. Errors on the observation, the signal, the next latent and the next signal against the latent size, for all six weights λ of the contrastive temporal term (λ = 0: reconstruction alone; λ = 1: the temporal term alone). Horizontal lines: the raw observation given directly to the same downstream networks (in the next-latent panel, hidden under λ = 0). Mean and standard error over three seeds. Intermediate weights retain reconstruction information while improving signal recovery and latent predictability over reconstruction alone.

Figure 10: Out of distribution, 2 sampling steps, selected trajectories. AutoEval trajectories with the recorded actions replayed for 29 frames. Top row: the recorded frames; below: the rollout of each world model from the same context frame, with its LPIPS.

Figure 18: OpenVLA in WorldGym with 2 sampling steps. One starting frame per panel, inside the five world models of Table 2 (one training seed), at frames 0 to 40; bold: the frames the judge sees. Beside each row: the judged outcome and the three votes.

Figure 21: Latent maps at equal reconstruction quality. The same frame encoded by the four encoders of the equal-reconstruction experiment, all with the ordinary decoder, one training seed. Columns and standardization as in Figure 20. Latent and contrastive prediction suppress fine spatial variation compared with reconstruction alone, whereas pixel prediction retains it.

Figure 22: Spatial spectra of the frozen latents. Radial amplitude spectra of the latent channels, as a share of their total amplitude; at equal budget, solid curves use the past-conditioned decoder and dashed curves the ordinary one. Mean and standard error over three training seeds, except the pretrained encoder (one). Latent and contrastive prediction reduce the high-frequency components at equal reconstruction, and latent prediction and inverse dynamics do so at equal budget.

Figure 7: Autoencoder losses over fine-tuning in the weight sweep. Reconstruction error (left) and error of the jointly trained latent predictor (right), for each temporal weight and decoder. One training seed; the predictor receives no gradient at λ = 0. Past conditioning lowers both errors at every nonzero weight, and larger weights trade reconstruction for a lower prediction error.

Figure 14: Out of distribution, 10 sampling steps, selected trajectories. AutoEval trajectories with the recorded actions replayed for 29 frames; rows as in Figure 10.
Figure 15: Out of distribution, 10 sampling steps, random trajectories. AutoEval trajectories with the recorded actions replayed for 29 frames; rows as in Figure 10.
Figure 12: In distribution, 2 sampling steps, selected videos. Held-out Bridge videos rolled out for 59 frames; rows as in Figure 10.

Figure 17: In distribution, 10 sampling steps, random videos. Held-out Bridge videos rolled out for 59 frames; rows as in Figure 10.

Figure 24: Distribution metrics as the temporal weight varies. FID and FVD of latent prediction at each weight against reconstruction (λ = 0), both with the past-conditioned decoder and the same training seed, in distribution; panels as in Figure 23. One training seed, and two more at λ = 0.7 (dots). Weights from 0.1 to 0.5 improve both metrics; at λ = 0.7, both are worse than at λ = 0, for all three training seeds.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.
authors: Chengzhi Liu, Yuxiang Lai, Yuzhe Yang, Yanqing Liu, Jiheng Hou, Yue Cao, Haonan Wang, Ruixi Fan, Lan Wang, Sheng Liu, Songyou Peng, Yale Song, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Xin Eric Wang, Jui-Hsin Lai, Youbao Tang
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing vision-language agents to infer implicit intent and update interaction states as requests evolve.
StreamVibe-Bench includes 4.1K evaluation and 85K training samples covering explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents.
StreamVibe-VL infers intent from continuous observations and adapts response timing and content dynamically.
StreamVibe-Harness uses hierarchical memory to maintain persistent user and environmental states across interactions.
The proposed systems report 10.7% better response timing and answer quality, plus a 12.3% gain in sustained proactive interaction.

papers.abstract: Latency-sensitive spoken agents must know not only which tool to call, but also when they have heard enough to act. Waiting for the turn to complete delays execution even when the request is already actionable. However, neither existing spoken agents nor spoken dialogue corpora define the earliest point at which a request becomes actionable. We introduce a synthetic spoken-dialogue pipeline that provides earliest-actionable-point supervision, marking when the observed speech grounds a tool and its required arguments. Through controlled task generation, speech synthesis and alignment, and gated annotation, we construct 26,694 dialogues totaling 786 hours across 48 domains, with disjoint training and test argument values. We additionally create an audio rendering of $\tau^2$-bench for external evaluation. We train an omni-modal language model on this corpus, enabling causal, chunk-level decisions and partial-transcript generation for downstream call completion. The model achieves tool-state macro-F1 scores of 0.48 and 0.47 on held-out dialogues and the external benchmark, respectively. For correct calls, the estimated mean lead over a turn-end cascade, using the same formatter, is 1.8-2.0 seconds in-domain and 1.1 seconds on $\tau^2$-bench. These results demonstrate a data-driven path toward spoken agents that act while listening. We will open-source the pipeline and the training scripts.
authors: Yizhou Peng, Chen Chen, Donghang Wu, Hexin Liu, Eng Siong Chng
bullets: Targets latency in spoken agents by detecting the earliest point where a tool and its required arguments are grounded.

papers.abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.
authors: Jonathan DeCastro, Thomas Balch, Emily Sumner, Deepak Gopinath, Laporsha Dees, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Elliot Weiss, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Todd Rowell, John Leonard, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
bullets: Targets the challenge of proactive yet understandable assistance in tightly coupled human–vehicle control.

Validated in three human-subject studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment covering high-speed racing and urban driving.
Intent conditioning improved torque alignment and collision rate; the work also reports deployment insights for safety-critical human–robot teaming.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning-execution-verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.
authors: Lingjun Mao, Jinglin Cao, Lukun He, Wenpeng Xu, Yuchen Yan, Hengyu Jin, Zijun Zhang, Jinzhou Tang, Songyao Jin, Ziche Liu, Yifei Shao, Junbo Huang, Fang Nan, Ruobing Han, Ziqiao Xi, Ziming Xu, Shuang Liang, Sibo Zhu, Wenyi Wu, Xinyue Wang, Yiming Huang, Xinkai Zou, Gao Zhu, Kun Zhou, Biwei Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between benchmarks for isolated robot capabilities and the integrated demands of open-world autonomy.
Introduces 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks across atomic, short-horizon, long-horizon, and open-ended scenarios.
Evaluates five task-level abilities: task discovery, contextual reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness.
Measures scenario-level autonomy, including how agents combine these capabilities to satisfy high-level user needs.
Experiments show a substantial manipulation–autonomy gap, benefits from agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and persistent challenges for open-world deployment.

papers.abstract: How do later loops in a pretrained looped language model repair two-hop retrieval? We study Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B by transplanting attention queries between loops at the same layer, head and final prompt position. On synthetic in-context questions, injecting the layer-indexed collection of loop-3 queries throughout loop 1 rescues 90% and 97% of questions answered incorrectly at loop 1 and correctly at loop 3, versus 24% and 21% for shuffled donors. The rescue also holds under greedy generation in Ouro-2.6B; in Ouro-1.4B it is limited to four-candidate ranking. Crossed donor-recipient swaps favor retrieval through the donor's bridge entity over copying its answer, although a substantial positional component remains in Ouro-2.6B. Late keys and values rescue far fewer targets. Freezing queries at their loop-1 values also damages two-hop accuracy more than a matched question that supplies the bridge. On natural questions, rescue is smaller and replicates only in Ouro-2.6B, and crossed swaps do not establish bridge redirection. These results identify a transferable collection of late-loop queries that supports bridge-conditioned retrieval on synthetic scenes; they do not locate where the bridge is computed or establish a single-vector handoff.
authors: Ziyu Mu, Zehua Wang
bullets: Transplanting loop-3 queries into loop 1 rescues many cases that fail early but succeed later: 90% in Ouro-1.4B and 97% in Ouro-2.6B, versus 24% and 21% with shuffled donors.
Crossed donor-recipient swaps favor retrieval via the donor’s bridge entity rather than copying its answer, though positional effects remain in Ouro-2.6B.
Late keys and values produce far fewer rescues; freezing queries at loop-1 values also harms two-hop accuracy.
Greedy-generation rescue holds in Ouro-2.6B but is limited to four-candidate ranking in Ouro-1.4B.
On natural questions, the effect is smaller and replicates only in Ouro-2.6B; the study does not identify where the bridge is computed.

papers.abstract: Driving video captured through a windshield violates the world-space consistency assumed by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the road scene exhibits parallax while cabin reflections remain attached to the camera, causing standard 3DGS to embed reflected content into the reconstructed scene. We introduce RIDE-Splat, a pipeline for reflection-free 3D reconstruction from posed driving video without clean images, reflection masks, or pretrained networks. RIDE-Splat assigns world-consistent transmission through the windshield to a 3DGS scene and the dominant camera-attached reflection to one shared, signed RGB image. It builds the clean reconstruction in two passes. First, it learns the 3D geometry and the signed reflection image, representing both added radiance and transmission attenuation. Then, it uses the reflection-removed training images to fit a clean 3DGS model. At inference, the reflection image is discarded, preserving the standard 3DGS rendering path. We also introduce the RIDE-Splat Dataset, the first 3D reconstruction benchmark for reflection removal from driving video -- with real driving scenes, physical windshield reflections in training views, and separately captured non-reflective evaluation images. Across the RIDE-Splat Dataset, XLD, and Wayve, RIDE-Splat outperforms 3DGS, DC-Gaussian, and RobustSplat on all nine aggregate metrics, improving PSNR by up to 3.59 dB and reducing LPIPS by up to 0.0876. We achieve the highest metrics in 38 out of 42 per-scene comparisons and removes windshield reflections that remain visible in the baselines while preserving the transmitted scene.
authors: Kevin David Hayes, Alex Hanson, Allen Tu, Pranav Asthana, Matthias Zwicker, Tom Goldstein
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between world-consistent road scenes and camera-attached windshield reflections in 3DGS.
Jointly models scene transmission with 3D Gaussians and dominant reflections using a shared signed RGB image.
Uses a two-pass process: estimate geometry and reflections, then fit a clean 3DGS model to reflection-removed images.
Introduces the RIDE-Splat Dataset with real driving scenes, physical reflections, and separate non-reflective evaluation views.
Outperforms the compared baselines across nine aggregate metrics on RIDE-Splat, XLD, and Wayve; reflection removal preserves the transmitted scene.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of RIDE-Splat. Given posed driving frames with windshield reflections, RIDE-Splat reconstructs a reflection-free 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene without paired clean images or reflection masks. Phase I: Coordinate-Based Joint Optimization (Sec. III-B) warms up scene geometry, then jointly separates a world-consistent 3DGS scene from a shared, signed 2D reflection layer. Phase II: Reflection Self-Localization (Sec. III-C) derives a continuous spatial weight from the recovered reflection layer and retrains the decomposition from scratch with this support fixed, preventing weak scene residuals from entering the final reconstruction. This refit adds no optimized parameters. At inference, the reflection layer is discarded and standard 3DGS rasterization renders reflection-free novel views.

papers.abstract: Recently, point-supervised temporal action localization has attracted increasing attention due to its low annotation cost (only one frame per action instance) and competitive detection performance. However, since point annotations are less complete than proposal annotations, existing methods mainly rely on multiple instance learning for snippet-level classification, which leads to a performance gap compared to fully supervised models. To bridge this gap, we propose P2P-Former, a novel point-to-proposal Transformer-based framework that effectively connects point-level supervision with proposal-level learning for temporal action localization. In this work, we identify two key challenges in transitioning from point-level supervision to full supervision: (1) how to generate reliable proposals as pseudo ground-truth, and (2) how to effectively integrate point-level cues into the fully supervised paradigm. To address the first challenge, we propose a Point-aware Proposal Generation (PPG) strategy that refines the confidence of proposals produced by a base locator using a point-aware importance estimation function, and then performs optimal matching between point annotations and candidate proposals to select reliable proposals as pseudo ground-truth. To tackle the second challenge, we introduce a Point-guided Semantic Enhancement (PSE) module that aggregates prototypes from point-annotated features and injects them into snippet features through Transformer-based interactions. Moreover, we design a Point-to-Proposal Constraint Loss (PPCL) that enforces each predicted proposal to include the annotated point, thereby encouraging more accurate localization. Extensive experiments on the THUMOS14 and ActivityNet-1.3 datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms several existing state-of-the-art approaches.
authors: Yunchuan Ma, Laiyun Qing, Sai Xu, Guorong Li, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses the performance gap between low-cost point supervision and fully supervised temporal action localization.
Uses Point-aware Proposal Generation (PPG) to refine candidate proposals and match them with annotated points as pseudo ground truth.
Introduces Point-guided Semantic Enhancement (PSE) to transfer point-derived prototypes into snippet features via Transformer interactions.
Applies Point-to-Proposal Constraint Loss (PPCL) to ensure predicted proposals contain the annotated action points.
Experiments on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet-1.3 show improvement over several existing state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed P2P-Former framework. A base action locator first generates coarse proposals, which are then evaluated using point-aware scoring and matched with point annotations via the Hungarian algorithm to obtain reliable pseudo labels. Point-labeled features are clustered to construct category prototypes, which are injected into a prototype-guided semantic enhancement block to enrich video tokens. The enhanced tokens are processed by a Transformer encoder and FPN, followed by classification and regression heads for temporal action localization. The model is trained with Lcls, Lreg, and the point-toproposal constraint Lp2p.

papers.abstract: Vision-language anomaly detectors describe normal and abnormal appearance with text, and their gains are commonly credited to the semantic content of these descriptions. This attribution is plausible in the zero-shot setting, but few- and full-shot detectors interpose a trained visual adapter, and in that setting it has not been isolated. Changing a description changes both its meaning and its geometry, so accuracy comparisons cannot separate the two. We ask what a fixed pair of text embeddings, or anchors, contributes to such a detector: semantic content, effective scale, or joint anchor geometry. For a single anchor pair, the answer is effective scale alone. The score reads the anchors only through their difference, and a trained adapter can rotate to follow any replacement direction, leaving that direction, and with it the linguistic content, unidentifiable. We prove that replacement anchors with the same difference-vector length permit exactly the same probability maps and attainable losses. Across seven medical datasets, three vision backbones, both supervision regimes, and three adapter families, scale-matched random and orthogonal anchors track correct prompts; breaking the scale match opens a gap that restoring it closes without text. The same pattern holds in MVFA and when MadCLIP's learned prompts are replaced by a text-free learned scale. When one adapter serves many categories, the answer expands to their joint arrangement. Rotating all category axes together changes nothing, as predicted. For the tested CLIP prompts, these axes are nearly collinear, and meaning-free rotations that spread them apart improve performance on both industrial benchmarks. Even under frozen zero-shot transfer, a random anchor frame transfers as well as the prompt frame: coordinate consistency, not meaning. What these detectors read from their prompts is scale and arrangement, not semantic content.
authors: Arda Baris Basaran, Mesut Ceylan, Elgar Fleisch, Filipe Barata
bullets: A single anchor pair contributes only through its difference-vector scale; its direction and semantic content are unidentifiable after adapter training.
Scale-matched random or orthogonal anchors reproduce correct-prompt behavior, while mismatched scale causes performance gaps.
With multiple categories, joint anchor arrangement matters: rotating all axes together has no effect, but spreading nearly collinear prompt axes can improve performance.
These findings hold across seven medical datasets, three vision backbones, two supervision regimes, and multiple adapter settings.
Even in frozen zero-shot transfer, coordinate consistency—not prompt meaning—explains comparable performance.

Middle: with one adapter serving many categories, a shared rotation preserves the arrangement of their axes; independent rotations keep each scale but change the arrangement. Right: a frozen adapter cannot rotate, so it must keep the anchor frame it was trained with, which need not be linguistic. Embeddings are schematic.

papers.abstract: Erasing all furniture from a single room image to generate its empty counterpart is valuable for XR applications such as diminished reality and virtual staging. The challenge is twofold: inpainting the furniture regions with realistic content, and doing so without distorting the room's 3D geometry. Prompt-driven image editors, such as FLUX.2, handle realism impressively, but their structural faithfulness is inferior to explicit layout conditioned inpainting. To improve geometric consistency, we propose a training recipe for finetuning a LoRA on 2,500 furnished-empty room pairs. FLUX.2 with our LoRA adaptor significantly improves geometric consistency while retaining the high texture fidelity. This single-photo inpainter can be an effective building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.
authors: Prakhar Kulshreshtha, Brian Pugh, Zachary Nussdorfer, Salma Jiddi
bullets: Addresses single-image room defurnishing for diminished reality and virtual staging.
Targets the trade-off between realistic inpainting and structural faithfulness.
Finetunes a LoRA using 2,500 furnished–empty room pairs.

Designed as a building block for depth-aware and 3D-consistent XR pipelines.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts. We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively. Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for $\pi_{0.5}$, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.
authors: Hanwen Cui, Yuanyuan Li, Qing Guo, Zhida Zhang, Chao Chen, Xi Chen, Jie Cao
bullets: Controlled ablations in FastWAM and OpenWAM isolate future-video prediction while holding architecture, initialization, data, and training steps fixed within each family.
Predictive supervision substantially improves success on clean, seen tasks: +24.38 and +72.91 percentage points in FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.
Trajectory analysis suggests gains reflect better execution within existing trajectory patterns, not only shifts in which patterns occur.
Under unseen tasks and environmental randomizations, improvements are inconsistent or absent, with both models performing poorly in the evaluated shifts.
Adding a lightweight training-only Transformer predictor to π₀.₅ raises success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that large pretrained video diffusion models are not required in this setting.

papers.abstract: A chunky gold-tone chain necklace bought online for 2.43 USD was photographed four ways: worn with formal attire against a wood-panelled wall, worn at a party, worn with casual clothing in a recycling yard, and laid flat with no person present. We asked six frontier language models to estimate its price in 1,164 independent and sequential API sessions (4,604 logged rows) and compared estimates across settings. Among the four models that answered image prompts, the same necklace was priced 1.9 to 3.3 times higher in the formal photograph than in the flat-lay (all p < 0.01). Against the yard photograph, the ratio ranged from 1.23 (Grok 4.5, not significant) to 3.57 (Kimi K3), with Claude Fable 5 at 3.32. A text-only version of the task, in which the setting is described in words, produced formal-to-yard ratios of 2.2 to 3.9 in all six models, so the effect does not require pixels. Flat-lay estimates themselves were 7.8 to 18.7 times the receipt price, so part of any headline "outfit multiplier" computed against the receipt is baseline overestimate, not a context effect. A single instruction to ignore clothing and setting significantly reduced the effect in one model (ratio of ratios 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.91) and not detectably in the others; telling the model the photo came from a company website or a personal account changed nothing significant. Asked afterward whether a different outfit would have changed their number, Claude Fable 5 said yes in 24 of 24 sessions, GPT-5.6 in 69%, and GPT-4o in 18%, while GPT-4o also refused 79% of image estimation prompts. The study isolates a mechanism with one object and one wearer at about 10 sessions per model and condition; we outline the replication needed next, with multiple objects and a human benchmark. Data, code, and raw outputs are released.
authors: Brianne Lee
bullets: The necklace’s formal-photo estimates were 1.9–3.3× higher than flat-lay estimates across responding models.
Formal settings also raised estimates relative to a recycling-yard scene, with effects varying by model.
Text-only descriptions produced similar context effects, indicating the bias does not require visual pixels.
Flat-lay estimates already exceeded the $2.43 receipt price by 7.8–18.7×, inflating receipt-based outfit multipliers.
An instruction to ignore context reduced the effect significantly in only one model; the study used one object and calls for replication across objects and human benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Tabular data is widely used in scientific applications, where complex layouts, including multi-level headers, merged cells, captions, and footnotes, make information extraction difficult. This is particularly important in pharmacokinetics (PK), where values must be correctly associated with the drug, species, dose, administration route, unit, and experimental condition. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduce adaptation cost but do not explicitly incorporate relationships between table values and surrounding headers. We introduce HARP-LoRA, a hierarchy-conditioned rank projection method for low-rank adaptation in scientific table understanding. HARP-LoRA extends projected LoRA by constructing token-specific intrinsic representations from the row- and column-header hierarchies of each data token. These representations condition the low-rank down-projection, incorporating hierarchical context while keeping the pretrained model and random projection tensors frozen. We evaluate HARP-LoRA on 950 manually annotated PK tables from 587 scientific articles and on WikiTableQuestions (WikiTQ) using Llama~3.2 3B, Llama~3.1 8B, and Gemma~3 27B. With Llama~3.1 8B, HARP-LoRA achieves a PK F1-score of 57.64\% and WikiTQ accuracy of 53.15\%, improving over LoRA by 1.42 and 6.56 points, respectively. With Gemma~3 27B, it achieves the best PK F1-score of 70.63\% and WikiTQ accuracy of 56.87\%. These results use only 172K, 197K, and 547K trainable parameters, far fewer than LoRA and TableLoRA. Overall, conditioning lightweight adapters on table-header hierarchies improves extraction from scientific tables and reasoning over flatter general-domain tables while maintaining parameter efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/hosseinsholehrasa/HARP-LoRA
authors: Hossein Sholehrasa, Mohammadhossein Amini, Doina Caragea, Remya Ampadi Ramachandran, Dan Wu, Zihang Shi, Zelin Li, Lindsey Hulbert, Eder Martinez, Xuan Xu, Majid Jaberi-Douraki

Evaluated on 950 annotated PK tables from 587 articles and WikiTableQuestions across Llama and Gemma models.
Using Llama 3.1 8B, it improves over LoRA by 1.42 PK F1 points and 6.56 WikiTQ accuracy points.
The approach uses only 172K–547K trainable parameters and reaches 70.63% PK F1 with Gemma 3 27B.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.
authors: Bahaeddin T\"urko\u{g}lu
bullets: Introduces Transformers and pre-training as the foundations of next-token text generation.
Explains fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, RAG, chain-of-thought prompting, and tool-using agents.
Covers efficiency techniques including FlashAttention and QLoRA, plus long-context use.
Provides tables, a life-cycle overview, and a checklist for evaluating claims.
Warns about data contamination, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and the need to check factual accuracy separately from helpfulness.

papers.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.
authors: Meryem Koksal, Yunzhe Wang, Volkan Ustun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing action-conditioned video world models, which typically support one agent or small fixed groups.

Introduces FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching for joint multi-agent video generation.
The abstract reports improved agent detection in density-matched settings and better rollout fidelity with diffusion forcing.
Provides a controlled testbed rather than a claim of broad real-world performance; its scope is artificial-life simulation.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP typically rely on independently parameterized transformer blocks across depth. We investigate the extent to which these blocks can instead be reused recurrently while preserving the transferable capabilities of CLIP. We study recursive transformer backbones in which a small set of $N$ transformer blocks is applied $M$ times per forward pass. By holding $N \cdot M$ fixed to the depth of a standard ViT-B, our models preserve computational depth while progressively increasing parameter sharing. We consider two recursive CLIP model families: rCLIP, where only the vision encoder is recursive, and r$^2$CLIP, where recurrence is also introduced in the text encoder. We study these models under both direct contrastive training and through knowledge distillation from a strong ViT-B/16 teacher pretrained on DFN-2B, using the substantially smaller CC3M and CC12M datasets. We evaluate the resulting models on zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval, and further study their adaptability through few-shot learning, visual grounding, and concept unlearning. Our results show that CLIP can tolerate substantial recurrent block reuse, although its effect depends on the encoder and downstream task. Recurrence also provides parameter efficiency by construction, since fewer distinct transformer blocks need to be stored and adapted. Our results establish recurrent block reuse as a practical design space for vision-language models and highlight its implications for knowledge transfer, downstream adaptation, and parameter efficiency.
authors: Szymon Mazurek, Alberto Presta, Micha{\l} Byra
bullets: Replaces independently parameterized transformer layers with a small set of blocks reused recurrently across depth while preserving total computational depth.
Introduces rCLIP with recursive vision encoding and r²CLIP with recurrence in both vision and text encoders.
Studies direct contrastive training and distillation from a strong ViT-B/16 teacher using smaller CC3M and CC12M datasets.
Evaluates zero-shot classification, cross-modal retrieval, few-shot learning, visual grounding, and concept unlearning.
Finds recurrence is a practical parameter-efficiency design space, but its benefits and costs depend on the encoder and downstream task.

papers.abstract: Adapting general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) to medical visual question answering (VQA) is valuable for helping clinicians read images and make diagnoses, but annotated data are scarce and provide only short answers, without reasoning annotations. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) fits these labels but overfits to them and amplifies their biases, eroding out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. Reinforcement learning (RL) better preserves generalization but never uses the gold answer as a training target: GRPO-style algorithms learn from the contrast between correct and incorrect answers within a group of sampled responses, so all-correct or all-wrong groups give no correctness signal. Existing SFT-RL hybrids either apply SFT and RL in separate stages or switch between them per question, or need reasoning traces from experts or stronger models, which medical VQA data lack. We propose GRASP, which combines RL and SFT in every update using only short answers: RL lets the model explore its own reasoning, SFT teaches the gold answer after that reasoning to supply the direct supervision RL lacks, and their balance adapts to how well the model answers each question. Tuning only about 1% of the parameters with LoRA, GRASP outperforms all compared training objectives both in domain and on OOD open-ended questions across Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3-8B and Gemma 3-4B. On an OOD benchmark spanning eight imaging modalities, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B beat all 10 compared general and medical VLMs in open-ended accuracy, including models trained on up to 2,600 times more data or with over 250 times more trainable parameters. We release MedTerse, a dataset of 12.9K short-answer questions, and our code at https://github.com/sea-comet/GRASP-MedVQA.

bullets: Addresses SFT overfitting and RL’s weak signal when sampled responses are all correct or all wrong.

On an eight-modality OOD benchmark, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B outperform 10 compared general and medical VLMs.
Introduces MedTerse, a 12.9K-question short-answer dataset, and releases the implementation.

papers.abstract: Visual-token compression is usually evaluated by clean accuracy and efficiency, but these averages do not reveal failures that compression introduces under an image shift where the uncompressed model stays correct. We introduce VTC-AUDIT, which estimates this incremental risk only on pairs where the full model is correct on both images and the compressed model is correct on the clean image. The four arms then cross two binary choices: which image selects the retained token positions, and which image supplies the visual features. We audit three open 8-9B vision-language models on four tasks and eight pre-specified shifts. We evaluate two training-free compressors---hard-pruning DivPrune and prune-and-merge ApET---at a matched 25% retained-position budget, producing 708,000 inference records. Reselecting positions on the shifted image, rather than reusing the clean-image positions, raises the failure rate in all six model-compressor settings. The increase is 3.04-9.60 percentage points for DivPrune and 2.05-4.20 percentage points for ApET, with every 95% interval above zero. Repeating the audit on a separately resampled second manifest reproduces all six increases. In a pooled monitor audit across the four benchmarks, support Jaccard instability fails the practical AUROC criterion of 0.65 in all six settings, whereas clean compressed-model uncertainty clears it. Thus, support turnover is a weak ranking signal under the audited benchmark mixture, while clean compressed-model uncertainty is substantially more informative. These results suggest that future visual-token compression evaluations should report conditional reliability alongside clean accuracy and efficiency.
authors: Isaac (Rucheng), Li
bullets: Measures incremental risk only when the full model remains correct under both clean and shifted images and the compressed model is correct on the clean image.
Crosses whether retained token positions and visual features come from the clean or shifted image, auditing hard-pruning and prune-and-merge compressors at a matched 25% budget.
Across three vision-language models, four tasks, and eight shifts, selecting positions from the shifted image increases failure rates in all six model–compressor settings.
The increases are reproduced on an independently resampled manifest, supporting the robustness of the finding.
Support Jaccard instability is a weak ranking signal, while clean compressed-model uncertainty is more informative in the pooled audit.
