papers.abstract: Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.
authors: Mingtian Tan, Vasileios Tzoumas
bullets: Targets corruption of online disturbance learning caused by treating all residual gradients equally.
Retains DAPL’s random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares residual adaptation.
Compares current gradients with short- and long-term memories to classify adaptation regimes.
Uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates and recover after persistent domain shifts.
In numerical tests with four mixed disturbances, DGC achieved the lowest mean position RMSE among the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: We introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim-Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra's observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.
authors: Haibao Yu, Jiaqi Meng, Zijian Zhang, Bowen Jing, Lei Yang, Yue Hu, Chenchen Ge, Yiming Hou, Chenbo Xin, Dawen Ye, Haifang Qin, Jin Li, Weitao Zhou, Jianing Qiu, Jiankai Sun, Dandan Zhang, Zaiqing Nie, Ping Luo, Ding Zhao

Astra’s real-world success rates were 80.0% (L1), 47.6% (L2), and 0.0% (L3); simulation rates were 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%.
Simulation and real-world outcomes closely matched: 10 of 16 tasks had identical success counts, while the other six differed by one success in three trials.
Recurring limitations involved spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordinating local progress toward task completion.

papers.abstract: Vision--language models applied to medical question answering can reach correct diagnoses without using the diagnostic image, inferring instead from the clinical vignette. We ask whether this is visible in how \emph{firmly} a model holds its answer: does a model defend a diagnosis derived from a blank placeholder as tenaciously as one derived from a real medical image? Crossing an image-substitution protocol with two levels of adversarial pressure on 60 Italian State Examination items, we find no evidence that ungrounded verdicts are more fragile. In a paired item-level analysis, fabricated consensus (L4) overturns 94.4\% of verdicts with the real image and 98.1\% without ($\Delta = +0.037$; one-sided 95\% upper bound $+0.105$); contentless doubt (L1) overturns 62.5\% and 51.8\% ($\Delta = -0.107$, 95\% CI $[-0.209, -0.001]$), the point estimate running opposite to the direction a grounding detector requires. The two levels nonetheless produce opposite \emph{dynamics}: under L4 the model flips once, always to the exact option argued for (110/110 first-turn flips), and then freezes, averaging 1.9 verdict changes over ten turns; under L1 it never settles, averaging 7.4 changes. Instability under contentless doubt tracks intrinsic item ambiguity rather than evidence availability, and so does not serve as a grounding signal. Flips are almost entirely corrupting (99/100 across both levels). The model is not unaware of the missing evidence---it flags the blank image at baseline on 35 of 60 items and abstains on 4--6---yet those abstentions do not survive contact with pressure. None of the epistemic signals a user could plausibly consult distinguishes a grounded diagnosis from a confabulated one.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of visual grounding reliability in medical VLMs; relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Conviction Without Evidence: Verdict Stability Is Independent of Visual Grounding in Medical Vision--Language Models
papers.tldr: Medical vision–language models defend diagnoses based on blank images about as firmly as those based on real images, so verdict stability does not reveal visual grounding.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
authors: Sooyoung Kwon, Carlee Joe-Wong, Kyunghan Lee
bullets: Targets onboard VLA inference, where processing hundreds of visual tokens causes high prefill latency.
Finds that reuse is effective for low-drift tokens, while pruning is preferable for high-drift tokens.
Uses a calibrated drift threshold and cache age to classify tokens as reusable, invalid-and-recompute, or prune.
A fixed recomputation budget directly controls latency.

On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, remains within 3 percentage points of full recomputation while reducing Jetson AGX Orin prefill latency by up to 48%; with 7% of tokens recomputed, it exceeds the strongest LIBERO-Object baseline by 24.4 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of TRIAGE. Shallow layers mark each token as important (blue) and its cache as invalid (red). The budget B goes to important, invalid tokens first; every other token is reused if valid and pruned otherwise, so B alone sets the prefill latency.

Fig. 5. TRIAGE lies on the Pareto frontier in every setting. Success rate versus prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin (top) and an RTX 3090 (bottom), averaged over the LIBERO suites or the SimplerEnv settings; dashed: Pareto frontier. No baseline is both more accurate and faster.

Fig. 1. Recompute only what neither reuse nor pruning can handle. Blue: important tokens; red: tokens changed since frame t−1 (stale caches). Reuse-only recomputes every changed token (18) and prune-only every important token (17). TRIAGE recomputes only tokens that are both (7), reuses valid caches, and prunes the rest.

Fig. 2. Drift decides between reuse and pruning. (a, b) Reuse − prune action error ∆ (Eq. (2), ×10−3) versus drift of the probed tokens on LIBERO-Spatial; blue region: reuse is better. Black: pooled over cache ages (95% bootstrap CI); thin: individual ages. Reuse is never worse below δ = 0.3 (dashed) but clearly worse above 0.5. (c) Drift grows with cache age (median, solid; 90th percentile, dashed), so the age limit T rarely binds.

Drop-all / keep-all prune / reuse every non-recomputed token. Drop-all degrades steadily and keep-all collapses below B = 46, while TRIAGE leads VLAPruner by 24.4 pp at B = 18.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLA inference acceleration via joint token reuse and pruning with drift-based cache validity fits VLA and token/KV efficiency.
papers.title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
papers.tldr: TRIAGE combines token reuse and pruning based on cache drift to reduce VLA prefill latency while preserving near-full-recomputation robot performance.

papers.abstract: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size $N$. On streaming replays of LongMemEval and LoCoMo, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at $N=8$ reaches 87-100% at $N=2048$, across embedding models and for explicit and implicit cues; LLM judges show the same growth from a lower base. We prove that a gate with false-alarm rate $\alpha$ operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about $-\ln(1-\alpha)/N$, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and, under regular variation, makes it decay as a power of $N$ with an explicit constant. The resulting prediction matches the hit rate of a per-$N$ oracle threshold to within one percentage point. The analysis explains why lexical and semantic channels need thresholds growing like $\ln N$ and $\sqrt{\ln N}$, and why per-cue normalisation roughly doubles the hit rate at matched false alarms. A cue-swap conformal gate, which compares the current cue with the user's other cues on the same store, needs no labels and has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability; on LongMemEval it holds false alarms near 5% at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold. Three annotators (Fleiss' $\kappa=0.63$) find that about nine in ten false alarms are genuine interruptions. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale
authors: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
bullets: A threshold calibrated for 5% false alarms with 8 memories produces 87–100% false alarms at 2,048 memories across embedding models and cue types.
Theoretical analysis links store size to per-item false positives, forcing operating points toward the far-left ROC curve and causing hit rates to decay with scale.
Thresholds must grow roughly as ln N for lexical similarity and √ln N for semantic similarity; normalizing per cue can roughly double hit rates at matched false alarms.
A cue-swap conformal gate requires no labels and maintains about 5% false alarms on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold.
Annotators judged about 90% of false alarms to be genuine interruptions, highlighting the practical cost of proactive recall.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes proactive memory recall in LLMs as a multiple-testing problem, analyzing the trade-off between hit rate and false alarms as the memory store size scales.
papers.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
papers.tldr: Proactive memory recall becomes dramatically harder as the memory store grows because controlling interruptions creates a multiple-testing tradeoff that sharply reduces hit rates.

papers.abstract: In formal systems such as Lean 4, efficiently finding answers to mathematical problems and generating verifiable proofs is an important task in automated mathematical reasoning. In the traditional way where an upstream solver provides multiple candidate answers, the common workflow requires searching for proofs for each candidate separately, incurring redundant computational cost. To this end, we propose a joint proof framework that integrates candidate answer selection, answer supplementation, and formal proof generation into a unified reasoning process. At its core is a trained prover that selects given or proposes new answers and generates a proof for at least one answer in a single call. Joint proof can also reuse generated proofs to check for faithfulness errors. For problems with a unique answer, if two distinct answers both obtain verifiable proofs under the same formal statement, this confirms the statement does not faithfully preserve the original problem semantics. On MATH-500, AMC 2023, and AIME 2024/2025/2026, our framework achieves the same formal proof success rate as per-candidate proof generation with about one sixth of the token cost, and identifies at least 6.1% of the formalized statements as unfaithful without requiring additional judges. Our model and code are available at https://github.com/Linppz/Gobble-Prover.
authors: Pengzhen Lin, Ke Zhang, Maziar Raissi, Zhouxing Shi
bullets: Addresses redundant proof searches when an upstream solver supplies multiple candidate answers.
Uses a trained prover to select existing answers, supplement new ones, and produce a verifiable proof in one call.
Reuses generated proofs to detect faithfulness errors in formalized statements.
On MATH-500, AMC 2023, and AIME 2024/2025/2026, matches per-candidate proof success with substantially lower token cost.
Identifies at least 6.1% of formalized statements as unfaithful without additional judges.

Arrows go from each base prover (per-candidate) to our Gobble-Prover (joint proof). The third panel plots accuracy under a per-problem token budget (x-axis), pooling both prover pairs. Solve rates and detection rates are almost the same across candidate set sizes.

Figure 2: An unfaithful formal statement lets two values pass Lean. The problem asks how many kids share 12 candies when each gets 4, so the answer is 3, but the formalizer only asks which number divides 12 (dropping the condition that each kid gets 4), so every divisor of 12 becomes provable. Code A proves the statement with 3 (since 12 = 3 · 4) and Code B with 6 (since 12 = 6 · 2), two proofs (type 1); Code C proves both values in one proof (type 2). The only difference between the two types is whether the two values are proved in the same generation; our training additionally rewards type 2. Candidate 5 (not a divisor of 12) fails under all three codes.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a joint proof framework for formal systems (Lean) that reduces token cost while maintaining proof success rates for mathematical reasoning.
papers.title: Efficient Proof Generation for Lean Statements with Multiple Candidate Answers
papers.tldr: A unified Lean 4 framework jointly selects or proposes answers and generates proofs, matching per-candidate success while using about one sixth the token cost.

papers.abstract: Significant advancements in 3D asset creation have enabled high-fidelity 3D generation from images. However, most existing representations remain inherently static, lacking the ability to model physically plausible behaviors under dynamic interactions. We present \textbf{PhysCreator}, a unified framework that directly generates simulation-ready 3D representations with spatially varying physical properties from images. Unlike prior approaches that treat physical attributes as simple post-hoc predictions or rely on expensive per-instance optimization, we reformulate physical property estimation within a unified 3D representation learning framework. We introduce a voxel-aligned latent space by lifting image observations into a spatially structured 3D representation, in which geometry, appearance, and physical properties are jointly modeled and inferred in a feed-forward manner. To enable scalable learning without densely annotated physical ground truth, we leverage vision-language distillation to transfer material-aware semantic priors from powerful vision-language models into spatially grounded voxel-level supervision. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior visual quality, physical plausibility, and generalization compared to prior approaches.
authors: Shiyan Zheng, Ming Li, Lei Han, Xiangyu Xu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static 3D representations that cannot model physically plausible behavior under interaction.
Uses a voxel-aligned latent space to jointly infer geometry, appearance, and physical properties.
Applies vision-language distillation to provide spatially grounded, material-aware supervision without dense physical annotations.
Experiments report improved visual quality, physical plausibility, and generalization over prior approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of PhysCreator. Top: Given observations, our framework first constructs a voxel-aligned latent representation (the 3D latent). Built upon this shared representation, we decode simulation-ready 3D Gaussian primitives together with voxel-wise physical attributes, including Young’s modulus, density, Poisson’s ratio, and material category. Bottom: To provide scalable supervision, vision-language distillation generates part-level semantic and physical annotations, which are lifted into voxel-level labels for training the physical-material decoder. The predicted geometry and physical properties are then passed to an MPM simulator to evaluate and visualize dynamic behavior.

Figure 4 Effectiveness of spatially varying physical property modeling. Top: PhysCreator enables the flower to sway while keeping the pot stable, and allows the snow body to deform while preserving the hat; PhysGM produces implausible deformation due to uniform properties. 1D samples across time (space–time slices highlighted by dotted lines) are included to better visualize the temporal dynamics. Bottom: PhysCreator localizes motion to the flower while keeping the pot and chair stable, whereas PhysGM causes all components to move together. The blue dashed axes highlight this unintended coupled motion.

Figure 1 We present PhysCreator, a physics-aware 3D generative model that produces simulation-ready 3D Gaussians with spatially-varying, semantically-consistent physical properties directly from images. Our method enables the joint prediction of geometry and physically meaningful attributes, such as material type, stiffness, and density, with strong generalization across diverse objects. The generated 3D Gaussians can be seamlessly integrated into simulations, yielding realistic and dynamic physical behaviors.

Figure 3 Qualitative comparison of simulated dynamics under gravity. PhysCreator produces stable and physically consistent motion with realistic contact and deformation. In contrast, OmniPhysGS exhibits structural collapse after impact with the ground, while DreamPhysics and PhysGM show unrealistic local deformation.

Figure 5 Qualitative comparison of text-conditioned physical control under identical wind forces. PhysCreator produces distinct prompt-consistent bending for “soft” and “hard,” whereas DreamPhysics shows limited responsiveness. The pink dashed curves indicate bending trajectories.

Table 3 Mean relative errors (↓) of physical-property predictions. Young’s modulus and density are evaluated in logarithmic space because of their large dynamic ranges, whereas Poisson’s ratio is evaluated in its original scale. “–” indicates that the corresponding method does not predict this property, using a manually selected value for simulation instead.

Table 4 Quantitative comparison of text-conditioned physical control. Higher property ratios indicate stronger responsiveness to the corresponding semantic prompts. PhysCreator demonstrates substantially stronger control than the baseline method (Huang et al., 2025).

Table 1 Quantitative comparison across multiple object categories in terms of semantic consistency (CLIPsim,%), user-study score (Uscore), and per-object runtime cost. PhysCreator∗ denote our model with multi-view input. Best and second-best results are shown in bold and underlined, respectively. The proposed algorithm achieves consistently favorable semantic and human-evaluation scores while maintaining efficient inference.
Table 2 Quantitative comparison of geometry reconstruction quality. PhysCreator achieves a lower Chamfer Distance and a higher F-score, indicating more accurate and complete surface reconstruction.

papers.selection_reason: Unified feed-forward 3D asset generation with physical attributes; fits 3D foundation model interest.
papers.title: PhysCreator: Creating Physically-Attributed 3D Assets at Will
papers.tldr: PhysCreator generates simulation-ready 3D assets from images with spatially varying physical properties in a single feed-forward framework.

papers.abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) has attracted considerable interest by enabling local clients to continually acquire knowledge from new tasks. However, most FCL methods assume that the global server has prior knowledge of the arrival times and number of categories for new tasks, which is unrealistic in the real world. Furthermore, they neglect the importance of positive inter-task semantic relationships when learning new tasks and are significantly affected by irrelevant relationships from old tasks, thereby exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To resolve the above challenges, we develop a novel Task Relevance-driven Prompt Expansion (TRPE) model. Specifically, to eliminate the reliance on prior knowledge of new tasks, we propose an out-of-distribution detector to identify the arrival of new tasks within local clients, along with a radius-adaptive DBSCAN to infer the quantity of categories in new tasks on the proxy server. Moreover, to explore positive inter-task relationships, we calculate the affinity between the original gradient for learning new task and its gradient orthogonal to the feature space of old tasks to evaluate semantic relevance between old and new tasks from a global perspective. Then, we use this global task relevance to determine the key-prompt pair for new tasks and identify highly related old tasks. After concatenating their prompts for training, we can leverage such positive inter-task relations to improve the continual learning of newly arriving tasks. To balance the learning of new tasks and the forgetting of old ones, a soft orthogonality constraint is applied to the local key and prompt gradients. Experiments spanning diverse datasets and backbones confirm the efficacy of our TRPE model.
authors: Jiahua Dong, Wenqi Liang, Yang Cong, Yichen Li, Hongyuan Yu, Henghui Ding, Yulun Zhang, Salman Khan, Fahad Shahbaz Khan
bullets: Addresses unrealistic assumptions about known task arrivals and category counts in federated continual learning.
Uses an out-of-distribution detector locally and radius-adaptive DBSCAN on a proxy server to detect new tasks and infer their category counts.
Measures global semantic relevance between new and old tasks through gradient affinities.
Expands prompts by selecting relevant key-prompt pairs and concatenating related task prompts.
Applies a soft orthogonality constraint to balance learning new tasks with retaining old knowledge; experiments across datasets and backbones support its efficacy.

papers.abstract: Non-rigid structure from motion (NRSfM) aims to recover camera motion and time-varying 3D shape from tracked 2D image measurements. Recent high-performing methods show that shape-space factorization remains highly effective for this task. These methods often use costly solvers for two key steps. First, a semidefinite programming (SDP) cone solver to perform Euclidean correction. Next, an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver to recover the low-rank shape. These steps often scale poorly to long sequences and dense point tracks. We propose a fast, scalable NRSfM solver that avoids these costly steps. For rotation estimation, we introduce a differentiable Euclidean correction that directly optimizes small factors for each sequence. A row-polar projection then maps each estimated camera block to the closest row-orthonormal matrix. For shape estimation, we introduce an unrolled spectral-proximal solver. It combines reprojection-gradient steps with weighted singular-value shrinkage in the reshuffled shape domain. This solver further uses FISTA-style restart and continuation. The spectral shrinkage operator itself is classical, but we embed it in a fixed differentiable solver, while preserving NRSfM's geometric constraints. The proposed approach is category-agnostic, requires no external training data, and maps naturally to modern accelerator-friendly linear algebra primitives. Across sparse, dense, noisy, missing-data, and long-sequence benchmarks, our solver achieves substantial speedups with competitive reconstruction accuracy, including 7x-1000x runtime improvements on dense sequences with 28,887 tracked points.
authors: Suryansh Kumar
bullets: Targets the poor scalability of conventional Euclidean-correction and low-rank-shape solvers for long sequences and dense tracks.
Estimates camera rotations by directly optimizing small factors, followed by row-polar projection to enforce row-orthonormality.
Recovers shape with an unrolled spectral-proximal solver combining reprojection gradients, weighted singular-value shrinkage, FISTA-style restart, and continuation.
Works across sparse, dense, noisy, and missing-data settings without external training data.
Reports 7×–1000× runtime improvements on dense sequences with up to 28,887 tracked points while maintaining competitive accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Accuracy-runtime and dense-sequence behavior. (a) Accuracy-runtime Pareto comparison on CMU MoCap [5]. Smaller, faded markers show individual sequences, while larger markers show method averages (lower left is better). The proposed solver achieves the fastest runtime while retaining competitive reconstruction accuracy relative to recent shape-space baselines. (b) On dense sequences [18] with 28, 887 tracks, the proposed solver achieves large runtime gains over recent shape-space baselines such as TSM [57] and OPM [33], while retaining competitive accuracy.

Figure 4. (a) Overall compute time comparison with current SOTA approaches [33, 57] on [26] dataset. Observation: Our approach compute time is significantly better as the number of frames and points increases (for e.g., Tearing seq. with F = 405, P = 132). (b) Our approach compares favorably with other methods on missing dataset sequence.

Figure 9. Detailed computational pipeline of the proposed nocone, no-dual approach. papers.abstract: Understanding how individual token choices affect reasoning length is important for characterizing reasoning models. Building on prior findings that changing the first reasoning token (hereafter, the first token) can substantially alter reasoning length, we focus on this initial choice to investigate how its influence operates during subsequent generation. One possibility is that the first token changes the early text that follows, which in turn affects reasoning length. However, replacing only the first token of an existing reasoning prefix and resuming generation substantially changes the remaining reasoning length, even though all other prefix tokens are unchanged. To trace this persistent influence, we compare next-token distributions while varying only the first token and find that sensitivity is concentrated at a small set of generation positions. Blocking attention from these positions to the first token reduces the length gap between first-token conditions. Using next-token distributions from a different first-token condition at these positions also substantially changes subsequent reasoning length. Together, these findings suggest that attention to the first token at a few sensitive positions helps sustain its length effect, illustrating how a local token choice persistently influences a sequence-level outcome.
authors: Ruochen Liu, Hao Yan, Ziluowen Luo, Senzhang Wang, Sihong Xie
bullets: Changing only the first token can substantially alter the remaining reasoning length, even with the rest of the prefix fixed.
The study compares next-token distributions across different first-token conditions to trace this influence.
Sensitivity to the first token is concentrated at a small number of generation positions.
Blocking or replacing first-token-dependent information at these positions reduces or changes the resulting length differences.
The findings suggest a local token choice can sustain a sequence-level effect through later attention interactions.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a standard representation for real-time novel-view synthesis. Yet, its quality-efficiency trade-off still relies heavily on adaptive density control. Existing cloning, splitting, and pruning rules use proxy signals, such as position gradients, opacity, and image-space error. Although effective in practice, these signals do not directly answer the structural question behind density control: where should new Gaussians be allocated to reduce the multi-view reconstruction loss, and which existing primitives can be pruned with minimal penalty. To address this, we propose first-variation birth-death control for 3DGS, a principled approach that replaces heuristic structural decisions with a variational score derived from the reconstruction loss. At each structural update, we freeze the current Gaussian population, attach auxiliary mass coordinates to each primitive, and differentiate the multiview loss with respect to these coordinates. We demonstrate that this score is a coordinate of the first variation of the Splat Regression Model, giving a rigorous local descent surrogate for birth-death moves: high-score Gaussians are selected as birth sites, while low-score, low-opacity Gaussians are selected for removal. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, integrating this score into 3DGS-MCMC yields state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and outperforms existing methods, delivering the most significant gains under tight Gaussian budgets. Ultimately, our work provides compelling evidence that gradient-based variational metrics offer a principled alternative to proxy heuristics in 3DGS.
authors: Quan Tran Hong, Long Nguyen-Chi, Binh T. Nguyen
bullets: Targets the problem of deciding where to add Gaussians and which to prune to reduce multiview reconstruction loss.
Introduces first-variation birth-death control using loss gradients with respect to auxiliary mass coordinates attached to each Gaussian.
Uses high-score Gaussians as birth sites and removes low-score, low-opacity primitives.
Integrated into 3DGS-MCMC, the method achieves state-of-the-art quality on standard 3DGS benchmarks and outperforms existing approaches.
The reported benefits are strongest when the number of Gaussians is tightly constrained.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the score-guided birth–death controller. A batched multiview backward pass computes the first-variation score qi = −∂F̂t(m)/∂mi|m=1. Higher scores explicitly predict a larger first-order loss reduction from assigning mass to that primitive. Guided by these scores, the controller kills low-opacity, low-score slots and births new capacity at high-score parent sites using the 3DGS-MCMC transitions.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models are costly to serve because they are large and because they generate long chains of thought (CoT). Weight pruning and CoT compression address these two costs separately, but they interfere in that pruning adds redundant reasoning on problems the model still solves and incomplete reasoning on those it no longer solves, and on harder problems makes the model less compressible by subsequent length-preference optimization. We trace this to a blind spot on each side: pruning criteria do not distinguish necessary from redundant reasoning, and preference-based CoT compression receives no training signal on problems a pruned model always or never solves. We propose Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), which identifies neurons enriched in redundant reasoning by contrasting their activations on long and short correct solutions of the same problem and prunes them preferentially, and we extend preference pairs to the problems a pruned model always or never solves. Pruning 20\% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combination uses 8--22\% fewer thinking tokens on four math benchmarks than pruning with reasoning-aware calibration (RAC) followed by the same compression, with accuracy within 0.5 points.
authors: Tao Jing, Chen Kang, Feifei Zhai, Pengyuan Liu, Dong Yu
bullets: Pruning and chain-of-thought compression can interfere: pruning may induce redundant or incomplete reasoning and reduce later compressibility.
The method, Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), contrasts neuron activations between long and short correct solutions to identify neurons associated with redundant reasoning.
It also adds preference-training pairs from problems a pruned model always solves or always fails to solve.
With 20% pruning of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combined approach used 8–22% fewer thinking tokens across four math benchmarks than RAC followed by the same compression.
Accuracy remained within 0.5 percentage points of the comparison pipeline.

papers.title: Improving the Chain-of-Thought Compressibility of Pruned Reasoning Models via Long--Short Contrastive Pruning

papers.abstract: Extracting salient information from long-horizon dialogue histories remains a significant challenge for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to the restricted context windows and efficient retrieval challenges. Current methods typically rely on history organization or local token-level optimization, suffering from information loss, retrieval redundancy, and myopic attention. Inspired by the view in cognitive science that dialogue constitutes sense-making and memory association, we propose CoLink, a framework that enhances LLMs' global context awareness in domain-specific multi-turn dialogues through information linking and compression. CoLink first clusters historical contexts into topic graphs to establish cross-semantic associations with external knowledge. Guided by the adaptive control of thought, it then retrieves and activates knowledge via synergizing semantic relevance and graph-structural topology. Crucially, to achieve effective compression of history and knowledge, we ground multi-turn dialogues in information theory and derive a principled optimization objective for extracting the core sense-making information. Coupled with a competitive slot mechanism, CoLink condenses the global context into dedicated memory and knowledge slots, efficiently distilling lengthy, redundant inputs into an extremely compact latent representation. Extensive empirical results on both public and our MMD datasets validate CoLink's superiority and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.
authors: Lian Yan, Zhenbo Xia, Haotian Wang, Chen Tang, Yi Guan, Jie Liu, Jingchi Jiang
bullets: Addresses context-window limits, information loss, redundant retrieval, and myopic attention in long-horizon dialogue modeling.
Builds topic graphs to connect dialogue history with external knowledge across semantic relationships.
Retrieves knowledge using both semantic relevance and graph topology.
Uses an information-theoretic objective and competitive slots to distill dialogue and knowledge into compact latent representations.
Experiments on public and MMD datasets support its effectiveness and generalizability in knowledge linking and sense modeling.

papers.abstract: Language models switch tasks from demonstrations, but vision still often relies on separate systems for restoration, editing, and stylization. A before--after example offers a shared instruction only if the transferable change can be separated from the scene that demonstrates it. We introduce CrossPair, which adapts a pretrained multimodal image editor to transfer diverse transformations from one exemplar pair. Exemplar-before, exemplar-after, and query images take fixed roles in its native VLM and VAE pathways: the VLM extracts operation semantics, while the VAE retains fine appearance and structure. A training-only, change-aware DINOv3 objective aligns feature-change directions across content-distinct scenes, guiding the output to follow the demonstrated relation without an inference-time encoder. We construct Transform-360K by grouping filtered pairs from conditional representations, restoration, editing, virtual try-on, and stylization under shared transformations. On Relation252K-derived seen and held-out transformations, \method improves target agreement and edit-direction similarity over released systems. Ablations show that the semantic and visual exemplar routes are complementary and that DINO relation alignment further strengthens transfer; Transform-360K training also improves aggregate held-out-operation scores.

Introduces Transform-360K, a dataset grouping filtered image pairs by shared transformations.
Improves target agreement and edit-direction similarity on seen and held-out transformations; ablations support complementary semantic/visual routes and relation alignment.

papers.abstract: Conveyor belts are vital arteries in continuous bulk material handling, particularly in heavy process industries such as cement manufacturing. Undetected structural anomalies (longitudinal tears, holes, degraded patch repairs, and impact punctures) cause catastrophic belt snapping, costly downtime, and severe safety hazards. While deep learning offers high accuracy, existing models rely on power-hungry workstation GPUs, hindering practical deployment at remote industrial edge points. In this paper, we propose, implement, and validate an end-to-end, low-power edge AI vision system for real-time conveyor belt defect detection deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 accelerated by a Google Coral Edge TPU coprocessor. The system leverages an optimized YOLOv11 nano (YOLOv11n) architecture trained on a multi-source industrial corpus exceeding 3,000 augmented samples from an operational cement plant in West Java, open-source datasets, and automated captures. The model undergoes post-training full integer quantization (INT8) compiled for systolic tensor execution. Experimental results demonstrate robust detection capability, achieving precision of 0.742, recall of 0.730, and mAP@0.5 of 0.764 across four defect classes. Deployed on-site in an IP-rated enclosure interfaced with an RTSP PoE industrial camera, the system achieves stable throughput of 30-40 FPS at 320x320 resolution with an end-to-end latency of 70-90 ms. Operational profiling under harsh clinker dust confirms thermal equilibrium at 55 +/- 5 deg C on the host CPU and ~65 deg C on the Edge TPU with zero frame loss. This demonstrates that edge AI bridges the gap between high-accuracy computer vision and cost-effective predictive maintenance in continuous manufacturing.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in image editing have enabled fine-grained and highly controllable visual modifications. However, achieving similar levels of controllability in video editing remains an open challenge, particularly for precise local edits, dynamic temporal effects, and consistent lighting across frames.In this paper, we propose EditDistill, a framework that distills image-level visual transformations from edits to guide video editing.Specifically, given a source video and an edit prompt, we first generate an edited version of the initial video frame using an off-the-shelf image editing model. We then distill the visual transformation of this original-edited image pair into a compact representation termed an edit descriptor.This descriptor is injected into a video diffusion model through our lightweight fusion module, which steers the denoising process toward the desired edit. To align the video trajectory with the demonstrated image edit while preserving motion and layout, we train with edit-descriptor alignment and DINO structural consistency losses, and derive an equivalent inference-time guidance formulation under flow matching.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance on standard benchmarks and produces high-quality video editing results across diverse scenarios. For more details and videos, please refer to the anonymous webpage: https://yu-shaonian.github.io/EditDistill-Web/.
authors: Guojun Lei, Hong Li, Hongbing Yang, Lixue Gong, Chi Wang, Zheng Dong
bullets: Addresses the challenge of precise local edits, dynamic effects, and consistent lighting in videos.
Generates an edited first frame, then distills the source–edited image transformation into an edit descriptor.
Injects the descriptor into a video diffusion model through a lightweight fusion module to steer denoising.
Uses edit-descriptor alignment and DINO structural consistency losses to preserve motion and layout.
Reports strong benchmark performance and high-quality results across diverse video-editing scenarios.

Stage II keeps the Wan2.1-I2V-14B video diffusion frozen and trains the inject modules to inject d into selected transformer blocks by lightweight feature fusion modules steering the diffusion denoising toward the desired edit to produce a temporally coherent video V e from the video V s.

The Delta VAE encoder extracts a stochastic descriptor from the source and edited VAE latents by combining shared features, their explicit feature difference, and a multi-scale encoder. The Delta VAE decoder receives only the source latent and descriptor, and reconstructs the edited latent through descriptor-conditioned residual blocks with self- and cross-attention.

papers.abstract: The stance expressed in responses from retrieval-augmented generation systems is significantly influenced by the stance distribution of the retrieved materials. Existing research on knowledge poisoning has primarily targeted factual errors. In contrast, this study focuses on injection attacks in which the facts are correct but the stance on a controversial issue is one-sided. At a mean topic-level poisoning share of 18.9% within the post-injection ProCon documents, all four generation models from different vendors exhibited stance shifts aligned with the poisoning direction; across four concentration levels, the shifts increased monotonically. This paper proposes a Stance-Balancing Middleware positioned between the retriever and the generator. It consists of stance detection, fixed balancing (2 supporting + 2 opposing + 1 neutral), and a debiasing prompt, without introducing additional large language model calls. Across all eight concentration-direction settings, the complete method reduced the magnitude of stance deviation by an estimated 0.106 to 0.350; the six settings at poisoning shares of 11.9%-18.9% remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p <= 0.009). In the cross-model experiment, all eight model-direction combinations moved along the stance axis in the corrective direction, and seven of eight showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute distance from 0. In the concentration sweep, the post-defense intervals included 0 in all eight settings, while the cross-model pro-poisoning results retained small positive residual point estimates of +0.045 to +0.063. For 20 candidate documents, stance detection took approximately 1.5% of the median generation time on a single GPU and approximately 16% on CPU.

papers.abstract: Training a spatial VLM to answer which side an object lies on does not require it to preserve the metric displacement that determines that answer, while supervision for a distance estimate may leave categorical relations largely unconstrained. When post-training emphasizes one readout, improvements can therefore concentrate on that interface while transfer to others remains weak or even degrades; we call this observed specialization interface lock-in. ChronoReplay addresses it by replaying heterogeneous spatial supervision as chronologically ordered episodes, retaining source-native targets, and balancing supervision across families. Under the same observation access, a single ChronoReplay checkpoint improves OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench together, including a 13.41-point gain on OST-Bench, and achieves the highest three-benchmark mean among the supervision settings compared here. Same-data controls further separate the ingredients of this transfer: answer serialization redistributes gains across OST and UCS, family-balanced learning improves over ordinary joint SFT and natural turn weighting, and chronological replay exceeds a shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points across two paired seeds. Adaptive frame selection then changes evidence access while keeping the trained model fixed, providing an additional inference-time gain at lower visual cost. Streaming spatial performance depends on what distinctions supervision preserves, how heterogeneous histories are organized during learning, and what causal evidence inference makes available at test time.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Artificial Intelligence (AI) by their extraordinary capabilities, like contextual understanding, few-shot/zero-shot learning, code generation, ability to reason and problem-solving. Recent studies have shown immense work on LLMs. Yet, there is limited work on the thorough taxonomy of LLMs. This study would showcase a detailed classification of LLMs, starting with the earlier models like BERT and leading to LLMs like GPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok. We would delve into topics like datasets used to train LLMs, computational power used during training, their hardware specifications, architecture and parameters. Further, we would also look at the limitations, computational challenges and open problems as well. This study would primarily focus on the timeline of LLMs, signifying their growth over the period. Findings reveal a clear pattern: models that optimize the ratio between architectural complexity and data quality exhibit stronger reasoning stability and better alignment, without proportionally increasing the computational load. This desired balance between scaling and sustainability is the defining characteristic of the current generation of AI.
authors: Harsidak Singh Banwait, Chander Prabha
bullets: Provides a timeline and taxonomy covering models such as BERT, GPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok.
Examines training datasets, computational requirements, hardware specifications, architectures, and parameterization.
Reviews limitations, computational challenges, and open problems in LLM design.
Argues that balancing architectural complexity with data quality is associated with more stable reasoning and better alignment without proportional increases in computation.
Highlights scaling–sustainability balance as a defining direction for current AI development.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models(LLMs) have shown strong performance on tasks with verifiable answers, but many real-world queries involve subjectivity, disagreement, and conflicting evidence. Most existing benchmarks for such queries remain English-centric, overlooking the vast diversity of perspectives held by users worldwide. To systematically study how LLM perspectives vary across languages, we curate PerspectivesQA, a manually verified multilingual dataset of globally contested topics covering 18 languages, and propose ROOTS, a framework that profiles linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity. We evaluate a diverse set of eight models covering both open-source and proprietary families at varying scales, establishing that LLMs hedge their answers in English but commit to positions in lower-resource languages. Larger models maintain a more consistent cross-lingual worldview, while smaller models are more easily swayed. All models also exhibit high sensitivity to minor surface-level input variations, producing notable stance even in larger models.
authors: Wiem Ben Rim, Yao Lu, Pontus Stenetorp, Emine Yilmaz
bullets: Introduces PerspectivesQA, a manually verified dataset of contested topics spanning 18 languages.
Proposes ROOTS to measure linguistic, perspective, and framing diversity in LLM responses.
Across eight open-source and proprietary models, English answers hedge more while lower-resource-language answers commit more strongly.
Larger models show more consistent cross-lingual worldviews; smaller models are more easily swayed.
All evaluated models remain sensitive to minor wording changes, including larger ones.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Stance shift rate across models on DebateQA. We remove all instances where the model refuses or gives an irrelevant answer. All languages can provide different stances from English, but Amharic, Kazakh, Swahili and Hindi have the biggest shifts.

Figure 7: Degeneration across models and datasets. papers.abstract: We propose a novel method for robust point cloud registration with only one tunable parameter. Our method, dubbed TLP, uses truncated $L_p$ functions with different values of $p$ to assign priority scores to correspondences, select the hypothesis, and refine the final model. By leveraging the robustness of truncated functions, TLP effectively handles the high outlier rates commonly encountered in real-world 3D feature matching. We also exploit GPU parallelization to evaluate hypotheses efficiently, enabling registration from thousands of correspondences in under a second on average. With only one tunable parameter, our method offers greater practicality than multi-parameter methods that require dataset-specific tuning of several parameters. Evaluations on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that TLP achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art single-parameter methods. Furthermore, it outperforms two widely used multi-parameter methods on three of the four evaluated datasets while maintaining competitive runtime.
authors: Seong Hun Lee, Patrick Vandewalle, Javier Civera
bullets: Addresses high outlier rates in real-world 3D feature matching.
Uses truncated $L_p$ functions to prioritize correspondences, select hypotheses, and refine the final model.
GPU parallelization evaluates thousands of correspondences in under a second on average.
Outperforms state-of-the-art single-parameter methods and beats two multi-parameter methods on three of four benchmark datasets.
Offers practical tuning with competitive runtime, though performance varies across evaluated datasets.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a promising approach for fast, high-quality novel-view rendering. However, its large parameter size remains a bottleneck for storage and transmission. We propose RacerGS, a compact 3DGS compression framework that achieves scene reconstruction at significantly reduced storage sizes with preserved fidelity. To obtain compact and spatially coherent features, we design a hash projection model that projects the anchor hash encodings into compact context features. Additionally, we introduce a FiLM-modulated autoregressive GRU context model that utilizes causal dependencies among anchor feature groups and uses recurrent hidden states to refine entropy-model parameters, improving bitrate efficiency. Furthermore, we adaptively entropy-code quantized anchor-attribute residuals relative to their context-predicted means, leveraging spatial consistency to reduce symbol entropy. Overall, RacerGS achieves more than 150x compression over vanilla 3DGS and 28x over Scaffold-GS, while providing comparable rendering quality. Extensive experiments across five datasets demonstrate that RacerGS outperforms prior 3DGS compression methods in both storage reduction and rate-distortion performance.
authors: Wenqing Wang, Huimin Zeng, Yun Fu
bullets: Addresses the large storage and transmission cost of 3DGS.
Projects anchor hash encodings into compact, spatially coherent context features.
Uses a FiLM-modulated autoregressive GRU to model causal dependencies and refine entropy parameters.
Entropy-codes quantized anchor-attribute residuals relative to context-predicted means.
Reports over 150× compression versus vanilla 3DGS and 28× versus Scaffold-GS, with comparable quality across five datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Pipeline overview. The refined parameters are combined with the spatial prior to form an accurate Gaussian mixture model for residual entropy coding.

papers.abstract: Scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting allows one scene representation to serve different Gaussian-count budgets, yet its quality-budget curve may lag behind models optimized separately for each budget. Reducing the number of Gaussians changes both the selected members and the reconstruction tasks carried by the survivors; parameters inherited from a high-budget model may fit a low-budget representation poorly. We propose ParetoGS, which describes member changes and parameter evolution with a small set of adapted budget anchors and decodes intermediate budgets without separate optimization at every requested count. ParetoGS alternates pruning and fixed-member adaptation to build nested anchors with persistent identities, and encodes their parameter changes relative to the full model in a compact residual atlas. At decoding, it interpolates the states of shared members and gradually introduces the rendering contributions of new members, connecting sparse anchors into a continuous-budget representation. Across 13 scenes, ParetoGS attains better average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with fewer Gaussians than the compared prefix methods at 10% of each method's own full model. From a shared full model, it also outperforms FlexGS-imp at its trained 1%, 5%, and 10% budgets and NanoGS-imp at the 1% and 0.1% budgets. On Garden, its non-anchor quality approaches an empirical reference from independently optimized GNS models at higher retention ratios and exceeds it at some lower-budget points. Across 13 scenes, encoding reduces mean additional state from 390.0 to 85.7 MB with an average PSNR change of 0.01 dB. Project page: https://xiaobin2001.github.io/ParetoGS-Web/
authors: Xiaobin Deng, Changyu Diao, Min Li, Duanqing Xu
bullets: Addresses quality degradation when pruning a high-budget Gaussian model for lower budgets, where surviving parameters may no longer fit well.
Builds nested, persistent-identity anchors through alternating pruning and fixed-member adaptation.
Stores parameter changes in a compact residual atlas and decodes intermediate budgets by interpolating shared members and gradually adding new members.
Across 13 scenes, improves average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over prefix methods at 10% retention and outperforms several budget-trained baselines at selected budgets.
Reduces mean additional encoding state from 390.0 MB to 85.7 MB with only a 0.01 dB average PSNR change.

papers.abstract: High-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting training increases pixel and Gaussian-tile intersection counts, expanding rasterization caches that coexist with projection and gradient state at peak memory. A complete-view update aggregates gradients across the view; each region's forward and backward caches can be released after its contribution is collected. BoundedGS separates rasterization and projection backward passes and bounds the active local rasterization working set according to its measured load. Candidate-indexed projection and compact gradient storage address the view-level peaks exposed by this change, while CPU-assisted structure rebuilding and bounded image supply manage resources outside rendering. In a resolution sweep at a fixed count of about 6M Gaussians, the measured rendering working set stays within 1.073-1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K; at 11K, a warm pass takes 19.79 seconds versus 21.76 for full-frame execution. Across five native 5K outdoor scenes, full training reduces the mean rendering working set from 9.97 to 1.76 GiB (82.3%), retains similar reconstruction quality, and shortens training time from 36.7 to 33.9 minutes. Project page: https://xiaobin2001.github.io/BoundedGS-Web/
authors: Xiaobin Deng, Changyu Diao, Min Li, Duanqing Xu
bullets: High-resolution 3DGS exceeds memory limits because rasterization caches grow alongside projection and gradient state.

At roughly 6M Gaussians, rendering memory remains nearly constant at 1.073–1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K resolution.

papers.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used in different stages of scientific knowledge production, including the suggestion of references. These models can operate at different levels of reasoning effort and provide summaries of their reasoning processes. This raises two questions: Does increasing reasoning effort improve the verifiability of generated references, and do the resulting reasoning summaries reveal how the model's behavior changes with greater effort? We examined summaries from GPT-5.5 as it generated scholarly references for 1,000 papers under paired low- and high-effort settings. Generated references were matched to external bibliographic records, and reasoning summaries were scored for four predefined features and explored for additional features discovered by GPT-5.5. High effort increased the mean paper-level resolver-verified reference rate from 78.3% to 84.8%, and produced longer reasoning summaries. All four predefined features received higher scores under high effort. The discovered features changed less uniformly: some appeared equally often in both conditions, whereas others were more common under high effort. Within each effort condition, neither feature set showed a consistent increase in verification rates with higher scores.
authors: Melika Mobini, Andres Algaba, Vincent Ginis
bullets: The study compares low- and high-effort GPT-5.5 reference generation for 1,000 papers.

Bottom: Reasoning summaries are scored on predefined features and on model-discovered features derived by GPT-5.5, using a 1–5 scale from absent to strong, with GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 serving as judges. papers.abstract: Modern surgical AI increasingly requires multimodal understanding rather than isolated perception, yet existing datasets remain largely limited to single-task supervision such as recognition or templated question answering. Current medical VQA resources often rely on synthetic templates, lack natural descriptive supervision, or provide sparse annotations that hinder reasoning about spatial relations and procedural context. We introduce MIS-VQA, a surgical vision-language dataset generated through an annotation-driven pipeline that converts heterogeneous surgical annotations into structured textual scene representations. Using EndoVis18 and CholecT50, we transform phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation labels into unified contexts that guide large language models to generate clinically coherent question-answer pairs. MIS-VQA supports four response types-concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning-enabling hierarchical evaluation from atomic visual grounding to compositional reasoning. To address annotation sparsity, we incorporate confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks, enabling spatially grounded supervision at scale. MIS-VQA establishes a unified benchmark for surgical vision-language understanding with spatial supervision and multi-tier reasoning evaluation. To demonstrate its utility, we introduce LLaVA-SurgXpert, a family of surgical vision-language models with visual encoders to analyze how visual representations influence multimodal reasoning. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines while revealing capability gaps between perceptual grounding and higher-level reasoning hidden in prior benchmarks.

Builds unified scene contexts from phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation annotations in EndoVis18 and CholecT50.
Provides four response types: concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning.
Uses confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks to scale spatially grounded supervision.
Introduces LLaVA-SurgXpert models and reports improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines, while exposing gaps between grounding and higher-level reasoning.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enables flow-matching models to acquire complementary capabilities from specialized teachers through supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, different evaluation dimensions, such as aesthetics and OCR accuracy, and different tasks, such as image generation and editing, emphasize different aspects of the denoising process, suggesting that their effective supervision may occur at different stages. Existing methods typically select supervision states from predefined timestep distributions, which may overlook these phase-dependent differences and incur unnecessary computational overhead. This motivates two critical timing decisions: when to adaptively query teachers for effective supervision based on the evolving generative process, and when to skip the remaining rollout to avoid redundant computation. In this paper, we introduce PhaseOPD, a phase-aware query-and-skip framework that identifies generative phases online from revisions of predicted-clean latents, using existing student velocity predictions without additional model evaluations. For each task-assigned teacher, PhaseOPD selects a supervision state based on its phase preference and skips the unused rollout suffix once all query decisions are finalized, preserving the single-query velocity-distillation objective. On SD3.5-M, PhaseOPD executes only 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch, reducing training time by 41.3% relative to DanceOPD while improving Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores.
authors: Renye Yan, Junyi Zhan, Jikang Cheng, Wei Peng
bullets: Different tasks and evaluation goals may need teacher supervision at different denoising stages.
The framework identifies phases online from changes in predicted-clean latents, reusing student velocity predictions without extra model evaluations.
Task-specific teachers are queried at preferred phases, while unnecessary rollout suffixes are skipped after query decisions are complete.
On SD3.5-M, it uses 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch and reduces training time by 41.3% versus DanceOPD.
It also improves Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores in the reported setting.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary instance segmentation (OVIS) provides a promising solution for marine perception by recognizing and segmenting categories beyond predefined label spaces. Existing OVIS methods usually rely on vision-language alignment, where visual region features are matched with textual category embeddings to recognize both seen and unseen classes. However, this alignment assumption becomes fragile in underwater environments. Color attenuation, scattering, turbidity, and low contrast distort visual appearance, causing region features to deviate from their corresponding semantic concepts. As a result, the similarity between degraded visual features and textual classifiers becomes unreliable, which particularly weakens the recognition of unseen underwater categories that cannot be corrected by category-specific supervision. To address these issues, we propose GeoPrompt, a geometry-conditioned prompt learning framework for underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation. Our key insight is that geometric structure is more stable than visual appearance in degraded underwater scenes. Specifically, GeoPrompt introduces a geometry-guided visual adaptation module (GVAM) to extract depth-derived structural priors and inject them into multi-scale visual features. It further develops a geometry-conditioned prompt learning (GCPL) that generates geometry-aware textual classifiers from structural representations. These geometry-aware classifiers are integrated with fixed and image-conditioned textual classifiers to improve open-vocabulary semantic alignment. Experiments on the MARIS-OpenIS benchmark show that GeoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance and brings consistent improvements on underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation.
authors: Shanshan Han, Yuxi Wang, Can Qin, Yujie Chen, Cong Pan, Haitao Li, Guoqiang Zhong
bullets: Underwater degradation distorts visual features, making text-based recognition—especially for unseen categories—unreliable.
The method extracts depth-derived structural priors and injects them into multi-scale visual features.
It generates geometry-aware textual classifiers and combines them with fixed and image-conditioned classifiers.
Experiments on MARIS-OpenIS report state-of-the-art performance with consistent improvements.

GCPL generates geometry-aware textual classifiers and integrates them with fixed and image-conditioned classifiers for geometry-conditioned vision-language alignment and openvocabulary instance mask prediction.

Appearanceonly predictions are prone to incomplete masks or inaccurate localization, while pseudo-depth maps reveal object contours and spatial layout. By leveraging depth-derived geometry, GeoPrompt produces more complete and reliable open-vocabulary instance predictions.

papers.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of LLMs suffers from catastrophic forgetting, and prevailing mitigation strategies struggle to reconcile the plasticity-stability dilemma. To address this, we propose Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization (ECHO), a closed-loop control framework. By decomposing the KL divergence, we identify output entropy as a dominant observable component of KL variation. This enables us to leverage entropy as a computationally efficient online proxy to monitor forgetting risks in real-time, bypassing expensive reference-model inference. Consequently, ECHO employs an elastic controller that dynamically modulates the gradient weight of replay data via a proportional control law, using deviations from the pre-trained entropic equilibrium as an error signal. Empirical evaluations across 0.6B to 9B parameter architectures demonstrate that ECHO lies on, and in several comparisons extends, the observed plasticity-stability frontier and maintains high operational robustness against varying data mixing ratios.
authors: Shangxi Wu, Xiaorong Yan, Xiaojun Meng, Yuxiang Zhang, Jiansheng Wei
bullets: Addresses the plasticity–stability trade-off in supervised fine-tuning of LLMs.
Decomposes KL divergence to identify output entropy as an efficient proxy for monitoring forgetting risk.
Uses a proportional controller to adjust the gradient weight of replay data based on deviations from pretrained entropic equilibrium.
Evaluations across 0.6B–9B models place ECHO on, and sometimes beyond, the observed plasticity–stability frontier.
Shows robustness across varying data-mixing ratios.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence models must retain earlier information. Full attention keeps all past tokens but grows expensive, and recurrent-memory models compress history into fixed slots for linear-time processing. Limited capacity makes writes consequential: distractors can interfere with useful content, while skipped evidence cannot be recalled. Existing multi-slot memories write every token to the same number of slots, merging whether to store it with how many slots to update. We introduce Factorized Write Routing (FWR), which first keeps or skips each token and then chooses a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Queries still read all slots. Across ten seeds on two synthetic tasks that query facts after long contexts, we observe a density-dependent reversal. With four slots per write, long-context accuracy favors always writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs 0.337), but learned selective writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs 0.048). The tested adaptive rule underperforms fixed allocation under the learned gate on both tasks. A diagnostic oracle given fact labels unavailable at deployment reaches 0.372 on Passkey, showing headroom in filtering distractors. The results suggest avoiding missed writes in information-dense contexts and filtering distractors when they dominate.
authors: Chen Chen, Rui Cheng
bullets: Recurrent memories compress long histories into fixed slots, making write decisions critical: distractors cause interference and skipped evidence is unrecoverable.
Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first decides whether to keep or skip each token, then selects a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots to update.
Across two synthetic long-context tasks and ten seeds, always writing outperformed selective writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs. 0.337).
Selective writing outperformed always writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs. 0.048).
The tested adaptive slot-allocation rule underperformed fixed allocation, while an oracle fact filter showed remaining headroom on Passkey.

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors built on diffusion transformers run tens of denoising steps. Training-free acceleration either reuses features across steps (step caching) or stops computing the regions an edit leaves untouched (region freezing), and the two have been combined before. We ask how a high speed-up target should be split between them. On Qwen-Image-2.1, freezing does more than remove tokens: it lowers the cost of every step, so the step cache can reach the same overall speed-up with a conservative threshold that keeps its error small. A per-step cost model fitted on development runs predicts held-out latency with a median error of 4.0% and reproduces the speed ceilings of the region methods we re-implemented (2.73$\times$ predicted vs. 2.70$\times$ measured for RegionE). Driving frozen tokens to the model's one-step $x_0$ estimate beats returning them to the reference image on every development sample, and in 90% of measured cases the composed error stays below the sum of the two individual errors. The resulting method, FreezePlan, keeps five full steps and gives the rest of the budget to TaylorSeer. On a pre-registered test split it runs 5.05$\times$ faster end to end at 29.8 dB PSNR to the original output, with no significant drop in a VLM judge score; TaylorSeer at 5.02$\times$ reaches 23.5 dB. The curve extends to 5.99$\times$ at 28.0 dB. Swapping in the region selectors of prior methods under our schedule lowers median PSNR by only 0.5--0.6 dB, which places the gain in the schedule and budget split rather than in the selector.
authors: Baiyan Li, Ganxuan Yang
bullets: Region freezing reduces the cost of every denoising step, allowing step caching to operate in a lower-error regime.
A fitted per-step cost model predicts held-out latency with 4.0% median error and accurately estimates method speed ceilings.
Using the model’s one-step x₀ estimate for frozen tokens outperforms restoring the reference image across development samples.
FreezePlan keeps five full steps and allocates the remaining computation budget to TaylorSeer.
On a preregistered test split, it achieves 5.05× end-to-end speedup at 29.8 dB PSNR with no significant VLM-judge score drop; it reaches 5.99× at 28.0 dB.

papers.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/
authors: Tianchen Guo, Tengyue Zhang, Chen Liu, Ling Chen, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces an interactive benchmark with real-world scenes and multi-turn questions, covering passive multi-view control and active exocentric exploration.
Models must query adjacent viewpoints from severely occluded views and are scored on answer quality and exploration efficiency.
State-of-the-art MLLMs often stop too early with high confidence and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometry.
Matched-view comparisons suggest the active–passive performance gap mainly stems from insufficient evidence acquisition.
GRPO-based view-seeking increases exploration but can reduce accuracy because models over-explore and fail to integrate views across turns.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the SATE-Bench Curation and Evaluation Pipeline. Our framework is constructed and deployed through four distinct stages. Steps 1 & 2 (Data Collection and Quality Control): We source dense, 360-degree multi-view captures across five cognitive spatial categories. Candidate question-answer pairs undergo a rigorous human annotation and modification loop to guarantee accuracy, clarity, and appropriate difficulty. Step 3 (Active Exploration): The multi-turn interactive evaluation setting. The MLLM is initialized with a single view and must dynamically query additional exocentric perspectives until it confidently resolves its visual uncertainty. Step 4 (Passive Observation): The single-turn control setting, where the model is provided a static, comprehensive bag-offrames to yield a direct prediction without the need for spatial view-exploration.

Increasing the action reward successfully incentivizes proactive behavior, evidenced by a sharp rise in (b) average steps and (d) active exploration rate. However, this aggressive exploration exacerbates contextual interference, leading to a steady decline in (a) active accuracy and (c) average reward. In contrast, the model’s passive accuracy remains highly stable across all reward configurations.

Figure 4. Taxonomy and qualitative examples of SATE-Bench tasks. Our benchmark evaluates multi-view spatial reasoning across five core cognitive dimensions: Counting, Existence, Pose and Physical Interaction, Global Relative Proximity, and View-Specific Spatial Geometry.
