papers.abstract: Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However, greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile these goals, we introduce \ours, a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. \ours constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query, structural--semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, \ours improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average while reducing answer-context length by 58.55\%. Our code is available at the $\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE}{repository}$.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models to new tasks, but identifying which weight changes support the resulting behavior remains difficult. Weight-space interpretability assigns semantic descriptions to these changes, called fine-tuning deltas. Such descriptions leave open how much task performance depends on the identified updates, particularly when other updates can support the same predictions. We address this gap by pairing reversion, which restores selected parameters to their pretrained values, with retention, which keeps only selected fine-tuning updates. We evaluate Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models on synthetic financial charts, Flowers102, EuroSAT, and FGVCAircraft with ViT-L/14, and on Flowers102 with ViT-B/16, using a shared recipe that tunes the final six visual blocks. Our contributions are threefold. First, attention value-output (VO) updates alone recover 43-87% of the accuracy improvement, although reverting them leaves chart accuracy unchanged. Cross-entropy loss preserves this contrast on Charts and EuroSAT, while correct-class score margins reveal additional contributions. Second, VO weights recover more loss improvement than all ten equally sized, layer-matched random subsets in each setting. VO and multilayer perceptron (MLP) retentions jointly correct 25-81% of pretrained errors, demonstrating overlapping recovered behavior, which we call operational redundancy. Third, removing semantically selected directions reduces VO-retained recovery more than matched-random removal in all five settings. Together, these results distinguish semantic alignment, removal cost, and retained recovery as complementary evidence about the functional role of fine-tuning updates within the evaluated CLIP recipe.

bullets: Fine-tuned CLIP models are evaluated on synthetic financial charts, Flowers102, EuroSAT, and FGVCAircraft using ViT-L/14, plus Flowers102 with ViT-B/16.

VO updates recover more loss improvement than matched random subsets across all evaluated settings.
VO and MLP retentions jointly correct 25–81% of pretrained errors, indicating operational redundancy in recovered behavior.
Removing semantically selected directions harms VO-retained recovery more than matched-random removal in all five settings.

papers.abstract: Indoor IoT cameras can support assisted living and activity-aware spaces, but exporting raw RGB frames raises privacy concerns by exposing facial, clothing, and household details that body-motion tasks often do not require. We present StickFigure, a pose-only IoT camera system that, during real-time monitoring, keeps raw frames local and ephemeral while exporting only compact skeleton streams sufficient for downstream human activity recognition (HAR). While pose estimation has matured on GPUs, extracting accurate pose streams on resource-constrained IoT cameras remains difficult. To overcome these challenges and enable on-device pose streams on (almost) any IoT camera, we present two core designs in StickFigure: an activation-aware pose backbone that allocates channel capacity after spatial downsampling and a lightweight hierarchical MLP refiner that selectively corrects elbow and wrist coordinates using intermediate visual features and kinematic context. We fully implement StickFigure and evaluate it on public benchmarks and real-world deployment. Compared with state-of-the-art MCU pose models, StickFigure achieves the highest pose accuracy and downstream HAR utility on both NTU RGB+D and Penn Action, while using 96.5% fewer parameters and 99.3% fewer MACs per frame than RTMPose-S-based baselines, achieving 0.107 s p95 latency on a representative STM32H753 MCU. We believe StickFigure establishes a new operating point for privacy-aware edge vision on massive IoT cameras.

Achieves strong pose accuracy and downstream HAR utility on NTU RGB+D and Penn Action benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map a language instruction and the current observation directly to actions, without checking whether the instruction has been completed. For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished. Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs. The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps. Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights. To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations. RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot.
authors: Jie Wang, Bo Zhang, Renzhi Lu, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses unnoticed failures in VLAs that can leave long-horizon tasks incomplete.
Uses code to coordinate a full-task VLA, a completion checker, and an atomic-skill VLA in a closed loop.
The coding agent selects which VLA executes actions and does not require updating the full-task VLA’s weights.
Introduces LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge, built from existing LIBERO demonstrations.
Improves X-VLA and π₀.₅ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, especially for long-horizon tasks, and recovers failures on a real robot.

Both policies stay frozen, so the same program wraps X-VLA and π0.5 without retraining. papers.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.
authors: Shahriar Kabir Nahin, Xiao Ye, Muhao Chen, Ben Zhou, Anshuman Chhabra
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between draft-model inference latency and distributional alignment with the target model.
Uses latency-aware structured pruning plus knowledge distillation to formulate draft-model design as an optimization problem.
Prunes up to 92% of the target model while maintaining strong speculative decoding performance across multiple domains and target-model scales.
The resulting draft models can plug into other token-alignment and distillation methods for additional gains.
Scope: effectiveness depends on measured latency and cross-entropy alignment with the target model’s responses.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction is important for embodied agents operating in complex environments whose semantic categories extend beyond fixed taxonomies. While recent studies have explored open-vocabulary occupancy in outdoor driving scenarios, indoor environments remain challenging due to dense occlusions, complex geometry, and fine-grained long-tailed semantics. To reduce the need for expensive voxel-level semantic annotations, we study a geometry-only supervision setting requiring only binary occupancy labels. We build upon Language-Embedded Gaussians as a unified representation coupling 3D geometry with language-aligned semantics. For geometry learning, we introduce an opacity-aware Poisson-based Gaussian-to-Occupancy formulation that enables stable volumetric aggregation under binary occupancy supervision. For semantic learning, we render Gaussian features into images and align them with a frozen open-vocabulary model, together with Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing during Gaussian splatting. Building on this framework, we further introduce Instance-Level Semantic Consistency to alleviate fragmented object predictions, and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to provide informative and less redundant multi-view semantic supervision. We also extend our framework to outdoor driving scenarios to evaluate its generality across substantially different environments. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves strong open-vocabulary occupancy performance, validating the effectiveness and generality of our framework. Code will be available at https://github.com/JuIvyy/LegoOcc.
authors: Changqing Zhou, Yueru Luo, Han Zhang, Zeyu Jiang, Changhao Chen
bullets: Targets indoor and outdoor scenes with dense occlusions, complex geometry, and long-tailed semantics beyond fixed taxonomies.
Uses binary occupancy labels for geometry, with an opacity-aware Poisson Gaussian-to-occupancy formulation for stable volumetric aggregation.
Aligns rendered Gaussian features with a frozen open-vocabulary model and applies Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing.
Introduces Instance-Level Semantic Consistency and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to improve fragmented and redundant multi-view predictions.
Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show strong performance and cross-environment generality.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Framework Overview. From a monocular image, a feed-forward Gaussian model produces Language-Embedded Gaussians. Training proceeds along two paths: Semantic learning, we differentiably render Gaussian features to the image with Progressive Temperature Decay and align them to a training-free open-vocabulary segmenter via a cosine objective Lfeat; Geometry learning, we convert Gaussians to occupancy using an opacity-aware Poisson-based Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator and supervise binary occupancy with Locc. At inference, the Language-Embedded Occupancy supports text-driven queries by computing cosine similarity between voxel embeddings and prompt embeddings, yielding open-vocabulary semantic occupancy without dense voxel-level semantic labels during training.

Fig. 6: Qualitative results on Occ-ScanNet. From top to bottom: (a) input images; (b) ground-truth semantic occupancy; (c) results from our re-implemented LOcc [23]; (d) LegoOcc; and (e) LegoOcc++. All compared open-vocabulary methods are trained with geometry-only supervision and evaluated using the closed-vocabulary annotations of Occ-ScanNet.

Fig. 5: Covisibility-aware support-view selection. Each example shows a reference view (left) and four support views. Fixed temporal selection often produces highly redundant observations (top). Our method filters views with either insufficient overlap or near-duplicate content according to geometric covisibility, and selects pose-diverse views from the remaining candidates (bottom), providing complementary observations while preserving shared scene geometry.

Fig. 1: Closed- vs. open-vocabulary occupancy. Conventional closed-vocabulary methods [5], [6] can recognize only categories predefined during training. In contrast, our openvocabulary formulation aligns language with 3D occupancy and supports text queries for arbitrary categories. Right column (Random Class): text-conditioned voxel scores are visualized as heatmaps, where darker red indicates a higher response to the queried category.

Fig. 7: Open-vocabulary qualitative comparison. Legends list the VLM-extracted object nouns used as text queries. (a) Input image. (b) Open-vocabulary 2D segmentation for the queried nouns. (c) LegoOcc 3D open-vocabulary occupancy, colored by the same categories. (d) LegoOcc++ 3D open-vocabulary occupancy, colored by the same categories.

Fig. 3: Comparison of temperature schedules. Linear decay decreases τ uniformly, whereas our exponential schedule rapidly approaches Tmin, allocating more iterations for the model to adapt to the low-temperature regime.

Fig. 8: Qualitative results on Occ3D-nuScenes. We show surround-view input images and semantic occupancy predictions from GaussTR and LegoOcc++, together with the ground truth. LegoOcc++ better preserves the overall road layout and longrange scene structure, yielding more complete occupancy predictions.

Fig. 4: Instance-level semantic consistency. Given an input image (left), a frozen open-vocabulary teacher (e.g., Trident [36]) provides semantic cues in image space (middle), which can be spatially fragmented and incomplete for the same object. In contrast, SAM produces category-agnostic instance masks (right) that more coherently capture complete object extents. We aggregate teacher features within each reliable SAM mask to form an instance-level semantic prototype, and encourage rendered LE-Gaussian features inside the same instance to align with this shared prototype.

TABLE II: Quantitative performance of 3D occupancy methods on the Occ3D-nuScenes dataset. We compare methods that do not rely on LiDAR supervision. Frames denotes the number of temporal frames required at inference, and methods requiring more than one frame are shown in gray. IoU scores for “others” and “other flat” classes are consistently zero and thus omitted. “Cons. veh.” denotes construction vehicles, and “drive. surf.” denotes drivable surfaces.

TABLE I: Monocular results on Occ-ScanNet. †We re-implement POP-3D [58] and LOcc [23] for the indoor monocular setting, and supervise geometry with ground-truth binary occupancy instead of the authors’ LiDAR-derived pseudo labels. We also adopt DepthAnything-v2 [70] as the backbone and use the same input resolution and training recipe as ours for fair comparison. For POP-3D, we project voxel centers to the image plane and sample language-aligned features at those locations to form a 3D grid of text-aligned embeddings for open-vocabulary reasoning. For LOcc, we prompt Qwen2.5-VL-7B [71] to extract object names and use Trident [36] to obtain training-free open-vocabulary segmentations.
TABLE VI: Model profile. FPS is measured on the same machine with a single RTX 4090 GPU, averaged over 1,000 runs after 100 warm-up runs.
TABLE IV: Ablation on temperature scheduling. We vary the temperature range (Tmin, Tmax), the test-time temperature τtest, and the scheduling strategy. “×” denotes no schedule.
TABLE III: Ablation on the Gaussian-to-Occupancy operator. We compare three aggregation rules: GaussianFormer2, Bernoulli, and Poisson, under both closed- and open- vocabulary settings.
TABLE VII: Model profile. FPS is measured on the same machine using a single RTX 4090 GPU.

TABLE V: Comparison of LegoOcc and LegoOcc++. Starting from LegoOcc baseline, we progressively introduce covisibility-aware support-view selection (Covis.) and SAMbased instance-level semantic consistency (SAM-Inst.).

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation for autoregressive (AR) video generation commonly first initializes an AR student and then refines it with distribution matching distillation (DMD). This refinement process faces two challenges. First, although initialization already yields a reasonably capable student, DMD obtains the refinement direction indirectly by estimating the full student score before forming the teacher-student correction. Second, detached-history training prevents the generator from assigning credit to a current chunk for its influence on subsequent chunks. We introduce Leta, a few-step distillation framework that addresses these challenges with ScoreDelta and FutureCredit. ScoreDelta directly estimates the teacher-student correction from denoising residuals, while FutureCredit learns an auxiliary cross-chunk update signal from vector-Jacobian products (VJPs) of next-chunk teacher residuals. Leta combines these signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in a single forward pass during generator updates. Teacher evaluations and credit VJPs are used only for estimator training. For ScoreDelta, we establish population equivalence to score-difference estimation and a conditional approximation advantage under limited capacity in a fixed-feature linear model. In our controlled experiments, Leta improves over DMD by 0.9 points on VBench and 0.66 on VideoAlign. This advantage persists at a higher generator update frequency (a generator-to-estimator update ratio of G:E=1:1), where Leta improves over DMD by 1.6 on VBench and 0.35 on VideoAlign. Project page: https://scdzx.github.io/Leta/.
authors: Zixuan Duan, Yabo Chen, Xunzhi Xiang, Xin Zhang, Haibin Huang, Yin Chen, Chi Zhang, Qi Fan
bullets: Addresses two DMD limitations: indirect score estimation and detached-history training.
ScoreDelta estimates the teacher–student correction directly from denoising residuals.
FutureCredit learns cross-chunk credit using vector-Jacobian products of next-chunk teacher residuals.
Combines both signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in one generator-update forward pass.
Controlled experiments report gains over DMD on VBench and VideoAlign, including at a 1:1 generator-to-estimator update ratio.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Literature and Linguistics Analysis Benchmark (LALA), comprising 236 open-ended questions written by experts in linguistics and literary studies, together with expert-provided ideal answers. By comparing models within families and at similar training scales using human and LLM judges, LALA identifies differences in linguistic competence associated with post-training, offering a framework for evaluating future models and guiding targeted improvements. We administered questions to 17 language models and evaluated their responses using both human expert assessment and two LLM evaluators, Sol and Qwen. Base models displayed little of the linguistic competence assessed by the benchmark, whereas their post-trained versions performed markedly better, suggesting that post-training plays a central role in making linguistic knowledge accessible and usable. Parameter count, by contrast, showed no statistically significant association with partial-credit performance, and competencies remained unevenly distributed across linguistic domains. We interpret this pattern as evidence that post-training adds linguistic competencies piecemeal, without producing a general linguistic intelligence capable of extending them beyond the learned policies that support them. Models performed best on logical relations between statements and selected discourse-level tasks, while even the strongest post-trained models continued to struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions. Human and Sol evaluations produced nearly identical model rankings in both the original and ReliableEval runs, supporting the replicability of the comparative results.
authors: Michael Foster, Barbara McGillivray, Gard B. Jenset, Jakub M\'acha, Jason Harding, Marcus Perlman, Devyani Sharma, Patrick Skeels, Jana Willer-Gold, Jeannette Littlemore
bullets: Introduces 236 expert-written open-ended questions with ideal answers spanning linguistics and literary studies.
Evaluates 17 models using human experts and two LLM judges, with largely consistent comparative rankings.
Post-trained models outperform base models, while parameter count has no significant association with partial-credit performance.
Models perform best on logical relations and some discourse tasks, but struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions.
Results suggest post-training adds competencies piecemeal rather than creating general linguistic intelligence beyond learned policies.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.
authors: Chi-Wei Chang, Mu-Tien Kuo, Kuan-Wei Lee, Meng-Hsun Tsai
bullets: The study evaluates 150 models from 25 data recipes, 3 pretraining seeds, and 2 post-training seeds using shared jailbreak prompts.
Same-pretraining-run copies have highly similar per-prompt non-refusal patterns (correlation 0.984), while changing the pretraining seed drops correlation to 0.811.
Changing the data recipe lowers correlation only slightly further, to 0.779; the pattern also holds at 150M and 300M parameters.
The best attack template transfers across pretraining seeds only 27% of the time, versus 67% across post-training seeds.
Per-prompt non-refusal behavior fingerprints the pretraining run: identification succeeds every time across 3,211 prompts and 98% of the time using 50 prompts.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Study design. papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that pretraining runs leave unique fingerprints affecting jailbreak susceptibility, providing insights into LLM robustness and data composition.
papers.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
papers.tldr: Which jailbreaks succeed depends far more on a model’s specific pretraining run than on its data recipe or safety-training seed.

papers.abstract: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
authors: Xuan He, Sining Zhoubian, Ruozhen Yang, Yuhao Wen, Zhineng Wang, Yuyang Hu, Ke Yang, Yuyu Zhang, Ping Nie, Jiawei Han, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Evaluates memory systems across multiple benchmarks and model backbones against naive RAG.

Studies how memory tax arises from system and evaluation factors and extends the concept to broader memory applications.
Advocates evaluating the net value and reliability of memory rather than standalone performance; code and results will be released.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces the concept of 'Memory Tax' to dissect the net value of memory systems in long-horizon agents, contrasting them with direct retrieval.
papers.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
papers.tldr: Dedicated agent memory can hurt performance relative to retrieving directly from raw history, so its value should be measured as benefits minus memory-induced losses.

papers.abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.
authors: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu

Tests held-out scene configurations and target changes under fixed training layouts.
Baseline action success drops from 41.6% on held-out configurations to 16.1% with changed instructions; oracle visual cues improve both settings.
Shows that perception accuracy does not consistently translate into robot behavior, motivating joint evaluation of spatial understanding and task completion.

papers.abstract: LVLM benchmarks tell us whether a model answers correctly, but not which visual conventions it has retained, nor where those conventions live. Sketches expose this hidden structure. A sketch removes texture, lighting, and photographic context while preserving the strokes humans judged sufficient for recognition. If an LVLM can operate on that abstraction, the surviving signal is structural rather than merely photometric. We introduce a training-free sketch probe with three readouts: temporal part-construction order, spatial attention-based grounding, and the mechanistic layer/head locus of grounding. We evaluate nine LVLMs on part order and five on the attention readouts, over two part-annotated sketch datasets. Three findings emerge. First, LVLM part order tracks human convention: models reproduce canonical orderings where human drawings converge, and become correspondingly variable where human orderings vary. Controls that blank, withhold, and mismatch the sketch locate this convention in the language model. Second, part-level grounding survives the abstraction: attention heads selected from the frozen model with an existing recipe recover part and object regions on object and scene sketches, with no grounding supervision. Third, the grounding signal concentrates in a narrow mid-network band whose location follows the base language model rather than parameter count in the two families we compare, and remains stable across object and scene sketches. The result is a practical diagnostic for sketch-driven LVLMs: no fine-tuning, no auxiliary segmenter, and a layer band that doubles as a head-selection prior, matching or improving grounding mAcc@0.1 in every model and dataset we tested.
authors: Chaitat Utintu, Ahmed Bourouis, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song
bullets: Introduces a training-free sketch probe measuring temporal part order, spatial grounding, and the mechanistic layer/head location of grounding.
Across nine LVLMs, part-construction order follows human conventions: canonical where people agree and variable where human order varies.
Across five LVLMs, attention-based grounding recovers object and part regions from object and scene sketches without grounding supervision.
Grounding concentrates in a stable mid-network layer band tied to the base language model rather than parameter count in the studied families.
The probe matches or improves grounding mAcc@0.1 in every tested model and dataset, without fine-tuning or an auxiliary segmenter.

papers.abstract: Camera motion recognition requires separating viewpoint changes caused by camera translation, rotation, or zoom from object motion and scene dynamics. Video-language models often rely on semantic cues and struggle with the geometric evidence needed for this task. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures such as V-JEPA offer strong spatio-temporal representations, but our experiments suggest that they underrepresent geometric cues in some regions. Under temporal-reversal supervision, V-JEPA improves overall but degrades on several motion families, whereas a weaker geometry-oriented VGGT predictor improves across all families. We refer to these geometrically underrepresented regions as geometric blind spots and propose Fovea-JEPA to identify and address them. Using V-JEPA as the base model and VGGT as a geometry expert, we construct intervention pseudo-labels from their prediction errors to weakly supervise a blind-spot predictor. The predictor produces token-wise response maps, which are aggregated into a clip-level intervention score to guide adaptive fusion of visual and geometric features. This selective intervention introduces complementary geometric information while preserving reliable visual predictions. Experiments on CameraMotionDataset, CameraBench, and ShotBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Fovea-JEPA, with gains of 9.67, 8.67, and 24.38 percentage points over previously reported state-of-the-art baselines, respectively. Code and models will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Xiangkun Shi, Hanhui Li, Shiyue Zhang, Chang Liu, Junwen Pan, Zhenbang Sun, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets geometric blind spots in video representations that hinder distinguishing camera motion from object and scene dynamics.
Uses V-JEPA as the base model and VGGT as a geometry expert to create error-based pseudo-labels for blind-spot supervision.
Aggregates token-level blind-spot responses into clip-level scores that guide adaptive fusion of visual and geometric features.
Reports gains of 9.67, 8.67, and 24.38 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art baselines on CameraMotionDataset, CameraBench, and ShotBench.
Scope: addresses camera-motion recognition through selective geometric intervention while preserving reliable visual predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Fovea-JEPA. Our dual-branch framework leverages visual-geometric complementary cues and hierarchical error-guided pseudo supervision to detect geometric blind spots. Subsequently, our framework adaptively retains robust visual semantic predictions or activates geometric compensation to correct visual prediction errors.

Figure 1: Motivation of Fovea-JEPA. Top: Fovea-JEPA estimates a blind-spot map Q and aggregates it into an intervention score q, which indicates whether intervention by a geometry expert (e.g., VGGT) is necessary. A high-q case activates geometric intervention to correct the V-JEPA prediction, whereas a low-q case preserves the original prediction. Bottom left: matchedbudget intervention controls. Applying intervention to high-q clips outperforms applying it to low-q or randomly selected clips, while retaining VGGT tokens with the highest q scores outperforms retaining those with the lowest scores or using random masks. Bottom right: Fovea-JEPA compared with state-of-the-art methods across three benchmarks.

Figure 3: Qualitative analysis of the learned intervention decisions. Each column pairs two clips with the same ground-truth camera motion. For high-q cases, q > τ activates the VGGT-guided intervention: the predictions from both V-JEPA 2.1 and VGGT are inexact, whereas Fovea-JEPA recovers the exact label set. For low-q cases, q < τ preserves the V-JEPA pathway, retaining its exact prediction despite an inexact VGGT prediction.
Figure 4: Clip-level intervention-budget analysis. The random curve is the expected same-budget accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Improves video-language models for camera motion recognition via geometric blind-spot intervention, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: Fovea-JEPA: Overcoming Geometric Blind Spots in V-JEPA for Camera Motion Recognition
papers.tldr: Fovea-JEPA improves camera-motion recognition by detecting where V-JEPA misses geometric cues and selectively injecting information from a geometry-focused predictor.

papers.abstract: Robots that learn from people often see several valid ways to do the same task: pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, open the microwave or move the kettle first. A policy that re-decides at every step can waver between these ways mid-task. We ask when the action head (the part of a policy that turns the state into actions) matters, and how it should make this choice. On a controlled task, heads that sample one way succeed far more often than a head that averages the ways when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take (+0.72 success with two ways); this trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran. We then present ElevateHead, a head that decides once at a learned decision point, commits to that choice for the episode, and exposes the choice as an input a user can set. We designed it by diagnosis: each version was frozen and tested on tasks it had not seen, and the next version changed only what a measured failure pointed to; predictions were registered before each run. The first four versions each fell below BeT on at least one held-out task. The fifth completed all four subtasks of the held-out Franka Kitchen task in 45.2% of episodes against 29.3% for BeT, the strongest baseline across our tasks (+0.160, 95% CI [+0.129, +0.188]); when a mode was forced, the first completed subtask matched it in 95% of successful episodes. Diagnosis also located where commitment breaks: varied start positions (repaired on the controlled task: commitment 0.22 to 0.81, success 0.74 to 0.91) and varied object placement (partly repaired: in an exploratory variant, commitment 0.03 to 0.59 on aligning with no detectable change in success). On held-out block stacking, version 4 was comparable to BeT and did not exceed it. A real-robot test with predictions fixed in advance is planned for a follow-up version of this paper.
authors: Tsung-Lung Yang
bullets: Per-step averaging can fail when demonstrations contain multiple valid strategies and observations do not reveal which strategy to choose; sampling performed better on one controlled task, but this trend did not generalize to all tasks.
ElevateHead selects a mode once, commits to it, and lets users set the selected mode explicitly.
Through iterative diagnosis on unseen tasks, the fifth version achieved 45.2% success on all four Franka Kitchen subtasks versus 29.3% for BeT.
Forced modes matched the first completed subtask in 95% of successful episodes, supporting controllable behavior.
Commitment was sensitive to varied starts and object placements; performance was comparable to BeT on held-out block stacking, and real-robot evaluation remains future work.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. ElevateHead in four ideas. Offline (gray): find the ways and the decision points in unlabeled demonstrations. Online (blue): at the first decision point a gate checks whether the choice is genuinely open; if so, one mode is drawn and kept for the rest of the episode; if not, the head acts without a mode.

papers.selection_reason: Action head design for multimodal imitation learning in robot manipulation.
papers.title: ElevateHead: Decide Once, Then Commit: When the Action Head Matters for Multimodal Imitation
papers.tldr: ElevateHead improves multimodal imitation by making one interpretable action-mode choice at a learned point and committing to it for the episode.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly enable robots to follow language instructions, understanding their navigation decisions becomes important for reliable deployment. Existing explainability methods overlook a key challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN): evidence for the current action may be distributed across historical and current observations and associated with different instruction stages. We identify instruction-stage insensitivity, where existing methods produce similar explanations despite changes across different navigation stages. To address this issue, we propose a stage-aware attribution framework for VLN. We first construct action-conditioned temporal instruction--visual attributions across observations. These attributions are projected into instruction space to estimate stage associations, which guide the aggregation of relevant historical evidence for refining the current explanation. An instruction-guided spatial filter further suppresses isolated responses while preserving compact, instruction-relevant regions. Experiments across multiple VLN policies and benchmarks show improved attribution quality over existing methods. We further demonstrate that our method acts as a diagnostic tool for analyzing failure cases, and validate its applicability to real-world navigation on a Unitree G1 robot.
authors: Yiyuan Yao, Xinpeng Ding, Minglei Chen, Fei Gao, Lihuo He, Jie Yuan, Aijun Li, Nannan Wang, Xinbo Gao
bullets: Addresses instruction-stage insensitivity in existing VLN explanations.
Builds action-conditioned temporal instruction–visual attributions across observations.
Projects attributions into instruction space to identify stages and aggregate relevant historical evidence.
Uses an instruction-guided spatial filter to remove isolated responses while preserving compact relevant regions.
Improves attribution quality across multiple policies and benchmarks, supports failure analysis, and transfers to a Unitree G1 robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of our framework. (a) We construct action-conditioned temporal instruction–visual attributions across historical and current observations. (b) We project each attribution into instruction space to estimate its associated instruction stage. (c) We weight historical observations by their stage correspondence with the current view and aggregate the resulting support to refine the current attribution. (d) We further use instruction–patch associations to suppress spatial noise while preserving decision-relevant visual evidence.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art methods across navigation stages. The same instruction is used throughout navigation, while the highlighted tokens are automatically induced by the action-conditioned instruction attribution at each decision step. For Steps 1, 7, and 21, we visualize early-history, recent-history, and current observations together with their attribution maps. Compared with existing methods, our explanations better follow the evolving instruction stage while retaining relevant evidence across historical and current views.

Fig. 8: Our method as a diagnostic tool for VLN policies. Our attributions reveal stage- and token-level causes of VLN failures. (a) Premature subgoal execution: attention shifts to a later subgoal too early. (b) Action-phrase neglect: the landmark is emphasized while its action phrase is underweighted. (c) Partial instruction grounding: only part of the relevant instruction is grounded.

Fig. 7: Real-world qualitative comparison on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Two representative navigation cases are shown across multiple decision steps. For each step, we compare egocentric attribution maps from DEX-AR [14] and our method, together with the corresponding third-person execution view. Our method better follows the evolving instruction stage and highlights decision-relevant visual evidence throughout real-world navigation

Fig. 1: Visual explanation challenges in VLN. (a) Explaining a generated token involves localizing its visual evidence while reducing interference from preceding tokens. (b) Explaining a navigation action requires recovering temporally distributed evidence across historical and current observations, while suppressing cross-stage interference from evidence associated with other instruction stages. Colored boxes schematically indicate stage-related regions. (c) Existing methods [14] are insensitive to instruction-stage transitions, exhibiting overlapping token attributions (top) and high cross-stage explanation similarity (bottom).

Fig. 6: Quantitative analysis of instruction-stage insensitivity. Top: token-level instruction attribution and frame-level similarity. Bottom: dataset-level comparison with the baseline, i.e., TAM [13]. Our method shows stronger sensitivity to instruction-stage transitions and more concentrated visual explanations.

Fig. 5: Effect of SF. Visualization of the base rank filter [13] and our uni-/bidirectional SF variants (Section III-E). Green and red boxes denote instruction-relevant and irrelevant regions, respectively.

Fig. 4: Effect of TR. Comparisons before and after TR show that stage-guided historical support reduces crossstage interference and yields more focused attribution on evidence relevant to the current navigation decision. Red boxes highlight the irrelevant regions.

papers.abstract: GEPA is among the strongest reflective prompt optimizers for language-model programs, but its system-aware merge operator is unstable across models: merge improves gpt-4.1-mini on average while degrading Qwen3-8B, an asymmetry noted but left unexplained by the GEPA paper. We investigate this instability across five datasets and two models. Our nine-configuration sweep over merge timing and merge operator shows that merge can improve both models when configured appropriately. This suggests that merge instability is better explained by configuration sensitivity than by an inherent flaw in the merge operator. We then test whether prompt-level features predict GEPA's merge-accept decisions and find that they do not, ruling out static-feature gating. As a proof of concept, a behavior-based probe built from these diagnostics avoids large merge failures in our multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks, although it does not consistently outperform NoMerge. Code is available as GEPA-MergeProbe at https://github.com/ChongZZZZ/GEPA_MERGE .
authors: Chong Zhao, Ruyi Yang, Changming Liu, Alice Zhao
bullets: Studies GEPA merging across five datasets, two models, and nine merge configurations.
Finds appropriate merge timing and operators can improve both gpt-4.1-mini and Qwen3-8B.
Shows static prompt features do not predict merge-accept decisions.
A behavior-based probe avoids large merge failures in multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks.
The probe does not consistently outperform NoMerge; code is released as GEPA-MergeProbe.

papers.abstract: Deep learning facilitates rapid single shot three dimensional (3D) reconstruction using fringe projection profilometry (FPP), but recovering accurate surface height from a single high frequency fringe image remains challenging because both long-range spatial consistency and fine geometric details must be preserved. Convolutional networks are limited in modeling long range dependencies, whereas window-based Transformers establish global interactions only progressively with increasing depth. To address these limitations, a hybrid Mamba Transformer network is proposed for fringe to height regression. The network adopts a Swin based U shaped architecture and introduces visual state space modeling at the intermediate resolution encoder stage. An axial and dilated vision state space (ADVSS) block is further developed to enhance prescan feature encoding through local, dilated, and axial depthwise convolutions while retaining four directional selective scanning. This design combines linear complexity long range modeling with direction aware preservation of local fringe structures. Experiments on a publicly available FPP dataset show that the proposed method outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet in mean absolute error(MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), absolute relative error, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Using only one deformed fringe image, the proposed method achieves an RMSE of 0.548 mm and an SSIM of 0.9985, reducing RMSE by 65.2% and 59.6% relative to UHRNet and HiDNet, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining selective state space modeling with hierarchical window based attention for accurate single-shot FPP reconstruction.
authors: Xinjie Zhou, XiaoLei Li
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving both global spatial consistency and fine geometric details in single-shot fringe projection profilometry.

On a public FPP dataset, outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet across MAE, RMSE, absolute relative error, and SSIM.
Achieves 0.548 mm RMSE and 0.9985 SSIM from a single deformed fringe image; evaluation is limited to the reported public dataset and metrics.

papers.abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.
authors: Qinsi Wang, Wei Wen, Chong Zhou, Saksham Suri, Zechun Liu, Lemeng Wu, Hai Helen Li, Yiran Chen, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Qi Qian
bullets: Addresses the difficulty and cost of evaluating egocentric assistants through real human interaction.

Provides a platform and benchmark for developing more capable interactive assistants.

papers.abstract: Automated classification of gastrointestinal (GI) findings in endoscopic images could support early diagnosis, but architectures are often chosen on accuracy alone. We present a controlled, reproducible benchmark of ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 for eight-class GI classification on the public Kvasir dataset (4,000 images), using a stratified split (400 test images) and stratified group 5-fold cross-validation over all images. In cross-validation, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 reached 92.12% and 91.70% accuracy, and a two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure showed equivalence within a +/-3 percentage-point margin (difference +0.43 points, 90% CI -0.33 to +1.18; p < 0.001). The architectures differed mainly in cost: ResNet50 had 3.6 times fewer parameters and 4.3 times fewer operations, 2.5-fold lower single-image CPU latency (69 vs. 177 ms) and 3.8-fold higher GPU throughput. Cross-validated calibration was similar (expected calibration error 0.021 vs. 0.023). An edge-oriented transformer, MobileViT-S, was most accurate on the test split (95.5%) but lost 9.4 points when an acquisition artefact present in some classes (the ScopeGuide inset) was occluded, whereas ResNet50 was not significantly affected. On 500 unseen polyp images with expert masks, both models' Grad-CAM maps focused on the lesion (3.6 times chance). On a de-duplicated external subset of GastroVision (1,998 images), accuracy fell to 78-80% for all three models and differences between them remained small. Accuracy differences between architectures were thus small relative to the effects of shortcut learning and domain shift, whereas efficiency differences were large. An efficient CNN is a defensible default for resource-constrained screening, but no model is deployment-ready without local validation.
authors: Akwasi Asare
bullets: On Kvasir’s eight-class task, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 were statistically equivalent within a 3-point accuracy margin.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a benchmark comparing the efficiency (latency, throughput) of ResNet50 and Vision Transformers, highlighting architectural trade-offs for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: An Efficiency- and Statistics-Aware Benchmark of ResNet50 and Vision Transformer for Explainable Multi-Class Gastrointestinal Diseases Classification
papers.tldr: ResNet50 matches ViT-B/16 accuracy for GI disease classification while being substantially more efficient, but shortcut learning and domain shift limit deployment readiness.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.
authors: Linfei Yuan, Rachel Holladay
bullets: Addresses long-horizon manipulation where object properties cannot be determined reliably from appearance.
Integrates task-directed information-gathering actions with interleaved planning and execution.
Plans optimistically, verifies interactive outcomes, and replans only the remaining necessary connections.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot across tasks involving movable objects, ink-filled pens, openable drawers, and empty containers.
Supports continued execution despite uncertain interaction outcomes and external disturbances.

Before each retained action, PRECHECK verifies executability (red blocks). Detected precondition mismatches trigger RECOVERYREPLAN (yellow blocks), which searches for a bridge to the next retained action or, if unsuccessful, to a later retained action. Each successful repair produces an updated plan combining the recovered bridge with the retained suffix. The system executes the bridge and resumes the retained plan, repeating state updates, validation, and on-demand repair until the goal is reached. papers.abstract: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Sitian Tu, Yuxuan Huang, Huichi Zhou, Zhangyue Yin, Jiahao Huang, Jingyuan Xu, Tianmiao Shi, Jin Shi, Nianxi Zhang, Yangmiao Zhang, Zhuolang Chan, Huiyan Hu, Chenchao Sheng, Yaqing Luo, Yue Chen, Huaxiu Yao, Meng Fang, Jun Wang
bullets: Introduces 120 expert-authored tasks with five sequential levels each, covering 600 levels, 89 professional roles, and 12 occupational domains.
Agents must pass each level to unlock later levels, testing accumulated experience rather than isolated task performance.
Compares single submissions with diagnostic feedback plus one revision; feedback improves median completion by 5.3 percentage points across 17 configurations.
The strongest system clears 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels for 23.3% of tasks, indicating substantial difficulty with sustained continual learning.
CLE may also support post-training LLMs to improve continual-learning capabilities.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic control requires simultaneous management of distinct functional demands under motor noise, energetic costs, and communication delays. We investigate how learning responsibility should be organised across modular controllers and the two arms in a simulated musculoskeletal system with two communicating recurrent controllers. Using a 2 x 2 design, we compare differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments. Task-aligned functional specialisation was strongest when differential objectives were combined with a fixed assignment aligned with contralateral control routing. This condition achieved the highest canonical-task performance and control efficiency, reaching 81.33% bimanual success. Its advantage over shared objectives increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties. Stronger specialisation also reduced hand-role flexibility: reversing the hand roles decreased bimanual success by 80.46 percentage points under Differential-Fixed training, compared with 1.51 percentage points under Shared-Balanced training. These results show that controller objectives and hand-task experience jointly determine functional organisation. Stronger role-specific specialisation favours performance and efficiency when roles remain stable, whereas more distributed training favours interchangeability when roles change.
authors: Jingwen Li, Levin Kuhlmann, Jason Friedman, Gideon Kowadlo
bullets: Studies functional specialisation in two communicating recurrent controllers controlling a simulated musculoskeletal bimanual system.
Compares differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments in a 2×2 design.
Differential objectives with fixed, contralaterally aligned assignments produced the strongest specialisation, performance, and control efficiency.
This condition reached 81.33% bimanual success; its advantage increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties.
Specialisation reduced role flexibility: reversing hand roles caused an 80.46-point success drop versus 1.51 points for Shared-Balanced training.

papers.abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Guile Wu, Shuangzhi Li, Xingxin Chen, Chengjie Huang, Sam Hosseini, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses high inference latency that limits real-world deployment of world action models.
Adaptively aggregates representations from different world-model layers based on the evolving action-denoising state.
Uses structured action supervision to modulate layer-wise gradients and improve representation learning.
Reduces inference cost by executing fewer world-model layers and caching relevant representations across denoising steps.
Experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks show low latency with competitive task success rates.

The structured action supervision mechanism modulates action-supervision gradients across world model layers during the backward pass. Together, these complementary designs reduce inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates.

(b) Spatial feature relationships at different world-model depths in Faster-WAM, visualized through cosine similarity between the reference location (close to the gripper) and other spatial locations. (c) Influence of individual world model layers at different denoising steps in Faster-WAM, measured by the relative change in predicted action velocity when the key/value pairs from a given layer are excluded from fusion. (d) Routing distance across denoising steps, measured by the total variation distance between two layer-wise fusion weight distributions.

papers.abstract: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons's hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29 m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.
authors: Basheer Al-Tawil, Magnus Jung, Ayoub Al-Hamadi
bullets: Addresses the train-deploy gap caused by idealized training trajectories versus noisy RGB-D pose and depth estimates at inference.
Uses a shared pipeline for pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing during both training and deployment.
Encodes recent hip-center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and predicts future velocities using a GRU head.
Achieves 0.29 m average ADE and 0.51 m FDE on ETH/UCY.
Has 262K parameters and runs in real time on modest hardware, including deployment on a TIAGo robot with a Jetson Orin.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Framework structure. Normalized observed velocities pass through a linear layer and several bidirectional Mamba blocks (forward + backward, merged by a learned gate). Fig. 5: Prediction Visualization on the ETH/UCY benchmark: Each column corresponds to one scene (ETH, UNIV, Zara1, Zara2, Hotel) and each row shows a different sample. papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection identifies inputs outside the training distribution. Rank-based analyses such as RankFeat and RankWeight suggest that OOD overconfidence is closely related to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces. Since weight averaging operates directly in parameter space and improves model generalization, we consider it for OOD detection from a dominant-component perspective. Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA) assigns a single coefficient to each checkpoint, limiting independent control of dominant weight components. We extend TWA with leading rank-one weight components extracted by Singular Value Decomposition as correction directions, whose contributions are learned through the in-distribution classification objective. On ResNet50, our method improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across the evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, both with and without Outlier Exposure. Mahalanobis-based evaluation yields mixed results, indicating that the benefit depends on the OOD scoring protocol. Target-layer analyses with MSP and Energy favor correction near the classifier.
authors: Akito Shinohara, Hiroaki Aizawa
bullets: OOD overconfidence is linked to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces.
The method extends Trainable Weight Averaging with SVD-derived rank-one weight corrections learned using the in-distribution classification objective.
On ResNet50, it improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, with and without Outlier Exposure.
Mahalanobis evaluation is mixed, and target-layer analyses favor applying corrections near the classifier.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can exploit shortcuts, i.e., correlations present in training data that may not hold at test time. This can lead to poor predictions when correlations shift. Most existing solutions for removing shortcuts operate at training time, requiring labeled training data, model weight access, and significant computational resources. Here, we study the problem of test-time shortcut removal. We propose a family of counterfactual test-time augmentation (CTTA) methods: given an example, each method uses an auxiliary model to generate counterfactual edits in which the shortcut value is changed, and then takes a weighted average of the LLM's predictions across these edits. We prove that the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor is a member of this CTTA family, and we characterize its weights. The weights depend on the training distribution, and therefore are, in general, not identifiable from the trained model and unlabeled test data. However, we present assumptions under which the weights can be obtained using the token probabilities of the trained LLM, and propose tests to detect violations of these assumptions. We use these tests to develop Select-CTTA, an aggregate method that selects among CTTA methods. Empirically, we find that Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches the performance of models fine-tuned on shortcut-balanced data.
authors: Katie Matton, Rosalind W. Picard, John Guttag, Maggie Makar
bullets: Addresses shortcut-induced failures under distribution shifts using only test-time intervention, avoiding labeled training data and model-weight access.
Uses an auxiliary model to create counterfactual edits and combines the LLM’s predictions with method-specific weights.
Proves the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor belongs to the CTTA family and characterizes its weights.
Introduces Select-CTTA, which chooses among CTTA methods using tests for assumptions needed to estimate weights from token probabilities.
Empirically, Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches shortcut-balanced fine-tuning performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Select-CTTA decisions on the reversed test split (p = 0.95). Each point represents one model, fine-tuning setting, and task combination. Positive values indicate that Model-Weighted CTTA outperforms Uniform CTTA. Select-CTTA selects the better-performing CTTA method in most settings.

Figure 1: Causal graph of the data-generating process. The label Y and shortcut S may be correlated (dashed bidirected edge). Y affects the text X only through XY . Shading indicates observed at test-time.

Underlined: not significantly different from the best (95% paired bootstrap interval of the difference includes zero). CTTA methods substantially outperform test-time baselines in most cases, with Select-CTTA consistently among the top-performing methods.

papers.selection_reason: Develops test-time counterfactual augmentation to remove shortcuts in LLM predictions, fitting deployment-time adaptation.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models hold immense potential for high-stakes applications in robotics, game engines, and immersive digital twins, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on perceptual similarity rather than the physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility. We introduce WMEval, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates interactive world models against Unity-based physical simulations. By leveraging Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle, we shift evaluation beyond perceptual visual assessment toward the objective state-based verification required for downstream applications. Spanning 9 diverse scenes, WMEval assesses action controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting. By executing matched action sequences in both the simulator and the world model, WMEval enables evaluation at both the perceptual level and the physical-causal level, using simulator-derived states as reference. Experiments on state-of-the-art models reveal significant room for improvement in dimensions that remain hidden by standard perceptual metrics but are vital for real-world deployments. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/WMEval.
authors: Lanxiang Hu, Yixin Huang, Abhilash Shankarampeta, Zilin Dai, Yuyuan Wu, Kun Qian, Junze Liu, Arvind Srinivasan, Mingjia Huo, Will Lin, Kai Zhong, Weiqi Zhang, Tian Wang, Qingjun Cui, Tajana Rosing, Hao Zhang
bullets: Evaluates world models across 9 diverse scenes using Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle.
Tests controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting.
Runs matched action sequences in both the simulator and world model, comparing perceptual and simulator-derived states.
Finds substantial weaknesses in state-of-the-art models that standard perceptual metrics fail to reveal.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as \emph{explanation drift}: models maintain predictive accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features to spurious correlations. This work identifies and resolves a previously overlooked structural flaw in explanation-aware CL: pixel-level saliency regularization derives supervision targets from the model's own frozen saliency maps, creating a \emph{self-referential drift loop} that actively reinforces spurious attention across tasks. We introduce \textbf{C$^3$L} (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning), which breaks this loop by anchoring regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts (e.g., ``curved beak'', ``striped pattern'') discovered offline, independent of model state, providing (i) target independence from model drift, and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency across every instance of a class. We identify that our concept-based objective, combined with approximate LRP relevance conservation, induces a \emph{crowding-out effect}: since concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction, enforcing high relevance within concept regions implicitly suppresses spurious background correlations without explicit penalization. \method does not require human-annotated concept sets, as it employs a fully automated concept discovery and spatial grounding. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks and over 20 baselines demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
authors: Yehonatan Elisha, Oren Barkan, Noam Koenigstein
bullets: Identifies a self-referential drift loop in pixel-level explanation regularization: frozen model saliency maps can reinforce spurious attention across tasks.
Anchors regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts discovered independently of the model, ensuring target independence and cross-instance consistency.
Combines concept-based regularization with approximate LRP relevance conservation, causing relevant concept regions to crowd out spurious background correlations.
Automatically discovers and spatially grounds concepts without human-annotated concept sets.
Across five benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, reports state-of-the-art accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious-correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: C3L Overview. Discriminative visual concepts are discovered offline via an LLM and spatially grounded using SAM 3, producing model-state-independent supervision targets that break the self-referential drift loop of prior pixel-level methods. During continual training, Lconcept anchors relevance to semantic regions via a crowding-out effect, while Lstab preserves background spatial structure against task-specific drift.

Figure 1: Mitigating Explanation Drift via Semantic Anchoring. Saliency maps for “Electric Guitar” sample after continual learning. Standard CL (PLAN) suffers from explanation drift, shifting attention to spurious background artifacts. While pixel-level methods (RRR) attempt to mitigate this, they result in noisy, non-specific attributions. Our C3L anchors model representations to semantically meaningful concepts, maintaining focus on diagnostic features like the fretboard and guitar body.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces C$^3$L, a continual learning method that uses semantic concept steering to break the explanation drift loop, offering a novel approach to preventing catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Semantic Concept Steering Breaks the Explanation Drift Loop in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: C$^3$L reduces continual-learning forgetting and explanation drift by steering relevance toward stable, automatically discovered semantic concepts rather than self-referential saliency targets.

papers.abstract: Language-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced language-driven 3D scene understanding by incorporating semantic and relational cues into reconstructed scenes. However, relation-aware grounding depends not only on representing such information, but also on whether the underlying scene-side evidence is reliable and sufficient. Multi-view semantic aggregation can incorporate weak observations, while object relations can remain under-observed along the available camera trajectory, leading to ambiguous evidence for target disambiguation. We present RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation that selectively refines semantic and relational evidence for 3D visual grounding. RelateGS suppresses unreliable observations during semantic feature uplifting and consolidates multi-view object observations into a persistent 3D graph. The graph further identifies under-observed object relations and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames to complement their evidence. Experiments on Sr3D+ and Nr3D demonstrate competitive 3D grounding performance, improving the previous best by 7.9 and 1.7 percentage points at Acc@0.25, respectively.
authors: Seongjun Choi, Sangyoun Lee
bullets: Addresses ambiguous target disambiguation caused by weak semantic observations and incomplete relational evidence.
Suppresses unreliable multi-view observations during semantic feature uplifting.
Builds a persistent 3D object-relation graph from multi-view observations.
Uses the graph to identify missing relations and re-query informative existing frames.
Improves prior best Acc@0.25 by 7.9 points on Sr3D+ and 1.7 points on Nr3D.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of RelateGS. Given a reconstructed 3D Gaussian scene and posed RGB-D observations, RelateGS selectively refines the scene-side evidence used for relation-aware grounding. At the Gaussian level, weak multi-view observations are filtered during semantic uplifting. At the object level, multi-view observations are consolidated into a persistent graph, whose current state identifies under-observed object pairs and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison of relation-aware 3D visual grounding on ScanNet. The ground-truth column shows the target object in green and distractor objects in red. For each method, green denotes the ground-truth target, yellow indicates a correctly grounded prediction, and red indicates an incorrect prediction. Compared with language-embedded Gaussian representations and RelateGS without relational re-querying (w/o RQ), the full RelateGS more reliably resolves targets from relational expressions by complementing underobserved relational evidence.

Figure 1. Motivation of RelateGS. Existing methods can suffer from (A) unreliable semantic evidence due to weak multiview observations and (B) insufficient relational evidence due to limited viewpoint coverage. RelateGS addresses these issues by (A) filtering weak observations during semantic feature uplifting and (B) complementing under-observed relations through graphguided re-querying of informative existing views.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison of open-vocabulary localization on LERF-OVS. Given the same language query, we compare the activation maps and localized regions produced by Occam’s LGS and RelateGS. Confidence-aware semantic uplifting suppresses weak multi-view observations, yielding more concentrated language responses around the referred object.
