papers.title: RelateGS: Reliable Semantic and Relational Evidence for 3D Scene Understanding with Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: RelateGS improves language-driven 3D grounding by filtering unreliable semantic evidence and actively strengthening under-observed object relations in Gaussian-splat scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to follow instructions in typed text, limiting broader deployment in natural speech. The traditional solution by prepending a speech recognition before VLA to convert speech into texts would incur additional latency and propagate errors. To address this, we present Speech-$\pi_{0.5}$, which maps raw speech directly to motor commands without explicit textual transcriptions. Specifically, built on $\pi_{0.5}$, we use a cross-modal projection to convert voice frames directly into audio tokens with significant response latency reduction. To further improve the accuracy, we adopt split LoRA adaptation with dedicated audio and task adapters, under a two-stage training. Speech-$\pi_{0.5}$ achieves $3\times$ lower response latency than ASR pipeline while maintaining competitive task success on LIBERO, and generalizes robustly to unseen accents where a single adapter degrades significantly.
authors: Enfu Nan, Pu Zhao, Yixiao Chen, Lin Zhao, Juyi Lin, Chen Wang, Weiwei Chen, Yanzhi Wang
bullets: VLA robots typically require typed instructions or an intermediate speech-recognition step.
The proposed model directly converts speech into motor commands, avoiding transcription latency and error propagation.
A cross-modal projection produces audio tokens, while split LoRA adapters separately handle audio and task adaptation.
The system achieves 3× lower response latency than an ASR-based pipeline with competitive LIBERO task success.
It generalizes robustly to unseen accents, unlike a single-adapter approach.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8% average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5% success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Lin Cao, Fenggang Zhang, Haotong Zhang, Yangtao Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao

Reaches 57.5% success across four real-robot tasks, improving by 32.5 percentage points over the comparison method.

papers.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-centric tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic objects across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-centric representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at https://github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
authors: Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer, Jan Eric Lenssen
bullets: Addresses the instability of patch-based and holistic tokens whose identities are tied to fixed image locations.
Learns tokens that track the same objects across motion, deformation, and partial occlusion.
Produces compact continuous latent representations for downstream flow-based video generation.
Matches class-conditional FVD on UCF-101 with 8× fewer latent tokens and lower latency.
Outperforms 1D tokenization baselines on Kinetics-600 frame prediction at low token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method Overview. TrackTok encodes an input video V into a 1D set of object-centric, semantically persistent, latent tokens Z . Its encoder E is composed of semantic feature extraction with V-JEPA 2.1 [16], the construction of input-dependent queries Q using centroids of k-Means clusters C, and a ViT performing attention based on semantic similarity instead of spatial position. The decoder D reconstructs the three-dimensional RGB video from the 1D latent set Z .

For each sample, we apply PCA on token features and map the top three components to RGB as color for the corresponding token impact mask. The visualization highlights the semantic object alignment and temporal tracking of tokens learned by TrackTok in contrast to AdapTok’s or LARP’s tokens, which are dominated by high-frequency textures and edges. Both baselines also show degraded reconstruction quality at 128 tokens. Furthermore, leveraging only V-JEPA 2.1 without our cluster queries (CQ) still results in tokens encoding fixed regions of the video. Refer to Appendix E for more uncurated examples.

papers.abstract: Language is a natural way to command robots, but converting a single instruction into a long-horizon, contact-rich hand-object interaction remains challenging: synthesized references are noisy, human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias, and fixed-reference tracking lets small errors snowball. We address this with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking. A distilled generalist tracker serves as the skill carrier, while a tightly aligned modulator performs three feedback corrections: reference modulation (continual adjustment of what to track), object-latent modulation (online adaptation of the object representation to recruit suitable skills), and positional-target modulation (small state-dependent refinements for execution). The tracker is learned via large-scale specialist to generalist distillation on a corpus of language-conditioned hand-object trajectories; the modulator is trained with RL under the same task objective, ensuring tight coupling. Across large-scale evaluations, AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object sets in both average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization. We further show zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, where adding the modulator yields substantial gains over a tracker-only variant. AdaDexTrack reframes language-conditioned dexterous manipulation as modulated tracking, replacing the open-loop, fixed-reference tracking with in-loop modulation that adjusts the reference, object latent, and positional target, yielding drift-resistant execution from noisy text references.
authors: Jianibieke Adalibieke, Qianwei Han, Xueyi Liu, Yuzhe Qin, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses noisy language-generated references, embodiment bias, and error accumulation in long-horizon contact-rich manipulation.
Combines a distilled generalist tracker with an RL-trained, tightly coupled modulator.
The modulator performs reference, object-latent, and positional-target feedback corrections.
Outperforms prior state of the art on unseen trajectories and objects in tracking error and success rate.

papers.abstract: Video world models (VWMs) are rapidly emerging as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation. However, most benchmarks only evaluate them as open-world video generators, using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that lack strict 3D spatial and kinematic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboWorM, a comprehensive, deployment-aware benchmark that leverages known hardware priors such as robot kinematic trees and fixed camera configurations, to systematically examine structural and spatiotemporal fidelity. RoboWorM curates 1,605 episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid morphologies, spanning both Markovian and long-horizon non-Markovian tasks under single- and multi-view setups. To explicitly measure physical consistency, we propose two deterministic, VLM-free metrics: KIVA for intra-view kinematic stability, and RIGIS for multi-view geometric consistency. By exploiting intrinsic robotic invariants, KIVA improves hallucination detection alignment with human annotations by 25.8% relative to the strongest frontier VLMs, while RIGIS achieves a 130% higher Spearman correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, since real-world deployment requires low inference latency, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct the first large-scale audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluating 9 state-of-the-art acceleration techniques across 3 leading world models (over 29,000 generated rollouts), we demonstrate how these acceleration methods can retain superficial visual quality while silently compromising deployment-critical physical constraints. Using our metrics, we achieve 2.3$\times$ maximum inference speed-up with minimal quality loss.

Duong, Jonas Fischer, Ngan Le, An Thai Le, Daniel Sonntag, Gim Hee Lee, James Zou, Mathias Niepert, Jan Peters, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Ngo Anh Vien
bullets: Introduces a deployment-aware benchmark covering 1,605 episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid robots, with single- and multi-view, short- and long-horizon tasks.

KIVA and RIGIS align more closely with human judgments than frontier VLMs, improving correlation by 25.8% and 130%, respectively.
Audits 9 acceleration methods across 3 world models and over 29,000 rollouts, showing that visual quality can remain high while physical consistency degrades.
Finds up to 2.3× inference speed-up with minimal measured quality loss.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong visual reasoners, yet remain limited in open-world, multi-step search that requires grounding images, selecting tools, and integrating web evidence. Existing approaches typically construct and filter fixed offline corpora whose question distributions cannot adapt as the target deep-search agent improves. Building on MTA-Agent's image-grounded QA construction, we present MTA-Zero, an online multimodal QA-Solver co-training framework for self-improving multimodal deep-search agents that requires no precomputed multi-hop corpus. Starting from image-grounded VQA seed contexts, a trainable QA Generator retrieves evidence and constructs verified multi-hop questions online. A separate deep-search Solver then selects tools, gathers evidence, and answers the generated questions. To focus generation on the Solver's learning frontier, we derive a Goldilocks reward for the QA Generator from the Solver's group-wise rollout success rate: questions solved by all rollouts or by none receive zero reward, whereas questions near the current frontier are favored. We optimize the two policies independently with GRPO, without sharing parameters or gradients. Across six multimodal deep-search benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-8B Solver from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy and achieves performance comparable to GPT-5 under the same agent workflow. The same framework also improves a newer Qwen3.6-27B Solver by 10.82 points. These results show that verified online question generation provides a policy-specific curriculum for continually improving multimodal deep-search agents.
authors: Xiangyu Peng, Jiaxin Zhang, An Yan, Yu Li, Ran Xu, Zeyuan Chen, Chien-Sheng Wu
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of fixed offline training corpora for open-world, multi-step multimodal search.

Uses a Goldilocks reward to prioritize questions at the Solver’s current learning frontier.
Independently trains the QA Generator and deep-search Solver with GRPO, without shared parameters or gradients.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy across six benchmarks; also boosts Qwen3.6-27B by 10.82 points.

papers.abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to an 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.
authors: Zhuoyuan Yu, Yuxing Long, Du Wang, Junyang Wang, Hongwei Fan, Hao Dong
bullets: Addresses policy degradation under changes in building layout, appearance, and language.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
authors: Sagnik Anupam, Utkarsh Lal, Aneesh Edara, Botong Zhang, Yao Tang, Jiatao Gu, Dinesh Jayaraman, Osbert Bastani
bullets: Evaluates VLMs on language-conditioned frame ordering, depthwise object ordering, and left-to-right pixel-coordinate ordering.
Uses stereo and wrist-camera images from real-world robots, with task difficulty controlled by the number of items to sort.

Introduces an autonomous pipeline for generating scalable training data.
Shows that supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on this data improve ordering performance and transfer to downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.
authors: Samarth Varshney, Ritu Yadav
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting RAG to specialized domains using only unlabeled corpora.
Probes answers with and without retrieved context, categorizing examples as known, solved, context-failure, or retrieval-failure.
Routes each category to reader, retriever, or parametric training signals; repeated probing adapts the mixture to the student.
Evaluated across 11 datasets in three domains and CS-Bench, it improves over budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2–6.4 points.
The method recovers closed-book performance whenever retrieval harms the base model; filtering out evidence-lacking contexts can cause readers to over-trust retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of TriageRAG. papers.abstract: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.
authors: Samarth Varshney, Ritu Yadav
bullets: Addresses persistence failures, where active constraints are forgotten, and relapse, where withdrawn constraints are still followed.
Uses a typed, revisable constraint state with tombstones, plus exact round-trip checks against automatically compiled ground-truth states.
Combines supervised state summarization and state-conditioned response training with preference learning from self-generated relapse contrasts.
Across two backbones, it reduces relapse by 8–22 points versus supervised self-training and improves conversation success by 8–19 points over the base models.
The approach has costs on general instruction-following benchmarks; weight interpolation is explored as a mitigation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of StateWise. Stage I induces two complementary skills from scripted trajectories whose ground-truth states are compiled from the edit history. Stage II lets the model generate state and response on fresh trajectories and keeps only turns that pass an exact round-trip check. Stage III turns the same check into a preference signal: the model’s relapsed generations are rejected responses, its round-trip-clean generations are chosen responses. No proprietary model, judge or human annotation is used in training.

papers.abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.
authors: Xiaodi Huang, Zilin Wang, Jinpeng Liu, Pengchuan Xiao, Zhenlei Shao, Zhang Zhang, Shuxiang Lu
bullets: Represents each token’s observation footprint as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times.

papers.abstract: Floor traction influences wheel-slip behavior, dead-reckoning accuracy, and the navigation performance of wheeled mobile robots that rely on wheel odometry. As these robots become increasingly common in GNSS-denied indoor environments, including automated manufacturing and retail facilities, their onboard measurements could also be used to characterize floor conditions and improve localization. In this study, a skid-steer robot was driven over five floor surfaces with distinct traction characteristics using commanded velocity profiles designed to induce wheel slip through repeated acceleration and direction reversal. Differences between the body velocity estimated from inertial sensing and the velocity obtained from wheel odometry were evaluated using the integrated relative-velocity error, phase-derived wheel-to-body response delay, and velocity-reversal response delay. Welch power spectral density analysis was additionally applied to characterize the frequency distribution of the velocity mismatch during positive and negative acceleration. Band-integrated spectral power, spectral centroid, and spectral decay rate were extracted from each recording and evaluated using linear discriminant analysis and multiclass classification. The response-delay measurements produced consistent surface-dependent trends, with the longest delays observed on soap and the shortest delays observed on carpet. The spectral features also provided clear separation among the tested surfaces, achieving a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These results demonstrate that both the magnitude and frequency domain characteristics of wheel-to-body velocity mismatch contain useful information about tire-surface interactions. Such information could support surface recognition and the development of slip-aware wheel-odometry weighting within robot state-estimation frameworks.

papers.abstract: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.

papers.abstract: A robot in a home it has never seen must open doors, drawers, lids and taps whose physics a picture does not show. Instructions such as "open the drawer halfway, gently" depend on that physics: how far a part travels, how it resists, and what locks it. We present Open-World Law-to-Action (L2A). A vision-language model (VLM) proposes, for each movable part, its motions, the terms of its law of motion, and what may lock it. Each proposal becomes a prior with a floor, so that touch can always overturn it. The robot identifies each part's law online by Bayesian linear regression with closed-form evidence, for parts that move in one way or in two, and keeps a hypothesis that an unseen part or motion locks the target. We prove that touch alone cannot rule this hypothesis out, derive when another look is worth its cost, and show that a constant load and friction cannot be told apart while a part moves one way. All experiments are in simulation, developed on some scenes and run once on held-out ones. In new kitchens the robot completes 80% of tasks from the VLM's proposals, against 98% when every part is known. Proposed physics raises success on objects that need new terms from 353 to 378-383 of 400 episodes, and a second look raises success in mixed scenes from 284 to 329 of 366 tasks. A mobile robot that takes nothing from the simulator completes 70 of 100 requests in new scenes, against 62 when the simulator says which part each box is (after one change made between two held-out tests).
authors: Mohamed A. Mabrok
bullets: Targets open-world tasks such as opening doors, drawers, lids, and taps according to force- and motion-sensitive instructions.
A VLM proposes part motions, motion-law terms, and possible locks; touch can revise these priors online.
Bayesian linear regression identifies one- or two-way motion laws while maintaining an unseen-lock hypothesis.

papers.abstract: Typed decision-making tasks in agents, such as UI element selection, product recommendation, and chart matching, require models to choose from a set of discrete candidates. While prior work demonstrates that text-only System One models achieve four key properties including candidate-order invariance, scalability, and cache reuse via separate request-candidate encoding, extending them to multimodal settings where candidates are visual remains underexplored. We introduce Iris, a framework that accommodates image, text, or hybrid candidates while preserving the core decision module. We prove that order invariance and exact cache reuse hold for any per-candidate encoder under Iris, and derive the closed-form latency reduction. We construct a visual-candidate benchmark from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16, deduplicated, order-shuffled, three generalization splits). Independent encoding (Iris) achieves 78.4 / 72.1 / 74.8 percent accuracy with zero-flip rate under candidate reordering. Joint encoding reaches 90.6 / 89.5 / 91.6 percent but suffers an 8 to 10 percent answer-flip rate when shuffled. To bridge this gap, we propose a design that encodes each candidate conditioned on the request state without inter-candidate cross-attention; it preserves strict order invariance, enables forked cache sharing, and attains 91.7 / 86.5 / 90.0 percent accuracy at one-third of OneJev latency with calibrated null probabilities (AUROC 0.93 to 0.97). Reusing image candidates across requests cuts latency by 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. On MetaEncoder benchmarks, Iris-4B achieves 100 percent on JevBench original and easy, outperforming 30B MetaEncoder and 27B OpenJev. Finally, we resolve a systems bottleneck on Ampere GPUs: reformulating Qwen3.5 patch-embedding Conv3d into its exact matrix-product form accelerates processing by 350x. Code, data, and checkpoints: https://github.com/lllfx/Iris.
authors: Fengxin Li
bullets: Targets typed-choice tasks such as UI selection, recommendation, and chart matching with visual candidates.
Uses per-candidate encoding, including request-conditioned encoding without inter-candidate cross-attention, to preserve strict order invariance and reusable caches.
The proposed design reaches 91.7/86.5/90.0% accuracy across three splits, with one-third of OneJev’s latency and AUROC 0.93–0.97 for calibrated null probabilities.
Reusing image candidates reduces latency by 37× at K=256 and 191× at K=2048.
An exact Conv3d-to-matrix-product reformulation accelerates Qwen3.5 patch embedding by 350× on Ampere GPUs.

papers.abstract: Unrolled variational networks achieve state-of-the-art performance for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but standard end-to-end training becomes prohibitively memory intensive as the number and width of cascades increase. We propose a memory-efficient training framework that updates a randomly sampled cascade while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss. The error signal is propagated from the end of the chain to the sampled cascade using an activation-light backward pass that avoids storing full chain activations, thereby decoupling training memory from chain length. A time-conditioned network shared across cascades further keeps the parameter count independent of chain length. The backward pass is approximate only through frozen normalization statistics, and a trained exact gradient control shows the approximation leaves reconstruction quality unchanged. The framework remains trainable at chain lengths and cascade widths where standard end-to-end backpropagation exhausts GPU memory. On fastMRI single-coil knee and multi-coil brain reconstruction, our method consistently outperforms other local training approaches. On high-SNR knee slices, our method surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and matches it at $4\times$, while on the complete brain validation set it surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and achieves comparable performance at $4\times$, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster per-iteration training. Code is available at https://github.com/emehillaj/scalable-unrolled-mri.
authors: Emiljo M\"ehillaj, Ender Konukoglu
bullets: Randomly samples a cascade for updating while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss.
Uses an activation-light backward pass to propagate error without memory scaling with chain length.
Shares a time-conditioned network across cascades, keeping parameter count independent of chain length.
Maintains reconstruction quality despite approximate gradients caused by frozen normalization statistics.
Outperforms other local-training methods and matches or exceeds E2E-VarNet in the reported fastMRI knee and brain settings, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster iteration training.

papers.abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.
authors: Nadun Rajapaksha, Sandun Herath, Devnith Wijesinghe, Isiri Amani Withanawasam, Hasindri Watawana, Ranga Rodrigo
bullets: Targets limited embedded knowledge and opaque reasoning in MLLMs for whole-slide image analysis.
Uses a visual branch with pathology foundation models to learn visual token inputs.
Uses a knowledge branch that queries a pathology-specific knowledge graph for morphological features and knowledge tokens.
Evaluated on WSI-Bench, where it reportedly surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods and presents reasoning as intuitive graphs.
Its modular knowledge path is designed to complement vision-aligned MLLMs and support other domains with curated knowledge graphs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overall pipeline architecture showing the connection of visual path (in blue) and knowledge path (in yellow). papers.abstract: Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49x but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54x, showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released.
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Post-training largely restores pruning-induced performance loss, including on OCR and grounding tasks.
A 282K-sample mixture spanning VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding supports a unified evaluation of 36 compression configurations.
In native-resolution MLLMs, the vision encoder dominates prefill time, making encoder-side pruning more impactful than projector-side pruning.
The best setup lightly prunes the encoder, aggressively prunes the projector, and keeps the LLM unchanged while preserving general understanding and reasoning at dense-model levels.
A 3.49× LLM-stage speedup translates to only a 1.54× end-to-end time-to-first-token improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Rethinks visual token pruning in MLLMs, introducing post-training recovery and joint compression strategies, fitting Efficient AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs
papers.tldr: Post-training can recover most of the accuracy lost to visual token pruning, while pruning location—not just token count—is critical for end-to-end MLLM speed.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
authors: Qingyuan Cai, Bo Zhang, Yongzhen Huang, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of robot data and the human–robot embodiment gap.
Learns factorized latent actions that disentangle shared manipulation primitives from embodiment-specific signals.
Transfers manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations to robots with different kinematic structures.
Supports both parallel grippers and dexterous hands.
Reports consistent gains over no-pretraining baselines on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing a coherent 3D scene from uncurated image collections remains challenging due to the presence of irrelevant or non-overlapping views. Recent work has shown that feed-forward reconstruction models contain internal view-consistency signals that support distractor rejection. However, reference-conditioned filtering relies on a curated clean reference, which is not guaranteed in practical image collections. To address this limitation, we introduce FreeView, a training-free framework that jointly selects a filtering reference and rejects distractor views from an uncurated collection. FreeView leverages collection-level consensus to identify a representative view that serves as a reliable reference for filtering. It then adapts view rejection to each input collection by combining complementary visual and geometric evidence. This approach preserves useful views under substantial appearance and viewpoint variations while rejecting distractors. FreeView integrates with both VGGT and pi^3, removing the need for a manually curated reference or manual calibration of view rejection. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate high clean-view retention and distractor rejection rates, leading to reliable 3D reconstruction from uncurated views.
authors: Junho Kim, Hyunyoung Choi, Seongwon Lee
bullets: Addresses irrelevant and non-overlapping views that can disrupt reconstruction.
Uses collection-level consensus to select a representative filtering reference.
Combines visual and geometric evidence to adapt view rejection to each collection.
Integrates with VGGT and pi^3 while preserving useful views under appearance and viewpoint variation.
Experiments across multiple datasets show high clean-view retention and distractor rejection, improving reconstruction reliability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of FreeView. Given an uncurated image collection, Consensus Reference Selection identifies a representative view through agreement among related images, establishing a reference for filtering without prior knowledge of which views are clean. Adaptive Dual-Cue Rejection combines complementary visual and geometric evidence to adapt view selection to each collection. Retaining views supported by either cue preserves useful observations under appearance and viewpoint variations, while rejecting views unsupported by both suppresses distractors. The retained views are then processed by VGGT or π3 for final reconstruction.

papers.title: FreeView: Robust 3D Reconstruction from Uncurated Views
papers.tldr: FreeView enables reliable 3D reconstruction from uncurated image collections by automatically choosing a reference view and rejecting distractors without training or manual calibration.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires locating small controls in cluttered screenshots and identifying which control a natural-language instruction refers to. Cropping and enlargement can expose local detail, but the resulting image may still leave ambiguity about the intended target. We propose PreView, an auxiliary preprocessor that improves the inputs to an existing grounding model without further training that model. PreView prepares two complementary types of input features: task-relevant views for localization and candidate-specific cues for target understanding. A trained lightweight auxiliary model predicts and refines a center, crops the screenshot into a local view, and enlarges that view for zoomed-in grounding. It also prepares a visual cue (i.e., a red-circle marker with a location hint) and a textual cue describing the candidate's identity or function. The frozen grounding model uses the prepared inputs to predict the final click. Across five benchmarks, PreView improves the average grounding accuracy of Qwen3-VL-2B, OS-Atlas-4B, and Qwen3-VL-4B without further training these grounding models. Extensive analyses examine the contributions of views and cues, center refinement, and visual input budgets.
authors: Wenjun Hou, Kaishuai Xu
bullets: Targets the difficulty of locating small, ambiguous controls in cluttered GUI screenshots.
Uses a lightweight trained auxiliary model to predict and refine a target center, then crop and enlarge a local view.
Adds candidate-specific cues: a red-circle location marker and text describing the candidate’s identity or function.
Improves average grounding accuracy across five benchmarks for Qwen3-VL-2B, OS-Atlas-4B, and Qwen3-VL-4B without retraining them.
Analyses assess the roles of views, cues, center refinement, and visual input budgets.

papers.abstract: Attribute-based person retrieval ranks surveillance images from a binary query of semantic attributes, but mean Average Attribute Degree of Match (mADM) drops on unseen cameras as predicted probabilities shift. Common pipelines rank gallery images by their L1 distance to the query, which penalizes a confident single-attribute mismatch no more than small uncertainties across many attributes, while post-hoc recalibration fitted on source validation data fails to transfer because the per-attribute maps fitted on source data do not match those of new cameras. We propose LENS (Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing), combining fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student. LENS regularizes mutually exclusive attribute groups with group cross-entropy in training, scores gallery images by the log-likelihood of the exact query, and smooths gallery logits over nearest neighbors using DINOv3 appearance features from the same forward pass. On held-out datasets, all three changes raise mADM: the likelihood score improves all six retrieval metrics for the main ensemble and mADM for all 48 development models, and training-free kNN smoothing improves all 46 tested development models. On the hidden test set of the UPAR 2027 benchmark, LENS reaches 68.17 mADM.
authors: Nguyen Dang Duy Tan, Vo Thanh Nguyen, Linh T. T. Tran, Huynh Nguyen Phat
bullets: Addresses mADM degradation caused by probability shifts across unseen cameras and limitations of L1-distance ranking.
Uses fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student, plus group cross-entropy for mutually exclusive attributes.
Ranks gallery images by the exact query’s log-likelihood rather than L1 distance.
Smooths gallery logits over appearance-based nearest neighbors using DINOv3 features from the same forward pass.
All evaluated changes improve reported development metrics; LENS achieves 68.17 mADM on the UPAR 2027 hidden test set.

papers.abstract: Pedestrian Attribute Recognition (PAR) predicts semantic attributes of individuals, such as gender, age, clothing and accessories, and its descriptions support attribute-based person retrieval and person re-identification. However, accurately recognizing fine-grained attributes across domains remains challenging due to occlusion, appearance variations, and shifts in image distributions. Ensembles of independently trained foundation encoders combine their logits with fixed fusion weights, so every attribute uses the same mix and the encoders are never trained together. We propose UniQuery, which instead jointly fine-tunes DINOv3 and CLIP for attribute-specific fusion. It combines two query heads, one for each encoder, with a joint query head whose attribute queries attend to tokens from both encoders, and the prediction is the average of the logits of the three query heads. We evaluate UniQuery on the benchmark of the UPAR Challenge 2027 at the WACV 2027 Real-World Surveillance workshop, where models are trained on PA100k, PETA and Market-1501 with a shared set of attributes. In leave-one-dataset-out experiments, UniQuery outperforms the independent ensemble in Challenge_Avg on both held-out datasets. Ablations show that learning fusion over independently trained encoders does not improve upon logit averaging in the mean over the two held-out datasets, while freezing the encoders lowers the Challenge_Avg of UniQuery. On the hidden test set of the benchmark, UniQuery achieves a Challenge_Avg of 0.8001.
authors: Nguyen Dang Duy Tan, Linh T. T. Tran, Huynh Nguyen Phat, Vo Thanh Nguyen
bullets: Targets fine-grained pedestrian attributes under occlusion, appearance variation, and domain shift.
Uses separate query heads for DINOv3 and CLIP plus a joint head whose queries attend to both encoders’ tokens.
Averages logits from the three heads for final attribute predictions.
Outperforms an independently trained ensemble in leave-one-dataset-out Challenge_Avg evaluations.
Achieves a Challenge_Avg of 0.8001 on the benchmark’s hidden test set; freezing encoders reduces performance.

papers.title: UniQuery: Unifying Vision Models with a Joint Query Head for Cross-Domain Pedestrian Attribute Recognition
papers.tldr: UniQuery jointly fine-tunes DINOv3 and CLIP with attribute-specific query-based fusion to improve cross-domain pedestrian attribute recognition.

papers.abstract: Pavement crack segmentation under low light is degraded by reduced contrast, shadows, headlight glare, joints, stains, and wet seams. Existing crack segmentation methods mostly assume good illumination. Low-light enhancement methods improve visual quality, but they do not explicitly preserve crack topology. To address these limitations, we formulate low-light crack segmentation as a degradation-aware, prompt-grounded structural defect segmentation problem and propose DROA-CLIPSeg, a parameter-efficient framework that adapts a frozen CLIPSeg vision language backbone using two lightweight modules. QKV Low-Rank Adaptation is injected into the Q/K/V projections of the vision and text encoders to improve crack-specific image text alignment without backbone fine-tuning. The proposed Domain Residual Orthogonal Adapter (DROA) decomposes intermediate features into a dominant crack-domain branch, which captures recurring low-light crack patterns, and an orthogonal residual branch, which preserves faint, thin, and fragmented evidence usually suppressed by noise, shadow, or over-smoothing. We also introduce CrackLingo-9K and CrackLingo-12K, text augmented versions of Crack9k and Crack12k with crack-aware prompts. Training only approximately 1.93 M parameters, corresponding to 1.3% of the full model, DROA-CLIPSeg outperforms 9 zero-shot and 4 fine-tuned vision language baselines on both splits, generalises zero-shot to MVTec AD across textures and defect morphologies, and is supported by extensive ablations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/VShuklacode/DROA-CLIPSeg
authors: Vinita Shukla, Partibha Jangra, Vinayak Pathak, Praful Hambarde, Amit Shukla
bullets: Addresses low contrast, shadows, glare, stains, joints, and wet seams that impair conventional crack segmentation.
Uses QKV low-rank adaptation to improve crack-specific image–text alignment without fine-tuning the backbone.
Introduces a Domain Residual Orthogonal Adapter that separates dominant crack patterns from residual faint, thin, and fragmented evidence.
Provides CrackLingo-9K and CrackLingo-12K, prompt-augmented versions of existing crack datasets.
Reports better performance than 9 zero-shot and 4 fine-tuned vision-language baselines, with zero-shot generalization to MVTec AD; results are limited to the evaluated datasets and settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts CLIPSeg for low-light crack segmentation using parameter-efficient adapters (QKV Low-Rank Adaptation, DROA), fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: DROA-CLIPSeg: Prompt-Guided Thin Crack Segmentation in Low-Light Conditions
papers.tldr: DROA-CLIPSeg enables thin pavement-crack segmentation in low-light imagery by adapting a frozen CLIPSeg model with lightweight, crack-aware modules that preserve faint structural evidence.

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
authors: Zelin Gao, Hao Ouyang, Jiapeng Zhu, Qiuyu Wang, Jingye Chen, Zichen Liu, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of visual priors when adapting bidirectional video diffusion models to causal, autoregressive generation.
Introduces MoBA attention, jointly combining teacher-forced causal prediction with bidirectional training for causal initialization.
Uses chunk-wise cross-attention to condition video on shared environment context and local instructions without revealing future prompts.
Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Causal pre-training with mixture attention for interactive video world models, enabling long-horizon autoregressive rollout.

papers.tldr: Mix Forcing converts bidirectional video diffusion models into efficient autoregressive world models while preserving visual quality and enabling long-horizon interactive generation.

papers.abstract: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.
authors: Xuebin Li, Jinpeng Xiao, Zong Chen, Pierluigi Arpenti, Bruno Siciliano, Jiebao Sun, Yiqun Li
bullets: Targets coordination across robots with different motion capabilities and a shared, unfixed payload.
Uses hierarchical CTDE: a centralized critic trains high-level coordination policies, while embodiment-specific low-level controllers execute commands.
Diffusion policies represent flexible, potentially multimodal coordination responses beyond single-Gaussian policies.
Robots act from local robot and payload observations without partner-state inputs or inter-robot communication.

Simulations report higher mean returns and velocity-tracking success, with lower velocity errors than evaluated baselines; real-world tests include quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot transport.

papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning with diffusion policies for heterogeneous cooperative robot transport.

papers.tldr: HA-DiPO enables heterogeneous robots to cooperatively transport an unfixed payload using decentralized diffusion policies trained with centralized critics.

papers.abstract: Simulation provides a low-cost sandbox where embodied agents can attempt tasks, observe outcomes, and learn from experience. Running many diverse simulation environments concurrently can consume substantial CPU and GPU memory because independently constructed scenes duplicate resources that remain unchanged across instances. We present Patchwork, a resource-sharing system for domain-randomized simulation, built around the representation $E=T+\Delta$: a shared template contains common resources, and a patch records the mutations needed to construct a target environment. Patchwork separates randomization sampling from replay and selects reusable templates together with patches that preserve each target environment's intended configuration. Its layered runtime shares compiled model structure and immutable assets while keeping mutable parameters and simulation state private to each instance. We implement Patchwork on robosuite and MuJoCo and evaluate it on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads. At 32 replicas, shared-template execution reduces CPU RSS by 88-92% relative to process-per-environment execution. Controlled experiments show how sharing shifts memory growth toward template diversity and unique asset content rather than instance count, within the supported sharing boundaries.
authors: Zixu Hao, Weijun Wang, Xiangyu Li, Liang Mi, Hao Wu, Yunxin Liu, Ting Cao
bullets: Addresses duplicated CPU and GPU memory from independently constructed simulation scenes.
Represents each environment as a shared template plus a mutation patch: E = T + Δ.
Separates randomization sampling from replay and keeps mutable parameters and simulation state private.
Implemented with robosuite and MuJoCo, evaluated on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads.
At 32 replicas, reduces CPU RSS by 88–92%; memory growth depends more on template diversity and unique assets than replica count within supported boundaries.

papers.tldr: Patchwork reduces the memory cost of running many domain-randomized embodied simulations by sharing reusable resources while preserving per-environment changes and state.

papers.abstract: Megapixel visual synthesis with latent diffusion models requires operating far beyond the resolutions at which these models are typically trained. Cascade refinement is a leading strategy for this setting: it starts from a base image at a native resolution and progressively upsamples it to the target resolution through multiple refinement stages. Each stage typically performs a pixel-space resolution transition followed by latent-space denoising. While prior acceleration efforts mainly focus on reducing denoising cost, we identify a complementary and underexplored bottleneck: the repeated movement of representations through the VAE. We call these operations pixel-space transitions. In cascade pipelines, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement, while final latents are decoded patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress boundary artifacts. We propose UltraFlash, a transition-efficient approach that accelerates these VAE-heavy operations. UltraFlash has two components. Latent Hyperloop replaces intermediate RGB round trips with a learned latent-space shortcut that approximates the decode-resize-encode transformation without repeated VAE decoding and encoding. Sparse Patch-based Decoding accelerates final reconstruction by addressing patch seams caused by inconsistent GroupNorm statistics and reusing cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into a state-of-the-art cascade baseline, UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by approximately 2x while improving image quality. These results show that optimizing pixel-space transitions can improve both efficiency and fidelity, offering an effective route toward fast, high-quality megapixel visual synthesis.
authors: Phuc Lai, Anh Nguyen, Phong Nguyen, Anh Tran
bullets: Targets an underexplored bottleneck in cascade refinement: repeated decoding, resizing, and re-encoding through the VAE.
Latent Hyperloop replaces intermediate RGB round trips with a learned latent-space approximation.
Sparse Patch-based Decoding reduces overlap between final reconstruction patches by reusing GroupNorm statistics, mitigating seams.
Integrated into a cascade baseline, UltraFlash approximately halves 4K generation latency and improves quality.
Focuses on VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions rather than only reducing denoising cost.

figures.caption: Figure 5: User preference study. Preference share of each method on three criteria. UltraFlash (gold bars) receives the highest share (∼30–33%) on all three.

Figure 2: UltraFlash targets transition costs common to cascade megapixel synthesis. Cascade pipelines often use pixel space twice: an intermediate RGB round trip before refinement and dense patch-wise VAE decoding for final output. UltraFlash accelerates both without changing the denoising/refinement stage. Latent Hyperloop removes repeated VAE decode/encode calls during intermediate transfer, while Sparse Patch-based Decoding reduces final decoding redundancy by enforcing consistent GroupNorm statistics across patches.

Figure 3: Shared GroupNorm statistics enable sparse final RGB decoding. When overlap is small, standard patch-wise decoding shows seam artifacts caused by independently computed GroupNorm statistics. Sparse Patch-based Decoding uses shared cached statistics to align normalization across patches, making adjacent patches decode consistently. The right plot shows that our method maintains consistently low boundary MSE across overlap factors when decoding with sparse overlaps.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces latency of VAE-heavy cascade visual synthesis; efficiency contribution to generative pipelines.
papers.title: UltraFlash: Accelerating Megapixel Visual Synthesis
papers.tldr: UltraFlash accelerates 4K latent-diffusion image synthesis by reducing costly VAE-based resolution transitions while improving image quality.

papers.abstract: Running a language model and a dense 3D map on one device means the two share one memory, and exceeding its limit is an out-of-memory failure. Map systems that keep a bounded working set bound it by a count of keyframes, but the memory one keyframe occupies varies widely with what it carries, so a count does not control what the working set occupies. The unit of admission is as poorly matched, since a radius around the pose, a fixed cell, or the graph neighbors of the last matched keyframe all move parts of the map that are not needed. We therefore propose two decisions. First, the memory the resident map uses is bounded directly, and the cost of every admission is known before any data is read, from per-keyframe resident sizes computed offline and carried with the map. Second, keyframes are admitted and released at a semantic spatial unit, the rooms and corridors of the building, so that the robot holds the zone it occupies together with the zone it is about to enter while the zones it has passed are released. Every admission measures the resident total, makes room, and only then reads, so the budget is never overshot. On two NVIDIA Jetson boards the budget holds in every run and the model gives up at most 0.8 percent of its throughput, whereas without it the operating system kills the model or the map. Under that budget, and over the environments evaluated, admission by semantic zone localizes 6-9 points more of the query frames than a geometric partition of matched zone count and about twice as much as the retrieval of RTAB-Map, at a lower ATE. Bounding memory lets the map and the model coexist, and moving the map in semantic zones makes the bounded map usable.
authors: Huichang Yun, Jaeyeul Kim, Seungho Yoo
bullets: Keyframe-count limits are unreliable because keyframes vary substantially in memory usage.
The system predicts each keyframe’s resident size offline and enforces a strict memory budget before reading new data.
It admits and releases map content by rooms and corridors, retaining the current and next zones while removing passed zones.
On two NVIDIA Jetson boards, the budget held in every run with at most 0.8% model-throughput loss.
Semantic-zone admission localized 6–9 percentage points more query frames than geometric partitioning and about twice as much as RTAB-Map retrieval, with lower ATE in the evaluated environments.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-bounded keyframe management for dense maps on robots, a form of embodied spatial memory.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Keyframe Management for Dense Maps on Memory-Constrained Robots

papers.abstract: Video world models are expected to generate videos that accurately follow specified camera trajectories while maintaining consistent 3D structures. However, existing models are predominantly trained on densely sampled videos with small inter-frame camera motions. When applied to sparse, large step trajectories, they often produce frozen frames, inaccurate camera motion, and severe geometric drift. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between the gradual viewpoint transitions seen during training and the large viewpoint changes required at inference time. To address this problem, we propose Dense Trajectory Teacher Distillation (DTTD), a post-training framework that transfers a model's generation capability from dense trajectories to large camera motions. Given a sparse trajectory, DTTD interpolates additional camera poses to construct a dense trajectory covering the same path. The frozen base model then generates reliable teacher videos along this familiar dense trajectory, and pose aligned teacher observations are used to evaluate candidate videos generated under the original sparse trajectory. In this way, the model serves as its own generation teacher, requiring neither additional video data nor a stronger external video generator. We further combine dense teacher supervision with geometry aware rewards that assess cross frame consistency and camera trajectory following, and use the resulting preferences for offline preference optimization. To stably expand the model's motion range, we introduce a cumulative curriculum that progressively incorporates larger motion steps while retaining simpler trajectories to reduce capability forgetting.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Existing models often fail on sparse, large-step camera trajectories, producing frozen frames, inaccurate motion, and geometric drift.
DTTD interpolates sparse camera paths into dense trajectories that the frozen base model can reliably generate.
Pose-aligned dense teacher videos supervise candidate outputs generated on the original sparse trajectory, without extra data or an external teacher.
Geometry-aware rewards measure cross-frame consistency and trajectory following for offline preference optimization.
A cumulative curriculum progressively increases motion difficulty while retaining simpler trajectories to limit capability forgetting.

papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.
authors: Zheng Zhang, Xiaoyang Tang, Shuaiqi Cheng, Jiakai Huang, Zhongbo Wu, Ziyi Zhang, Yuan Si, Zeyu Liu, Weibo Gao, Shunyu Liu, Shan You, Fei Wang, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao

Highlights the need for more reliable world models before using them to guide deployment decisions.

papers.abstract: Video spatial reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand how objects are arranged and related across viewpoints. While these models can recognize objects in individual frames, integrating these observations to solve complex spatial tasks remains challenging. We examine route planning as a representative task and observe that existing models become substantially less accurate as the number of required turns increases, with several models achieving accuracy close to random guessing on routes requiring three or more turns. This finding suggests that recognizing landmarks alone is insufficient: models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GeoLift, a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction. It then uses shared geometric regions, called superpoints, to associate observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map enables explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and provides geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift improves Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including an increase in route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and achieves 59.8% accuracy on MindCube. These results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training.
authors: Xinglin Li, TingTing Long, Jingzhi Zhou, Jiajing Chen, Jian Yang, Jin Xie
bullets: Existing MLLMs struggle to connect landmarks across viewpoints, with accuracy dropping sharply on routes requiring three or more turns.
GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained feed-forward geometry models for training-free 3D reconstruction.
Shared geometric regions called superpoints associate the same objects across views without a learned matcher.
The resulting 3D map supports explicit spatial-relation and multistep-route computation, plus distance and size estimation.
It raises Qwen3-VL-4B’s VSI-Bench average from 55.4% to 64.1% and route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, while reaching 59.8% on MindCube.

The resulting view-consistent map supports a toolbox of deterministic spatial operations, including occupancy-grid construction and A* route search. papers.abstract: High-resolution remote sensing (RS) imagery provides fine spatial detail over large areas, making it essential for fine-grained scene understanding. Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation (RRSIS) aims to segment regions described by natural language, yet many existing methods rely on sequential alignment--fusion pipelines with limited joint modeling of cross-scale visual hierarchies and linguistic dependencies. Moreover, dense attention mechanisms struggle with the sparsity and wide spatial dispersion of RS targets, while current datasets offer limited structured evaluation of multi-target references, multi-hop relational reasoning, and multi-granularity descriptions, limiting both model development and evaluation. To address these challenges, we propose a Cross-Scale Sparse Attention Model (CSSAM), which aligns multiscale visual features with complex referring expressions through two key modules. The Cross-scale Modality-aligned Fusion Module (CMFM) performs unified cross-scale cross-modal fusion, while the Dynamic Multimodal Sparse Hybrid Attention (DMSHA) selectively attends to informative visual--textual tokens, reducing dense visual interactions. Furthermore, we introduce M$^{3}$RRSIS-D, a RRSIS dataset explicitly designed around three core reasoning dimensions: multi-target (M$^{1}$), reference-dependent multi-hop (M$^{2}$), and multi-granularity (M$^{3}$) expressions. Extensive experiments on M$^{3}$RRSIS-D and two public RRSIS benchmarks demonstrate that CSSAM achieves competitive performance across accuracy, fine-grained reasoning, and high-IoU localization metrics, validating its effectiveness for complex semantic reasoning in realistic RS scenarios. Code, dataset, and model weights will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Yuxi Li, Lu Si, Xia Liao, Yidong Shen, Zheng Wei, Jun Zhang, Xin Yuan
bullets: Targets the difficulty of segmenting spatially sparse, widely dispersed regions described by complex natural-language references.
Uses CMFM for unified cross-scale cross-modal fusion and DMSHA to selectively attend to informative visual–textual tokens.
Introduces M³RRSIS-D, covering multi-target, reference-dependent multi-hop, and multi-granularity expressions.
Experiments on the new dataset and two public benchmarks report competitive accuracy, fine-grained reasoning, and high-IoU localization.
Code, data, and model weights are planned for release upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
authors: Jingmeng Zhou, Seson Sun, Binyao Xu, Lingming Zhang, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Weiming Hu, Jin Gao, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Incorrect actions can create behavioral inertia: retained off-route history prevents the agent from turning when needed.
MOON adds two lightweight modules to a frozen VLN policy: a deviation judge that triggers history clearing and a recovery policy trained from alarm states.
On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MOON improves its frozen base success by 5.2 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively, and achieves the highest R2R-CE success among compared methods.
A random-trigger ablation shows that recovery depends on clearing history at the right time, not merely clearing it.
MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON without retraining.
