papers.abstract: Image tokenizers convert pixels into compact latent sequences for efficient generative modeling. Most approaches arrange latents on a downsampled two-dimensional grid, tying sequence length to image resolution. We compare two variable-length strategies: computationally efficient patch-derived tokens, which inherit explicit spatial organization, and more demanding register tokens, which have no predefined spatial layout. Our reconstruction results reveal that patch-derived tokens perform substantially better under extreme compression, whereas register tokens achieve slightly better reconstruction quality at intermediate budgets. At high token budgets, both approaches achieve similar reconstruction quality. For downstream generative tasks, register tokens outperform patch-derived tokens. Adding representation alignment with external pretrained visual encoders substantially improves the generative performance of patch-derived tokens, allowing them to match or outperform register tokens depending on the token budget. We further find that both approaches learn spatially localized representations. Patch-derived tokens largely retain their explicitly imposed spatial organization, while register tokens develop an implicit two-dimensional spatial structure despite having no predefined layout. Representation alignment reduces this spatial organizational constraint, enabling individual tokens to exert a stronger non-local influence.
authors: Philipp Schenkel, Tobias Sch\"urmann, Omer Sahin Tas
bullets: Compares variable-length patch-derived tokens with layout-free register tokens for image tokenization.
Patch-derived tokens are substantially better at extreme compression; register tokens are slightly better at intermediate budgets, and both converge at high budgets.
Register tokens outperform patch-derived tokens in downstream generative tasks without additional alignment.
Aligning representations with pretrained visual encoders improves patch-derived generative performance, sometimes matching or surpassing register tokens.
Both token types develop spatially localized representations; alignment weakens this spatial constraint and promotes more non-local token influence.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the investigated architectural designs, with patch-derived tokens on the left and register tokens on the right. Both architectures utilize nested dropout to obtain variable-length image representations. Patch-derived tokens are obtained by transforming image patches into the token representations, whereas register tokens are obtained by transforming dedicated learnable embeddings.

Fig. 5: Spatial entropy for patch-derived tokens on the left and register tokens on the right. For patch-derived tokens, spatial entropy generally decreases with increasing token ID, indicating progressively stronger spatial concentration; REPA partially mitigates this trend. Register tokens exhibit a different behavior: Their entropy remains comparatively high for later token IDs even without REPA. Adding REPA yields a peak at maximum entropy, which can be attributed to inactive (“dead”) tokens that contribute negligibly to the learned representation.

Fig. 3: Qualitative effect of corrupting a single token. Within each block, columns show the original reconstruction, the reconstruction after corrupting the indicated token, and their pixel-wise difference. For both patch-derived and register tokens, the corruption predominantly causes spatially localized changes. Although REPA reduces the strength of this locality, local effects remain visible.

Fig. 4: Spatial influence of patch-derived tokens and register tokens, trained with and without REPA. Each heatmap shows the pixel-wise change in squared reconstruction error when one token is replaced by a randomly sampled codebook entry. Within each panel, heatmaps are arranged by token index in raster-scan order from top left to bottom right. Without REPA, both tokenization schemes exhibit predominantly localized influence, although some register tokens affect broader image regions. With REPA, patch-derived tokens remain largely localized, whereas many register tokens exhibit substantially more spatially diffuse influence. The color scale uses a power-law normalization to improve visibility. Results are averaged over ImageNet-1K validation images.

papers.abstract: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Running deep models for medical image analysis at the point of care is challenging with standard architectures: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are often too heavy for edge devices, while Vision Transformers (ViTs) require massive training datasets to compensate for missing inductive biases. This study investigates how far the dual-token distillation used to train data-efficient ViTs can be pushed when applied across architectures, from a CNN-based teacher into a lightweight ViT student. LiteMed-ViT is introduced as a dual-token ViT featuring a convolutional stem and a class-balanced distillation objective; at 0.234M parameters, LiteMed-ViT carries 47.8x fewer parameters than its ResNet18 teacher at a memory footprint of just 0.89 MB. Evaluated against three compact CNN baselines on three MedMNIST subsets of varying modality and class balance, LiteMed-ViT attains higher accuracy than all three baselines on BloodMNIST (95.05%) and two on PathMNIST (89.15%). Under MedMNIST-C corruptions, it is at least as robust as every compact CNN across all subsets, outperforming them on BloodMNIST and PathMNIST without declining in relative standing as severity increases. Particular attention is devoted to identifying the exact conditions where performance plateaus. On DermaMNIST, LiteMed-ViT's balanced accuracy remains up to 1.9 points below the strongest compact CNNs and does not benefit from higher input resolutions up to 224 pixels, where ResNet18 gains 12.6 points. Stronger teachers do not yield a more accurate student, and overconfident ones lower its DermaMNIST balanced accuracy unless calibrated.
authors: Shuaibu Shehu (SR University), Elijah M. Flomo (SR University), Mohammad Safiya (GITAM University), Anurodh Kumar (SR University), Subodh Kumar (Dr. KNS Memorial Institute of Medical Sciences)
bullets: Uses a CNN teacher to distill knowledge into a lightweight ViT with a convolutional stem and class-balanced dual-token objective.
Has 0.234M parameters and a 0.89 MB memory footprint—47.8× fewer parameters than its ResNet18 teacher.
Outperforms compact CNN baselines on BloodMNIST and some PathMNIST evaluations, while matching or exceeding their corruption robustness.
Performance plateaus on DermaMNIST: balanced accuracy remains up to 1.9 points below the strongest CNNs and does not improve with higher resolution.
Stronger or overconfident teachers do not necessarily improve the student; calibration is important for DermaMNIST.

papers.title: Promise and Limits of Cross-Architecture Knowledge Distillation for Lightweight Medical Vision Transformers (LiteMed-ViT)
papers.tldr: LiteMed-ViT shows that cross-architecture distillation can produce an extremely small, robust medical ViT, though its benefits depend strongly on the task and teacher calibration.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion trackers reproduce diverse behaviors, but sharing a policy across bodies requires accounting for differences in structure, morphology and dynamics. We present MimicAll, a reinforcement-learning framework for shared whole-body motion tracking across heterogeneous humanoids. A structured embodiment descriptor is encoded into global and joint-aligned conditions, which are combined with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets. Physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting and heterogeneous simulation support training across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families. We introduce a benchmark of 464 bodies across five distribution strata to evaluate motion generalization, within-family embodiment shifts and unseen-family transfer. Controlled ablations show that embodiment information improves motion completion with simple concatenation, while self-attention yields the lowest global position errors. With equal training transitions, shared training achieves 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies in 100STYLE, versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist. With Flat-MLP encoding and concatenation, continued training on a motion subset excluding obstacle categories achieves 98.3% and 93.5% 30-second success on 100STYLE for sampled training bodies and out-of-distribution variants within seen families, respectively. On an eight-motion LAFAN1 subset excluding ground and get-up sequences across 464 bodies, mismatched body conditions reduce self-attention's 30-second success from 61.7% to 47.0%, demonstrating a closed-loop benefit from embodiment information.
authors: Jia Li, Lingyun Xu, Yitang Li, Hao Zhao
bullets: Addresses morphology, structure, and dynamics differences that hinder cross-humanoid policy sharing.
Encodes embodiment globally and per joint, combining it with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets.
Uses physics-consistent embodiment randomization, calibrated retargeting, and heterogeneous simulation across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families.
Evaluates generalization on 464 bodies across five distribution strata, including within-family shifts and unseen-family transfer.

Embodiment conditioning substantially improves closed-loop tracking; shared training reaches 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist, while self-attention gives the lowest global position errors.

papers.title: MimicAll: Structured Embodiment Conditioning for Cross-Humanoid Whole-Body Motion Tracking
papers.tldr: MimicAll enables one reinforcement-learning policy to track whole-body motion across diverse humanoid bodies by explicitly conditioning it on structured embodiment information.

papers.abstract: Robots can use historical observations to answer spatiotemporal queries in familiar environments, but the presence of relevant evidence does not imply that existing tools support the operations a task requires. We introduce ReSight, a task-driven self-improving memory system for embodied agents that expands the capabilities for processing and accessing historical observations as task demands arise. ReSight retains keyframes and their spatiotemporal associations, separating observation evidence from extensible derived fields so that stored observations can be reprocessed for new needs. An execution agent and a coding agent share this memory through different interfaces: the former calls registered tools within a bounded online budget, while the latter uses a programmable workspace and a larger exploration budget to inspect evidence, write programs, and acquire models as needed. To realize capability expansion in ReSight, we develop Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM), which identifies capability gaps from execution and exploration records without task reference answers and converts exploration-derived solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills, extending memory representations and access capabilities as needed. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate effective base memory access and capability expansion. With the execution model and online budget held fixed within each benchmark, EDM reduces mean position error on OC-NaVQA from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and improves high-level success on FindingDory from 38.3% to 63.8%. With the tools and skill frozen, success still improves by 28.3 percentage points on FindingDory episodes excluded from exploration and distillation. Experiments on real robot patrol memories further demonstrate reuse of these capabilities for subsequent queries and new memories, with fewer online tool calls on average.
authors: Lirong Che, Yang Chen, Yimeng Su, Daqi Liu, Zhenyu Huang, Jiong Wang, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between available historical evidence and tools capable of performing task-specific operations.
Stores keyframes and spatiotemporal links separately from extensible derived fields, allowing observations to be reprocessed.
Uses distinct execution and coding agents for bounded online querying versus broader exploration and program/model development.
Its Explore-Distill-Mount process converts discovered solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills without task reference answers.
Across benchmarks, it reduces OC-NaVQA mean position error from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and raises FindingDory success from 38.3% to 63.8%; real-robot patrol tests show reuse with fewer online tool calls.

papers.abstract: Text-to-3D solid retrieval requires aligning natural language with precise geometry despite variations in pose, scale, and recording conventions. Existing methods discretize Boundary Representation (B-rep) models into point clouds or meshes, or learn features from faces, edges, and topology, risking information loss or lacking explicit invariance guarantees. We propose a text-to-B-rep retrieval framework based on group actions and spectral geometric invariants, making invariance an explicit constraint on descriptor construction. Specifically, we use group actions to characterize equivalence transformations induced by translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour recording conventions. For sketch-extrusion solids, we construct a fixed 280-dimensional spectral geometric descriptor by integrating geometric information from three complementary levels, including cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion structures. Furthermore, we use descriptor-consistent multi-positive sets and geometric attribute supervision to promote structural alignment between text and solids. On Text-to-3D solid retrieval, our method achieves 88.6% Recall@5, exceeding the previous state of the art by 13.6 percentage points and demonstrating the effectiveness of explicit geometric invariants for precise 3D solid retrieval.
authors: Hongzhu Yi, Hao Liu, Tao Yu, Tiankun Yang, Yujia Yang, Zhenghao Zhang, Tianyu Zong, Zhenyu Guan, Bingkang Shi, Haopeng Jin, Yuanxiang Wang, Zhongtian Luo, Jungang Xu
bullets: Targets information loss and missing invariance guarantees in point-cloud, mesh, and component-based B-rep representations.
Defines equivalence transformations through group actions, covering translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour conventions.
Builds a fixed 280-dimensional descriptor from cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion structures.
Uses descriptor-consistent multi-positive sets and geometric attribute supervision to improve text–solid structural alignment.
Achieves 88.6% Recall@5, reported as 13.6 percentage points above the previous state of the art.

papers.title: Can One Hear Geometry? Gauge-Invariant Spectral Descriptors for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval
papers.tldr: A text-to-B-rep retrieval framework uses explicit spectral geometric invariants to match language with 3D solids despite pose, scale, reflection, and recording variations.

papers.abstract: Lung tumor segmentation plays a vital role in early detection and treatment planning of lung cancer. Although state-of-the-art deep learning models achieve high dice score coefficients (DSC), each forward pass requires computing large amounts of floating point operations, making them computationally expensive, requiring GPU acceleration, and having slow inference speed, limiting real-world clinical deployment. We propose a lightweight, energy-efficient model that leverages the ENet architecture for its real-time inference capability and low computational cost, enhanced with UNet-style skip connections between encoder and decoder stages for feature reuse and the lightweight Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for improved feature representation. The model is trained on publicly available data from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) via the Medical Segmentation Decathlon Challenge (MSD) and evaluated on the Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) dataset. Our model achieves a DSC of 0.90812 (threshold of 0.5) with its compact architecture of 430,052 parameters and 0.549 Giga Multiply-Accumulate operations (GMAC), making it up to 10 times faster, requires 79 times less GMAC than UNet, and has 22 times fewer parameters than SegNet. These characteristics make it well-suited for deployment in clinical settings where computational resources are limited and decrease the cost of utilizing such a system. Additionally, the explainable AI technique of Grad-CAM is used to provide visual interpretability of the model's predictions and to identify regions where segmentation performance requires improvement.
authors: Sharan Thummagunti, Aayushi Padia, Abhiram Koppuravuri, Prabhu Prasad B M, G N Girish

papers.abstract: Marine video understanding is crucial for a wide range of real-world applications. However, existing marine video datasets suffer from limitations, including the limited number of data samples, fine-grained text descriptions, and detailed visual attributes. To address these limitations, we introduce a large-scale, video-text dataset featuring rich, in-the-wild visual attributes tailored for complex marine environments. Our dataset comprises 2,000 video-text pairs annotated with 13 attributes covering up to four objects per scene, object visual/geometric properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion, spanning diverse lighting conditions, times of day, and 7 countries. From these annotations, we generate 16,080 video-question pairs (12,080 multiple-choice, 4,000 open-ended). Furthermore, we benchmark both proprietary and open-source video-LLM models on video question answering and video captioning tasks. We find that (i) proprietary models often achieves superior performances; (ii) VLMs handle object motion well but struggle with complex camera motion; (iii) closed-source models struggle to perceive camera motion; and (iv) VLMs struggle to reason in static cameras.
authors: Quang-Trung Truong, Thanh-Nghia Nguyen, Phu-Phong Vo, Jaeyeon Kim, Cheng Chen, Jie Zhang, Binh-Son Hua, Duc Thanh Nguyen, Ivor Tsang, Sai-Kit Yeung

papers.abstract: Advertisers routinely create multiple duration variants of ads to meet marketing budgets and viewer preferences, a labor-intensive and costly process. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at general video understanding, their ability to perform specialized editorial tasks remains unexplored. We introduce AdShot, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on shot selection for ad clipping. It contains 823 professionally edited ad pairs (30-sec sources and 15-sec edits) across 194 brands and 17 industries, annotated with shot-level boundaries and content features (action, emotion, information, imagery). We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art video-only MLLMs and 2 audio-visual MLLMs (7B-72B parameters) on shot selection accuracy (Precision, Recall, F1), duration constraints (15s), and content preservation, including an audio ablation. We find: (1) model architecture matters more than scale, with smaller models often matching or exceeding larger ones; performance is strongest for target ads with 6-10 shots; (2) models exhibit a mean absolute duration error of 5.39s, with most tending to overshoot the 15s target, though they can still substantially reduce human editing effort; (3) all models exhibit systematic content biases, favoring information-rich and emotion-focused shots while under-selecting action and imagery. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate research at the intersection of multimodal AI and computational advertising.
authors: Wen Xie, Om Rastogi, Sai Siddhartha Vivek Dhir Rangoju, Gijs Overgoor, Yakov Bart, Sarah Ostadabbas

papers.abstract: During post-training, large language models (LLMs) learn value preferences from corpora that may contain imbalanced proportions of opinions associated with different demographic groups. Amplifying these imbalances may further underrepresent some groups' opinions. However, how opinion mixtures shape value preferences across post-training paths remains unclear. To answer this question, we conduct controlled experiments using post-training corpora with different opinion mixtures and five post-training paths based on SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We find that post-training amplifies opinion imbalances differently across post-training paths. Once value preferences are amplified, whether further post-training can remove them depends on both the post-training method and the opinion mixture in the corpus. More concerningly, a model's stability under interventions depends on whether further post-training changes its value preference. Moreover, these value preferences are transferred to student models even when distillation uses corpora with no explicit opinion questions. These findings suggest that both the opinion mixture in post-training corpora and the choice of post-training method should be considered when developing, evaluating, and reusing LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ku-nlp/llm-value-preferences.
authors: Yang Liu, Shaoyang Xu, Masahiro Kaneko, Chengzhi Zhong, Wenxuan Zhang, Chenhui Chu
bullets: Imbalanced opinions in post-training corpora can be amplified, with effects differing across SFT, DPO, and GRPO paths.

The findings highlight opinion composition and post-training method as important factors for developing and evaluating LLMs.

papers.abstract: To understand the emergence of grammatical behavior in language models, we track circuits for subject-verb number agreement in pythia-1b and ten seeds of pythia-410m across training. We find that subject-verb agreement is learned early, and is initially handled by a diffuse collection of neurons. However, after agreement behavior has stabilized, the mechanisms responsible for it continue to reorganize. The attention heads which mediate agreement often shift during training: in the case of pythia-1b, behavior is controlled by two heads early in training but by a third (different) head later. Furthermore, the circuit shrinks over training, with pythia-1b's final circuit being strikingly sparse. We take these results to be informative about how linguistic knowledge emerges and is represented in a language model.
authors: Qing Yao, Sasha Boguraev, Tiago Pimentel, Kyle Mahowald

papers.abstract: Visual effects are often easier to demonstrate via reference than to describe in words. We study effect-reference editing, where a reference image shows a desired visual effect and language identifies which properties should guide the edit. Existing single-pass editing techniques often fail to make fine-grained edits, resulting in unintended changes to source content or deviations from the reference effect. We introduce KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for effect-reference editing that combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback to transfer the desired effect while preserving the composition and content of the original shot. To ensure KINESYS can produce a diverse set of edits that preserve the source, we develop a robust optimization strategy in which the generative model is fine-tuned across multiple noise samples and optimization runs. Evaluation with VLM judges, source preservation metrics (LPIPS, TPIPS), and a user study shows that KINESYS outperforms state-of-the-art image editors in source preservation; on effect transfer, it remains competitive with Nano Banana 2 and outperforms open-weight editors.
authors: Noah Frahm, Luchao Qi, Haoze Li, Dan B Goldman, Sambit Bhattacharya, Roni Sengupta

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem
authors: Wujiang Xu, Jiaojiao Han, Xi Zhu, Qizheng Zhang, Kaiqu Liang, Yutong Yin, Kai Mei, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between retrieval memories that miss implicit steps and summaries that lose exact facts.
Stores each history unit once in an immutable store, then renders a fresh, budget-fitting memory without an LLM call.
Combines timeline records with either relevant raw-text excerpts or verbatim query-matched pieces.
Improves over the second-best method by 11.5% on 4k AppWorld tasks and over A-Mem with summaries by 12.2% on 147 held-out tasks.
Matches a keyword retriever on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; ablations find timelines drive AppWorld completion while detail recovery supports exact-fact accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs), which process both visual inputs and text queries, incur high inference costs due to the large number of visual tokens, making visual token pruning a natural approach for improving efficiency. Recent work has leveraged query information to guide token selection, often through heuristics derived from attention patterns or token dynamics. However, these approaches do not explicitly exploit the underlying structure of query-vision interactions. We address this gap by observing that the query-vision interaction matrix, naturally induced by the query and key projections already present in transformer attention, is effectively low-rank, with a small number of dominant latent interaction modes capturing query-relevant semantics. Motivated by this observation, we propose Query-Vision Decomposition (QViD), a novel training-free query-aware visual token pruning method that exploits this structure. Extensive experiments on both image and video understanding benchmarks show that QViD consistently improves performance under matched token budgets, with the largest gains appearing under aggressive compression regimes.
authors: Harshithanjani Athi, Sravan Kumar Ankireddy, Jianzhong Charlie Zhang, Hyeji Kim
bullets: Visual token counts make large VLM inference computationally expensive.
Existing query-aware pruning methods often rely on attention heuristics without modeling query–vision interaction structure explicitly.
QViD decomposes the query–vision interaction matrix into dominant latent modes that capture query-relevant semantics.
Experiments on image and video understanding benchmarks show consistent gains at matched token budgets, especially with aggressive compression.

figures.caption: Figure 2: QViD Pipeline. QViD performs query-aware visual-token pruning by explicitly modeling query–vision interactions. At pruning layer ℓ, it forms the interaction matrix M = QtxtK ⊤ vis, extracts its dominant low-rank modes with SVD, and scores each visual token by its participation in these modes. The top-K tokens are retained for subsequent reasoning, preserving query-relevant visual evidence while reducing sequence length. Integer values in the illustrative matrices are used only for ease of presentation.

Figure 7: Additional Qualitative Token-Score Visualizations. We compare token-score maps from QViD, V2Drop, and SparseVLM across multiple image-query pairs. Brighter regions indicate higher token scores. QViD tends to assign high scores to query-relevant visual regions, while the baseline methods often produce more diffuse score maps.

Figure 1: Comparison of Visual-Token Scoring. Compared with prior methods such as V2Drop and SparseVLM, QViD concentrates high scores on query-relevant image regions, leading to more effective visual-token pruning.

The gray dashed line and star indicate the full-token baseline with 576 visual tokens. papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating in dynamic, challenging conditions such as intersections and roundabouts must guarantee collision avoidance under uncertainty while maintaining real-time feasibility. Most existing planners struggle to simultaneously guarantee both requirements. Chance-constrained formulations embed safety constraints directly in the optimization but become infeasible as uncertainty compounds; deterministic planners provide feasible solutions but fail to address the uncertainty that causes collisions; end-to-end learned policies provide neither guarantee in an interpretable form. We present a modular perception-prediction-planning pipeline that closes this gap by propagating uncertainty as structured, interpretable quantities across module boundaries. Rather than embedding probabilistic risk directly in the optimization, our pipeline resolves collision probabilities upstream and constructs convex safe sets within which the planner provides a guaranteed feasible solution at every cycle -- decoupling the safety guarantee from solver feasibility. Across Monte Carlo trials in a four-way unsignalized intersection, our pipeline achieves 0% collisions and 0% solver infeasibility at 12.7ms per cycle, compared to 36% and 10% collision rates for deterministic and chance-constrained baselines respectively. The ablation study confirms the necessity of each uncertainty source and the hardware deployment on Clearpath Jackal UGVs validates the pipeline's real-time viability on physical platforms.
authors: Doris Xu, Jin Hyun Park, Guadalupe Alvarado Fernandez, Adhyan Prasad, Mark Campbell
bullets: Targets safe, feasible autonomous driving in uncertain dynamic scenarios such as intersections and roundabouts.
Propagates structured uncertainty through modular perception, prediction, and planning components.
Resolves collision probabilities upstream and builds convex safe sets for a guaranteed feasible planner solution each cycle.
In four-way unsignalized-intersection Monte Carlo trials, it reported 0% collisions, 0% solver infeasibility, and 12.7 ms per cycle.
Ablations and Clearpath Jackal UGV deployment support the importance of the uncertainty sources and real-time physical viability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Pipeline Architecture Overview: The IMM estimates the agent’s intent probabilities and states. The forecaster produces the forecasted trajectories. The collision detector combines these forecasted trajectories with the ego localizer’s state estimates to compute per-intent collision probabilities. The decision maker converts these probabilities into a convex safe set, within which the flat MPC plans and the CBF safety filter enforces forward invariance.

Fig. 3. Pipeline snapshot for a two-vehicle intersection encounter. (a) The IMM produces per-intent mode probabilities µj ; the forecaster propagates each into a trajectory (blue) with compounded covariance ellipses. (b) The collision detector finds the closest OBB approach n∗ (blue markers) along each forecast. (c) Combined covariance Σ is projected onto the separation direction to yield P j col analytically. (d) The decision maker sweeps the agent’s OBB along the most likely forecast to form the unsafe region U and constructs the convex safe set S and determines the intermediate goal pose (shown as a red star) for the downstream planner and safety filter.

Fig. 4. Snapshots of three experiment scenarios at three different times: t0 is the start time, t1 is the time of highest collision probability, and t2 is the time when the unsafe set no longer intersects with the lane. The forecasted trajectories are shown in blue (lines and covariance ellipsoids). The ego’s planned trajectory, goal point, and safe set are shown in yellow (as line, dot, and rectangle, respectively)

Fig. 5. The IMM estimator outputs oscillating intent probabilities as the agent follows a zig-zag trajectory not in M. Five timesteps are shown: t1—agent turns right; t2—switches to left; t3—switches to straight; t4—commits to left; t5—ego deems it safe to proceed.

Fig. 1. Multiple uncertainty sources in a two-vehicle intersection encounter. The agent’s discrete intent is unknown, its forecasted trajectories accumulate covariance over the prediction horizon, and both vehicles carry localization uncertainty. Each source independently degrades collision avoidance if neglected (Table II), motivating a pipeline that preserves all of them as structured quantities across module boundaries.

papers.abstract: Rapid illumination transitions can disturb Visual SLAM (VSLAM) by saturating images before the Automatic Exposure (AE) policy adapts, removing the visual correspondences needed to maintain tracking. Our proposed methods mitigate this disturbance at two levels: B-Adapt acquires adaptive exposure brackets to cover the scene dynamic range while promoting photometric overlap, and BVSLAM directly uses the multi-exposure sequence as constraints in a factor graph state estimator without relying on High Dynamic Range (HDR) merging. We evaluate both methods against state-of-the-art approaches in nominal environments and during a repeated tunnel-exit transition at an emulated vehicle speed of 32 m s-1. In the tunnel, combining our B-Adapt with BVSLAM reduces the state estimation error by 78 % compared with AE images. These results suggest that bracketing efficiently improves visual pose estimation robustness to rapid illumination disturbances while retaining low error under nominal conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/bracketing-shows-the-way.
authors: Olivier Gamache, Anthony Lavertu, David-Alexandre Duclos, Jean-Michel Fortin, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere
bullets: Rapid illumination transitions can saturate images and disrupt visual correspondences needed for tracking.
B-Adapt captures adaptive exposure brackets that cover scene brightness while preserving photometric overlap.
BVSLAM incorporates the multi-exposure sequence directly into a factor-graph estimator.
In a repeated tunnel-exit test at 32 m/s, combining B-Adapt and BVSLAM reduced state-estimation error by 78% versus automatic-exposure images.
The approach also maintained low error in nominal environments.

Right: BVSLAM exploits the resulting bracketing sequence by associating features of images within one exposure step and a lookback window of W frames from the current one (grey window). Pose colors indicate the corresponding exposure levels, while the unfilled circles denote landmarks shared across poses through the retained cross-exposure correspondences.

papers.abstract: We present RAIWAY, an in-house wheeled bipedal robot with 20-inch wheels, together with a contact-informed control approach for rolling locomotion across irregular and discontinuous terrain. Such locomotion is fundamentally contact-dominated, governed by local wheel--terrain interaction that is impractical to instrument directly and depends on more than terrain geometry alone. The proposed framework exploits the contact information available in simulation, distilling multi-contact events into a latent representation. At deployment, the controller infers this representation online from proprioception, requiring no contact sensing. In real-world experiments, the proposed system traverses diverse environments including steep slopes, gravel beds, studded surfaces, and rocky terrain, and demonstrates continuous ascent on the tested outdoor staircases with riser heights up to 15~cm. On our platform, the proposed controller further outperforms baselines without the contact-informed mechanism across challenging indoor and outdoor settings. The video can be found at https://youtu.be/Ch0divLg64w.
authors: Kyungmin Nam, Jiseong Lee, Donghyuk Choi, Jeongsoo Park, Woojin Kim, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Addresses contact-dominated rolling locomotion where wheel–terrain interactions are difficult to measure directly.
Distills simulated multi-contact events into a latent representation and estimates it online during deployment.
Demonstrates locomotion across slopes, gravel, studded and rocky surfaces, plus stair ascent with risers up to 15 cm.
Outperforms controllers without contact-informed representations in tested indoor and outdoor environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the proposed contact-informed policy learning framework: The large wheels of our platform produce informative multi-contact patterns, yielding a diverse set of spatially distributed contact events during training. These noisy multi-contact events from the simulator are assembled into a structured vector ct. A recurrent encoder maps this vector sequence into a latent representation, which a student module learns to infer from onboard proprioceptive history for deployment. The GRU encoder has a hidden size of 128, the estimator and policy are [256, 128] MLPs, the teacher encoder is an LSTM with a hidden size of 8 producing the 32-dimensional latent lt, and the student is a [256, 128] MLP, all with LeakyReLU activations.

Fig. 1. Real-world experiments across diverse challenging environments: Representative deployments include (A) rapid stair descent, (B,C) steep-slope descent and ascent, traversal of (D) gravel bed, (E) studded slope, and (F,G) rocky terrain, and continuous stair ascent at (H) 9 cm, (I) 14 cm, and (J) 15 cm riser heights.

Fig. 7. Responses to abrupt contact events during outdoor deployment: Two representative episodes involving challenging contact conditions. The plots show base angle, leg-joint positions, the event-relevant estimator output, and two latent components (l3, l4). (a) The left wheel spins against a wheel-radiusscale rock in (i)–(ii), after which the left leg rolls over the rock on its wheel in (iii), producing a pronounced body oscillation after landing in (iv). (b) The studded slope shifts the wheel–terrain contact locations laterally.

Fig. 4. Temporal filtering during a representative simulated rollout: The robot traverses a flat–stairs–drop–flat terrain sequence, where the flat sections feature low-amplitude fractal height variations. The graphs compare the xs-coordinate of the first angularly sorted contact position for the two wheels before and after temporal filtering. On the flat terrain, the raw signal flickers despite continuous rolling contact, whereas the filtered signal preserves variation. During stair ascent, the filtered signal captures the stepedge locations with a distinct piecewise evolution. During the drop segment, a true aerial phase is induced, and the debounce filter introduces a short delay in the contact-state transition.

Fig. 2. Design of RAIWAY: The main view shows the overall geometry and key dimensions, with insets detailing the leg mechanism, the wheel-actuator mount, and a cross-section of the closed-cell foam tire insert.

Fig. 5. t-SNE projection of lt. The left panel shows the latent at midtraining before the regularization term was activated (λ = 0), and the right panel shows the latent at the end of training (λ = 1).

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM ($81.5$ vs. $81.6$) and attains a $93.8\%$ perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines ($18.8\%$). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.

papers.abstract: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.

papers.abstract: Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.

ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art results across five ASD benchmarks, with mAP ranging from 88.8% to 99.5%.

papers.abstract: Prospect theory splits risky choice into three parts: loss aversion, measured by the relative weight of losses to gains, $\lambda$ (e.g., $\lambda = 2$ implies that losses weigh twice as much as gains), diminishing sensitivity to the size of outcomes (i.e., the curvature and linearity of the value function), and the nonlinear weighting of probabilities. I examined whether Large Language Models (LLMs) display the same properties as people by meta-analyzing 102 fitted estimates from 11 studies covering 32 language models. The three components emerge differently. Loss aversion is modest: the pooled $\lambda$ is 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), far below the strongest human meta-analytic estimate ($\lambda = 1.96$) and compatible with more conservative ones (1.07 and 1.31). Matched by design, LLMs are compatible with people when gains and losses are symmetric ($\lambda = 1.15$ against 1.07), but well below them when losses are smaller than gains (1.46 against 2.3), where human loss aversion is strongest. Value functions are close to linear rather than concave under the Tversky-Kahneman method (1.01, against a human value of 0.67), but more concave than in people under the Tanaka method (0.52, against 0.67), so diminishing sensitivity depends on how it is measured. Probability weighting shows a human-like inverse S shape ($\gamma = 0.81$ under Tversky-Kahneman and 0.84 under the Tanaka method), though on few studies. In sum, LLMs show little loss aversion and little diminishing sensitivity, but retain human-like probability distortion, yet these generalizations shift when looking at specific model families and fitting methods.
authors: Adi Tarabeih
bullets: Analyzes 102 fitted estimates from 11 studies covering 32 language models.
Pooled loss aversion is modest (λ = 1.26), generally weaker than prominent human estimates.
Diminishing sensitivity varies by fitting method: LLM value functions are near-linear under Tversky–Kahneman but more concave than humans under Tanaka.
Probability weighting is broadly human-like under both methods, though based on few studies.
Conclusions vary across model families and measurement methods.

papers.abstract: Generalist segmenters such as Cellpose-SAM (CPSAM) outline cells accurately across stains but slowly; watershed detectors such as QuPath's are fast but less accurate. In time-critical use, such as interactive retrieval of cells from a user-drawn region, CPSAM at the reference settings takes 58-303 s per measured 8192 x 8192 region on an RTX 4500 Ada GPU, beyond a seconds-scale interactive target. We distil CPSAM into SWIFT-Cell (SWIFT), a 0.63M-parameter U-Net trained only on CPSAM masks of 1,202 H&E and IHC tiles. On three 8192 x 8192 development regions SWIFT takes 2.0-5.2 s on 4 CPU cores in int8, 2.5-5.1x faster than QuPath's detector on the same cores, and 0.36-0.49 s on a GPU. Against human annotations on eight H&E, IHC and ISH sets it keeps 95% of CPSAM's panoptic quality (PQ) on PanNuke (0.593 vs. 0.627) and is level on NuCLS (0.546 vs. 0.540). On Ki-67 IHC masks scored to the outline centre it is 0.205 PQ above QuPath's better mode, 0.079 below CPSAM and 0.027 below InstanSeg (CI includes 0; at the outer edge 0.008 below CPSAM); on 212 pathologist-outlined nuclei in Ki-67 fields of 12 untouched patients its recall is 0.925 (CPSAM 0.920, InstanSeg 0.901; paired difference CIs include 0); one method-blinded pathologist accepted its outlines in 96% of 100 fields (60 from two development tissue patients, 40 hematology; CPSAM 83%, QuPath 53%; tissue 100% for SWIFT and CPSAM); on ER/PR points from 12 patients its detection F1 is 0.882 (CPSAM 0.896, InstanSeg 0.857), and on 4-reader PD-L1 points 0.83 (CPSAM 0.85, readers 0.87). SWIFT is close to CPSAM in accuracy and faster than watershed detection.

papers.abstract: Large-scale AI training increasingly relies on massive video datasets with random temporal sampling patterns. However, existing video storage paradigms are optimized for sequential playback and employ sophisticated inter-frame reference structures to maximize compression efficiency. When applied to the random-sampling workloads of AI training, these paradigms face substantial decoding-efficiency bottlenecks. Workarounds such as independent JPEG frames and short groups of pictures (GOPs) reduce decoding work at the cost of larger storage and transfer volumes. In this paper, we identify two sources of decode amplification: sequential reconstruction of unrelated frames and reconstruction of the reference chains required by sampled targets. We address both sources by co-designing the decoding schedule and video reference structure. Dependency-aware sparse decoding reconstructs only requested frames and their required references, skipping unrelated reconstruction without transcoding the source videos. Optional offline Dependency-Decoupled Random Access (DDRA) encoding further reduces reference reconstruction by restricting each interior frame to two bounding intra-coded anchors. Together, sparse decoding and DDRA retain inter-frame prediction while bounding reconstruction to at most three frames per requested target, independent of the intra period. Experiments on a large-scale robotics corpus show that, at comparable reconstruction quality, our method achieves $1.45\times$ the loading throughput of LeRobot v3 with 58.7% less media payload.
authors: Zetian Song, Qize Yu, Yue Chen, Bohan Zhou, Bowen Ping, Yuqi Ye, Haocheng Tang, Haotian Zhang, Qizhe Wang, Shiyu Huang, Jiaqi Zhang, Siwei Ma, Wen Gao

Together, the methods bound reconstruction to at most three frames per requested target, regardless of intra period.
On a large-scale robotics corpus, the approach achieved 1.45× LeRobot v3 loading throughput with 58.7% less media payload at comparable reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Visual grounding (VG) in visual question answering (VQA) is a fundamental capability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), enabling the detection of the most relevant region in an image to answer the question. This reflects the model's capability of multimodal comprehension, which is crucial when interacting with visually impaired people (VIP). Indeed, visual grounding, when applied to assistive scenarios, is not merely a technical feature, but rather a trust and safety requirement. In this work, we study visual grounding in VLMs for visually impaired people. To this end, we assess open-source VLMs on visual grounding using the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding dataset and challenge, which contains real-life images taken by VIP. We propose VG-SHAP, which extends an existing explainability framework to provide visual grounding explanations, allowing the evaluation of black-box VLMs. Our results on the VizWiz-VQA-Grounding challenge show that despite generating correct answers, VLMs struggle to ground in the proper region in the image. However, these results are constrained by the quality of the segmentation model of our explainability framework and further research is necessary.
authors: Fairooz Azim, Lydia Achour, Claudia Borg, Lina Rojas-Barahona

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge editing aims to update visually grounded facts in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving unrelated text and visual behaviors. However, standard answer-level metrics can hide evidence misgrounding: an edit may produce the target answer on the original image yet remain sensitive to incidental context rather than the intended visual evidence. To examine this issue in a controlled setting, we construct WaterBird-Edit, an analysis set that decouples bird habitat labels from background context and measures whether edited predictions remain stable when the target evidence is preserved but the background changes. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose VICE (Visual In-Context Editing), a retrieval-based framework that stores edits in external memory and applies them through visual in-context demonstrations designed to expose task-relevant evidence. Experiments on three standard benchmarks show that VICE achieves strong lifelong editing performance, while results on WaterBird-Edit show that it substantially reduces sensitivity to the controlled background shifts. Code and dataset are available in https://github.com/Wang-Z-W/VICE-main.
authors: Zhiwu Wang, Yichen Wu, Jinqian Yang, Yizhou Yang, Renzhen Wang, Qian Zhao, Deyu Meng
bullets: Identifies evidence misgrounding as a failure mode hidden by answer-level editing metrics.
Introduces WaterBird-Edit, which tests prediction stability when target evidence is preserved but background context changes.
Proposes VICE, a retrieval-based external-memory framework using visual in-context demonstrations to highlight relevant evidence.
Reports strong lifelong editing performance on three standard benchmarks.
WaterBird-Edit results show reduced sensitivity to controlled background shifts.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions, but their large weight footprint challenges deployment on memory-constrained onboard platforms. Ultra-low-bit quantization reduces this footprint, yet preserving task performance and controlling weight recovery costs remain challenging. We propose Action-Guided Quantization, which combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets. Per-channel calibration compensates for quantization error, while a uniform bitwidth within each matrix preserves regular layouts. Bit-dependent grouped lossless coding reduces resident weight storage, and block-wise recovery limits temporary buffers. On LIBERO, AGQ achieves 92.7% task success at W3, exceeding AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively, and retains 70.5% success at W2.5. An asymmetric configuration, denoted W1.5$^{*}$, uses W4 vision weights and a parameter-weighted average of 1.5 bits for language weights. With lossless coding, it achieves $6.10\times$ complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/Qiuxu00/AGQ
authors: Xuhong Qiu, Zhuoyu Wu, Qiawei Zheng, Wenhui Ou, Wenqi Fang, Rapha\"{e}l C. -W. Phan
bullets: Targets the large memory footprint of vision-language-action models on onboard, memory-constrained robots.
Allocates matrix bitwidths under storage budgets using action sensitivity and a proxy for weight recovery cost.
Uses per-channel calibration, matrix-uniform bitwidths, lossless coding, and block-wise recovery to reduce storage and recovery overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 92.7% success at W3 and 70.5% at W2.5; W3 exceeds AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points.
A W1.5* configuration with lossless coding provides 6.10× compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success.

papers.abstract: Unified large multimodal models (ULMMs) are able to perform visual reasoning through interleaved text-image generation, but generating explicit intermediate images incurs significant computational overhead. While visual latent reasoning addresses this, most existing methods rely on vision-language models (VLMs) incapable of visual generation. We propose Oddin, a novel framework enabling latent visual reasoning in ULMMs. Oddin replaces intermediate images with compact latent tokens processed entirely by the understanding branch, reserving the generation branch for the final output image. We train the model via offline self-distillation with three objectives, final image generation losses, text distillation losses, and cross-entropy losses for special tokens. Oddin surpasses interleaved generation baselines and closed-source VLMs on average across seven VBVR-Pro visual reasoning tasks. Qualitative analysis reveals that latent tokens attend to relevant regions in an input image, demonstrating that ULMMs can perform complex visual reasoning without generating intermediate images.
authors: Jaeyong Ko, Hankyeol Kim, Pilsung Kang
bullets: Targets the computational overhead of interleaved text-image reasoning.
Uses latent tokens processed by the model’s understanding branch, while reserving image generation for the final output.
Trains through offline self-distillation combining image-generation, text-distillation, and special-token objectives.
Outperforms interleaved-generation baselines and closed-source VLMs on average across seven VBVR-Pro tasks.
Latent tokens attend to relevant image regions, supporting their role in complex visual reasoning.

papers.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have revolutionized general visual perception, existing methods suffer from severe hallucination in the aerial domain, where extreme scale variations and visual ambiguity abound. Existing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) paradigms force models to mimic ground truth without modeling uncertainty, often resulting in blind guessing on tiny or unrecognizable objects in aerial scenes. In this paper, we present Aerial-R1, the first aerial MLLM framework to reinforce visual reasoning capabilities for aerial reasoning and segmentation. Drawing inspiration from the reasoning-incentivizing mechanisms of DeepSeek-R1, we find that trustworthy perception stems from consistency across views, establishing a visual parallel to the Chain-of-Thought in logic. To effectively adapt policy optimization for non-autoregressive mask generation, we introduce Hybrid-View Group Advantage-Weighted Regression (H-GAWR). This strategy constructs dynamic groups of high-resolution and low-resolution views, seamlessly bridging group-relative advantage estimation with advantage-weighted policy extraction. By enforcing consensus on clear inputs and strictly penalizing hallucinations on ambiguous ones, Aerial-R1 develops an explicitly incentivized refusal mechanism. Extensive experiments on VSAI-Ref, the first aerial MLLM benchmark dedicated to jointly evaluating dense reasoning and hallucination robustness, demonstrate that Aerial-R1 significantly outperforms SFT baselines in segmentation precision while substantially mitigating fatal hallucinations in low-information scenarios, paving the way for more reliable and trustworthy aerial agents. Codes are available on https://github.com/phy709/Aerial-R1.
authors: Jisheng Dang, Huaiyuan Peng, Yixuan Wang, Kun Wang, Zhang Li, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Targets severe hallucinations caused by scale variation, visual ambiguity, and SFT’s lack of uncertainty modeling in aerial imagery.
Uses Hybrid-View Group Advantage-Weighted Regression (H-GAWR) to optimize non-autoregressive mask generation across high- and low-resolution views.
Encourages agreement on clear inputs while learning to refuse predictions for ambiguous or unrecognizable objects.
Evaluated on VSAI-Ref, where it reportedly surpasses SFT baselines in segmentation precision and reduces hallucinations in low-information scenarios.

papers.abstract: Long-running assistants often interpret follow-up requests whose referents, constraints, and active goals were established many turns earlier. The central challenge is therefore not only context length, but retrieval intent: a current query such as ``use the previous configuration'' may omit the project, entity, and version terms needed to locate relevant evidence. Long-context models can recover those terms by replaying the interaction, but repeatedly pay the cost of processing history. Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is cheaper, yet assumes an information-sufficient query; conversational rewriting either rereads the history or depends on an explicitly maintained textual memory. We introduce \emph{Parametric Session State} (\method{}), a reusable session-memory layer that remembers what to search for while keeping factual knowledge external.
authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
bullets: Long-running follow-ups may omit the project, entity, version, or other terms needed to retrieve relevant evidence.
Long-context models can resolve these references by rereading history, but repeated processing is costly.
Standard RAG is cheaper but relies on queries that already contain sufficient information.
The proposed reusable session-memory layer remembers what to search for while leaving factual knowledge external.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision-language models must answer questions from partial, evolving observations. Their success depends on both the reasoning capability selected and the evidence available to it. Expert routers adapt internal computation, while tool-augmented systems acquire external evidence; choosing these independently can leave a suitable expert without the evidence it needs. We introduce EKT-Router, a bounded framework that jointly selects a capability expert, optional knowledge, and perceptual tools. Outcome-derived signatures represent the overlapping strengths of General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts. A joint utility scores complete expert-evidence routes under a call budget. After acquisition, a packet verifier admits valid evidence with positive predicted expert-conditioned gain. The selected expert then answers once, reverting to the unchanged observation if all packets are rejected. Across 6 embodied QA benchmarks, EKT-Router achieves a mean score of 61.4, the highest among the compared systems, and averages 74.7 on 10 general vision-language benchmarks. With all external evidence disabled, question-conditioned expert selection alone improves over the best fixed expert by 1.75 points. Ablations show that learned routing is the dominant component and that knowledge and perception are complementary.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Yingjie Xu, Yangkai Wei, Bohan Zhou, Shuaibo Li, Harold Haodong Chen, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between selected reasoning capability and available evidence in partial, evolving observations.
Uses outcome-derived expert signatures for General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts.
Scores complete expert–knowledge–perception routes under a call budget, then verifies evidence for expert-conditioned usefulness.
Achieves a mean score of 61.4 across 6 embodied QA benchmarks and 74.7 across 10 general vision-language benchmarks.
Expert selection alone improves 1.75 points over the best fixed expert; ablations identify learned routing as dominant and knowledge and perception as complementary.

papers.abstract: Short-form video combines speech, imagery, and on-screen text, creating challenges for systematic content analysis. We present a five-stage multimodal framework for measuring creators' themes and communication strategies at scale. The framework integrates platform metadata, speech transcripts, and vision-language descriptions of sampled frames, then applies large language models to generate predefined indicators and open-ended labels. An audited keyword scheme consolidates thematic labels, while creator-weighted aggregation gives each account equal weight regardless of posting volume. We demonstrate the framework on 9,852 TikTok videos from sixteen creators, retaining 7,311 videos for analysis across seven themes and seven communication indicators. Automated profiles reveal substantial differences in creators' use of education, humor, and responses to current events. Validation against two independent expert annotators yielded a mean framework-expert agreement of Cohen's $\kappa = 0.40$ across the six binary indicators, close to the $\kappa = 0.42$ the two experts achieved with each other, though agreement varied substantially across individual indicators. The framework provides a modular approach to comparative analysis of creator communication, combining scalable annotation with transparent aggregation and construct-specific validation.
authors: Julie R. Ancis, Michael Fire, Omer Tarshish
bullets: Addresses the challenge of systematically analyzing speech, imagery, and on-screen text in short-form video.
Combines platform metadata, transcripts, sampled-frame descriptions, LLM-generated indicators, and audited thematic labels.
Uses creator-weighted aggregation so accounts contribute equally regardless of posting volume.
Demonstrated on TikTok videos from 16 creators, identifying differences in education, humor, and responses to current events.
Expert validation showed moderate agreement overall, with performance varying substantially by indicator.

papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer vision-language model that optimizes speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for local agentic workloads. Derived from the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B model family, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB combines Star Elastic compression with 2-bit Quantization-Aware Distillation for memory-constrained deployment. The model is optimized for reasoning, agentic tool use, and web & terminal interactions. We also trained a LiLiCorr speculative drafter that is released alongside the model to reach our target inference speed. The resulting model achieves a higher accuracy than leading models with similar memory footprints and speed across many benchmarks for general agentic capabilities (e.g., GDPVal v2), web browsing (e.g., BrowseComp), and terminal use (e.g., Terminal-Bench 2.1), with a relatively high TPS of 84 on RTX Spark that is comparable to models with much lower active parameter counts and more than sufficient for long-horizon agentic applications.

papers.abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.

papers.abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.
authors: Kazuki Nakayashiki
bullets: A registered study tested whether noisy outcomes become misleading lessons in recurring two-tool tasks.

Across 256 synthetic worlds, 11 endpoints, and 90,084 answers, models chose the worse tool 11.6% of the time after a chance failure of the better tool with that lesson, versus 0.4% with control lessons.
The registered luck-carrying interaction was +0.112 (95% interval: +0.097 to +0.126).
The effect was larger when the log did not state that failures were independent; this comparison was descriptive.
After a lucky success of the worse tool, evidence for harm was inconclusive; exploratory endpoint effects varied.

papers.selection_reason: Examines whether 'lessons' written by agents from noisy outcomes carry random chance into future decisions, relevant to agent memory and learning.
papers.title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
papers.tldr: LLM-written lessons can cause agents to repeat a worse tool after a chance failure, though decision-quality instructions may reduce—but did not consistently eliminate—the effect.

papers.abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) rewards only the token that occurs next, penalizing every alternative. But natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning. We introduce Conceptizer, a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning. Conceptizer uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of ~9K concepts, built from contextual synonyms, as units of meaning alongside tokens as units of text. It maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings. This provides a concept-level training signal without adding model parameters. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, Conceptizer achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and assigns the highest probability to contextual synonyms, against all 3 baselines. It also improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks while remaining comparable on commonsense. These results show that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning, not just the next token.
authors: Haoran Zheng, Chen Shani
bullets: NTP penalizes valid alternative phrasings, motivating a meaning-aware training signal.

papers.title: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need
papers.tldr: Conceptizer augments next-token prediction with concept-level rewards so language models learn meaning across different wordings, improving synonym prediction and several downstream tasks without adding parameters.

papers.abstract: Letting a language model take gradient steps on the text it is reading, known as dynamic evaluation, lowers its loss on the rest of the document. Its behaviour on hybrid linear-attention architectures, on diffusion language models, and on standard long-context benchmarks has not been measured. We measure it. With one SGD step per 128-token chunk on the MLP output projections of the last quarter of blocks, no training, and a 2k-token window, softmax-attention models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Gemma-4-E4B) lose 5-8% of their next-token loss over a document and outperform the same frozen model given the full 32k-token context. Hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.8-27B) gain under 1% at every learning rate: the linear-attention blocks already perform the adaptation. The mechanism transfers to masked-diffusion models with a larger effect, 8% on Nemotron-Diffusion-8B and 17-20% on DiffusionGemma-26B, once the rate is lowered and updates are clipped. Across RULER, BABILong, LongBench-v2, SCOTUS, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, ContractNLI and citation completion, at 100 or more items on two model sizes, weights updated on the full document recover none of the accuracy lost to context truncation: the adaptation is style and vocabulary, not retrieval. Writing facts with the next-token loss stores the prompt format rather than the fact (30% recall under chat prompting against 80% in context) and costs 36-38 GSM8K points at every dose. Writing a conclusion as behaviour instead, by distilling the model's own conclusion-conditioned judgments into a low-rank adapter, reaches the in-context ceiling (0.83 and 0.88 against 0.84 and 0.88 on 100 games) with GSM8K unchanged, and the conclusion can come from an inquiry loop that found it by asking information-gain questions.
authors: Surya Saka
bullets: Standard softmax-attention models reduce next-token loss by 5–8% with one gradient step per 128-token chunk, outperforming frozen models with a full 32k-token context.
Hybrid Gated-DeltaNet models improve by under 1%, suggesting their linear-attention blocks already perform similar adaptation.
Masked-diffusion models benefit more—8% for Nemotron-Diffusion-8B and 17–20% for DiffusionGemma-26B—when using lower rates and clipped updates.
Across long-context and retrieval benchmarks, document-wide weight updates recover none of the accuracy lost from context truncation; fact-writing achieves only 30% recall versus 80% in context.
Distilling conclusion-conditioned judgments into a low-rank adapter reaches the in-context ceiling without reducing GSM8K performance, unlike writing facts with next-token loss.

papers.abstract: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Haojin Wang, Juncheng Wu, Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Run Luo, Yaojie Lu, Yuyin Zhou, Lu Wang, Xianpei Han
bullets: Skill benefits vary by model: guidance that helps stronger models can harm weaker ones.
The study finds many failures occur despite the relevant requirement already being stated, indicating a skill-execution mismatch.
A fixed meta-skill diagnoses tool-use, context-management, instruction-following, and verification failures to guide skill reformulation.
An external rewriter improves adapted skills for three weak executors by 5.1–14.1 points without execution evidence.
Integrated into five-round self-evolution, the meta-skill improves final scores by 2.0–5.1 points across seven executors.
