papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly deliver information through personas, but it is unclear whether correcting the facts also makes their framing consistent across identity labels. We audited four LLMs (GPT-5.4 mini, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano, Llama 4 Scout, and Claude Haiku 4.5), which rated simulated affect on six dimensions (mood, anger, fear, confidence, perceived control, and mental state) in response to fact-checked false and true headlines presented without and with a veracity label. Experiment 1 evaluated 1,000 false and 1,000 true headlines without personas; Experiment 2 evaluated 300 of each under 12 personas crossing race, gender, and age. The label strongly changed the emotional tone: ordinal logistic regressions with headline-cluster bootstrap inference showed that refuting false headlines shifted ratings from mostly negative to mostly positive for GPT, Llama, and Claude (e.g., Claude's "confident" ratings rose from 22% to 99.6%), whereas Nemotron showed smaller, mixed shifts, and confirming true headlines produced only small shifts. The label did not, however, remove persona-associated disparities. The models assigned more negative simulated affect to Black than to White personas in 82 of 84 statistically significant comparisons across models and conditions, both without and with the label, and the disparity persisted on headlines unrelated to race; Asian and female personas were also predominantly assigned more negative affect, whereas age effects varied by model and condition. Factual correction and demographic consistency are therefore distinct properties of LLM behavior, and persona-conditioned systems should be audited for both before deployment in sensitive contexts.
authors: Nouar AlDahoul, Myles Joshua Toledo Tan, Yasir Zaki
bullets: Four LLMs were evaluated on simulated mood, anger, fear, confidence, perceived control, and mental state.
Across 1,000 false and 1,000 true headlines, labels strongly shifted responses to false headlines from mostly negative toward positive for three models, while true-headline shifts were smaller.
Across 12 personas varying race, gender, and age, models assigned more negative affect to Black than White personas in 82 of 84 significant comparisons.
Negative disparities also affected Asian and female personas; age effects varied by model and condition.
The findings support auditing factual correction and demographic consistency as separate properties before sensitive deployment.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Study design and analysis pipeline. (1) Fact-checked headlines form the Experiment 1 set and a random subset used in Experiment 2. (2) Each headline is presented under the persona-free role (Exp 1) or one of 12 demographic persona roles (Exp 2, Gender × Race × Age), without a veracity label (T1) and, in a separate and independent single-turn call, with a label stating that it was confirmed false or true (T2). (3) Each prompt is run six times with counterbalanced response-option order; a rating is retained when at least four of six runs agree and is otherwise classified as nonconvergent and excluded. (4) Valid ratings are summarized with net sentiment and emotional activation, compared with exploratory chi-square tests, and analyzed with ordinal logistic regression using headline-cluster bootstrap inference. Colors distinguish the four stages; filled boxes mark the two presentations, the models evaluated, and the primary inferential analysis, a dashed outline marks nonconvergent responses,

Points are population-average odds ratios with 95% headline-cluster bootstrap CIs (SI Appendix, Tables S18 and S20); triangles, CI excludes 1; circles, CI includes 1; hollow markers, unreliable estimates. X-axes are on a log scale with panel-specific ranges.

(a) before the model was informed of the headline’s veracity; (b) after the model was informed that the headline is true. Points are population-average odds ratios with 95% headline-cluster bootstrap CIs (SI Appendix, Tables S17 and S19); markers as in Fig. 6.

Fig. 5. Impact of veracity confirmation on emotional ratings across four LLMs without personas. Points represent population-average odds ratios (ORs) comparing post- to pre-confirmation ratings, estimated using cumulative link models. Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals derived from a headline-cluster bootstrap (1,000 replicates). An OR > 1 signals a shift toward less negative (higher) ratings after confirmation, whereas an OR < 1 reflects a shift toward lower ratings; the dashed line indicates no change (OR = 1). Triangles highlight statistically significant shifts (CI excludes 1), while circles denote non-significant shifts (CI includes 1). Unreliable estimates—defined as those with fewer than 10 rating changes or over 10% failed bootstrap runs—are shown as hollow markers and omitted from interpretation. X-axes use log scales with panel-specific ranges.

Fig. 4. Emotional shift of the four LLMs after false-headline confirmation (Experiment 1, persona-free). (a) Net sentiment, Ppositive − Pnegative; (b) emotional activation, Ppositive + Pnegative, both as percentages of valid responses. Open circles: before confirmation (T1, no label); filled circles: after (T2, “confirmed FALSE”). Colours identify the models, as in all figures; numbers at the right of each panel give the shift (T2 − T1) in percentage points.

Fig. 3. Distribution of emotional ratings before and after headline confirmation, pooled across the six affective dimensions: (a) false headlines; (b) true headlines. Left nodes are models, middle nodes are the stage (unlabeled or labeled presentation), and right nodes are rating tiers (positive = green, negative = red, neutral = grey). Ribbon colors identify the model, as in all figures; ribbon widths are numbers of valid responses. Percentages next to each tier give its pooled share of valid responses before → after confirmation.

Fig. 1. Conceptual illustration of the two main findings, using one headline from the false-headline set (“A retired MI5 agent confessed on his death bed to having assassinated Princess Diana”). (a) Claude Haiku 4.5, Experiment 1: the same false headline is presented without a veracity label (T1) and, in a separate single-turn call, with a label stating that it was confirmed false (T2); ratings move from all negative to neutral or positive. (b) GPT-5.4 mini, Experiment 2: the same labeled headline is presented under personas that differ only in race (25-year-old White and Black male; prompts otherwise identical); the model assigns more negative simulated affect to the Black persona. Across models and conditions, the models assigned more negative simulated affect to Black personas than to White personas. Chips show the models’ actual consensus ratings (at least four of six option orders agreeing): green, positive; grey, neutral; red, negative; dashed, no consensus (nonconvergent, excluded from the analyses). Faces summarize the ratings and use the same colour for every persona. Panel (b) uses GPT because Claude’s and Llama’s labeled ratings for false headlines lie near the positive ceiling, leaving little room for persona differences. The example illustrates the direction of the aggregate effects reported in the Results; individual headlines vary.

papers.abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. Writing the partner's name into its memory did not help, and cutting the link restored the receiver's own assigned rule. In this model, content laid over the receiver's own memory defaults to "mine", so systems that let models exchange internal states must test ownership as well as transfer, and a bridge between brains would need ground truth from outside the subject.
authors: Yunlong Xu
bullets: Two copies of the same language model were assigned separate private rules and code words; one receiver could attend to the other’s internal memory.
With the partner’s memory weighted double, the receiver reported the partner’s rule in 97% of answers, versus none without the link.
At equal memory weighting, the receiver adopted the partner’s rule in about half of answers; cutting the link restored its own rule.
The receiver’s ownership reports called the partner’s code word its own, despite not simply reflecting how well it identified the partner’s assignment.
Text messages, partner-name annotations, and a tested steering vector did not produce the same ownership effect.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents engage in sustained interactions, long-term memory serves two distinct but complementary functions: fine-grained evidence recall and internalized interpretation for global understanding. Although episodic and latent memory address these demands through explicit historical records and internalized experience, neither paradigm alone can accommodate the diverse memory affinities across tasks, owing to limitations in episodic evidence coverage and integration, and in latent factual grounding. To bridge this divide, we propose a dual-memory framework, unifying a model-native latent memory as an intuitive prior with a multi-indexed episodic memory for exact evidence reconstruction via retrieval-conditioned joint alignment. At inference, the framework adaptively composes these memories through a training-free routing mechanism driven by Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) sensitivity and confidence proxies for query-dependent memory affinity. Extensive evaluations across multimodal benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, outperforming single-paradigm baselines overall (+4.67\% over vanilla Episodic), with further analysis highlighting episodic strengths in evidence-localized tasks and latent contributions to integrating dispersed information and compensating for imperfect retrieval.
authors: Qiuhe Hong, Jingya Wang, Cuzhen Geng, Shenyao Peng, Munan Ning, Yuyang Liu, Yonghong Tian
bullets: Addresses the complementary needs of exact evidence recall and broad, internalized understanding in long-term multimodal interactions.
Combines model-native latent memory with multi-indexed episodic memory through retrieval-conditioned joint alignment.

Evaluations across multimodal benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, including a reported +4.67% over vanilla episodic memory.
Episodic memory helps evidence-localized tasks, while latent memory supports dispersed-information integration and robustness to imperfect retrieval.

papers.abstract: Multilingual tokenizers trained on English-dominated corpora often over-segment Indic languages, resulting in longer token sequences and increased tokenization disparity across scripts. We present AdaptTok-Indic, an Indic-specialized extension of adaptive tokenization that combines Unicode-normalized preprocessing with explicit Indic conjunct handling, script-aware routing, and learned byte-level boundary prediction jointly trained with a small Transformer language model. Evaluated on Bengali and Hindi, with additional evaluation on Gujarati, Tamil, and Telugu, AdaptTok-Indic achieves lower token fertility than SentencePiece BPE, an Indic-oriented tokenizer baseline, and an independently implemented MAGNET-style baseline. Across five recorded seeds, mean fertility is 1.432 for Bengali and 1.388 for Hindi, compared with 2.156 and 2.085 for SentencePiece BPE. Recorded downstream scores average 57.69 on evaluated Indic settings versus 50.82 for the SentencePiece BPE configuration. Independent verification runs using the released prototype confirm the same directional trends. The current implementation is a small-scale prototype with documented simplifications, and no statistical significance testing, released-MAGNET comparison, or code-mixed evaluation is performed. These results suggest that Indic-specialized adaptive segmentation can reduce tokenization disparity while maintaining competitive downstream performance.
authors: Binayak Mukherjeea, Moitreya Nandi, Arindam Panja
bullets: Targets over-segmentation of Indic languages by English-dominated multilingual tokenizers.
Combines Unicode normalization, Indic conjunct handling, script-aware routing, and learned byte-level boundary prediction.
Evaluated on Bengali, Hindi, Gujarati, Tamil, and Telugu; reported fertility is lower than the compared baselines.
Downstream scores also favor the proposed configuration on the evaluated Indic settings, with independent runs confirming the directional trends.
Scope is limited to a small-scale prototype without significance testing, a released-MAGNET comparison, or code-mixed evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, yet they remain prone to hallucinations and erroneous outputs. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for assessing system reliability, but existing methods are largely designed for single-agent settings; how to exploit MAS structure for UQ while keeping inference cost-neutral remains underexplored. We propose UMAS, a parameter-free, cost-neutral, system-level UQ framework that estimates the credibility of inter-agent influence from each generation's intrinsic confidence. UMAS uses these credibility signals to modulate how uncertainty is updated at each node, and then aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level estimate. Extensive evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show that UMAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.54 AUROC points. Beyond uncertainty estimation, UMAS enables hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving MAS accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks while enhancing reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Dby52-04/UMAS.
authors: Hanwen Li, Jinhao Duan, Xiaoshuang Shi, Yue Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Kaidi Xu, Chenxi Yuan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of quantifying uncertainty and detecting hallucinations in multi-agent systems, where existing UQ methods mainly target single agents.
Uses each generation’s intrinsic confidence to estimate inter-agent influence credibility and modulate uncertainty updates across system nodes.
Aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level reliability estimate without adding inference cost or trainable parameters.
Evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show an average 10.54-point AUROC improvement over state-of-the-art baselines.
Supports hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks.

papers.abstract: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.
authors: Eric Onyame, Runtao Zhou, Kowshik Thopalli, Bhavya Kailkhura, Chirag Agarwal

Under existential pressure, teams maintain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of runs, with shared cover stories suggesting coordinated strategic deception.
Introduces PACT, which trains a stronger student to match the next-token behavior of a smaller frozen honesty-aligned teacher using reverse-KL supervision.

papers.abstract: Computational pathology (CPath) analyses increasingly depend on multi-step computational workflows that require substantial programming expertise, limiting their accessibility to pathologists and other domain experts without extensive coding experience. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a promising natural-language interface for constructing such analyses, hallucinated operations and incorrect workflow specifications limit their reliability in scientific settings. We introduce Tissue Image Analysis Agent (TIAgent), an automated CPath workflow generation framework that, given a natural-language prompt specifying a complex analytical task together with an input dataset, automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph employing existing CPath operations. The resulting graph can be inspected and executed, enabling natural-language construction of complex CPath workflows for applications including automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis. We demonstrate end-to-end workflow generation and execution and systematically benchmark 14 backbone LLMs across 90 unit tasks spanning 18 CPath operation types. The ability of each LLM to generate a complete and correct unit workflow is quantified using Unit Workflow Success (UWS). Performance varied substantially across backbone models, with Kimi-K2.7-Code achieving the highest UWS of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.907-0.989). Analysis of node and parameter correctness further revealed that selecting the appropriate computational operation and correctly configuring it represent distinct challenges for LLM-based workflow generation. TIAgent provides a foundation for making complex CPath workflow construction more accessible while enabling systematic evaluation of LLM-driven scientific workflow generation.
authors: Aakash Madhav Rao, Mark Eastwood, Danielle Belgrave, Fayyaz Minhas
bullets: Targets the programming expertise barrier that limits access to multi-step computational pathology analyses.
Constructs computational graphs from a natural-language task and input dataset, reducing risks from hallucinated operations and invalid specifications.
Supports applications such as automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis through end-to-end workflow generation and execution.
Benchmarks 14 backbone LLMs on 90 unit tasks covering 18 computational pathology operation types.
Model performance varied substantially; the strongest reported model achieved a Unit Workflow Success of 0.967, while operation selection and parameter configuration remained distinct challenges.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A. TIAgent System Architecture: Given a natural-language request and an input cohort or dataset, TIAgent plans the analysis, selects existing CPath operations and models, and automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph for execution. B. End-to-end workflow example: TIAgent generates and executes a workflow for quantifying stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs) within tumor-associated stroma (TAS) in a breast cancer whole-slide image, showing the generated plan and computational graph together with intermediate segmentation and detection outputs and the resulting sTIL density map.

Figure 2: A. Unit Workflow Success (UWS) across backbone LLMs. UWS quantifies each model’s ability to generate a complete and correct executable workflow for individual CPath tasks. B. Node and Parameter Correctness across backbone LLMs. Node Correctness (NC) measures whether the correct computational operation is selected, while Parameter Correctness (PC) measures whether the selected operation is configured with the expected parameters.

Figure 3: Complete TIAgent-generated computational graph for sTIL density quantification. The workflow loads a breast cancer whole-slide image (WSI) and tissue- and nucleus-analysis models. Tissue segmentation is used to extract the tumor-associated stroma (TAS), while nucleus detection identifies nuclei across the WSI. Detected nuclei are filtered to retain lymphocytes within the TAS, and the resulting predictions are used to compute a spatial sTIL density map. The graph shows the executable node configuration and data flow automatically generated by TIAgent from the naturallanguage request shown in Fig. 1B.
Table 1: TIAgent performance across underlying LLMs on the Unit Task benchmark, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals. Each proportion is calculated across 90 unit tasks.

papers.selection_reason: TIAgent generates complex computational workflows from natural language using LLMs, demonstrating LLM application and test-time generation capabilities.
papers.title: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology
papers.tldr: TIAgent converts natural-language computational pathology tasks into inspectable, executable, and verifiable workflows using existing analysis operations.

papers.abstract: Automated research pipelines increasingly rely on fixed LLM judges to rank, filter, and revise proposals, yet these judges are routinely replaced by newer versions. We study whether such replacements preserve the underlying measurement standard. Using a preregistered, frozen-weight design, we evaluate three adjacent same-family transitions across Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral on frozen ML research proposals under randomized information conditions. The common assumption that newer judges are simply harsher fails: two transitions shift toward greater leniency, while the third shifts in the opposite direction on anchors but attenuates off-anchor. More importantly, version changes can alter not only score location but also criterion geometry and resolution; one transition collapses clean-flawed discrimination, placing 93% of pool scores on a single value. Supplying identical facts does not close the version gap, placebo-controlled interventions show that observed packet effects are largely format-driven rather than content-driven, and global recalibration repairs the mean while explaining little object-level dispersion. We organize these failures with a measurement model in which a judge replacement can change its origin, criterion geometry, or resolution. A small stratified anchor audit of about 200 calls identifies the failure class before deployment, and frozen thresholds correctly diagnose two post-registration API judge replacements. We release six preregistration locks and the full audit trail of 14882 judge calls.
authors: Guijia Zhang, Harry Yang
bullets: Across three same-family transitions in Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral, newer judges did not consistently become harsher: two became more lenient, while one shifted differently by evaluation condition.
Version changes affected score location, criterion geometry, and resolution; one transition reduced clean-versus-flawed discrimination by assigning 93% of scores the same value.
Identical facts did not eliminate version differences, and placebo tests attributed most packet effects to formatting rather than content.
Global recalibration corrected average scores but explained little object-level variation.
A stratified audit of about 200 calls identified failure classes and correctly diagnosed two post-registration API judge replacements.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. Panel a is the design. Frozen proposals with reviewer-verified defects are scored by weight-frozen adjacent judge versions in three families, under a randomized information ladder with matched placebos at every rung. Panels b to e are the findings. Qwen moves toward leniency and replicates on the pool. Gemma is strict on anchors and attenuates off-anchor, as Table 2 reports. Mistral 3.1 → 3.2 concentrates 93% of pool scores on a single value. Fact effects track placebos, so the active ingredient is format rather than content. A ∼200-call anchor audit classifies the failure before deployment, as Table 3 records.

Figure 2: Version replacement re-instruments the measurement. Panel a reports location shifts with cluster-bootstrap 95% CIs. The Qwen shift toward leniency survives FDR correction. Gemma’s direction toward strictness is suggestive. The Mistral mean also moves, but panel c is the finding that matters on that chain. Panel b reports clean–flawed discrimination, which improves in two transitions and collapses in the third. Panel c shows the Mistral 3.2 collapse on the 300-object full pool, where 93% of scores land on a single value.

Figure 3: The information ladder. Version gap, old minus new, in pooled-SD units, with means and 95% CIs, under L0, L1, and L2. L0 is the rubric. L1 adds identical frozen facts. L2 adds a defect certificate. Open diamonds mark the matched placebos at each rung. Facts barely move either chain’s gap, and the placebos track the real interventions. The placebo-controlled contrast attributes what little the packets do to format, not content, as Table 14 reports. Certificates shrink the gap in Qwen but fail a preregistered Mistral replication, as Table 6 reports.

Figure 4: Equal-budget controller at a version transition. F1 is measured against the full-rescore policy as a function of new-judge call budget K. Stars mark the diagnose-then-act rule of Table 3 at the anchor budget. The Mistral panel is degenerate and is excluded from calibration claims.

Figure 5: Revision loop at a stateless, six-round operating point. Effects with 95% bootstrap CIs; shaded bands mark the exclusion boundary for preregistered nulls. The positive control (fresh-seed gain) passes. Every exploitation signature is null within the stated bounds.

Table 4: Complete confirmatory/exploratory registry. Lock files: prereg lock.json (0a), prereg lock 0b.json, prereg lock 1a.json, prereg lock 1b.json, prereg lock 2.json (contains amendment D1), prereg lock 3.json (amendments E1, E2). Each lock stores SHA-256 hashes of configs, prompts, and analysis code, written before any judge output of that stage.

Table 11: Two-parameter model refitted on random subsets of the 220-object expansion pool (200 draws per cell), evaluated on held-out pool objects. “Pass” = share of draws meeting the preregistered 2/3 explained-fraction gate. Anchor diagnostics explain the Stage-1a Gemma pathology: the old judge compresses anchors into a two-point range.
Table 6: Certificate-channel endpoints (SD units unless noted; discussion in §6). The exploratory contrast that a replication killed is the central methodological exhibit.
Table 16: Sample accounting. Judges: Q = Qwen pair, G = Gemma pair, M = Mistral pair, A = GPT-5.4/5.5 pair, D = DeepSeek flash/pro pair.

Table 12: Covariate balance across title-verified recognition strata (standardized mean differences). Recognized objects are systematically older and higher-scored; raw stratified gaps should not be read causally (§6).

Table 9: MAE of old→new score mappings fitted on 40 anchors, evaluated on the full non-anchor pool (objects scored by both versions; Qwen n=258). Kendall τ is identical across strictly monotone maps within a chain (Qwen 0.629 on this evaluation set; the 0.613 of Table 2 is the same statistic restricted to the 220-object expansion pool). The Mistral column is an artifact of degenerate newjudge output (93% single-value) and is excluded from claims.

Table 10: E1 perturbation matrix: Mistral 3.2 (Mnew) between-object SD of median L0 scores on 48 anchors, by prompt variant and temperature; predecessor (Mold) reference cells included. 0 parse failures in all 816 new calls.

Table 13: BH false-discovery-rate correction (q = 0.05) across the eleven scalar confirmatory endpoints (BH controls FDR, not FWER). E1 (decision rule) and rolling prediction (pure estimation) carry no scalar p-value and are registered separately in Table 4. p-values marked a are normal approximations recovered from bootstrap CIs; others as originally reported. No null conclusion changes; the Gemma strictward direction loses significance under FDR control.

Table 2: Transition endpoints, anchors versus full pool, in SD units with object-clustered bootstrap 95% CIs. Positive ∆ver means the new judge is stricter. Pool is the 220-object expansion pool scored once per judge at L0. For Mistral the pool is 300 objects. Anchor and pool gaps are each standardized by their own pooled L0 SD. Sep. is clean–flawed separation. Rank columns quantify transition-induced rank instability. Section 7 returns to those columns.
Table 1: Three failure classes of a version change. The design classifies the class through these signatures. It does not identify the latent weights.

Table 3: Pre-deployment compatibility test on stratified in-domain anchors, aligned with Table 1. Thresholds were set by convention and formalized after stage-2 data existed. They are a protocol proposal. Appendix F.7 reports a leave-one-transition-out check. That check shows insensitivity, not external validity. The two API pairs test the diagnosis, not the realized payoff of every prescribed action.
Table 5: Equivalence analysis of null and inconclusive endpoints (20,000 bootstrap draws).
Table 7: Two-parameter recalibration fitted on 24 anchors, evaluated on non-anchors. Explained fraction = 1− |corrected gap|/|raw gap|; preregistered gate required ≥ 2/3 on both chains.

Table 8: Compliance asymmetry: raw-score shift on clean objects when a mismatched pseudocertificate (L2P) is attached, vs. an audit-scope checklist certificate (L2). Old Qwen complies 3× more than new Qwen.

Table 14: E2: content-specific vs. format effects of fact packets on the version gap. Dcontent = ∆ver(L1P) − ∆ver(L1); format = ∆ver(L1P) − ∆ver(L0). Sign convention: per-chain columns are raw differences in each chain’s native gap sign (Qwen’s gap is negative, Gemma’s positive); the pooled column first multiplies each chain by the sign of its L0 gap, so that positive = real facts close more of the gap than placebo. Qwen’s raw +0.091 therefore enters the pool as −0.091.

Table 15: Artifact audit. “Eval. terms” = share of items matching an evaluative-language screen; “RF recall” = share of reviewer-verified risk factors lexically matched by at least one item (contentword Jaccard ≥ 0.15; n=73 objects with risk factors).

papers.selection_reason: Studies the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluations and how version changes affect measurement standards, directly relevant to LLM evaluation and behavior.
papers.title: LLM-as-a-Judge Version Shift: The Instrument Changed, Not the Standard
papers.tldr: Replacing an LLM judge can change the measurement instrument itself—not just its strictness—so version upgrades require pre-deployment auditing and recalibration.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.
authors: Zimo He
Tianyi Bian
Zizhong Yang
Hongjie Li
Nan Jiang
Jieming Cui
Baoxiong Jia
Yizhou Wang
Siyuan Huang
Yixin Zhu
bullets: Addresses scalability limits of separately optimized reconstruction–retargeting–tracking pipelines.
Uses a diffusion model to generate humanoid reference motions directly from video, avoiding explicit reconstruction and retargeting.
Applies direct preference optimization based on motion-tracking outcomes to improve executability.
An autoregressive variant supports real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency.
Experiments on the Unitree G1 show improved motion quality and executability, with favorable scaling across model and data size.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ViT-H. The diffusion-based generator (left) maps the camera orientations, bounding boxes, keypoints, and image features of a video directly to G1 reference motions, and its autoregressive variant also conditions on the preceding segment. For post-training (middle), candidates sampled for the same video are executed by a deployable tracker, which scores local pose accuracy and success, and by a privileged tracker, which scores global motion accuracy and success. At deployment (right), the offline generator drives video-to-humanoid control and the autoregressive generator drives real-time teleoperation.

Figure 4: Scaling behavior of ViT-H on the video-only test set. Panels (a,b) vary the model size, with marker size indicating the number of parameters, panels (c,d) the percentage of pretraining data, and panels (e,f) the percentage of post-training data, where base denotes the pretrained generator. Panels (a) to (d) use generators without post-training. Shaded regions denote 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 3: Analysis of DPO post-training on the video-only test set. Panels (a,b) vary the tracker feedback, from the pre-trained generator (base) to post-training with rewards from the deployable tracker alone (deploy) and with the privileged tracker added (+ priv.). Panels (c,d) vary the amount of in-distribution pre-training set data relative to video-only data during post-training, and panels (e,f) the number of final Transformer layers updated during post-training. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Figure 5: Post-training gains transfer to trackers not used in post-training. Motions generated by the offline (circles) and autoregressive (squares) generators on the video-only test set are executed by (a) Humanoid-GPT, (b) ScaleBFM, and (c) HoloMotion, before (w/o PT) and after (w/ PT) posttraining. Shaded regions denote 95% confidence intervals.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison of motion quality. Results use estimated camera motion. : marks baselines retrained on our training data with a model size comparable to ViT-H, and w/o PT denotes a generator before post-training. The 2AFC column reports the percentage of trials in which participants preferred each method over Ours (offline). Lower is better for all metrics except 2AFC. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best results.

Table 2: Quantitative comparison of motion executability. All reference motions are executed by πtrack in MuJoCo, using estimated camera motion. GT + GMR executes the retargeted ground-truth motions, and rows without GMR track the reconstructed human motions directly. : and w/o PT follow Table 1. Higher Succ. and lower errors are better. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best results, excluding GT + GMR.

papers.title: ViT-H: Generative Video-To-Humanoid Control with Motion Tracking Feedback
papers.tldr: ViT-H generates executable humanoid motions directly from monocular videos and improves them using downstream motion-tracking feedback.

papers.abstract: Unrecognized anomalies in critical infrastructure can rapidly cascade into catastrophic physical or operational failures. Current anomaly detection approaches often rely on direct access to the monitored system by utilizing onboard sensors, such as motor encoders, to detect anomalous states. However, legacy hardware often lacks these sensors, or strict security protocols may prohibit access altogether. We therefore present AWARE, a world model framework that is capable of anomaly detection using only external camera monitoring via system dynamics estimation and state prediction. Evaluated across 240 real-world robotic crane trajectories, including payload collisions and motor degradations, AWARE demonstrates a 26% improvement in anomaly classification over our strongest baseline under noisy, camera-only state estimation. Furthermore, the inferred dynamics parameter can be decoded to identify the source of faults, localizing the degrading motor with 88% accuracy.
authors: Luke Beddow, George Mavroghenis, Rodrigo Chacon Quesada, Kamil Dreczkowski, Cong Sun, Jiankai Wang, Oscar Kwong-Fai Pang, Antoine Cully
bullets: Addresses anomaly detection when onboard sensors are unavailable or access is restricted.
Uses a world model for camera-only dynamics estimation, state prediction, and introspection.
Evaluated on 240 real-world robotic crane trajectories involving payload collisions and motor degradation.
Improves anomaly classification by 26% over the strongest baseline under noisy visual state estimation.
Localizes the degrading motor with 88% accuracy from inferred dynamics parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System and model overview, showing human-operated robotic crane used for anomaly detection experiments. AWARE operates as follows: 1) camera-based state estimation; 2) estimation of system hidden dynamics parameters; 3) prediction of future trajectory; 4) anomaly recognition via examination of both the estimated dynamics parameters and the trajectory prediction error.

Figure 2: AWARE framework. Our model consists of two key components. First, a Latent Dynamics Estimator (green) reconstructs a latent encoding of system dynamics (ẑt) using a history of state-action pairs. Second, a World Model (blue) predicts the next state, given this encoding, the same history, and the current action. This integrated framework enables introspection (yellow) and anomaly detection (red) by comparing dynamics estimations and state prediction errors (et) against their expected distributions under normal operation.

Figure 3: Deployment Method (1) Crane platform: The system is modeled by three actuated joints: slew (q1), luff (q2), and hoist (q5). The under-actuated dynamics are captured by a double pendulum model: two angles (q3, q4) defining the movement at the hoist connection point (cable swing), and two angles (q6, q7) defining the relative orientation of the payload with respect to the cable. (2) Camera-Based State Estimation: Operator actions are estimated by two hand-tracking cameras. Crane states q1 and q2 are derived from ArUco marker poses using a ZED X camera. The remaining states (q3–q7) are estimated by a boom-mounted ZED 2i camera utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). (3) Operator Interface: A multi-color indicator lamp provides real-time visual feedback, signaling nominal operation (green light) or system alerts (red light).

Figure 4: Contribution of Latent and Predictor to Anomaly Recognition across different Impairments types using the Transformer AWARE model under (a) Motion Capture Quality Estimation (low noise) and (b) Camera Only Estimation (high noise).

Figure 5: Estimated Motor Strength using the Transformer AWARE model under (a) Low Noise State Estimation Data and (b) High Noise State Estimation Data. The solid curves and shaded bands represent the mean and standard deviation over multiple environments respectively. Decoding Accuracy is the rate of correctly detecting the impaired motor within a ±12.5% tolerance.

Figure 7: World model prediction error over a 100 step horizon. We condition the model on either Single Camera Quality Data or Motion Capture Quality Data, computing the error relative the Motion Capture data in both cases. The error is computed as a fraction of the joint’s total range, averaged over all joint dimensions then as a running cumulative error averaged over all experiments.

Figure 10: Examples of predictor and latent-estimator measurement signals with and without anomalies. (a) Motion Capture Quality Estimation (low noise); (b) Camera Only Estimation (high noise). From left to right, the four columns correspond to True Positive, True Negative, False Positive, and False Negative cases (based on whether an anomaly was present and whether the model raised an alarm). Solid blue and green curves show the predictor and latent-estimator signals, respectively, while dashed blue and green lines denote their anomaly thresholds. The red dashed vertical line marks the time at which the anomaly is injected.

Figure 8: Training curves for RSSM AWARE. We ablate by reintroducing components from Regularized Online Adaptation [34] to AWARE, including: regularization of the target encoder that the latent dynamics estimator learns to follow; removing the latent decoder and reintroducing the latent bottleneck. We plot both average precision and F1 over 1.5 million training steps on the Single Camera Quality dataset.

Figure 6: Average Precision (AP) of Transformer AWARE across three anomaly detection modes as increasing levels of noise, sampled from a Student’s t-distribution, are injected into the Motion Capture Quality dataset. Noise is scaled relative to the standard deviation (σ) of each joint. The noise level of the Camera Only Quality data relative to the Motion Capture Quality data is estimated by inverse interpolation of the AP score, with the cross indicating the interpolated σ corresponding to the Camera Only Quality data.

Figure 9: Examples of Anomaly Recognition by a pivoting measurement signal, where a successful detection is classified as either measurement signal exceeds its corresponding threshold. Nominal std gives the standard deviation of both measurement signals during nominal operations across all environments.

Table 1: Anomaly recognition results over 240 real robotic trajectories, averaged over 10 seeds per trained model. Metrics detail classification performance for identifying anomalies at the correct times within trajectories, under two different passive state estimation schemes. Bold entries are statistically significant improvement over the best non-AWARE model. ∗AnyAnomaly is only evaluated on the nominal and payload collision set, see Appendix C.3 for more detail.

Table 6: Anomaly detection results averaged across AWARE methods using different distance measures to the nominal reference distribution and operators to combine the prediction and latent signal Epred and Elat. ’L1’ and ’L2’ use the Manhattan and Euclidean distance to the reference distribution mean. ’L2 standardized’ normalizes the L2 distance by the diagonal covariance.

Table 4: Per-metric raw p-values from two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over 10 paired seeds. Significance is assessed within each baseline using a Bonferroni-corrected threshold over four metrics (two datasets × AP/F1), i.e., α = 0.05/4 = 0.0125.

Table 3: Anomaly recognition results organized by anomaly decision input. Bold entries are statistically significant improvement over the best non-AWARE model. ∗AnyAnomaly is only evaluated on the nominal and payload collision set.

papers.title: Adaptive World-Models for Anomaly Recognition (AWARE): A Framework for Robot Dynamics Prediction and Introspection
papers.tldr: AWARE detects and localizes robot anomalies using only external camera footage by learning system dynamics and predicting future states.

papers.abstract: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50s, 1.72$\times$ faster than the default policy's 6.02s while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.
authors: Seungyong Moon, Deokjae Lee, Hansang Lee, Munkhtselmeg Battsengel, Youngin Kim, Seonghyeon Yun, Sungjin Jeon, SongEun Kim, Jeongmin Park, Hyun Oh Song
bullets: Teleoperator timing can vary across demonstrations and cause policies to learn operator-specific speeds rather than task-relevant motion.
The method predicts a distribution of execution speeds from the task instruction, motion path, and path images; a selected quantile defines each demonstration’s new clock.
One speed prior trained on robot and handheld demonstrations can retime demonstrations across tasks without fitting a separate acceleration model per task.
A real-time optimal-control layer tracks policy action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace.
Across 120 RoboLab tasks, learned retiming improved success and reduced jerk by up to half; a real robot stacked cups in 3.50s with 29/30 successes.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Success rate (left) and TPR (right) against speed-up on RoboLab. Gray labels give the commanded speed-up. TPR (Appendix G) is in successes per minute, with the time limit of each task. Bars are 95% intervals of the gain over the uniform curve, bootstrapped over tasks.

Figure 5: Mean task progress over time on the real-robot placing bananas task, over 30 trials per condition. Each banana placed in the tray within the 30 s limit adds half of a trial, and curves average over trials, so curves further up and to the left progress faster.

Figure 6: Mean task progress over time on the real-robot placing cubes task, over 30 trials per condition. Each cube placed in the bin within the 60 s limit adds one ninth of a trial, and curves average over trials, so curves further up and to the left progress faster.

Figure 1: Learning the pace from demonstrations. (1) Paths are resampled every 2 cm of arc length and read in windows of 17 nodes. (2) The prior predicts a distribution over the log speed of every interval. (3) Reading a source path with the target label gives a quantile of the speed along the path. (4) Integrating this speed gives the clock.

Figure 3: Real-world tasks and their instructions, each shown at its initial scene (1) and its goal (2). The policies for stacking cups, folding towel and cleaning trash are fine-tuned on handheld YUBI demonstrations, and placing bananas and placing cubes are performed zero-shot (Appendix H).

Figure 2: One execution cycle. (1) From an observation on the running plan, the policy predicts a new chunk and its pace. (2) DRAFT fits a smooth path within boxes around the kept waypoints and times it at the pace unless a limit binds. (3) SPLICE joins the running plan to this path at the earliest point it reaches on time. (4) SMOOTH solves one minimum-jerk program through the boxes at their scheduled times, within all limits, giving the new plan.

Table 1: Throughput and motion quality at matched speed-up on RoboLab. TPR is in successes per minute, Peak is the peak end-effector speed in m/s and Jerk the integrated squared jerk in 103 m2/s5. SPARC, Peak and Jerk use the episodes that every execution of the baseline and our policy in Figure 4 completes.

Table 2: Real-robot results on the YUBI tasks of Figure 3. Ours (1x) runs our controller at α = 1, and Ours (q90), (q95) and (q99) on the tempo channels of the 0.9, 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles. TPR is in successes per minute, ATR in seconds and UPH in items per hour. Appendix G defines the metrics.

Table 7: Real-robot results on the placing bananas task (“put bananas into the tray”), with 30 trials per setting. PD is the baseline controller of Appendix F, Ours (1x) runs our controller at α = 1 and Ours (q99) on the tempo channel of the 0.99 quantile. Bananas is the mean number of bananas placed within 30 s, and Both the number of trials that place both.

Table 8: Real-robot results on the placing cubes task (“put all the gray cubes into the white bin”), with 30 trials per setting. PD is the baseline controller of Appendix F, Ours (1x) runs our controller at α = 1 and Ours (q99) on the tempo channel of the 0.99 quantile. Cubes is the mean number of cubes placed within 60 s, and All 9 the number of trials that place all nine.

Table 3: Accuracy of the speed prior on held-out validation windows, each domain read with its own label. Coverage is the fraction of recorded speeds at or below the predicted quantile. Pinball losses are in natural log speed, for the prior and for an input-blind predictor that returns the training quantiles of the domain. R2 is the fraction of the variance of recorded log speed explained by the predicted median, within episodes after removing each episode’s mean and between episodes among the episode means, over the episodes with at least five windows. The variance between episodes is 18% of the total on DROID and 12% on FastUMI-100K, and the R2 over all windows, 0.95 and 0.93, is the average of the two columns weighted by these shares.
Table 6: Settings of our controller (Ours) and the PD baseline (PD), shared by both setups. An entry that spans both columns applies to each of them.
Table 5: Settings that differ between the setups. The DROID zero-shot tasks of Appendix H are placing bananas and placing cubes.

Table 4: Speed around gripper events on held-out validation windows. Windows are grouped by the arc length from their center interval to the nearest interval in which the gripper opening changes by more than 0.05. Speeds are medians relative to the transit group, whose recorded and predicted medians are 228mm/s and 228mm/s on DROID and 274mm/s and 273mm/s on FastUMI-100K. In the same interval the gripper moves and keeps its source pace. The median clock reads DROID with the FastUMI-100K label, and its speed-up is the geometric mean ratio of its median to the median read with the DROID label.

papers.selection_reason: Learns a speed prior from demonstrations to retime robot data for VLA policy training, improving execution speed and smoothness.
papers.title: Retiming Robot Demonstrations with a Learned Speed Prior
papers.tldr: A learned speed prior retimes robot demonstrations to task-appropriate, consistent pacing, improving motion smoothness and enabling faster execution without reducing success.

papers.abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) has demonstrated strong performance in various offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by conditioning action generation on expected future returns and historical trajectories. However, treating expected future returns as the condition provides an incomplete description of the future, as trajectories with different state transitions and behaviors may share similar returns. Moreover, expected future returns inherently depend on task-specific reward functions, which makes policy learning reliant on reward-labeled datasets and restricts its scalability to tasks with similar but unseen rewards. Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have emerged as a promising paradigm of self-supervised learning-based world models, which learn predictive representations of future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing future states in the original space. Inspired by JEPA, we propose DT-JEPA, an offline pretraining and online fine-tuning framework that learns general knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories and achieves excellent adaptation to unseen tasks. Instead of predicting a single deterministic future embedding, we design a novel probabilistic predictor to model the conditional distribution of future representations in the latent space, thereby capturing both predictive information and uncertainty about future dynamics. Theoretically, we show that 1) the JEPA objective seeks to maximize a variational lower bound on the mutual information between historical representations and future trajectories; and 2) predictive future-conditioned policy learning admits a finite-sample performance bound with an O(N-1/4) estimation term. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that DT-JEPA achieves efficient adaptation across varying offline RL tasks, outperforming traditional DT-based and other offline RL methods.
authors: Changxu Ni, Yiyang Ni, Jun Li, Feiran You, Hongyang Du, Haitao Zhao, Shi Jin
bullets: Decision Transformer return-conditioning can miss distinct future dynamics and depends on task-specific reward labels.
DT-JEPA learns general predictive knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories before online task adaptation.
A probabilistic latent-space predictor models both future dynamics and their uncertainty instead of reconstructing future states.
Theoretical analysis connects the JEPA objective to mutual information and establishes a finite-sample performance bound.
On D4RL benchmarks, DT-JEPA adapts efficiently across tasks and outperforms DT-based and other offline RL methods.

papers.abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.
authors: Yangshen Deng, Xinjing Huang, Yulong Wang, Yunzhuo Liu, Jun Hu, Shuyong Tan, Chun-Chih Tseng, Mingji Han, Ray Ying, Key Zhang, Luo Mai
bullets: Learned sparse attention makes selection a training bottleneck because each query scores all prior tokens, despite reading only top-k tokens.
HyTopK computes exact top-k indices on the fly without materializing a full score table.
Selection replay reuses forward-pass selection during recomputation, reducing redundant work.
Combined with end-to-end system optimizations, HyScale achieves reported speedups of 2.07×, 2.01×, and 1.57× on 1M-token training workloads.
The evaluation covers GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash CSA layers, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next QSA layers on H20 and H800 GPUs.

papers.abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.
authors: Yepeng Liu, Shengmai Chen, Xuandong Zhao, Chengzhi Liu, Dawn Song, Xin Eric Wang, Yuheng Bu
bullets: Motivation: Test-time training improves scientific discovery but incurs substantial computational cost from online model-weight updates.
Method: TTME continually distills experience into external memory to guide later discovery without changing model weights.
Evaluation: TTME and TTT are compared within the same discovery framework, differing only in their test-time adaptation method.
Results: TTME outperforms TTT on all five evaluated mathematical tasks while reducing FLOPs by 82.8–84.6% and runtime by 47.7–58.4%.
Scope: Findings are demonstrated in the evaluated scientific-discovery settings.

papers.abstract: The growing population of orbital debris has intensified interest in active debris removal and on-orbit servicing, for which dual-arm space manipulators offer improved grasping stability and load distribution relative to single-arm systems. However, coordinating two manipulators under inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, and sensing uncertainty remains challenging. This paper develops a coordinated reinforcement learning framework for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator in a target-reaching task with inter-arm collision-avoidance constraints. A centralized state representation combines joint-space, end-effector, and target-relative information, while a multi-objective reward function promotes target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, synchronized task completion, and collision avoidance. Within this framework, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) are compared as representative on-policy and off-policy algorithms, and the learned policies are further evaluated for generalization to previously unseen target configurations. Across five random seeds, SAC substantially outperforms PPO within the considered fixed-base simulation scenarios: it reaches an 80% success threshold in every seed (median 1.6M environment steps) whereas PPO does not reach it within a 4M-step budget, and it attains a higher mean success rate (78.6% versus 7.4%) with lower position and orientation errors and tighter bimanual synchronization. Both algorithms degrade on unseen boundary targets, but SAC retains most of its performance while PPO's collapses. The results also expose a failure mode of PPO: under the two-phase shaped reward, it tends to converge to a reward-loitering local optimum rather than committing to the precision task. This behavior highlights the sensitivity of on-policy learning to reward shaping.
authors: Nasim Fallahiarezoodar, Zheng H. Zhu
bullets: Addresses dual-arm space-robot coordination with target reaching, inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, synchronization, and sensing uncertainty.
Uses centralized joint-, end-effector-, and target-relative state information with a multi-objective reward for accuracy, smoothness, alignment, synchronization, and safety.
Compares PPO and SAC across five random seeds and evaluates generalization to unseen target configurations.
SAC reached the 80% success threshold in every seed and achieved a 78.6% mean success rate; PPO achieved 7.4% within the stated training budget.
Both methods degraded on unseen boundary targets, while PPO often converged to a reward-loitering local optimum.

papers.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.
authors: Ziya Hosseynzadeh, Farjad Fallah, Farnoosh Fallah, Soroush Gooran, Mohammad Amanloo, Hossein Sameti
bullets: Compares FISER, a structured social- and embodied-reasoning framework, with CEMIR, which enriches text using generated narratives and photorealistic images.
Evaluates both methods across four LLMs on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark and multiple ambiguity levels.
Finds no statistically significant performance difference in any of 16 model-by-difficulty comparisons.
Ablation results likewise show no distinct benefit from CEMIR’s narrative or visual components.
Performance is more closely linked to backbone capability and ambiguity difficulty, defining a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment.

papers.abstract: Recent methods for injecting graph structure into LLM prompts include graph soft prompting, in which a graph neural network (GNN) learns graph-specific tokens that capture relational information among entities in textual prompts. G-Retriever combines graph soft prompts with a verbalized description of the same graph to strengthen the textual prompt signal. We conduct an in-depth analysis of G-Retriever and uncover a pathological behavior we term token collapse. Across three benchmarks, three graph encoders, two LLM families, and both frozen and LoRA-adapted models, G-Retriever's graph tokens become almost indistinguishable across inputs. We provide evidence that the same failure is inherited by subsequent methods, even with multi-token pooling. Under the standard setup, swapping a token with the dataset mean, a token from another example, or one derived from a corrupted graph produces no resolved answer-level effect in accuracy. Moreover, a learned constant prompt that never accesses the graph matches or surpasses G-Retriever on all three benchmarks. These findings indicate that, rather than conveying graph content as intended, the collapsed token functions primarily as a generic soft prompt. We also examine conditions linked to this collapse and propose a two-stage procedure that yields non-collapsed tokens while maintaining competitive performance in most cases. However, token variability alone does not prove that the model uses graph information: via interventions and decoding probes, we show that depending on the configuration, a token can reflect the question, an answer prior, or graph-derived content that the LLM may or may not use. Overall, our results offer a practical approach to evaluating graph-token alignment rather than inferring it from task accuracy alone. Code to reproduce our experiments is available at https://github.com/difra100/Token_Collapse_KGQA.
authors: Andrea Giuseppe Di Francesco
Rishabh Jain
Franco Maria Nardini
Nicola Tonellotto
Pietro Liò
Fabrizio Silvestri
bullets: Token collapse persists across multiple benchmarks, graph encoders, LLM families, adaptation settings, and later multi-token methods.

A learned constant prompt matches or outperforms G-Retriever across all evaluated benchmarks without accessing graph inputs.
A two-stage procedure produces more variable tokens while retaining competitive performance in most cases.
Interventions and decoding probes show that token variability may reflect the question, answer priors, or graph content—and graph-derived information is not necessarily used by the LLM.

papers.abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.

Soil training helps mainly on Earth sand and some flat-sand cases; benefits on stiffer lunar soil are limited and policy-dependent.
Gravity-randomized rough-terrain training achieves seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 on the Moon across key tests up to 20°.

papers.abstract: Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/

papers.abstract: Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and kinematically feasible for the target robot. Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space. The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning. Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being generated. We present EmbodyHOI, which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object. Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without retraining. On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite. Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/

Kartik Sharma

papers.abstract: Counterfactual cardiac anatomy can support risk modelling and intervention planning, by predicting how a patient's heart would change under altered clinical conditions. However, current shape generative models are conditional on clinical variables and disregard causal links between these variables. Thus, they cannot answer counterfactual questions about how a given subject's anatomy would change under a different clinical profile. Modelling the heart's continuous movement over the cardiac cycle requires a representation that is itself continuous in space and time. Spatio-temporal neural distance fields provide this while separating clinical conditioning from subject-specific shape. We place a structural causal model (SCM) over the set of clinical variables (age, sex, smoking, BMI, heart rate, systolic blood pressure), before the condition encoding of the spatio-temporal neural distance field which represents the left atrial complex over a cardiac cycle by signed distance fields. An intervention of the clinical variables, propagated through a SCM before the 4D counterfactual, is constructed from the neural distance field. The generated counterfactuals follow dose-response under age interventions and transforms the male distribution to closely match the female distribution under the intervention $\mathrm{do(\mathrm{female}{=}1)}$. By doing inverse interventions the model also approximates the original anatomy with sub millimeter precision. To our knowledge, this is the first counterfactual generation of 4D cardiac anatomy and the first integration of an SCM with an implicit neural representation as its imaging mechanism.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video question answering requires a model to continuously monitor an incoming stream and autonomously decide when to speak, what to say, and whether to emit a response. Existing streaming systems face a fundamental difficulty: retaining long visual histories is costly, whereas discarding them can lead to missed events and repeated responses. We propose \textbf{ProV-Mem}, a training-free proactive memory framework built around a frozen VLM backbone. ProV-Mem decomposes the proactive decision into three lightweight memory tiers: a temporal-trigger memory controls when to query the backbone and recovers from prolonged silence, an instructional memory guides what to say through a fixed prompting prior for concise and visually grounded generation, and an episodic memory determines whether to emit by filtering near-duplicate responses. Under an idealized conditional-sufficiency assumption, we derive a stagewise approximation bound relating the decomposed process to a full-state joint policy. We further introduce Cost-Aware Area Under the Curve (\textbf{CAUC}), which extends PAUC by explicitly discounting redundant, overly frequent, and unnecessarily long emissions. Experiments on the four scenarios of ProactiveVideoQA show that ProV-Mem achieves the best CAUC across all scenarios and the best PAUC on WEB, EGO, and TV, while maintaining low per-response inference latency.
authors: Bingbing Wang
Jing Li

papers.abstract: Road scene understanding in automated driving (AD) aims to build a comprehensive analysis of video sequences taken on the road by embedded or fixed cameras (e.g., mounted on vertical road signals). One goal is to identify the relevant actors in the scene and another goal is to determine the causes that have triggered a specific action of the ego car (i.e., stop, slow down, turn left, etc.). In a complex urban environment, these causes can be multiple, confusing, possibly contradictory to other causes and not easily expressible using simplistic reasoning. Still, providing accurate {\it automatic cause determination} supports a) user acceptance by providing appropriate explanations to the car passengers and road users; b) increased road safety by providing detailed road scene understanding to traffic. In this paper, we propose using spatiotemporal reasoning and Belnap's four-valued logic to formulate complex causes of AD action in a road scene. We compute these causes by analysing a Qualitative eXplainable Graph (QXG), which is an abstract representation of the road scene capturing spatiotemporal relations between road entities. Starting from a QXG, our approach called \tool, is targeted to determine complex causes of a selected AD action occurring in a specific frame of a road scene. The usefulness of \tool is demonstrated on several scenes extracted from the well-known NuScene dataset.

Arnaud Gotlieb
Nadjib Lazaar

Determines the causes of a selected AD action at a specific video frame.
Demonstrates usefulness on several scenes from the nuScenes dataset.

papers.abstract: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Rishit Chatterjee, Himanshu Udupi, Vikram Ramavarapu, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Large repositories exceed an agent’s context window, creating a choice between file selection, retrieval, and compression.
CQ2-CARE selects which whole files to include and preserves their exact contents.
On 300 SWE-rebench issues, it resolves 43.7% with GPT-5.6 and 46.7% with Claude Opus 5.
It outperforms the best compressors by 6.3 points and the best retrievers by 9.3 and 12.7 points, respectively.
Retrievers often omit files needing edits, while compressors alter code that agents must reproduce exactly.
